Module 1·1 dayMust

How the web works

11 topics · about 1.5 h of reading

As a Java developer you already know one side of the web: a Spring Boot controller receives a request and returns a response. This module shows you the other side — what the browser does before, during and after that request. You will learn how a URL is split into parts, how DNS finds your server, what an HTTP request and response really contain, and how the browser turns HTML, CSS and JavaScript into pixels on the screen.

Everything in the later modules builds on this. HTML (Module 2) and CSS (Module 3) are files the browser downloads and renders. JavaScript (Module 4) and React (Module 5) run inside the browser and call your API (Module 6). When something breaks between React and Spring Boot, the browser DevTools covered at the end of this module are how you find out which side is at fault.

  • Explain the client–server model and the request–response cycle clearly in an interview.
  • Split any URL into scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment, and know which parts reach the server.
  • Describe DNS resolution in a few clear steps.
  • Read a raw HTTP request and response, and choose the right method and status code.
  • Walk through what happens when you open a page, and how the browser renders it.
  • Tell static from dynamic sites, MPAs from SPAs and CSR from SSR — and place a React + Spring Boot app correctly.
  • Use the DevTools Elements, Console, Network, Application, Sources and Lighthouse panels to debug real problems.

Browser, server and the request–response cycle

The browser (the client) always starts the conversation by sending an HTTP request; the server answers with exactly one response — an HTML page, a CSS or JavaScript file, an image or JSON data.

The web is built on the client–server model. A client is a program that asks for something. A server is a program that waits for requests and answers them. On the web, the usual client is a browser — Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari. The server is a program listening on a network port (a numbered "door" on a machine), for example the embedded Tomcat inside your Spring Boot app on port 8080, or Nginx on port 443.

The word "server" means two things: the machine (a cloud VM, a container) and the program running on it. When someone says "the server is down", they may mean either. In these notes, "server" means the program unless stated otherwise.

The request–response cycle

Every interaction on the web follows the same pattern:

  1. The client opens a connection to the server and sends a request, for example "GET me /products/42".
  2. The server runs some code — it reads a file from disk, or calls your controller, service and repository, which query the database.
  3. The server sends back exactly one response: a status code (200, 404, 500…), some headers and usually a body.
  4. The client uses the response — the browser renders HTML, applies CSS, runs JavaScript, or hands JSON to your React code.

For a Java developer, a useful picture is a method call over the network. The request is like the method name plus its arguments; the response is like the return value. The differences matter, though: a network call is slow (milliseconds, not nanoseconds), it can fail halfway, and the server does not remember you between calls.

What a server can send back

The server tells the browser what kind of data the body contains using the Content-Type header. The browser decides what to do with the body based on it.

BodyContent-TypeWhat the browser does with it
HTML documenttext/htmlParses it and builds the page
Stylesheettext/cssApplies the styles to the page
Scripttext/javascriptRuns it in the JavaScript engine
Image, font, videoimage/png, font/woff2, video/mp4Displays it, or uses it to draw text
Dataapplication/jsonHands it to your JavaScript (for example a React component)

One page is never one request. The browser first downloads the HTML, then discovers the stylesheets, scripts, images and fonts it references and requests each of them. A React app then makes further requests for JSON data. A busy shopping page easily makes dozens of requests — you will see every one of them in the Network panel.

Try it: your own server and client

The smallest possible "server" is a Spring Boot controller. The browser is the client.

import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class HelloController {

    @GetMapping("/api/hello")
    public Map<String, String> hello() {
        // Spring converts the Map to JSON and sets Content-Type: application/json
        return Map.of("message", "Namaste from Spring Boot");
    }
}

Start the app and open http://localhost:8080/api/hello in the browser. The browser sends a GET request; Tomcat hands it to Spring's DispatcherServlet, which calls your method; the return value goes back as the response body.

{"message":"Namaste from Spring Boot"}

Web server vs application server

In production you often see two kinds of server, one in front of the other.

Web server (Nginx, Apache httpd)Application server (Spring Boot + embedded Tomcat)
Main jobServe static files fast, terminate HTTPS, forward requestsRun your Java code: controllers, services, database calls
Typical contentThe React build (index.html, JS and CSS files), imagesJSON from your REST API, or HTML from Thymeleaf templates
Runs Java?NoYes
Common extra rolesReverse proxy, load balancer, gzip compression, cachingSecurity, transactions, validation, business rules

A reverse proxy is a server that receives requests from browsers and forwards them to another server behind it. A common setup: Nginx serves the React files directly and forwards every request that starts with /api to Spring Boot.

Ports you will meet every day

PortUsually
80HTTP (browsers use it when the URL starts with http:// and has no port)
443HTTPS (the default for https://)
8080Spring Boot's default (server.port)
5173The Vite dev server for your React app
5432 / 3306PostgreSQL / MySQL
6379Redis

localhost is the name for your own machine; it resolves to 127.0.0.1 (IPv4) or ::1 (IPv6). During development the browser, the Vite server and Spring Boot all run on localhost, just on different ports.

Rule: the client always speaks first

In plain HTTP the server cannot send anything to a browser that did not ask. For live updates — order tracking, chat, stock prices — applications use WebSockets (a two-way connection) or Server-Sent Events (a one-way stream from server to browser), or the browser simply asks again every few seconds (polling).

Rule: HTTP is stateless

Each request is independent. The server does not automatically remember that the same user sent the previous request. Logins, carts and preferences work only because the client sends something with every request — a cookie with a session id, or an Authorization header with a token. You will see how in HTTP requests and responses.

Edge case: the browser is not the only client

curl, Postman, a mobile app, another microservice or an attacker's script can all send the same requests your React app sends. Anything only the browser enforces — a hidden Delete button, a disabled field, HTML form validation — can be bypassed in seconds. The server must validate and authorise every single request.

Mistake: "the admin API is safe because normal users never see the button"

Hiding a button is a user-interface decision, not security. Protect the endpoint itself on the server, for example with Spring Security rules or @PreAuthorize (see Spring Boot · Module 4).

In real projects

A common production layout: the React build sits on a CDN or behind Nginx, the Spring Boot API runs as several instances behind a load balancer, and all instances share one PostgreSQL database. Because HTTP is stateless and the instances share nothing in memory, any instance can serve any request — that is what makes scaling out easy.

Interview angle: "Explain the client–server model"

  • The client (browser, app) sends a request; the server processes it and returns one response.
  • The client always initiates; HTTP is stateless, so state travels in cookies or tokens.
  • Mention the layers: browser → load balancer or Nginx → Spring Boot → database.
  • Close with the security point: never trust the client; validate and authorise on the server.

URL anatomy: scheme, host, port, path, query, fragment

A URL tells the browser which protocol to use (scheme), which server to contact (host and port), which resource to ask for (path), extra parameters (query) and a position inside the page (fragment) — and the fragment never reaches the server.

A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the address of a resource on the web. You type URLs, put them in links, and call them from fetch(). Spring Boot reads parts of them with @PathVariable and @RequestParam. Knowing each part precisely saves you from many small bugs.

PartIn the exampleMeaningSent to the server?
SchemehttpsThe protocol. https = HTTP over an encrypted TLS connection.Decides how to connect
Hostshop.example.comDomain name (or IP address) of the server. DNS turns it into an IP.Yes, in the Host header
Port8443Which port on that machine. Omitted = default (80 for http, 443 for https).Used to connect
Path/products/42Which resource. Maps to @GetMapping("/products/{id}").Yes
Query?color=red&size=mKey–value parameters after ?, separated by &. Maps to @RequestParam.Yes
Fragment#reviewsA position inside the page — usually the element with id="reviews".No — browser only

Scheme

Besides http and https you will meet mailto: (open an email client), tel: (dial a number), ws: and wss: (WebSockets), file: (a local file — opening an HTML file by double-clicking gives you a file:///C:/... URL) and data: (data embedded in the URL itself). Modern browsers mark plain http sites as "Not secure"; production sites use https.

Host and port

The host can be a domain (shop.example.com), an IPv4 address (192.168.1.20) or an IPv6 address in square brackets ([::1]). shop is a subdomain of example.com. Host names are case-insensitive: SHOP.Example.com is the same server.

The port is written after a colon. You rarely see it in production because sites use the defaults, but in development it is everywhere: http://localhost:5173 (Vite) and http://localhost:8080 (Spring Boot).

Path

The path identifies a resource on the server. Unlike the host, the path is usually case-sensitive — Spring MVC treats /Products/42 and /products/42 as different paths. REST APIs use the path to name resources: /api/orders/1042, /api/customers/7/orders.

Query string

The query string starts with ? and holds key=value pairs joined with &. Use it for optional inputs: filters, sorting, paging and search terms. A key can repeat: ?tag=veg&tag=spicy binds to List<String> tag in Spring.

// GET /api/products?category=snacks&page=2&sort=price
@GetMapping("/api/products")
public Page<ProductDto> list(@RequestParam String category,
                             @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
                             @RequestParam(defaultValue = "name") String sort) {
    // ...
}

// GET /api/products/42  -> id = 42
@GetMapping("/api/products/{id}")
public ProductDto one(@PathVariable long id) {
    // ...
}

Fragment

The fragment (also called the hash) starts with #. The browser keeps it to itself: it scrolls to the element whose id matches, and JavaScript can read it with location.hash. It is never sent in the HTTP request, so your Spring Boot logs never show it. Older single-page apps used it for routing (/#/orders/42) precisely because changing the fragment does not reload the page.

Percent-encoding

Only a limited set of characters may appear in a URL as-is. Others — spaces, &, ?, #, non-English text — must be percent-encoded: each byte becomes % plus two hex digits. A space becomes %20, @ becomes %40, & becomes %26. In HTML form submissions (and in Java's URLEncoder) a space in the query string becomes + instead.

encodeURIComponent("Asha & Co");   // "Asha%20%26%20Co"
encodeURIComponent("मसाला");        // "%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B2%E0%A4%BE"
decodeURIComponent("Asha%20%26%20Co"); // "Asha & Co"
import java.net.URLEncoder;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

String q = URLEncoder.encode("Asha & Co", StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
System.out.println(q);
Asha+%26+Co

Reading a URL in code

Never split URLs by hand with string methods. Both languages have a parser. Paste this into the browser console:

const url = new URL("https://shop.example.com:8443/products/42?color=red&size=m#reviews");
console.log(url.protocol);               // "https:"
console.log(url.hostname);               // "shop.example.com"
console.log(url.port);                   // "8443"
console.log(url.pathname);               // "/products/42"
console.log(url.search);                 // "?color=red&size=m"
console.log(url.searchParams.get("size")); // "m"
console.log(url.hash);                   // "#reviews"
console.log(url.origin);                 // "https://shop.example.com:8443"

const api = new URL("https://shop.example.com/api/products");
api.searchParams.set("q", "dosa mix & chutney"); // encodes for you
console.log(api.toString());
// "https://shop.example.com/api/products?q=dosa+mix+%26+chutney"
import java.net.URI;

URI uri = URI.create("https://shop.example.com:8443/products/42?color=red&size=m#reviews");
System.out.println(uri.getScheme());   // https
System.out.println(uri.getHost());     // shop.example.com
System.out.println(uri.getPort());     // 8443
System.out.println(uri.getPath());     // /products/42
System.out.println(uri.getQuery());    // color=red&size=m
System.out.println(uri.getFragment()); // reviews

Origin: the part that matters for security

An origin is the combination scheme + host + port. https://shop.example.com and https://shop.example.com:443 are the same origin (443 is the default). http://localhost:5173 and http://localhost:8080 are different origins because the ports differ. Browsers isolate data per origin (cookies work a little differently, by domain), and a page from one origin calling an API on another origin triggers CORS checks — the reason your first React-to-Spring call fails in development. Module 6 explains the fix.

Rule: encode every value you put into a URL

Build query strings with URLSearchParams / url.searchParams in JavaScript and UriComponentsBuilder or URLEncoder in Java. A raw & or # inside a value silently cuts it short or starts a new parameter.

Convention: path for identity, query for options

Use the path to identify a resource (/api/orders/1042) and the query for filtering, sorting and paging (/api/orders?status=SHIPPED&page=0). Use lowercase, hyphen-separated path segments: /order-items, not /OrderItems.

Edge cases

  • url.port returns an empty string when the port is the default — new URL("https://a.com:443/").port is "". Java's URI.getPort() returns -1 when no port is written.
  • URLs have practical length limits. Spring Boot's embedded Tomcat limits the request line plus headers to 8 KB by default (server.max-http-request-header-size); a longer URL gets an error response before your controller runs. Send large data in a POST body.
  • A trailing slash can matter: since Spring Framework 6 (Boot 3), /api/orders/ no longer matches a mapping for /api/orders by default.

Mistake: putting secrets or personal data in the URL

URLs end up in browser history, server and proxy logs, analytics tools and the Referer header sent to other sites. Never put passwords, tokens, Aadhaar or PAN numbers in a query string. Send them in a request body or header over HTTPS.

Interview angle

  • "Name the parts of a URL" — scheme, host, port, path, query, fragment; give default ports.
  • "Is the fragment sent to the server?" — No; the browser uses it for in-page navigation and JavaScript reads it via location.hash.
  • "What is an origin?" — scheme + host + port; different ports mean different origins, which is why CORS appears between Vite (5173) and Spring Boot (8080).
  • "Path variable or request param?" — path identifies the resource, query refines the result.

DNS in short: from a name to an IP address

DNS is the internet's phone book: it turns a name like shop.example.com into the IP address the browser connects to, and every step caches the answer for a time called the TTL.

Computers connect to IP addresses — 203.0.113.10 (IPv4) or 2001:db8::10 (IPv6). Humans remember names. The Domain Name System (DNS) is the distributed database that maps names to addresses. Before the browser can send a single byte of HTTP, it needs the IP address of the host in the URL.

How a lookup works

  1. Browser cache. The browser remembers recent answers. If it looked up the name a minute ago, it is done.
  2. Operating system. The OS checks its own cache and the hosts file — a local text file that maps names to IPs and wins over real DNS.
  3. Recursive resolver. The OS asks a resolver — usually your ISP's, your company's, or a public one such as Google (8.8.8.8) or Cloudflare (1.1.1.1). The resolver does the hard work and caches results for everyone who uses it.
  4. Root servers. If the resolver has nothing cached, it asks a root server, which answers "I don't know, but here are the servers for .com".
  5. TLD servers. The top-level domain servers for .com (or .in, .org) answer "ask the name servers of example.com".
  6. Authoritative server. The domain's own name server (often run by the DNS provider, such as Route 53 or Cloudflare) gives the final answer: the IP address and a TTL (time to live, in seconds).
  7. The resolver returns the IP to your machine; everyone on the way caches it until the TTL runs out.

Record types you should know

RecordHoldsExample use
AAn IPv4 addressshop.example.com → 203.0.113.10
AAAAAn IPv6 addressshop.example.com → 2001:db8::10
CNAMEAn alias to another namewww.example.com → example.com, or a name pointing to a cloud load balancer's host name
MXMail servers for the domainWhere email for @example.com is delivered
TXTFree textDomain ownership proofs, email anti-spoofing (SPF)
NSThe domain's name serversDelegation from the TLD to your DNS provider

Look it up yourself

nslookup works on Windows, macOS and Linux; dig is common on Linux and macOS; PowerShell has Resolve-DnsName. The output below is illustrative — real addresses and the exact layout differ.

$ nslookup shop.example.com
Server:   192.168.1.1
Address:  192.168.1.1

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:     shop.example.com
Address:  203.0.113.10

$ dig +short shop.example.com
203.0.113.10

"Non-authoritative" means the answer came from a resolver's cache, not directly from the domain's own name server. That is normal.

Java does the same lookup when you open a connection. You can trigger it directly:

import java.net.InetAddress;

public class DnsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        for (InetAddress address : InetAddress.getAllByName("localhost")) {
            System.out.println(address);
        }
    }
}
localhost/127.0.0.1
localhost/0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1

The hosts file: DNS on your own machine

The hosts file lets you map a name to an IP without any DNS server. Developers use it to test with a realistic name. Editing it needs administrator rights.

# Windows: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts
# Linux and macOS: /etc/hosts
127.0.0.1   shop.test

Now http://shop.test:8080 reaches the Spring Boot app on your machine. Use the reserved .test ending for such names; it will never clash with a real domain.

Rule: DNS gives an IP address, never a port

A and AAAA records hold only an address. The port comes from the URL — written explicitly, or the default for the scheme. If your app listens on 8080 and the URL has no port, the browser tries 80 or 443 and fails, however correct the DNS is.

Edge cases and the errors you will see

  • Chrome shows DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN when a name does not exist (a typo, or a record not created yet).
  • In Java, a failed lookup throws java.net.UnknownHostException — common when a microservice's host name is misspelt in application.yml.
  • Changes are not instant. Old answers live in caches until their TTL expires, so a server migration can look "half done" for a while. Lower the TTL a day before a planned change.
  • The JVM caches lookups too (controlled by the networkaddress.cache.ttl security property), so a long-running Java process can keep using an old IP.

Mistake: forgetting an entry in the hosts file

You add 127.0.0.1 api.myapp.com for a test, forget it, and weeks later the "production" site on your laptop is really your local server. When a site behaves strangely only on your machine, check the hosts file first.

Going deeper

DNS normally runs over UDP port 53. Browsers can also use DNS over HTTPS (DoH) for privacy. Caching layers, resolvers and DNS-based load balancing are covered in CS Fundamentals · Module 2 and DevOps · Module 2.

Interview angle: "How does DNS resolution work?"

Answer in order: browser cache → OS cache and hosts file → recursive resolver → root → TLD → authoritative server → answer cached for the TTL. Name the A, AAAA and CNAME records, and mention that DNS returns only an IP, never a port.

HTTP requests and responses

HTTP is the request–response protocol of the web: a request carries a method, a path, headers and an optional body; a response carries a status code, headers and an optional body — and every request stands alone.

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) defines the messages a client and server exchange. HTTPS is exactly the same protocol, sent through an encrypted TLS connection. Every API you build in Spring Boot and every fetch() call you write in React is HTTP, so this is one of the most important topics in the whole page.

Anatomy of a request

In HTTP/1.1 a message is plain text. This is what the browser sends when your React app loads an order:

GET /api/orders/1042 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI3In0.signature
Cookie: lang=en
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ...
  1. Request line: the method (GET), the request target (path + query: /api/orders/1042) and the protocol version.
  2. Headers: Name: value lines with extra information — which site (Host), which formats the client accepts, credentials, cookies.
  3. An empty line marks the end of the headers.
  4. An optional body — empty for GET, JSON or form data for POST, PUT and PATCH.

Anatomy of a response

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 55
Cache-Control: no-store
Date: Sun, 18 Oct 2026 10:15:00 GMT

{"id":1042,"status":"DELIVERED","total":1499,"items":2}

The status line has the version, a three-digit status code and an optional reason phrase. Then come headers, an empty line and the body. Content-Length is the body size in bytes (55 here).

A request that creates something usually carries a JSON body and gets 201 Created back:

POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 29

{"productId":42,"quantity":2}
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /api/orders/1043
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":1043,"status":"PLACED"}

The same thing in Spring Boot

import java.net.URI;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orderService; // your own service class

    public OrderController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public OrderDto get(@PathVariable long id) {
        return orderService.find(id);                 // 200 OK + JSON body
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(@RequestBody CreateOrderRequest req) {
        OrderDto saved = orderService.place(req);
        URI location = URI.create("/api/orders/" + saved.id());
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(saved); // 201 + Location
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> cancel(@PathVariable long id) {
        orderService.cancel(id);
        return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();    // 204, no body
    }
}

Methods

The method (also called the verb) says what the client wants to do. Two properties matter in interviews. A safe method does not change anything on the server. An idempotent method has the same effect on the server whether you send it once or ten times — important because networks retry requests.

MethodUse it toBodySafeIdempotent
GETRead a resource or a listNoYesYes
POSTCreate a resource or trigger an action (place order, pay)YesNoNo
PUTReplace a resource completelyYesNoYes
PATCHChange part of a resourceYesNoNot guaranteed
DELETERemove a resourceUsually noneNoYes
HEADLike GET, but only the headersNoYesYes
OPTIONSAsk which methods are allowed; used by the CORS preflightNoYesYes

Idempotent is about the effect, not the response. Deleting order 1042 twice leaves the server in the same state as deleting it once, even though the second call may return 404. Sending "POST /api/orders" twice creates two orders — which is why payment APIs ask for an idempotency key header so they can detect a retried POST.

Status codes

The first digit gives the class:

ClassMeaningThink of it as
1xxInformational"Keep going" — rarely seen directly
2xxSuccess"Done"
3xxRedirection"Look somewhere else" (or "use your cached copy")
4xxClient error"You sent something wrong"
5xxServer error"We broke"
CodeNameTypical cause in a Spring Boot app
200OKA controller method returned an object
201CreatedResponseEntity.created(uri) after a POST
204No ContentResponseEntity.noContent() after a DELETE
301 / 308Moved Permanently / Permanent RedirectA URL changed for good (308 keeps the method and body)
302 / 307Found / Temporary Redirectreturn "redirect:/login"; in Spring MVC sends 302
304Not ModifiedThe browser's cached copy is still valid (ETag matched)
400Bad RequestMalformed JSON, or @Valid validation failed
401UnauthorizedNot logged in, or a missing/expired token — really "unauthenticated"
403ForbiddenLogged in but not allowed, for example @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") failed
404Not FoundNo mapping for the path, or the entity does not exist
405Method Not AllowedA POST sent to a GET-only mapping
409ConflictDuplicate email, or an optimistic-locking version clash
415Unsupported Media Type@RequestBody received a body without Content-Type: application/json
429Too Many RequestsA rate limiter rejected the call
500Internal Server ErrorAn unhandled exception, such as a NullPointerException
502 / 503 / 504Bad Gateway / Service Unavailable / Gateway TimeoutNginx or the load balancer could not get a good answer from your app in time

Headers you will use every week

HeaderSent byPurpose
HostClientWhich site — one IP address can host many sites. Required in HTTP/1.1.
AcceptClientFormats the client can handle, for example application/json
Content-TypeBothFormat of this message's body
Content-LengthBothSize of the body in bytes
AuthorizationClientCredentials, usually Bearer <token>
Cookie / Set-CookieClient / ServerSend stored cookies / ask the browser to store one
Cache-ControlBothCaching rules: no-store, max-age=3600…
LocationServerWhere a new resource lives (201) or where to go (3xx)
OriginBrowserThe origin of the page making a cross-origin request — used by CORS
Access-Control-Allow-OriginServerWhich origins may read the response (CORS)

Common body formats: application/json for APIs, application/x-www-form-urlencoded (name=Asha&city=Pune) for classic HTML forms, and multipart/form-data for file uploads.

State on top of a stateless protocol: cookies and tokens

Because HTTP is stateless, a login must be proven again on every request. Two common ways:

  • Session cookie. After login the server responds with Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=8F2A…; Path=/; HttpOnly. The browser stores it and automatically adds Cookie: JSESSIONID=8F2A… to every later request to that site. The server looks up the session by id.
  • Token. After login the server returns a token (often a JWT). Your JavaScript stores it and adds Authorization: Bearer <token> to each API call. The browser does not do this automatically.

Cookie flags matter: HttpOnly (JavaScript cannot read it), Secure (sent only over HTTPS) and SameSite (limits sending on cross-site requests). The JWT flow is covered in Spring Boot · Module 4 and the browser side in Module 6.

Caching in one paragraph

The browser keeps copies of responses according to Cache-Control. max-age=31536000, immutable suits Vite's hashed build files (index-a1b2c3.js): the name changes whenever the content changes. no-store means "never store" — right for personal data. With an ETag header the browser can ask "has it changed?" and get a cheap 304 Not Modified with no body.

HTTPS

HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS. Before any HTTP is sent, the browser and server perform a TLS handshake: the server presents a certificate proving it owns the domain, and both sides agree on encryption keys. After that, nobody in between — public Wi-Fi, an ISP — can read or change the messages. The default port is 443. A page loaded over HTTPS that tries to load a script over plain HTTP is blocked by the browser as mixed content.

HTTP versions

VersionRuns overKey idea
HTTP/1.1 (1997)TCPText messages; connections are reused (keep-alive), but each carries one request at a time, so browsers open several connections per host (Chrome allows six)
HTTP/2 (2015)TCPBinary frames; many requests in parallel on one connection (multiplexing); compressed headers; header names always lowercase
HTTP/3 (2022)QUIC over UDPFaster connection setup; one lost packet no longer stalls every request; good on mobile networks

The meaning — methods, status codes, headers — is the same in all three versions. Only the way bytes travel changes. DevTools shows the version in the Network panel's Protocol column (http/1.1, h2, h3).

Try it with curl

curl -i prints the status line and headers; curl -v also shows what was sent (lines with >) and received (lines with <).

$ curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/hello
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sun, 18 Oct 2026 10:15:00 GMT

{"message":"Namaste from Spring Boot"}

$ curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/orders \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"productId":42,"quantity":2}'
HTTP/1.1 201
Location: /api/orders/1043
Content-Type: application/json
...

Notice HTTP/1.1 200 with no "OK": Tomcat leaves out the optional reason phrase. Clients only use the number. Transfer-Encoding: chunked means the body was streamed in pieces instead of declaring a Content-Length up front.

Tip: curl on Windows

In Windows PowerShell 5.1, curl is an alias for Invoke-WebRequest, which takes different options. Type curl.exe to run real curl (it ships with Windows 10 and 11), or use Git Bash.

Rules

  • GET must not change server state. Links, prefetchers and crawlers follow GET URLs freely.
  • A 204 response and a 304 response have no body.
  • Send Content-Type: application/json with a JSON body, or Spring rejects @RequestBody with 415.
  • Header names are case-insensitive (content-type = Content-Type); values often are not.

Conventions for REST APIs

  • Nouns in paths, methods for actions: POST /api/orders, not POST /api/createOrder.
  • Return the most specific status code: 201 + Location on create, 204 on delete, 404 for a missing id, 400 with field errors for bad input.
  • Return errors as JSON with a consistent shape. Spring supports the standard Problem Details format (application/problem+json).

Edge cases

  • A GET request with a body has no defined meaning; many servers and proxies drop it, and fetch() refuses it with TypeError: Request with GET/HEAD method cannot have body.
  • Cache-Control: no-cache does not mean "do not cache" — it means "store it, but check with the server before every use". Use no-store to forbid storing.
  • With 301 and 302, browsers may change a redirected POST into a GET. 307 and 308 keep the method and body.
  • Browsers and fetch() follow redirects automatically, so your code sees the final response, not the 302.

Wrong: 200 for everything

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"success":false,"error":"Order not found"}

Right: the status code tells the truth

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"title":"Not Found","status":404,"detail":"Order 1042 not found"}

More common mistakes

  • Using 401 when the user is logged in but lacks permission — that is 403.
  • Making "Delete" a GET link (/orders/1042/delete); a browser prefetch or crawler can trigger it.
  • Forgetting that fetch() does not throw on 404 or 500 — you must check response.ok (see Module 6).

Interview angle

  • GET vs POST: GET reads, is safe and idempotent, sends data in the URL and can be cached and bookmarked; POST creates or acts, sends data in the body and is not idempotent.
  • PUT vs PATCH: PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent; PATCH changes some fields and is not guaranteed idempotent.
  • 401 vs 403: 401 = who are you? (authenticate); 403 = I know you, and the answer is no.
  • Stateless: each request carries everything needed; sessions and JWTs add state on top.
  • HTTP/2: multiplexing many requests over one connection; HTTP/3 moves to QUIC over UDP.

What HTML, CSS and JavaScript each do

HTML describes what is on the page (structure and meaning), CSS describes how it looks (presentation), and JavaScript describes what it does (behaviour) — three languages, three jobs, one page.

Every web page, from a plain blog to a Flipkart product page, is built from the same three technologies. The browser understands only these three, so every framework you will meet later (React, Tailwind, Bootstrap) is just a smarter way of producing HTML, CSS and JavaScript in the end.

The three jobs

HTML (HyperText Markup Language)
A markup language: you wrap content in tags that say what it is — a heading, a paragraph, a link, a form field. HTML gives the page its structure and meaning. It is not a programming language: no variables, no loops, no logic.
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)
A style language: rules that say "all headings are dark blue, cards have rounded corners, on phones show one column". CSS controls presentation — colours, fonts, spacing, layout, animation. It is declarative too: you describe the result, the browser works out how.
JavaScript (JS)
A real programming language that runs inside the browser. It reacts to clicks, validates input, changes the page, calls your Spring Boot API with fetch() and updates the screen with the answer. It controls behaviour.

A Java developer's mapping

If you think in layers, the browser side has its own layering:

ConcernFrontendSomething similar in your Java world
Structure and contentHTMLThe data model / the view template (Thymeleaf, JSP)
PresentationCSSFormatting and layout rules, kept separate from logic
BehaviourJavaScriptThe controller and service code
DataJSON from fetch()The DTOs returned by your REST controllers

The golden rule is separation of concerns: keep the three in separate files (index.html, styles.css, app.js), so each can change without breaking the others. React later blends HTML-like markup and JavaScript in one file, but it still produces the same three things for the browser.

The same button, three ways

Start with HTML only. This is a page with a heading and a button. It works, but it looks like a 1995 page and the button does nothing:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Chai counter</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Chai counter</h1>
  <p>Cups today: <span id="count">0</span></p>
  <button id="add">Add a cup</button>
</body>
</html>

Add CSS in a separate file and link it from the <head> with <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">:

body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  max-width: 24rem;
  margin: 2rem auto;
  text-align: center;
}

h1 { color: #7a3e00; }

button {
  padding: 0.6rem 1.2rem;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 0.5rem;
  background: #c76b00;
  color: white;
  font-size: 1rem;
  cursor: pointer;
}

button:hover { background: #a85a00; }

Add JavaScript in a third file and load it at the end of the page (or with defer, see How the browser renders a page):

const countEl = document.getElementById("count");
const button = document.getElementById("add");
let cups = 0;

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  cups++;
  countEl.textContent = cups;   // changes the page without any server call
});

Now each file has one job. Change the colours and you only touch styles.css. Change the counting logic and you only touch app.js. The browser connects them through the DOM: JavaScript finds elements with document.getElementById and changes them; the id in the HTML is the shared name.

What each language cannot do

  • HTML cannot compute anything or react to events. The only "behaviour" it has is built in: links navigate, forms submit, <details> opens.
  • CSS cannot read data or make decisions beyond selectors, media queries and a few functions like calc(). It can animate and respond to hover and screen size, but not call an API.
  • JavaScript can do everything, but doing it with JavaScript is often slower and more fragile than using HTML or CSS. A rule of thumb: use HTML if it can, CSS if it can, JavaScript only when you must. A dropdown built with <details>, or a smooth hover with a CSS transition, needs no script.

Where each one lives

TechnologyFile extensionAdded to the page withContent-Type
HTML.htmlIt is the page itselftext/html
CSS.css<link rel="stylesheet" href="…"> in the headtext/css
JavaScript.js (or .mjs)<script src="…" defer></script>text/javascript

JavaScript is not Java

The names are a marketing accident from 1995. The two languages are unrelated. JavaScript is dynamically typed, uses prototypes and functions as first-class values, has a single-threaded event loop, and runs in the browser (and on servers through Node.js). Module 4 teaches it properly, with Java comparisons at each step. TypeScript, a typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript, is covered in Module 7.

Rule: the browser only runs HTML, CSS and JavaScript

Whatever tool you use — React, Vite, Tailwind, Sass, TypeScript — its output for the browser is those three file types (plus images, fonts and WebAssembly). Build tools exist to turn friendly source code into that output.

Convention: no inline styles, no inline handlers

Avoid style="color:red" and onclick="..." inside HTML. They mix the concerns, are hard to override and make a strict Content-Security-Policy impossible. Use classes in CSS and addEventListener in JavaScript.

Mistake: using JavaScript to do layout or styling work

Beginners write scripts that compute widths and set pixel positions. CSS Flexbox, Grid and media queries do this faster, survive window resizing and need no code. Reach for script only for behaviour.

Interview angle: "What do HTML, CSS and JavaScript do?"

  • HTML = structure and meaning, CSS = presentation, JavaScript = behaviour; all three are loaded by the browser from separate files.
  • HTML and CSS are declarative; JavaScript is a programming language.
  • Mention that JavaScript changes the page through the DOM, and that frameworks still output these three.

What happens when you open a page

Typing a URL triggers a chain: parse the URL, find the IP through DNS, open a TCP and TLS connection, send an HTTP request, receive HTML, then fetch every linked file and render the page.

"What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?" is one of the most common interview questions, for freshers and for experienced developers. A good answer is a clear sequence of steps, with one or two details at each step. The full network story belongs to CS Fundamentals · Module 2; here is the version a full-stack developer should be able to tell.

The sequence

  1. Parse the input. The browser decides whether you typed a URL or a search term. For https://shop.example.com/products/42 it splits scheme, host, port and path (see URL anatomy).
  2. Check the caches. HSTS list (a site that must use HTTPS), service worker, HTTP cache. A fresh cached copy skips the network completely.
  3. DNS lookup. The browser turns shop.example.com into an IP address (see DNS in short).
  4. TCP connection. The browser opens a reliable connection to that IP on port 443 with the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP instead.
  5. TLS handshake. For HTTPS, the server sends its certificate, the browser verifies it against trusted authorities, and both sides agree on session keys. From now on, everything is encrypted.
  6. HTTP request. The browser sends GET /products/42 with headers, plus cookies stored for that site.
  7. Server work. Often a load balancer or Nginx receives it first and forwards it to one of your app instances. Your controller calls the service and repository, the database answers, and the server builds the response.
  8. HTTP response. Status line, headers and the body — usually HTML. The browser starts working on the first bytes while the rest is still arriving (streaming parse).
  9. Render and load sub-resources. While parsing, the browser finds <link>, <script> and <img> tags and sends more requests — each reusing the same connection where possible. Then it builds the DOM, applies styles, calculates layout and paints (see How the browser renders a page).
  10. JavaScript runs. Scripts may change the page and make fetch() calls to your API. The page is "interactive" once the main script has run.

Where the time goes

On a first visit to a site, DNS, TCP and TLS each cost at least one round trip before a single byte of your page is requested. This is why a server far away feels slow even when your code is fast, and why CDNs (servers close to users) and connection reuse matter. On the second request to the same host, the browser reuses the open connection and skips steps 3–5. The DevTools Network panel shows the split for each request: DNS lookup, initial connection, SSL, waiting (the server's time) and content download.

A tiny trace you can run

The -w option of curl prints the timing of each phase. Run this in a terminal (use curl.exe in PowerShell):

$ curl -s -o /dev/null https://example.com \
    -w "dns=%{time_namelookup} connect=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} \
first_byte=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n"
dns=0.012 connect=0.045 tls=0.110 first_byte=0.180 total=0.185

The numbers are in seconds and cumulative; yours will differ. Subtract neighbours to see each phase: here DNS took 12 ms, TCP 33 ms, TLS 65 ms, and the server about 70 ms. On Windows PowerShell write NUL instead of /dev/null.

What changes for a React + Spring Boot app

The first HTML response is tiny — an almost empty page with a <div id="root"> and a script tag. The browser then downloads the JavaScript bundle, runs React, and React calls your API (GET /api/products/42) to fetch JSON and draw the page. So there are two rounds: one for the app shell, one for the data. Static, dynamic, MPA, SPA and SSR explains the trade-offs.

Edge cases

  • A cached page may be shown without contacting the server at all (Cache-Control: max-age), which is why you sometimes do not see a change you just deployed. Hard reload with Ctrl+Shift+R bypasses the cache.
  • A redirect (301/302) adds a whole extra round trip, and http:// to https:// redirects are common. HSTS lets the browser skip that redirect next time.
  • If the TLS certificate is expired or does not match the host name, the browser shows a full-page warning (NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID or similar) instead of your site.
  • If the server is down, you see ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED; if it never answers, ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT.

Tip: answer in layers, not in a list of acronyms

Interviewers want to see that you understand the order and the purpose of each step. Say what each step achieves ("DNS gets the IP", "TLS makes the connection private"), then ask whether they want more depth on any layer.

Interview angle: "What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?"

  • URL parse → cache check → DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP request → server processing → response → parse HTML, fetch CSS/JS/images → render → run JS.
  • Add one Java-flavoured detail: the request reaches Tomcat, then DispatcherServlet, your controller, the service and the database.
  • Mention connection reuse, caching and CDNs as ways to make it faster.

How the browser renders a page

The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree, calculates the size and position of every box (layout), draws them (paint) and layers the result on screen (composite) — and a plain script tag stops the parser until the script has run.

The browser does not show HTML as it arrives. It runs a pipeline — the critical rendering path — every time it shows a page. Knowing the pipeline explains three things a full-stack developer meets constantly: why a page can flash unstyled content, why script placement matters, and why some CSS changes are cheap while others make the page janky.

1. HTML becomes the DOM

The parser reads HTML bytes, turns them into characters, then into tokens (start tag, end tag, text) and then into nodes that form a tree: the DOM (Document Object Model). The DOM is a live, in-memory object tree — each element is an object with properties and methods that JavaScript can read and change. Think of it as the parsed object graph of the document, like the object graph Jackson builds from JSON.

<body>
  <h1>Menu</h1>
  <ul>
    <li>Dosa</li>
    <li>Idli</li>
  </ul>
</body>

The parser is forgiving: if your HTML has a missing end tag, the browser repairs the tree instead of failing. That is convenient but hides mistakes, so validate your HTML (Validating HTML). Parsing is also incremental: the browser starts building the DOM from the first bytes while the rest of the file downloads.

2. CSS becomes the CSSOM

The browser parses every stylesheet into the CSSOM (CSS Object Model), a tree of rules with their final values. Unlike HTML, CSS cannot be used piece by piece: a rule at the bottom of the file can override one at the top, so the browser needs all the CSS before it can safely draw. That makes CSS render-blocking: the browser will not paint anything until the stylesheets in the head have loaded. This is why you put the stylesheet link in the head and keep CSS files small.

3. The render tree

The browser combines DOM and CSSOM into the render tree: only what will actually be displayed, with computed styles attached. Elements with display: none and everything in the <head> are left out. Elements with visibility: hidden are in the tree (they take space) but not drawn. Pseudo-elements such as ::before are in the render tree although they are not in the DOM.

4. Layout (reflow)

Layout works out the exact size and position of every box, in pixels, for the current window size. Percentages and rem units become real numbers here, and boxes are placed according to flow, Flexbox, Grid and positioning rules. One change high up the tree (a bigger image, a font that finishes loading) can change the position of everything below it, so layout is expensive. A second layout caused by a later change is called a reflow.

5. Paint

Paint turns boxes into pixels: backgrounds, borders, text, shadows, images. The browser records the draw commands for each layer. A change that only affects colour, such as a hover background, needs paint but not layout.

6. Composite

The page is split into layers (elements with transform, opacity animations, position: fixed, video and so on). The GPU draws the layers in the right order and combines them — compositing. A change to transform or opacity on its own layer only needs this last step, which is why animations should use them (Transitions and animations).

You change…Stages that re-runCost
width, margin, font-size, adding elementsLayout, paint, compositeHighest
background-color, box-shadowPaint, compositeMedium
transform, opacityComposite onlyLowest

Scripts block the parser

JavaScript can change the DOM while it is being built (document.write can even add HTML). So when the parser meets a plain <script src="app.js">, it stops, downloads the script, waits for pending stylesheets (the script may read styles), runs it, and only then continues. A big script in the head therefore leaves the user looking at a blank page.

Two attributes fix this. Both download the script in parallel with the HTML parsing; they differ in when it runs.

TagDownloadRuns whenOrder kept?Use for
<script src>Blocks the parserImmediatelyYesAlmost never in the head
<script defer>In parallelAfter the HTML is fully parsed, before DOMContentLoadedYes, in document orderYour app code; scripts that touch the DOM
<script async>In parallelThe moment it arrives (may interrupt parsing)NoIndependent scripts such as analytics
<script type="module">In parallelDeferred by defaultYesModern ES modules (Vite uses this)
 
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
  <!-- runs after parsing, in order: first vendor.js, then app.js -->
  <script src="vendor.js" defer></script>
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
  <!-- independent; runs whenever it loads -->
  <script src="analytics.js" async></script>
</head>

The older advice was "put scripts just before </body>". defer in the head is better: the download starts earlier and the order is still guaranteed. A Vite-built React app has exactly this shape:

<body>
  <div id="root"></div>
  <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
</body>

Page load events and metrics

  • DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is parsed and deferred scripts have run (images may still be loading).
  • load fires when everything, including images and stylesheets, has finished.
  • First Contentful Paint (FCP) is when the first text or image appears. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) is when the biggest visible element appears; good is under 2.5 seconds. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures unexpected jumps of the layout; Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures how quickly the page reacts to clicks. Lighthouse and the Performance panel report them.

Watching it happen

You can see the DOM change live. Open DevTools on any page, go to the Console and run:

const p = document.createElement("p");
p.textContent = "Added by JavaScript";
document.body.append(p);      // DOM changes -> layout and paint run again
document.body.children.length; // how many direct children body has now

The new line appears at once, and you can find it in the Elements panel. The DOM is the truth the browser draws; the HTML file you downloaded is only where it started.

Rule: CSS in the head, scripts with defer

Link stylesheets in the <head> so the first paint is already styled. Load your own scripts with defer (or type="module") so they never block parsing and always see a complete DOM.

Edge cases and errors

  • An async or defer attribute on an inline script (no src) does nothing; defer is ignored there. Only type="module" inline scripts are deferred.
  • A script that runs too early gets null from getElementById and fails with TypeError: Cannot read properties of null. The element does not exist yet. Use defer.
  • Images without width and height have no size until downloaded; the layout then jumps (bad CLS). Set the size in HTML (Images).
  • Web fonts can make text invisible or swap suddenly while loading; font-display: swap shows a fallback font first.

Mistake: reading layout values in a loop while changing styles

Reading element.offsetHeight forces the browser to run layout right away. Alternating "write style, read size, write style, read size" in a loop causes a reflow every iteration (layout thrashing). Batch all reads first, then all writes. React does much of this batching for you.

Interview angle: "How does the browser render a page?"

  • HTML → DOM; CSS → CSSOM; both → render tree → layout → paint → composite.
  • CSS blocks rendering; a normal script blocks parsing; defer keeps order and runs after parsing; async runs as soon as it loads, in no fixed order.
  • Layout is the costly stage; animate transform and opacity to skip it.
  • Reflow = layout again; repaint = paint again.

Static vs dynamic sites, MPA vs SPA, CSR vs SSR

A static site serves ready-made files, a dynamic site builds pages per request; a multi-page app loads a new HTML page per click, a single-page app loads one page and swaps content with JavaScript; and the HTML can be built in the browser (CSR) or on the server (SSR).

These terms are mixed up constantly, because they answer different questions. Keep three questions apart: (1) is the content fixed or generated? (2) does a click load a new page or update the current one? (3) where is the HTML produced? Your full-stack project will be: dynamic data, single-page app, client-side rendering.

Static vs dynamic

A static site is a folder of finished files — HTML, CSS, JS, images. The server just hands them over; nothing is computed per user. A dynamic site runs code on the server for each request, usually reading a database, so two users can see different content.

StaticDynamic
ExamplesPortfolio, docs, a company landing pageFlipkart, IRCTC, a banking dashboard
Server workRead a file, send itRun code, query the database, build the response
SpeedVery fast; served from a CDNDepends on your code and database
HostingFree or cheap: GitHub Pages, Netlify, S3 + CDNNeeds a running server, e.g. Spring Boot
Security surfaceTinyLarge: login, input, database

The line is blurry, because a static page can call a dynamic API after it loads. The React build is static files; the data it shows is dynamic. Static site generators (Hugo, Jekyll, Astro, Next.js in export mode) build HTML files ahead of time from templates and data.

Multi-page apps (MPA)

In a multi-page application every link click or form submit makes the browser request a new HTML document. The server (Spring MVC with Thymeleaf or JSP, PHP, Django, Rails) returns the complete page. The browser throws the old page away, including its JavaScript state, and renders the new one.

@Controller
public class OrderPageController {

    private final OrderService orderService;

    public OrderPageController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
    public String show(@PathVariable long id, Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("order", orderService.find(id));
        return "order";   // Thymeleaf template order.html -> full HTML page
    }
}

MPAs are simple, work without much JavaScript, and are good for SEO since each URL returns finished content. The cost: every navigation reloads the whole page, even the header and sidebar.

Single-page apps (SPA)

A single-page application loads one HTML page and one JavaScript bundle once. After that, clicking a link does not reload anything: JavaScript changes the URL with the History API, calls fetch() for JSON, and rewrites parts of the DOM. React with React Router, Angular and Vue work this way. It feels like a desktop app — fast transitions, state preserved — and the server becomes a pure JSON API.

SPA strengths

  • Smooth, app-like navigation; no full reloads
  • Clean split: one team builds the UI, another the REST API
  • The same API can serve a mobile app
  • The static build is cheap to host on a CDN

SPA weaknesses

  • Larger first download; blank screen until JavaScript runs
  • SEO and link previews are harder, since the first HTML is nearly empty
  • More moving parts: routing, state, auth tokens, CORS
  • Deep links need server configuration (see below)

Client-side vs server-side rendering

Rendering here means producing the HTML for the page content. Client-side rendering (CSR): the server sends an empty shell; the browser's JavaScript builds the content. Server-side rendering (SSR): the server sends HTML that already has the content; the browser shows it at once. Thymeleaf, JSP and PHP are server-side rendering in the classic sense. Frameworks like Next.js render React components on the server, then hydrate the page: React attaches event handlers to the already-present HTML so it becomes interactive.

CSR (plain React + Vite)SSR (Thymeleaf, Next.js)
First HTMLEmpty shellFull content
Time to first contentSlower (download, run JS, call API)Faster
SEO and link previewsWeaker (crawlers must run JS)Strong
Server costLow (static files + API)Higher (renders on every request)
After first loadVery fast navigationDepends on the framework

A related idea is static site generation (SSG): render the pages once at build time and serve them as static files — the best of both for content that rarely changes.

Where a React + Spring Boot app fits

The standard architecture in this course: a CSR single-page app in React, talking to a REST API in Spring Boot over JSON. In development, two servers run (Vite on 5173, Spring Boot on 8080). In production, there are two common layouts:

  • Separate hosting. The React build lives on a CDN or Nginx; the API lives on its own domain or under /api behind the same proxy. Teams can deploy independently.
  • One jar. Copy the Vite dist folder into Spring Boot's src/main/resources/static; Boot serves both files and API. Simple to deploy, but UI and API now ship together.
import org.springframework.stereotype.Controller;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;

@Controller
public class SpaForwardController {

    // The browser URL /orders/7 is a React route, not a server resource.
    // On a hard refresh the server must return index.html;
    // React Router then decides what to show.
    @GetMapping({"/orders/{id}", "/profile"})
    public String forward() {
        return "forward:/index.html";
    }
}

That last point catches many beginners: with a SPA, a refresh on /orders/7 sends that path to the server, which has no such file and answers 404. The fix is to return index.html for every non-API path (this is the try_files line in Nginx, or a fallback rule on static hosts).

Rule: in a SPA the server must never return an HTML error page to the API

Your React code calls response.json(). If the API answers with the SPA's index.html or a Whitelabel HTML error page, parsing fails with SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<'. Keep /api/** separate and make it always return JSON.

Convention: prefix all API routes with /api

A clear prefix lets Nginx or Spring route /api/** to controllers and everything else to the React app, and keeps SPA routes and API routes from clashing.

Edge case: SEO for a SPA

Google can run JavaScript, but other crawlers and social-media link previews (WhatsApp, LinkedIn) often read only the raw HTML. For public pages that need search ranking or good previews, use SSR/SSG (Next.js, Thymeleaf) or pre-render. For apps behind a login — dashboards, admin tools, CRMs — SEO does not matter and a SPA is perfectly fine.

Mistake: choosing a SPA for every project

A five-page company website or a blog is better as a static site or server-rendered pages. Pick the architecture from the need: public content → static/SSR; interactive app → SPA.

In real projects

Many service-company projects still use Spring MVC + Thymeleaf or JSP (MPA, SSR). Most product-company and startup teams build React + REST API. Large public sites such as e-commerce increasingly use Next.js for SSR with a Java backend behind it.

Interview angle

  • SPA vs MPA: one HTML page + JSON calls versus a full HTML page per navigation. Mention routing without reload, SEO and initial load.
  • CSR vs SSR: who builds the HTML — browser or server — and the effect on first paint and SEO.
  • Where does your project fit? React SPA (CSR) + Spring Boot REST API, JWT or session auth, Nginx serving the build.

Browser DevTools: opening them, Elements and Console

DevTools is the debugger built into your browser: the Elements panel shows and edits the live DOM and CSS, and the Console shows errors and runs JavaScript — together they answer "what is the page doing, and why?".

For a frontend developer, DevTools is what the IDE debugger and log files are for a Java developer. These notes use Chrome (Edge is identical, Firefox is very similar). You will keep DevTools open for most of your working day, so learn it early.

Opening it and the shortcuts worth knowing

ActionWindows / LinuxmacOS
Open or close DevToolsF12 or Ctrl+Shift+ICmd+Option+I
Open straight on the ConsoleCtrl+Shift+JCmd+Option+J
Inspect element (pick from page)Ctrl+Shift+CCmd+Shift+C
Toggle device toolbar (phone view)Ctrl+Shift+MCmd+Shift+M
Command menu (run any command)Ctrl+Shift+PCmd+Shift+P
Hard reload (ignore cache)Ctrl+Shift+RCmd+Shift+R
Show or hide the Console drawerEscEsc
Open a file in SourcesCtrl+PCmd+P

You can also right-click anything on a page and choose Inspect. DevTools can dock to the bottom, the right or a separate window (the three-dots menu); the right side suits wide monitors. The command menu is a quick way to find features by name — type "screenshot" to capture a full-page screenshot, or "dark" to switch themes.

The Elements panel

The Elements panel shows the live DOM — not the HTML file you downloaded, but the tree as it is right now, including everything JavaScript added. This is why "View Source" (Ctrl+U) of a React app shows an empty <div id="root"> while Elements shows the whole page.

  • Select and expand nodes in the tree on the left; the page highlights the matching element, and hovering a node shows its size.
  • Edit HTML live. Double-click text or a tag, change it, press Enter. Right-click a node for Edit as HTML, Delete element, Copy → selector, Break on → attribute modifications, and Force state → :hover (to style a hover state without keeping the mouse there).
  • Drag nodes to reorder them and see the effect immediately.
  • Search the DOM with Ctrl+F — by text, CSS selector or XPath.

Changes are made only in your browser's memory. Refresh the page and they are gone; nothing is saved to the server. That is perfect for experiments — and a reminder to copy a working change into your source files.

Styles, Computed and the box model

Select an element and look at the right-hand side.

Styles
Every CSS rule that applies to the element, from most to least specific. A rule that lost the fight is shown with a line through it (strikethrough). Each rule shows the file and line number (click it to jump to Sources). Edit a value, or tick and untick the checkbox beside a declaration to switch it on and off. Click + to add a new rule. Colour swatches open a colour picker; arrow keys change numbers (Shift+arrow changes by 10).
Computed
The final value of every property after the cascade — for example 1rem becomes 16px, and an inherited colour is shown. Expand a property to see which rule supplied the value. Use it when you ask "why is this 24px?".
Box model diagram
A nested picture of the element's content, padding, border and margin with the numbers. Hover a layer to highlight it on the page. It makes spacing bugs obvious (see The box model).
Layout (Flexbox, Grid)
Elements with display: flex or grid get a small badge in the tree. Click it to draw overlays that show the flex items or grid lines and track sizes. Essential for learning Flexbox and Grid.
Event Listeners / Accessibility
Lists the JavaScript listeners attached to the element, and its accessibility tree entry (role, name) — handy for checking forms and buttons.

Tip: the fastest CSS debugging loop

Inspect the element, look in Styles for a struck-through rule (it lost), look in Computed for the winning rule, untick declarations until the page looks right, then copy the change into your CSS file. Do not guess and re-save repeatedly.

The Console panel

The Console does two jobs: it prints messages from the browser and your code, and it is a JavaScript REPL (read–eval–print loop) where you can run code in the context of the current page — much like jshell for Java, but connected to the live page.

Reading messages
  • Errors (red): an uncaught exception such as Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name'), a failed request (Failed to load resource: 404), or a CORS block. The right-hand link shows the file and line; the arrow expands the stack trace.
  • Warnings (yellow): deprecations and framework warnings such as React's "Each child in a list should have a unique key".
  • Info and logs: output of your console.log() calls. Use the level filter and the text filter box to cut the noise.
Logging helpers
console.log("order", order);          // object is expandable
console.table(orders);                // array of objects as a table
console.error("Payment failed", err); // red, with a stack trace
console.warn("Cart is empty");        // yellow
console.group("Checkout");            // indent related logs
console.log("step 1");
console.groupEnd();
console.time("load");                 // start a timer ...
// ... code to measure ...
console.timeEnd("load");              // ... prints: load: 12.3 ms
console.dir(document.body);           // inspect as an object, not as HTML
Using it as a REPL
document.title                           // "Chai counter"
document.querySelectorAll("a").length    // 14
$$("img").filter(i => !i.alt).length    // images missing alt text
$0                                       // the element selected in Elements
$_                                       // the result of the last expression
$("h1").textContent = "Hello"            // $ is a shortcut for querySelector
localStorage.getItem("token")            // read saved data
fetch("/api/hello").then(r => r.json()).then(console.log)
await (await fetch("/api/hello")).json() // top-level await works in the Console

$, $$, $0 and $_ exist only in the Console, not in your source files. Press Up for earlier commands, and use the Preserve log setting so messages survive a page reload. Multi-line code: Shift+Enter adds a new line.

Convention: remove debug logging before you commit

A stray console.log(user) can leak personal data in production, where anyone can open the Console. Keep logs temporary, or use a logging helper that is switched off in production builds. ESLint's no-console rule catches them.

Edge cases

  • console.log(obj) shows a live reference: if the object changes later and you expand it afterwards, you see the new values, not the values at the time of logging. Use console.log(JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))) or structuredClone(obj) for a snapshot.
  • Browser extensions add their own errors to the Console. Test in an Incognito window (extensions are off by default) when an error looks unrelated to your code.
  • An error in the Console only says what failed in the browser. A 500 from your API shows up as a red network line, but the real cause is in the Spring Boot log.

Interview angle

  • "How do you debug a UI problem?" — inspect the element, read Styles/Computed for CSS, read Console errors, check Network for failed calls, then set breakpoints in Sources.
  • "View Source vs Elements?" — Source is the original response; Elements is the live DOM after JavaScript ran.

DevTools Network panel: reading every request

The Network panel lists every request the page makes with its status, size and timing, and shows the headers, payload and response of each — it is where you find out whether a bug is in React or in your Spring Boot API.

Open the panel before loading the page: open DevTools, click Network, then reload. Requests that happened earlier are not recorded. As a full-stack developer, this is the panel you will use most when connecting React to Spring Boot (Module 6).

The request list

Each row is one request. Useful default columns: Name (file or last path segment), Status, Type (document, script, stylesheet, fetch, xhr, image…), Initiator (which file or line made the request), Size (transferred over the network, versus the unpacked size below it), Time and Waterfall. Right-click the column header to add more, for example Protocol (h2, h3), Method and Domain.

The summary bar at the bottom shows the request count, total transferred data and the timings of DOMContentLoaded (blue line) and load (red line) on the waterfall.

Filtering to find your API calls

  • The type buttons — All, Fetch/XHR, JS, CSS, Img, Media, Font, Doc, WS, Wasm, Manifest, Other. Click Fetch/XHR to see only calls your JavaScript made with fetch() or XMLHttpRequest: this is your API traffic with the static files removed.
  • The filter box accepts text and special filters: /api/ matches URLs, method:POST, status-code:500, -domain:google.com to exclude, larger-than:100k.
  • The search icon (Ctrl+F) searches inside headers and response bodies of all requests.

Inspecting one request

Click a row to open a detail pane with tabs.

TabWhat it showsUse it to…
HeadersGeneral info (URL, method, status, remote address), response headers, request headersCheck Content-Type, Authorization, Set-Cookie, CORS headers, caching headers
PayloadQuery string parameters and the request body (JSON or form data), with a "view source" toggleConfirm what React actually sent
PreviewThe response formatted: a JSON tree, a rendered image or HTMLRead the data comfortably
ResponseThe raw response body textSee exactly what the server returned, including HTML error pages
InitiatorThe call stack that made the requestFind which component fired a call
TimingBreakdown: queueing, DNS lookup, initial connection, SSL, request sent, waiting for server response (TTFB), content downloadTell a slow server from a slow network
CookiesCookies sent and received, with flagsDebug sessions and SameSite problems

In the Timing tab, "Waiting for server response" (TTFB, time to first byte) is the time your Spring Boot code and database took. A large value there means optimise the backend; a large "Content Download" means the response is too big.

Reading the status column

The Status column is your first clue, because it tells which side owns the problem.

You seeIt usually meansFirst thing to check
200 with unexpected contentServer answered, but with the wrong data (often HTML instead of JSON)Response tab
304Browser cache validatedNormal; no action
400 / 415Your request was wrongPayload and Content-Type
401 / 403Token missing or user not allowedRequest Authorization header
404Wrong URL or missing entityRequest URL, /api prefix, proxy config
500Server exceptionSpring Boot console log
(failed) with net::ERR_…No response at all: server down, DNS, or a CORS blockIs the server running? Console CORS message
Two rows, an OPTIONS then the real callA CORS preflight requestYour CORS configuration (Module 6)

Settings that save hours

  • Preserve log: keep the list when the page navigates or reloads. Without it, a redirect after a form submit wipes the evidence — tick it when debugging a login.
  • Disable cache: skips the browser cache while DevTools is open. Always on during development, so you never debug stale files.
  • Throttling: the dropdown that reads "No throttling" lets you pick Fast 4G, Slow 4G, 3G or Offline. Indians on mobile data do not get your office Wi-Fi speed, so test your loading states and spinners with it. Offline shows how your app handles a lost connection.
  • Block request URL (right-click a row): pretend a file or API fails to test your error handling.
  • Record (red circle) and Clear (the stop icon) control capture.
  • Export HAR (download arrow): saves everything as a HAR file to share with a teammate.

Copy as cURL: replay a request outside the browser

Right-click a request → Copy → Copy as cURL (bash or cmd). You get a complete command, including cookies and tokens. Paste it into a terminal to reproduce the call without the UI, edit it, or import it into Postman (File → Import → paste raw text). If the curl call works but the browser fails, the problem is browser-only: CORS, cookies or caching. If both fail, the problem is on the server.

curl 'http://localhost:8080/api/orders' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9...' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"productId":42,"quantity":2}'

Mind the secrets: the copied command contains your real token. Do not paste it into chat groups or tickets.

A worked debugging example

The orders page is blank. Steps: open DevTools → Network → tick Preserve log and Disable cache → reload → click Fetch/XHR. You see GET /api/orders in red with status 401. In Headers, the request has no Authorization line, so the token was not attached — the bug is in the React code that builds the request, not in Spring Boot. Had the status been 500, you would read the Response tab (Spring Boot's error JSON) and then the server log. Two minutes, no guessing.

Rule: look at the Network panel before you read any code

Decide first which side is wrong: was the request correct? what status came back? what was in the body? Only then open source files. This one habit separates efficient full-stack developers from frustrated ones.

Mistake: trusting the Console message for a failed CORS call

For a CORS failure the Network panel may show the request as (failed) or with a status that JavaScript cannot read, while the Console explains "blocked by CORS policy". The server might actually have processed the request. Check the Spring Boot log to see if it arrived.

Edge cases

  • With "Disable cache" off, you may see (disk cache) or (memory cache) in the Size column — no network request happened.
  • Responses larger than a limit may show as "Failed to load response data" in Preview; use "Open in new tab" or curl.
  • WebSocket traffic appears under the WS filter; click the row and use the Messages tab.

Interview angle

  • "How do you debug a failing API call from React?" — Network tab, Fetch/XHR filter, check status, request headers and payload, response body, then Spring Boot logs; replay with Copy as cURL or Postman.
  • "What is TTFB?" — time to first byte; mostly your server's processing time plus network latency.

DevTools: Application, Sources, Lighthouse and device mode

Application shows what the browser stores (localStorage, cookies), Sources lets you pause running JavaScript at breakpoints, Lighthouse audits performance, accessibility and SEO, and device mode tests phone screens.

Application panel: what the browser stores

The Application panel lists the data your site keeps in the browser. On the left, open the Storage section.

Local storage
Key–value strings (about 5 MB per origin) that stay until deleted. Read in JavaScript with localStorage.getItem("theme"). You can double-click a value to edit it, or click the delete icons. Many apps store a JWT here (a security trade-off covered in Spring Boot · Module 4).
Session storage
Same API, but cleared when the tab closes and separate per tab.
Cookies
Name, value, domain, path, expiry and the flags HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite. A JSESSIONID from Spring Security appears here. HttpOnly cookies are visible in DevTools but not to JavaScript.
IndexedDB, Cache storage, Service workers
Bigger structured storage and offline-app features, used by PWAs. Know they exist.

Clear site data (Application → Storage → Clear site data) resets everything for the site — the quickest way to test "first-time visitor" and to log out cleanly when a stale token causes strange behaviour.

localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
localStorage.getItem("theme");     // "dark"
localStorage.removeItem("theme");
localStorage.clear();              // everything for this origin
document.cookie;                   // readable cookies only (not HttpOnly ones)

Sources panel: breakpoints and stepping

console.log debugging works, but a debugger lets you pause the program and look at every variable — exactly like IntelliJ's debugger. In Sources, open a file (Ctrl+P), and click a line number to set a breakpoint. Trigger the code (click the button) and execution freezes on that line.

  • The Scope pane shows local and closure variables; the Call Stack pane shows how you got here; Watch evaluates expressions you add.
  • Controls: resume F8, step over F10, step into F11, step out Shift+F11.
  • Conditional breakpoint: right-click a line number → Add conditional breakpoint → order.id === 1042. It stops only when true.
  • Logpoint: like a breakpoint, but prints a message without stopping and without editing code.
  • The right-hand lists include XHR/fetch breakpoints (pause when a URL matches), DOM breakpoints (pause when an element changes) and Event listener breakpoints (pause on any click).
  • Writing debugger; in your code pauses it whenever DevTools is open. Remove it before committing.
  • Also tick Pause on exceptions to stop at the line where an error is thrown.

Vite and other tools bundle and compile your code. Source maps let DevTools show your original files (OrderList.jsx) instead of the bundled output, so breakpoints land on the lines you wrote. They are on by default in development.

Lighthouse: an automatic audit

The Lighthouse panel runs an audit and scores four areas from 0 to 100: Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices and SEO. Choose Mobile or Desktop, tick the categories, click Analyze page load. The report lists problems with advice, such as "Image elements do not have explicit width and height", "Buttons do not have an accessible name" or "Document does not have a meta description". Run it in an Incognito window with extensions off, so results are consistent. Scores vary a little from run to run, and a local dev server is slower than a production build, so audit the production build (npm run build then npm run preview) for real numbers.

Device mode: test phones without a phone

Press Ctrl+Shift+M. The page appears in a resizable frame. Pick a device (iPhone, Pixel, iPad) or choose Responsive and drag the handles; the width in pixels is shown at the top. It simulates screen size, device pixel ratio, touch events and the mobile user agent, and the three-dots menu adds a media-query ruler and network throttling. It is not a real phone — fonts, scrolling and performance differ — so test on a real device before release. See Responsive design.

Other panels in one line each

  • Performance: record a timeline of CPU, rendering and scripting to find slow frames and long tasks.
  • Memory: heap snapshots to find memory leaks in the browser.
  • Security / Privacy and security: certificate and mixed-content information.
  • React Developer Tools (a browser extension): adds Components and Profiler panels that show the React component tree, props and state. Install it before Module 5.

Tip: a debugging workflow for "it works on my machine"

  1. Console: any red error?
  2. Network: failed or wrong request?
  3. Elements: is the element present, what are its computed styles?
  4. Application: stale token or cached data? Clear site data.
  5. Sources: breakpoint where the data goes wrong.

Mistake: storing secrets in localStorage or in front-end code

Anything in the browser — localStorage, the JavaScript bundle, environment variables compiled into it — can be read by the user in seconds with DevTools. API secret keys and database passwords belong on the server only. Vite exposes only variables prefixed VITE_ to the browser, and those are public.

Edge cases

  • Local storage is per origin: localhost:5173 and localhost:3000 have separate storage.
