Module 2·About 4 daysMust

HTML

10 topics · about 1 h of reading

HTML is the skeleton of every web page. A React component, a Thymeleaf template and a hand-written file all end up as HTML in the browser, so you must know it well even if you never write a raw .html file at work. Good HTML gives you accessibility, search ranking, working forms and a layout that CSS can style easily. Bad HTML (a page made of <div> soup) fails all four.

This module teaches HTML the way professionals use it: the right element for the job. Module 3 styles what you build here, Module 4 and Module 5 make it interactive, and the forms you learn here are what your Spring Boot controllers receive and validate (Spring Boot · Module 2). You will finish by building a personal profile page.

  • Write a valid HTML5 page and explain every line of the boilerplate.
  • Choose the correct element for text, links, images, lists and tables.
  • Structure a page with semantic elements such as header, nav, main, article and footer.
  • Build accessible forms with labels, the right input types and validation attributes, and explain why the server must validate again.
  • Make a page usable with a keyboard and a screen reader, and check it with Lighthouse.
  • Add meta tags for SEO and link previews, and validate your HTML.

HTML basics and the page boilerplate, line by line

An HTML document is a tree of elements written as tags with attributes; every page starts from the same small boilerplate — doctype, html with lang, head with charset, viewport and title, and a body.

HTML is text. A browser reads it and builds the DOM (see How the browser renders a page). You can write it in any editor — VS Code is the usual choice — save it as index.html and double-click the file to open it. For live reload while you edit, use the Live Server extension or the Vite dev server.

The boilerplate

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Asha Rao - Java Developer</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
    <script src="app.js" defer></script>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello, world</h1>
  </body>
</html>
<!doctype html>
Tells the browser to use modern standards mode. Without it, browsers fall back to quirks mode, which imitates 1990s behaviour and breaks CSS layouts in odd ways. Always the first line. It is not a tag, and it is case-insensitive.
<html lang="en">
The root element; everything else lives inside it. lang declares the page language so screen readers pick the right pronunciation, translation tools know what to translate and search engines classify the page. Use hi for Hindi, en-IN for Indian English.
<head>
Information about the page — nothing inside it is displayed (except the title in the tab).
<meta charset="utf-8">
The character encoding. Without it, "₹" or "नमस्ते" may appear as garbage like â‚¹. Keep it within the first 1,024 bytes, so put it first in the head. Also make your server send Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 (Spring does by default).
<meta name="viewport" ...>
Tells mobile browsers to use the real device width instead of pretending to be a 980-pixel-wide desktop. Without it, your responsive CSS does not work on phones (see Responsive design). Do not add user-scalable=no; zooming is an accessibility need.
<title>
The text of the browser tab, bookmarks and search results. Required, unique per page, ideally 50–60 characters.
<link rel="stylesheet" href="...">
Loads a CSS file. Put it in the head so the page is styled on first paint.
<script src="..." defer></script>
Loads JavaScript without blocking the parser (see defer and async).
<body>
Everything the user sees.

In VS Code, type ! and press Tab (Emmet) to generate this skeleton.

Elements, tags and attributes

An element is a start tag, content and an end tag. Attributes are extra settings in the start tag, written as name="value".

<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org" target="_blank">MDN Web Docs</a>
<!--   ^ tag name   ^ attribute      ^ attribute         ^ content   ^ end tag -->
  • Void elements have no content and no end tag: <br>, <hr>, <img>, <input>, <meta>, <link>. In HTML you write <img ...>, not <img ... /> (the slash is allowed and ignored; JSX in React requires it).
  • Boolean attributes are on when present: <input required disabled>. disabled="false" is still disabled — remove the attribute to turn it off.
  • Always quote values with double quotes. Tag and attribute names are case-insensitive but lowercase is the convention.
  • Global attributes work on any element: id (unique in the page), class (one or more names, for CSS), title (tooltip), hidden, tabindex, lang, data-* (your own data, e.g. data-product-id="42", read in JavaScript as el.dataset.productId).

Nesting rules

Elements nest like brackets in Java: the last one opened is the first one closed. <p><strong>text</strong></p> is right; <p><strong>text</p></strong> is wrong. Some elements restrict their children: <ul> may contain only <li>; a <p> cannot contain a <div> or another <p> (the browser closes the paragraph early); an <a> cannot contain another <a> or a <button>; a <table> expects rows, not random elements.

Block vs inline

Block elementsInline elements
LayoutStart on a new line, fill the full widthSit inside a line of text, only as wide as their content
Width and heightCan be setIgnored for width/height; vertical margin has no effect
Examplesdiv, p, h1–h6, ul, section, form, tablespan, a, strong, em, img, code, label

Block or inline is just the default display value; CSS can change it (The box model and display). In the HTML spec the stricter idea is the content model: flow content, phrasing content and so on — an inline element should hold only phrasing content.

Comments and whitespace

<!-- This is a comment. The browser ignores it, but it is visible in View Source. -->
<p>Many     spaces   and
new lines collapse    into single spaces.</p>

HTML collapses runs of spaces and line breaks into one space. To force a line break use <br> (for addresses and poems only, not for spacing; use CSS margin), and for preformatted text use <pre>. Never put secrets in comments — users see them.

HTML entities

Characters that mean something to HTML must be written as entities when you want them as text. Entities start with & and end with ;.

You wantWriteNotes
<&lt;Otherwise it starts a tag
>&gt;Optional but tidy
&&amp;Also in URLs inside attributes: ?a=1&amp;b=2
"&quot;Needed inside a double-quoted attribute
Non-breaking space&nbsp;Keeps two words together; do not use for layout
©&copy;Or just type ©, since the file is UTF-8
₹&#8377;Numeric code; or type ₹ directly

With charset="utf-8" you can type most characters directly; entities are essential only for <, & and quotes in attributes. To show HTML code on a page, escape it: <code>&lt;p&gt;</code> displays as <p>. This is also how XSS attacks work in reverse: a framework escapes user text for you (React does); Thymeleaf's th:text escapes, th:utext does not.

Rules

  • Start every page with <!doctype html>, set lang, declare charset and the viewport meta, and give a <title>.
  • id values must be unique per page and contain no spaces.
  • Close every element that needs closing, and nest properly.

Conventions

  • Lowercase tags and attributes, double quotes, two-space indentation.
  • Name files in lowercase with hyphens: contact-us.html. The home page is index.html, which servers return for /.
  • Class names describe meaning (product-card), not looks (red-big).

Edge cases

  • The browser never rejects bad HTML; it repairs it silently. A missing </div> may break the layout far below the actual mistake, and the result differs between nested cases. Validate (see Validating HTML).
  • Omitting <html>, <head> and <body> tags is legal — the parser adds them — but always write them.
  • Duplicate ids do not raise an error; getElementById just returns the first one.

Mistake: using <br> and &nbsp; to create space

Stacks of <br><br><br> or non-breaking spaces make spacing that cannot be controlled or made responsive. Use margin and padding in CSS.

Interview angle

  • "What does <!doctype html> do?" — triggers standards mode instead of quirks mode.
  • "Why the viewport meta tag?" — so mobile browsers use the device width; required for responsive design.
  • "What are void elements? Block vs inline?" — give examples and the layout difference.

Headings, text, links and generic containers

Use headings for outline (one h1, no skipped levels), p for paragraphs, strong and em for meaning, a for links with correct URLs and rel attributes, and div or span only when no meaningful element fits.

Headings

<h1> to <h6> form the outline of the page, like chapter and section titles in a book. Screen-reader users jump from heading to heading to scan a page, and search engines use them to understand it. So choose levels by structure, never by size — change the size with CSS.

  • One <h1> per page: the main topic ("Asha Rao — Java Developer").
  • Do not skip levels: an h2 is followed by h3, never directly by h4.
  • Do not use a heading just to make text big or bold.
<h1>Asha Rao</h1>
  <h2>Projects</h2>
    <h3>Library Management System</h3>
    <h3>Expense Tracker API</h3>
  <h2>Skills</h2>

Paragraphs and text-level elements

<p> is a paragraph. Inside text, choose the element by meaning:

ElementMeaningLooks like (default)
<strong>Strong importance or warningBold
<em>Stress emphasis (changes the sentence meaning when read aloud)Italic
<b>Draw attention, no extra importance (a keyword)Bold
<i>Alternate voice: a foreign word, a technical term, a thoughtItalic
<mark>Highlighted for reference (a search hit)Yellow background
<code>, <kbd>Code; keyboard inputMonospace
<blockquote>, <q>Long quotation; short inline quotationIndented; with quote marks
<abbr title="...">Abbreviation with expansionDotted underline
<sub>, <sup>, <small>Subscript; superscript; side commentsSmaller text

The rule: strong and em carry meaning (a screen reader changes its voice); b and i are only styling-like hints. If you want bold looks without meaning, use CSS font-weight. Also useful: <hr> (a thematic break between topics), <br> and <pre> (keeps whitespace, used with <code> for code blocks).

Links

The anchor element <a href="..."> is what makes the web a web. The href can be a lot of things.

<!-- Absolute URL: another site -->
<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML">MDN HTML guide</a>

<!-- Relative URL: another file in your site -->
<a href="projects.html">Projects</a>           <!-- same folder -->
<a href="blog/first-post.html">First post</a>  <!-- sub-folder -->
<a href="../index.html">Home</a>               <!-- one folder up -->
<a href="/about">About</a>                    <!-- root-relative: from the site root -->

<!-- In-page anchor: jumps to the element with id="contact" -->
<a href="#contact">Contact me</a>
<h2 id="contact">Contact</h2>

<!-- Other schemes -->
<a href="mailto:asha@example.com?subject=Hello">Email me</a>
<a href="tel:+919876543210">Call +91 98765 43210</a>

<!-- Download a file -->
<a href="files/asha-rao-cv.pdf" download>Download my CV (PDF)</a>

Absolute vs relative: an absolute URL has the scheme and host; a relative one is resolved against the current page's URL. Use relative links inside your own site so it works on localhost, staging and production alike. Be careful with a leading slash: /about starts from the host root, so it breaks when the site is deployed in a sub-path like /myapp/ (for example on GitHub Pages).

Opening in a new tab

<a href="https://github.com/asharao" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">
  My GitHub (opens in a new tab)
</a>

target="_blank" opens a new tab. Modern browsers already treat it as noopener, but writing rel="noopener noreferrer" is still the standard habit and protects older browsers: noopener stops the new page from controlling yours through window.opener (a phishing trick), and noreferrer hides your page's URL from the target. Warn users when a link opens a new tab, and do not do it for ordinary internal links — users can choose that themselves.

Writing good link text

Screen-reader users often list all links on a page without the surrounding text. So the link text must make sense alone: "Download my CV" is good; "click here" and "read more" are bad. Do not use a bare long URL as the text either.

div and span: the last resort

<div> (block) and <span> (inline) have no meaning. They are neutral boxes for grouping elements so CSS or JavaScript can target them. Use them only when no semantic element fits — a wrapper for a layout, a styled word inside text. Overusing div is called "div soup", and is the most common beginner problem (see Semantic HTML).

Wrong: headings for looks, links without meaning

<h4>Welcome</h4>       <!-- chosen for its size -->
<h1>Menu</h1><h1>Cart</h1> <!-- two h1 -->
<a href="/docs">click here</a>

Right: structure first, style with CSS

<h1 class="page-title">Welcome</h1>
<h2>Menu</h2>
<a href="/docs">Read the documentation</a>

Rule: links go somewhere, buttons do something

Use <a href> to navigate to a URL and <button> to perform an action (open a menu, save). An <a> without href is not keyboard-focusable, and a button used as a link cannot be opened in a new tab.

Edge cases

  • A link to an id that does not exist does nothing (no error). Anchors are case-sensitive.
  • mailto: and tel: open the user's mail or phone app, which may not exist on a desktop.
  • The download attribute works only for same-origin URLs.
  • In a SPA with React Router you use a router <Link>, which renders an <a> but prevents a full page load.

Interview angle

  • <strong> vs <b>, <em> vs <i> — meaning versus appearance.
  • "Why rel="noopener noreferrer"?" — stop window.opener access and hide the referrer.
  • "Absolute vs relative URL?" — with or without the origin; relative links stay portable between environments.

Images, figures and lists

An image needs a useful alt text and explicit width and height; lists use ul, ol or dl depending on whether order or name–value pairs matter; figure and figcaption attach a caption to content.

Images

<img src="images/asha.jpg" alt="Asha Rao smiling at her desk" width="400" height="300">

<!-- Below the fold: load only when near the screen -->
<img src="images/project-1.png" alt="Dashboard showing monthly expenses as a bar chart"
     width="800" height="450" loading="lazy">

<!-- Decorative image: empty alt -->
<img src="images/divider.svg" alt="" width="200" height="10">
src
The image URL (relative or absolute). A wrong path shows a broken-image icon and a 404 in the Network panel.
alt
Text replacement: read by screen readers, shown when the image fails to load, and used by search engines. Always present.
width and height
The image's intrinsic size in pixels (numbers only, no px). The browser uses them to reserve space before the image downloads, which prevents the page jumping (layout shift). CSS such as max-width: 100%; height: auto; still makes it responsive.
loading="lazy"
Downloads the image only when it comes near the viewport. Use it for images below the fold, never for the main hero image at the top.
srcset and sizes
Offer several sizes so the browser picks the best for the screen. A brief example is below.
<img src="hero-800.jpg"
     srcset="hero-400.jpg 400w, hero-800.jpg 800w, hero-1600.jpg 1600w"
     sizes="(min-width: 800px) 800px, 100vw"
     alt="Mumbai skyline at sunset" width="800" height="450">

The w numbers are the file widths. sizes says how wide the image will be displayed, and the browser chooses the smallest file that fits the screen's pixel density. A phone on mobile data then downloads 400 pixels, not 1,600.

Writing alt text

  • Describe the purpose, not just the picture: for a photo in an article, say what it shows; for a logo that links home, say "Company name – home".
  • Decorative images (borders, background flourishes) get alt="" so screen readers skip them. Omitting alt entirely is worse, because the reader may read out the file name.
  • Do not start with "image of" or "picture of"; the screen reader already announces it as an image.
  • If the text is in the image (a banner saying "50% off"), repeat that text in the alt.
  • Keep it short, about one sentence. A complex chart needs a nearby text description.

Image formats

FormatBest for
JPEGPhotos
PNGScreenshots, images that need transparency
WebP / AVIFSmaller modern replacements for JPEG and PNG; widely supported
SVGLogos, icons, simple illustrations — vector, sharp at any size, can be styled with CSS

Compress photos before using them; a 4 MB camera photo on a profile page is a classic performance bug. Resize to the largest size you actually display.

figure and figcaption

<figure>
  <img src="images/er-diagram.png" alt="ER diagram of customers, orders and products"
       width="600" height="400">
  <figcaption>Figure 1: Database design of the shop project</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure> wraps self-contained content referenced from the text — an image, a diagram, a code listing — and <figcaption> is its caption. Do not use it for every image; use it when a caption makes sense.

Lists

Lists tell assistive technology "these items belong together" and announce "list, 3 items".

<!-- Unordered: order does not matter -->
<ul>
  <li>Java</li>
  <li>Spring Boot</li>
  <li>PostgreSQL</li>
</ul>

<!-- Ordered: order matters -->
<ol>
  <li>Clone the repository</li>
  <li>Run the build</li>
  <li>Start the app</li>
</ol>

<!-- Description list: terms and their descriptions -->
<dl>
  <dt>Email</dt>
  <dd>asha@example.com</dd>
  <dt>City</dt>
  <dd>Pune</dd>
</dl>
  • <ol> accepts start="5", reversed and type="a" (letters). <li value="10"> sets one item's number.
  • Lists nest: put the inner <ul> inside an <li>, not beside it.
  • Navigation menus are lists of links: <nav><ul><li><a>…</a></li></ul></nav>. CSS then removes the bullets and lays the items out in a row.
  • <dl> fits key–value data such as a profile summary, glossary or product specifications.

Audio, video and embeds (brief)

<video controls src="demo.mp4" width="640"></video> and <audio controls src="song.mp3"></audio> need no plugin. Always provide controls; avoid autoplay with sound. <iframe> embeds another page (YouTube, Google Maps) — give it a title for accessibility, and remember that you are loading a third party's code.

Rule: every img has an alt attribute; informative images have meaningful text

Missing alt is the most common accessibility failure on the web, and Lighthouse reports it. Decorative images use alt="".

Convention: set dimensions and lazy-load below the fold

Always write width and height. Add loading="lazy" to images further down the page, but never to the largest image above the fold, or the page appears to load slower.

Edge cases

  • A relative src works when you open the file from disk, but breaks if the folder structure changes on the server. Check case: Photo.JPG and photo.jpg are different files on Linux servers, though Windows ignores case, so a page that works on your laptop can fail in production.
  • An image inside a link needs alt text that describes the link target, since the image is the link's only text.

Mistake: building a list with line breaks

Typing "- Java<br>- Spring" is not a list; screen readers do not announce it and CSS cannot style the items individually. Use ul and li.

Interview angle

  • "Why set width and height on images?" — to reserve space and avoid layout shift (CLS).
  • "What is alt for and when is it empty?" — screen readers, broken images and SEO; empty for decorative images.
  • "ul vs ol vs dl?" — unordered, ordered, name–value pairs.

Semantic HTML and page layout

Semantic elements such as header, nav, main, article, section, aside and footer say what each part of the page is, which gives screen readers landmarks, search engines context and you maintainable markup — a div says nothing.

A semantic element describes its meaning, not its looks. <nav> means "navigation links"; <div> means nothing. Compare the Java equivalent: naming a class OrderService instead of Class1. The page may look identical, but the meaning is available to tools.

Why semantics matter

  • Accessibility. Browsers build an accessibility tree from your HTML. Screen readers offer shortcuts to jump to landmarks like "main" or "navigation". With only divs, a blind user must read the whole page linearly.
  • SEO. Search engines weigh content in main and headings higher than repeated navigation.
  • Maintainability. <footer> tells the next developer more than <div class="f2">.
  • Built-in behaviour. Native elements bring keyboard support, default styles and features for free (button, details, dialog).
  • Reader mode and browser features find the article content only if it is marked up.

The layout elements

ElementMeaningNotes
<header>Introductory content: logo, title, navA page header, or the header of an article or section
<nav>A block of major navigation linksMain menu, table of contents. Not every group of links. Label several navs with aria-label
<main>The unique main content of the pageOnly one visible per page; not inside header, nav, footer
<section>A themed group of content, normally with a headingIf it has no heading, it is probably a div
<article>Self-contained piece that makes sense aloneBlog post, news story, product card, comment
<aside>Side content related to the main contentSidebar, pull quote, ads, related links
<footer>Closing content: copyright, contact, linksPage or section footer
<address>Contact information for the nearest article or the pageNot for any postal address, only the contact of the author or owner
<time datetime="...">A date or time in machine-readable form<time datetime="2026-10-18">18 Oct 2026</time>
<figure>, <details>, <dialog>Captioned content; disclosure widget; modal or non-modal dialogBuilt-in interactive widgets, no JavaScript needed for details

section vs article vs div

articlesectiondiv
TestCould it be published on its own (syndicated)?Is it a themed chapter that has a heading?Is it only a wrapper for styling or scripting?
ExampleOne blog post, one product card"Projects", "Skills" in a profileA wrapper for a CSS grid
Has a meaningYesYes (with heading)No

When in doubt, ask: "does this have a heading, and is it part of the page outline?" If yes, section. "Could I move it to another site and it still makes sense?" article. Otherwise div. Using div is fine; it is overusing it that hurts.

A full semantic page skeleton

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Asha Rao - Java Full-Stack Developer</title>
</head>
<body>
  <a class="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>

  <header>
    <p class="logo">Asha Rao</p>
    <nav aria-label="Main">
      <ul>
        <li><a href="#about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="#projects">Projects</a></li>
        <li><a href="#contact">Contact</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <main id="main">
    <h1>Asha Rao - Java Full-Stack Developer</h1>

    <section id="about">
      <h2>About me</h2>
      <p>I build REST APIs with Spring Boot and interfaces with React.</p>
    </section>

    <section id="projects">
      <h2>Projects</h2>
      <article>
        <h3>Expense Tracker API</h3>
        <p>Posted <time datetime="2026-08-02">2 August 2026</time></p>
        <p>A Spring Boot and PostgreSQL service for personal budgets.</p>
      </article>
    </section>

    <aside>
      <h2>Currently learning</h2>
      <p>React and Docker.</p>
    </aside>
  </main>

  <footer id="contact">
    <address>
      <a href="mailto:asha@example.com">asha@example.com</a>
    </address>
    <p>&copy; 2026 Asha Rao</p>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

A div version of the same page would look the same after styling, but the screen reader would report no landmarks at all. With the semantic version, header becomes the "banner" landmark, nav "navigation", main "main", aside "complementary" and footer "contentinfo" (header and footer map to these only when they are direct children of the body).

Rule: one main, one h1, landmarks not nested wrongly

A page has exactly one visible <main>, and it is not inside header, footer, nav, aside or article. Give each nav a label if there is more than one.

Convention: choose the element first, add classes second

Write <nav class="site-nav">, not <div class="nav">. Semantic element for meaning, class for styling hooks. Add a "skip to main content" link as the first focusable element so keyboard users can bypass the menu.

Exceptions

  • Semantic tags carry almost no default styling (section, nav and main are just blocks), so the visual result is unchanged. The benefit is for tools.
  • Do not wrap everything in a section. A group made only for layout is a div.
  • <header> inside an <article> is the article's header, and is not a page-level banner landmark.

In real projects

React components should return semantic markup too: a <Navbar> renders a <nav>, a <ProductCard> renders an <article>. A component library that renders only divs makes your whole app inaccessible — check what it outputs in Elements.

Interview angle: "What is semantic HTML and why use it?"

  • Elements named by meaning; benefits: accessibility landmarks, SEO, readable code, native behaviour.
  • List header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer and explain section vs article vs div.
  • Say "only one main per page".

Forms: form, labels, inputs and buttons

A form collects user input and sends it as name=value pairs to a server; every control needs a name (so it is sent), a label (so people know what it is) and the right type (so the browser helps).

Forms are how users log in, register, search and check out, so they are the most important HTML you will write. The browser's built-in form support does a lot: keyboards, mobile keyboards, autofill, validation hints and submission. Your Spring Boot controller is the other half of the story: it receives what the form sends.

The form element

<form action="/register" method="post">
  <label for="fullName">Full name</label>
  <input type="text" id="fullName" name="fullName" autocomplete="name" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>
  • action: the URL that receives the data. Left out, the form posts to the current page.
  • method: get (the default) puts the data in the query string — right for searches and filters, so the URL can be shared. post sends it in the request body — right for anything that changes data or is private. (The HTML method attribute accepts only get and post; there is no HTML form that sends PUT or DELETE. Spring's hidden _method filter and JavaScript fetch() cover those.)
  • enctype: how the body is encoded. Default application/x-www-form-urlencoded; use multipart/form-data when the form has a file input.

When the user clicks submit, the browser collects every named control and sends name=value pairs. The form above produces this request:

POST /register HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

fullName=Asha+Rao&email=asha%40example.com

Spring MVC binds these to a controller method:

@Controller
public class RegisterController {

    // fullName and email come from the form's name attributes
    @PostMapping("/register")
    public String register(@RequestParam String fullName,
                           @RequestParam String email) {
        // validate again on the server, then save
        return "redirect:/welcome";
    }
}

The name attribute is what is sent

The name attribute becomes the key. A control without name is not submitted at all. id is a different thing: it links a label to a control and gives CSS and JavaScript a handle. Normally you set both, with the same text. In a React app that sends JSON, the names are less important but the field-to-DTO mapping logic is the same.

Labels

Every control needs a visible <label>. Connect it in one of two ways:

<!-- 1. for + id (the usual way) -->
<label for="city">City</label>
<input id="city" name="city" type="text">

<!-- 2. wrap the control -->
<label>
  City
  <input name="city" type="text">
</label>

A connected label gives the control its accessible name, so a screen reader says "City, edit text". It also makes the label clickable: clicking the text focuses the input, or ticks a checkbox — a big help for small touch targets. In React the attribute is written htmlFor, because for is a reserved word in JavaScript.

Mistake: placeholder as a label

placeholder is a hint inside the empty field (placeholder="e.g. 9876543210"). It disappears as soon as you type, often has low contrast, and is not a reliable accessible name. Always add a real label; use the placeholder only for an example format.

Input types

The type attribute picks the control. The right type brings a suitable mobile keyboard, built-in validation and sometimes a native picker, at zero cost.

TypeUse forNotes
textNames, titles, any short textThe default if type is missing or unknown
emailEmail addressEmail keyboard on phones; checks for an @ format
passwordSecretsMasks the characters; add autocomplete="current-password" or "new-password"
numberQuantities, agesSpinner arrows, min/max/step. Not for phone numbers, PIN codes or card numbers
telPhone numbersNumeric keypad; no format check — add pattern if you need one
urlWeb addressNeeds a scheme such as https://
searchSearch boxesMay show a clear (x) button
date, time, datetime-local, monthDates and timesNative date picker; value format is 2026-10-18 (ISO), whatever the display
checkboxYes/no, or pick manySent only when ticked, with the value (default on)
radioPick one of a fewRadios with the same name form a group
fileUploadNeeds method="post" and enctype="multipart/form-data"; accept=".pdf,image/*", multiple
hiddenData the user does not seeAnyone can edit it in DevTools — never trust it
range, colorSlider; colour pickerRarely needed
submit, reset, buttonButtons made with inputPrefer the <button> element

Other controls

<label for="role">Role</label>
<select id="role" name="role" required>
  <option value="">Choose one</option>
  <option value="dev">Developer</option>
  <option value="qa">Tester</option>
  <option value="ops" selected>DevOps</option>
</select>

<label for="bio">About you</label>
<textarea id="bio" name="bio" rows="4" cols="40" maxlength="500"></textarea>

<label>
  <input type="checkbox" name="newsletter" value="yes">
  Send me the newsletter
</label>

<fieldset>
  <legend>Preferred contact method</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="contact" value="email" checked> Email</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="contact" value="phone"> Phone</label>
</fieldset>
  • <select> sends the chosen option's value, not its visible text. If an option has no value, the text is sent. Use multiple for multi-select, <optgroup label> to group options.
  • <textarea> holds multi-line text. The initial text goes between the tags (it has no value attribute). Resize it with CSS.
  • Radio buttons share a name: that is what makes them mutually exclusive. Each radio needs a different value. Wrap related radios or checkboxes in <fieldset> with a <legend> naming the question; screen readers then announce "Preferred contact method, Email, radio button".
  • <datalist> gives suggestions to a text input: <input list="cities"><datalist id="cities"><option value="Pune">…</datalist>.
  • <output>, <progress> and <meter> display results and values.

Buttons

ButtonWhat it does
<button type="submit">Submits the form. This is the default type for a button inside a form.
<button type="button">Does nothing by itself; for JavaScript-driven actions
<button type="reset">Resets fields to their initial values (rarely wanted)

The classic bug: a button that submits the form by accident

A button inside a form without a type is a submit button. So a "Show password", "Add another phone number" or "Cancel" button reloads the page or posts incomplete data. Write type="button" on every button that is not meant to submit.

<!-- Wrong: submits the form when clicked -->
<button onclick="togglePassword()">Show</button>

<!-- Right -->
<button type="button" onclick="togglePassword()">Show</button>

Use <button> rather than <input type="submit">: a button can contain text, icons and markup, and it is easier to style. A disabled button (disabled) cannot be focused or clicked, and its value is not submitted. To tell the server which button was pressed, give it a name and value.

Useful attributes on controls

autocomplete
Helps the browser autofill: name, email, tel, street-address, postal-code, username, current-password, new-password, one-time-code. Autofill saves users time and works better with correct values; do not set autocomplete="off" on login fields.
autofocus
Focuses a field on load. Use rarely; it can disorient screen-reader users.
readonly vs disabled
readonly can be focused and is submitted but cannot be edited; disabled cannot be focused and is not submitted.
inputmode
Chooses the mobile keyboard: inputmode="numeric" gives digits without the number-input quirks (good for OTP and PIN codes).
form
Associates a control placed outside the <form> with it, by form id.

A realistic form: login-style signup

<form action="/api/signup" method="post" novalidate>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Create your account</legend>

    <p>
      <label for="su-email">Email</label>
      <input id="su-email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email"
             required aria-describedby="su-email-hint">
      <small id="su-email-hint">We never share your email.</small>
    </p>

    <p>
      <label for="su-pw">Password (at least 8 characters)</label>
      <input id="su-pw" name="password" type="password" minlength="8"
             autocomplete="new-password" required>
    </p>

    <p>
      <label>
        <input type="checkbox" name="terms" required>
        I accept the terms and conditions
      </label>
    </p>

    <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
  </fieldset>
</form>

aria-describedby links the hint text to the field, so a screen reader reads the hint after the label. (novalidate here switches off the browser's built-in checks so that your own JavaScript can show custom messages; leave it out if you want the defaults — see Form validation.)

Rules

  • Every control has a visible label connected with for/id or by wrapping.
  • Every control you want sent has a name.
  • Radio buttons in a group share a name; group them with fieldset and legend.
  • Any button inside a form that is not meant to submit has type="button".
  • A file upload form needs method="post" and enctype="multipart/form-data".

Conventions

  • One field per row and labels above fields (easier on mobile); mark required fields clearly in the label text, not by colour alone.
  • Choose input types for the data: email, tel, date; set autocomplete values.
  • Use method="get" for search forms, post for everything else; never put passwords in a GET query string.

Edge cases

  • An unticked checkbox is absent from the request, not sent as false. Spring binds a missing boolean parameter to false only if you declare @RequestParam(defaultValue = "false"); otherwise a missing required parameter gives MissingServletRequestParameterException (400).
  • Number inputs return strings. An empty number field is sent as an empty string, which binding turns into a conversion error for int (MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException), so use Integer with required = false when a field is optional.
  • Pressing Enter in a text field submits the form via its first submit button. A form with no submit button but one text field also submits.
  • Nested forms are not allowed.

In real projects

In React you rarely use the browser's default submit. You keep the field values in state, call event.preventDefault(), and send JSON with fetch() (Module 5 and Module 6). All the HTML rules above still apply — labels, types, autocomplete, button types — because React renders the same elements.

Interview angle

  • "GET vs POST in a form?" — query string vs body; GET for idempotent searches, POST for changes and secrets.
  • "Why does a button inside a form submit it?" — default type is submit.
  • "Which attribute decides the key sent to the server?" — name, not id.
  • "How do you group radio buttons?" — same name, fieldset/legend for accessibility.

Form validation: attributes, the constraint API and the server

HTML validation attributes (required, min, max, minlength, maxlength, pattern, type) give instant feedback in the browser, but they are only for user experience — the server must validate every request again.

Validation checks whether input is acceptable before it is processed. Browsers can do much of it declaratively, with no JavaScript. When the user submits, the browser checks every control; if one fails, it blocks the submission, focuses the first invalid field and shows a message.

Validation attributes

AttributeWorks onMeaning
requiredMost controlsMust not be empty (checkbox: must be ticked; radio group: one must be chosen)
type="email", "url"inputValue must look like an email or URL
minlength, maxlengthText, textarea, passwordLength limits. maxlength also stops typing at the limit
min, maxnumber, range, date, timeValue limits: min="18" max="60", min="2026-01-01"
stepnumber, range, dateAllowed increments; step="0.01" for money, step="any" for no restriction
patterntext, tel, email, url, password, searchA regular expression the whole value must match
multipleemail, fileSeveral values allowed (comma-separated emails)
 
<label for="mobile">Mobile number</label>
<input id="mobile" name="mobile" type="tel" inputmode="numeric"
       pattern="[6-9][0-9]{9}" maxlength="10" required
       title="10 digits, starting with 6, 7, 8 or 9">

<label for="age">Age</label>
<input id="age" name="age" type="number" min="18" max="60" required>

<label for="pin">PIN code</label>
<input id="pin" name="pin" type="text" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]{6}"
       required>

The pattern is anchored automatically (as if wrapped in ^(?:…)$), unlike Java's find(); it is similar to String.matches(). The title attribute text is appended to the browser's error message to explain the format. Keep patterns simple: strict email or phone regexes reject real people.

CSS hooks: :valid, :invalid and :user-invalid

input:user-invalid {
  border-color: #b00020;     /* only after the user has interacted */
}
input:user-valid {
  border-color: #1b7f3b;
}

:invalid matches an empty required field the moment the page loads, so the form looks full of errors before the user types anything. :user-invalid and :user-valid apply only after interaction, and are supported in current browsers; for older ones, add the :focus or a class from JavaScript. Never signal an error by colour alone — add text.

The constraint validation API (brief)

JavaScript can read and customise the browser's validation. Every control has validity (an object of flags), validationMessage, checkValidity() and setCustomValidity().

const form = document.querySelector("#signup");
const email = document.querySelector("#su-email");

email.addEventListener("input", () => {
  if (email.validity.typeMismatch) {
    email.setCustomValidity("Please enter a valid email, like asha@example.com");
  } else {
    email.setCustomValidity("");   // empty string = valid again
  }
});

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  if (!form.checkValidity()) {
    event.preventDefault();        // stop the submit
    form.reportValidity();         // show the browser's error bubbles
  }
});

Useful validity flags: valueMissing (required), typeMismatch (email/url), patternMismatch, tooShort, tooLong, rangeUnderflow, rangeOverflow, stepMismatch and valid. A form with novalidate skips the automatic check but you can still call these functions. Forgetting to clear a custom message with setCustomValidity("") leaves the field permanently invalid — a very common bug.

Client-side validation is not security

Everything in the browser can be bypassed. A user can delete the required attribute in DevTools, disable JavaScript, or skip the browser entirely and send the request with curl or Postman. So:

  • Client-side validation exists for user experience: quick, friendly feedback without a network round trip.
  • Server-side validation exists for correctness and security: it is the only validation you can trust. The server must re-check everything — required fields, lengths, formats, ranges, business rules (is this email already registered? is the stock available?) — and never assume the browser did it.

In Spring Boot you do this with Bean Validation annotations and @Valid (covered in Spring Boot · Module 2). Keep the same rules on both sides so the user does not get surprised.

import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;

public record SignupRequest(
        @NotBlank @Email String email,
        @NotBlank @Size(min = 8, max = 72) String password,
        @AssertTrue(message = "You must accept the terms") boolean terms) {
}

// In the controller:  public ResponseEntity<?> signup(@Valid @RequestBody SignupRequest req)
// A failed rule returns 400 Bad Request with details of the field errors.

Also show the server's errors on the page. When the API returns 400 with field errors, your front-end code should display each message next to the matching field (Module 6).

Showing helpful errors

  • Say what is wrong and how to fix it: "Password must be at least 8 characters", not "Invalid input".
  • Put the message next to the field and connect it with aria-describedby; set aria-invalid="true" on the bad field.
  • Do not clear what the user typed. Do not validate on every keystroke before the user finishes; validate on blur or submit.

Rule: the server is the only validator you can trust

Treat all input as hostile: validate type, length, range and format on the server, encode output, and use parameterised queries. HTML attributes are conveniences.

Edge cases

  • type="number" accepts e (as in 1e5) and allows a minus sign; minlength/pattern do not apply to it. For a PIN, use text with inputmode="numeric" and pattern.
  • minlength and required are checked only when the user edits the value — a pre-filled value shorter than minlength passes until edited.
  • disabled controls are never validated; readonly ones are skipped for the "required" check too.
  • The look and wording of the browser's error bubble differs between browsers and cannot be fully styled; custom designs use novalidate with JavaScript.

Mistake: "the form already checks it, so the API does not need to"

This is how invalid or malicious data reaches the database. Add @Valid and constraints on every request body and parameter, even for forms that look strict.

Interview angle

  • "Client-side vs server-side validation?" — UX versus security; do both; server is mandatory.
  • "Name HTML5 validation attributes." — required, min, max, minlength, maxlength, pattern, type.
  • "How can the client-side check be bypassed?" — DevTools, curl/Postman, disabled JavaScript.

Tables for tabular data

Use table, thead, tbody, tfoot, caption and th with scope for data that has rows and columns — never for page layout.

A table presents data that has a natural grid: an invoice, a marks sheet, a train timetable, an employee list. If you would put it in a spreadsheet, it is a table. If you only want things side by side, it is not — use CSS Flexbox or Grid.

Structure

<table>
  <caption>Employees by department, October 2026</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Name</th>
      <th scope="col">Department</th>
      <th scope="col">Salary (₹)</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Asha Rao</th>
      <td>Engineering</td>
      <td>1,200,000</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Ravi Kumar</th>
      <td>Finance</td>
      <td>950,000</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
  <tfoot>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row" colspan="2">Total</th>
      <td>2,150,000</td>
    </tr>
  </tfoot>
</table>
ElementJob
<table>The whole table
<caption>The table's title; first child; announced by screen readers
<thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>Header rows, body rows, summary rows. They let you style sections and keep headers when printing
<tr>A row
<th>A header cell (bold and centred by default)
<td>A data cell

The browser adds a <tbody> automatically if you leave it out. In your Java code you often generate such tables from a list: Thymeleaf's th:each, or in React orders.map(o => <tr key={o.id}>…</tr>).

Accessibility: th and scope

A screen reader announces a cell together with its headers ("Salary, 1,200,000"), and it needs to know which headers apply. Use <th> for every header cell and add scope="col" (this header applies to the column below) or scope="row" (applies to the row). For complex tables with several header levels, headers and id link cells to headers explicitly. Always give the table a <caption> that says what it shows.

Merging cells: colspan and rowspan

<tr>
  <th colspan="2">Name (first and last)</th>   <!-- spans 2 columns -->
  <th rowspan="2">Marks</th>                  <!-- spans 2 rows -->
</tr>

colspan="n" stretches a cell across n columns; rowspan="n" across n rows. Cells that are covered must not be written again, or the grid shifts. Merged cells make tables harder for assistive technology, so use them only when they truly help.

Styling and responsive tables

Browsers draw tables with small gaps and no lines. CSS adds the polish:

table {
  border-collapse: collapse;       /* one line between cells, not double */
  width: 100%;
}
th, td {
  padding: 0.6rem 0.8rem;
  border-bottom: 1px solid #ddd;
  text-align: left;
}
td.number { text-align: right; }   /* align numbers to the right */
tbody tr:nth-child(even) { background: #f6f6f6; }   /* zebra stripes */

.table-scroll { overflow-x: auto; }  /* wrapper: scroll sideways on a phone */

Wide tables overflow small screens. The usual fix is a wrapper element with overflow-x: auto (as in the book you are reading right now, where tables become cards on phones). Do not shrink the font to unreadable sizes.

Rule: tables are for data, never for layout

Layout tables (a 1990s trick) break on small screens, confuse screen readers and mix structure with presentation. Use Flexbox or Grid (Flexbox, Grid).

Conventions

  • Always: caption, thead with th scope="col", tbody.
  • Right-align numbers (and use consistent decimals); left-align text.
  • Keep tables simple: a long table with sorting, paging and filtering is built with JavaScript (or a library) on top of this markup.

Edge cases

  • Text directly inside a <table> or <tr> is moved out by the browser (to above the table). Only tr, th, td and the section elements belong there. In React, whitespace or a stray string inside <tbody> gives a "validateDOMNesting" warning.
  • A row with fewer cells than the others does not fail; it leaves a blank area.
  • An empty list should show a message row such as "No orders yet", with <td colspan="3">, not an empty table.

Mistake: using td for headers, or tables to place a form and a picture side by side

A bold <td> is not a header; use <th> so assistive tools can relate the cells. Side-by-side layout belongs to CSS.

Interview angle

  • "When should you use a table?" — only for tabular data; layout with CSS.
  • "What do th scope, caption, colspan do?" — accessibility association, the title, and merging columns.

Accessibility basics

Accessibility means everyone can use your page — with a keyboard, a screen reader, low vision or a slow hand — and most of it comes free if you use the right native elements, alt text, labels, visible focus and enough colour contrast.

Accessibility (often written a11y, "a", 11 letters, "y") is designing so that people with disabilities can use your site. That includes blind users with screen readers, people with low vision or colour blindness, people who cannot use a mouse, deaf users, and people with temporary limits (a broken arm, bright sunlight). It also helps everyone: keyboard shortcuts, captions in a noisy bus, large tap targets. In India alone, millions rely on assistive technology, and in many countries (and for many government and enterprise clients) accessibility is a legal or contractual requirement, usually measured against WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. Interviewers increasingly ask about it.

How assistive technology reads your page

The browser turns the DOM into an accessibility tree: each node has a role (button, link, heading, checkbox), a name (its text or label), a state (checked, expanded, disabled) and a value. A screen reader reads this tree aloud. You can see it in DevTools: Elements → Accessibility pane. Native HTML elements fill in role, name, state and keyboard behaviour automatically; divs give nothing.

1. Use the right element — the foundation

Wrong: a clickable div

<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

Right: a real button

<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

The div version cannot be reached with Tab, does not react to Enter or Space, and is announced as plain text. To fix it you would need role="button", tabindex="0" and key handlers — everything a <button> already does. The same goes for links (<a href>), checkboxes, <select> and <details>.

2. Text alternatives

Images need meaningful alt (decorative: alt=""); icon-only buttons need a name; videos need captions; links need descriptive text (see Images). An icon button:

<button type="button" aria-label="Close dialog">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16">…</svg>
</button>

3. Labels and instructions

Every form control has a connected label (Forms). Errors are text, placed next to the field and linked with aria-describedby. Do not rely on placeholder text, colour or position alone.

4. Keyboard access and focus order

Many users never touch a mouse. Everything you can do with a pointer must work with the keyboard:

  • Tab moves to the next focusable element, Shift+Tab back, Enter activates links and buttons, Space activates buttons and ticks checkboxes, arrow keys move between radio buttons and inside menus, Esc closes dialogs.
  • Focus order follows the DOM order. So write the HTML in a logical reading order, and do not use CSS (order, positioning) to reorder things visually in a way that makes the Tab sequence jump around.
  • Avoid positive tabindex values (tabindex="3"); they create a confusing custom order. Use tabindex="0" (join the natural order) or tabindex="-1" (focusable by script only, e.g. to move focus to a dialog heading) when you must.
  • Add a skip link ("Skip to main content") as the first focusable element, so keyboard users do not have to tab through the whole menu on every page.
  • Visible focus. The outline that shows where you are must stay. Never write outline: none without a replacement. Use :focus-visible, which shows the ring for keyboard users but not for mouse clicks:
:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #1a56db;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  left: -999px;               /* off screen until focused */
}
.skip-link:focus {
  left: 1rem;
  top: 1rem;
  background: white;
  padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
}

5. Landmarks and headings

Use header, nav, main, aside and footer (Semantic HTML) and a logical heading hierarchy. Screen-reader users navigate by them, much as sighted users scan visually.

6. Colour and contrast

  • WCAG AA asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (about 24px, or 19px bold) and for UI parts such as input borders and icons.
  • Light grey text on white is the most common failure. Check colours with the DevTools colour picker (it shows the ratio) or Lighthouse.
  • Do not convey meaning with colour alone — a red border should come with an error message and perhaps an icon. About 1 in 12 men has some colour-vision deficiency.
  • Support zoom and text resize: use relative units (rem) so text enlarges to 200% without breaking the layout, and do not disable pinch zoom.
  • Respect prefers-reduced-motion for animations (Transitions and animations). Touch targets should be at least about 44 by 44 pixels.

7. ARIA — the last resort

ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes (role, aria-*) that add semantics when HTML has none. The first rule of ARIA: do not use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute can do the job. Wrong ARIA is worse than none, because it makes false promises to the screen reader. A few safe, common attributes:

AttributeUse
aria-label="Search"Gives a name when there is no visible text (icon buttons, a second nav)
aria-labelledby="id"Names an element from other visible text, e.g. a dialog from its heading
aria-describedby="id"Adds extra description such as a hint or error message
aria-hidden="true"Hides decorative content from assistive technology. Never on focusable elements
aria-expanded="true|false"State of a toggle button that shows or hides something
aria-live="polite"Announces changes inside a region, e.g. "3 items in cart" or a form error
aria-current="page"Marks the current link in a navigation
role="alert"An important, time-sensitive message announced at once

ARIA changes only what is announced. It adds no keyboard behaviour: a div role="button" still needs tabindex="0" and key handlers. This is why native elements win.

<button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="menu">Menu</button>
<ul id="menu" hidden>
  <li><a href="/profile">Profile</a></li>
</ul>

Your script flips aria-expanded and removes hidden together, keeping the visual state and the announced state in sync.

Testing

  1. Unplug the mouse. Tab through the whole page: can you reach everything, in a sensible order, always seeing where you are? Can you open and close menus and dialogs?
  2. Zoom to 200% and check the layout and reading order.
  3. Run Lighthouse (Accessibility category) and fix every item. Also try the browser extension axe DevTools.
  4. Inspect the Accessibility pane in DevTools to verify role and name.
  5. Listen once. Turn on a screen reader (NVDA is free on Windows; VoiceOver is built into macOS and iOS; TalkBack on Android) and navigate your own page for five minutes. It will teach you more than any checklist.

Automated tools find only about a third of real problems, such as missing alt text or low contrast. They cannot tell if your alt text is meaningful. Manual testing is part of the job.

Rules

  • Everything that can be clicked can also be reached and operated with the keyboard.
  • Focus is always visible; never remove the outline without a better one.
  • Text contrast is at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text).
  • First rule of ARIA: use a native element first.

Edge cases

  • display: none and visibility: hidden hide content from screen readers too; to hide something visually but keep it for them, use a "visually hidden" utility class (clip the box to 1px). aria-hidden does the opposite: visible but not announced.
  • Placeholder-only inputs, auto-playing carousels and time-limited pop-ups all fail users; give a way to pause or extend.
  • In a SPA the page does not reload on navigation, so screen readers do not announce the new page. Move focus to the new page's heading and update the document title.

Mistakes

  • outline: none with no replacement.
  • A div or span with a click handler instead of a button or link.
  • "Click here" links, missing alt text, heading levels chosen for size.
  • Putting aria-label on everything; it overrides visible text and can contradict it.

Interview angle: "How do you make a site accessible?"

  • Semantic HTML first; alt text; labels for forms; keyboard operable with visible focus; sufficient contrast; ARIA only when needed.
  • Mention testing: keyboard-only, Lighthouse or axe, a screen reader, zoom.
  • Quote WCAG AA contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text.

Meta tags and SEO basics

Meta tags in the head describe your page to browsers, search engines and social sites — title, description, Open Graph for link previews, favicon, robots and canonical — and good SEO is mostly semantic HTML, useful content and fast pages.

SEO (search engine optimisation) is making pages easy for search engines to find, understand and rank. Meta tags are the head-level part of it. They also control how your link looks when someone pastes it into WhatsApp, LinkedIn or Slack.

The essential tags

<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

  <title>Asha Rao - Java Full-Stack Developer in Pune</title>
  <meta name="description"
        content="Portfolio of Asha Rao: Spring Boot, React and PostgreSQL projects.">

  <link rel="canonical" href="https://asharao.dev/">
  <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="32x32">
  <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
  <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
  <meta name="theme-color" content="#1a56db">

  <!-- Open Graph: link previews -->
  <meta property="og:type" content="website">
  <meta property="og:title" content="Asha Rao - Java Full-Stack Developer">
  <meta property="og:description" content="Spring Boot, React and PostgreSQL projects.">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://asharao.dev/images/og-card.png">
  <meta property="og:url" content="https://asharao.dev/">

  <!-- X (Twitter) card -->
  <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
</head>
<title>
The blue headline in search results and the browser tab. Make it unique per page, descriptive, with the main keywords first, about 50–60 characters (longer titles get cut).
meta name="description"
The grey summary under the title in search results. Search engines may rewrite it, and it is not a ranking factor by itself, but a clear 120–160 character summary gets more clicks. Unique per page.
Open Graph (og:*)
A protocol created by Facebook and used by WhatsApp, LinkedIn, Slack, Telegram and others to build link preview cards. Without it they guess, often badly. og:image should be an absolute URL, around 1200 × 630 pixels. The twitter:card tag controls the card on X; other twitter:* tags fall back to Open Graph.
Favicon
The small icon in the tab and bookmarks. Browsers also request /favicon.ico automatically, and a 404 here shows in your server log — add one.
link rel="canonical"
Tells search engines the preferred URL when the same content is reachable at several (with and without www, with tracking parameters), so ranking is not split.
meta name="robots"
content="noindex" asks search engines not to list the page (use on admin, thank-you and login pages); nofollow asks them not to follow its links. Default is index and follow. A separate robots.txt file at the site root tells crawlers which paths not to fetch — it is public and is not security.
meta name="theme-color"
Colours the browser toolbar on mobile.

SEO basics that matter more than tags

  • Useful content that answers what people search for. No amount of markup rescues empty pages.
  • Semantic HTML: a single descriptive h1, logical h2/h3, main, lists, alt text (images also appear in image search). Meaningful link text rather than "click here".
  • Clean URLs: /blog/spring-boot-jwt, not /post?id=8372; lowercase, hyphens, stable (use 301 redirects when you must change one).
  • Speed and mobile friendliness: Google ranks on mobile experience and Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS). Compress images, use loading="lazy", set image sizes, defer scripts.
  • HTTPS everywhere.
  • A sitemap.xml listing your pages helps crawlers discover them.
  • Structured data (JSON-LD, schema.org) can add rich results like star ratings; mention it if asked, and learn it when you need it.

The SPA caveat

A plain React + Vite app sends an almost empty HTML file, and fills in content with JavaScript. Google can execute JavaScript but does it later and less reliably; many other crawlers and every link-preview bot (WhatsApp, LinkedIn) read only the raw HTML. In a SPA, the <title>, description and Open Graph tags in index.html are the same for every route, so every shared link looks identical. Options:

  • For logged-in apps, ignore SEO — crawlers cannot log in anyway.
  • Update the title per route with JavaScript (React Helmet or React 19's built-in support for rendering <title> and <meta> inside components) — helps tabs and Google, not link-preview bots.
  • For public content, use server-side rendering or static generation (Next.js, or Thymeleaf pages from Spring Boot), or a pre-rendering service. See CSR vs SSR.

Check your tags

View the page source (Ctrl+U) to see what a crawler sees without JavaScript. Run Lighthouse's SEO category. Platforms such as the LinkedIn Post Inspector and Facebook Sharing Debugger show your link preview; they cache results, so re-scrape after changes.

Rule: every page has a unique title and description

Identical titles across a site ("My App") hurt both users with many tabs open and search engines. Generate them from the page data.

Convention: put the page name before the site name

"Order 1042 - My Shop" is better than "My Shop - Order 1042", since the tab and the result snippet show the start first.

Edge cases

  • robots.txt blocks crawling, not indexing: a blocked URL can still appear in results if others link to it. To keep a page out, allow crawling and use noindex.
  • Never put private data in robots.txt or meta tags — they are public. Protect secrets with authentication.
  • Relative og:image URLs often fail; use absolute https URLs.
  • The keywords meta tag is ignored by Google; do not bother.

Interview angle

  • "What meta tags do you add?" — charset, viewport, title, description, Open Graph, canonical, robots as needed, favicon.
  • "SEO problem with a React SPA?" — empty initial HTML; fix with SSR/SSG or pre-rendering for public pages.

Validating HTML and the most common mistakes

Browsers silently repair broken HTML, so you must check it yourself with the W3C validator and an editor linter — most problems are unclosed tags, bad nesting, duplicate ids, missing alt and labels, and div soup.

Why validate

A Java compiler refuses to compile broken code; a browser never refuses broken HTML. It guesses what you meant, and different browsers can guess differently. A missing end tag may only show up as a strange layout far from the real mistake. Validation is the "compiler error" step for HTML.

Tools

  • W3C Markup Validation Service (validator.w3.org): paste your HTML, upload a file or give a URL. It lists errors and warnings with line numbers. Warnings about a missing lang or an empty heading matter; for the fragment you paste, ignore "missing doctype" if you only pasted a part.
  • Editor feedback. VS Code highlights some problems; the extension "HTMLHint" or ESLint with HTML plugins add rules. Prettier formats your markup and makes nesting mistakes visible through indentation.
  • DevTools Elements panel. Compare it with your source: if the tree is not what you wrote, the parser repaired something.
  • Lighthouse for accessibility and SEO issues, and the axe extension for accessibility rules.

A checklist of the most common mistakes

MistakeWhy it hurtsFix
Missing <!doctype html>Quirks mode, strange CSSFirst line of every page
No lang, charset, viewport or titleGarbled text, broken mobile layout, poor accessibilityUse the boilerplate
Unclosed or badly nested tagsLayout breaks elsewhereIndent, use the validator
Block element inside <p> or <a> inside <a>The parser splits your structureCheck the content model
Duplicate idWrong element selected; label points to the wrong inputUnique ids; use classes for repeats
Skipped or multiple headings (h1 to h4)Broken outlineOne h1, no skipped levels
Missing alt; "click here" linksInaccessible, poor SEOMeaningful alt and link text
Inputs without labels; placeholder as labelUnusable for screen readersConnect a label
Button without type inside a formAccidental submittype="button"
div/span with onclickNo keyboard, no rolebutton or a
Div soup, no landmarksNo structure for toolsSemantic elements
Tables for layout; <br>/&nbsp; for spacingFragile, inaccessibleCSS
Inline styles and presentational tags (<center>, <font>)Hard to maintain; obsoleteCSS classes
Unescaped < or & in textText swallowed as a tagUse &lt; and &amp;
Wrong file case or path (Img/Logo.PNG)Works on Windows, 404 on LinuxLowercase file names, check the Network tab

An example, found and fixed

Wrong: five problems

<div class="title">My Skills</div>
<p>
  <div id="list">Java, SQL</div>
</p>
<img src="me.jpg">
<a href="cv.pdf">click here</a>
<div id="list">React</div>

Right: meaning, structure, accessibility

<section>
  <h2>My skills</h2>
  <ul>
    <li>Java</li>
    <li>SQL</li>
    <li>React</li>
  </ul>
</section>
<img src="me.jpg" alt="Asha Rao" width="200" height="200">
<a href="cv.pdf">Download my CV (PDF)</a>

The problems fixed: a visual "title" div instead of a heading; a block div inside a p; a duplicate id; a missing alt and image size; a "click here" link.

A good habit for the daily workflow

  1. Write semantic markup first, without any CSS.
  2. Open the page and read it as plain text. Does it make sense in order? That is what a screen reader and a crawler see.
  3. Run the validator and Lighthouse.
  4. Only then add CSS and JavaScript.

Tip: turn CSS off to test your structure

In DevTools, or with an extension, disable all styles. A well-built page is still readable and in the right order — headings, lists, links and forms all make sense. A page that collapses into chaos was built on divs.

Edge case: React and JSX

React uses JSX, which looks like HTML but is stricter and differs: className instead of class, htmlFor instead of for, every tag must be closed (<img />, <br />), and attributes are camelCase (tabIndex, maxLength). All the HTML rules in this module still apply to what JSX produces. See Module 5.

Interview angle

  • "Does a browser show errors for invalid HTML?" — no, it repairs it silently; use the validator.
  • "What are common HTML mistakes?" — pick four from the table: nesting, missing alt/labels, duplicate ids, div soup, button without type.

Interview questions — HTML

What does <!doctype html> do, and what is quirks mode?

It tells the browser to render the page in standards mode following the HTML5 rules. Without it, the browser enters quirks mode, which imitates old browser behaviour (for example different box sizing and table inheritance) and breaks modern CSS layouts. It must be the first line.

Why do we need the viewport meta tag?

Mobile browsers pretend to be about 980px wide so old desktop sites fit, then scale down. width=device-width, initial-scale=1 makes the layout viewport equal to the real device width, so media queries and responsive CSS work. Without it, your mobile layout shows as a shrunken desktop page.

What is semantic HTML? Why does it matter?

Using elements that describe meaning (header, nav, main, article, section, footer, button) instead of generic divs. It gives screen readers landmarks, helps search engines understand content, brings built-in behaviour such as keyboard support, and makes code easier to read.

section vs article vs div?

article is self-contained content that could stand alone (a blog post, a product card). section is a themed group of content with a heading. div has no meaning and is only a wrapper for styling or scripting. Use div only when nothing semantic fits.

What is the difference between block and inline elements?

Block elements start on a new line and take the full available width; their width, height and vertical margins work. Inline elements flow within a line of text, are as wide as their content and ignore width and height. CSS display can change either default; inline-block mixes both.

<strong> vs <b> and <em> vs <i>?

strong and em carry meaning (importance, stress) and change how a screen reader speaks. b and i only draw attention or mark another voice, with no extra importance. For purely visual bold or italic, use CSS.

What does target="_blank" need, and why?

Add rel="noopener noreferrer". noopener prevents the new page from controlling the original through window.opener, and noreferrer hides the referrer. Modern browsers imply noopener, but the explicit attribute is still the habit.

How do you write good alt text? When is it empty?

Describe what the image conveys in its context in a short sentence, without "image of". Decorative images get alt="" so screen readers skip them. Images that are links describe the link's target. The attribute must always be present.

How do labels work, and why is placeholder not a label?

A label connected with for and the control's id (or wrapping the control) provides the accessible name and enlarges the click target. A placeholder disappears when typing, often has poor contrast and is not reliably announced, so it can only be an example hint.

A button inside a form reloads the page when clicked. Why?

The default type of a button is submit. Set type="button" for buttons that are not meant to submit, or call event.preventDefault() in the handler.

Which attribute decides what the server receives for a field? What if it is missing?

The name attribute is the key in the request. A control without name is not submitted. id is for labels, CSS and JavaScript. Unchecked checkboxes and disabled controls are also not sent.

GET vs POST for a form?

GET adds the fields to the URL as a query string; it is visible, bookmarkable and cached, so it is right for searches and filters. POST sends them in the body; use it for changes and sensitive data such as passwords. HTML forms support only these two methods; PUT and DELETE need JavaScript.

Is HTML5 form validation enough? Why validate on the server too?

No. Client-side validation (required, pattern, min, type=email) improves user experience but can be removed in DevTools or skipped entirely by calling the API with curl or Postman. The server must validate every request, for example with @Valid and Bean Validation in Spring Boot.

How do you make a page accessible? What is the first rule of ARIA?

Use semantic elements, meaningful alt text and labels, make everything keyboard operable with visible focus, keep contrast at 4.5:1 or better, and test with a keyboard, Lighthouse and a screen reader. The first rule of ARIA is not to use ARIA when a native HTML element does the job, since ARIA adds announcements but no behaviour.

Which meta tags matter for SEO and sharing?

A unique title and description, the canonical link, the robots meta (for noindex), a favicon, and Open Graph tags (og:title, og:description, og:image) for link previews. Page speed, headings and semantic HTML matter even more than tags.

Cheat sheet — HTML

  • Boilerplate doctype, html lang, meta charset, viewport, title, CSS link, script defer
  • Void elements br, hr, img, input, meta, link — no end tag
  • Entities &lt; &gt; &amp; &quot; &copy;
  • Headings one h1, no skipped levels, chosen for structure not size
  • Meaning strong/em carry meaning; b/i do not
  • Links href absolute or relative; #id anchors; mailto:, tel:; new tab needs rel="noopener noreferrer"
  • Images always alt (empty if decorative), width + height, loading="lazy" below the fold
  • Lists ul unordered, ol ordered, dl name–value
  • Landmarks header, nav, main (one only), aside, footer
  • section / article / div themed with heading / stand-alone / no meaning
  • Forms action, method; only controls with name are sent
  • Labels label for = control id; placeholder is not a label
  • Input types text, email, password, number, tel, url, search, date, checkbox, radio, file, hidden
  • Radios same name; group in fieldset + legend
  • Buttons default type is submit; use type="button" for others
  • Files need method="post" + enctype="multipart/form-data"
  • Validation required, min, max, minlength, maxlength, pattern, type
  • Server validates again client validation is for UX only
  • Tables caption, thead/tbody/tfoot, th scope, colspan/rowspan; never for layout
  • Accessibility native elements, keyboard + visible focus, contrast 4.5:1, labels, alt, skip link
  • ARIA last resort; aria-label, aria-describedby, aria-expanded, aria-hidden
  • SEO / meta unique title + description, Open Graph, canonical, robots, favicon
  • SPA caveat empty first HTML hurts SEO and link previews; use SSR or SSG for public pages
  • Validate W3C validator, Lighthouse, axe; browsers silently repair broken HTML

Practice — HTML

  1. Boilerplate from memory. Create index.html without copying: doctype, lang, charset, viewport and title. Done when the tab shows your title and Lighthouse reports no meta issues.
  2. Document outline. Write a page about yourself with one h1, three h2 sections and a few h3s, using only text. Done when it reads sensibly with no CSS at all.
  3. Links lab. Add an absolute link, a relative link to a second page, an in-page anchor to a section, a mailto:, a tel: and a downloadable file. Done when every link works from a different folder structure.
  4. Images and figures. Add a profile photo and one project screenshot with correct alt, width, height and loading, and wrap the screenshot in figure and figcaption. Done when the Elements panel shows no layout shift when the image loads on Slow 4G.
  5. Build the personal profile page (roadmap build). Semantic HTML only, no CSS: skip link, header with nav, main with h1, "About", "Skills" (a list), "Projects" (an article per project with links to GitHub opened safely in a new tab), "Experience or education" (a table with caption and th scope), an aside for "Currently learning", and a footer with address. Done when the validator reports 0 errors.
  6. Contact form. Add a contact form to the profile page: name, email, mobile (tel with a pattern), preferred contact method (radio group in a fieldset), topic (select), message (textarea with maxlength), a consent checkbox, and a submit button. Done when every field has a label, name and autocomplete, and invalid input is blocked with clear messages.
  7. Break the form on purpose. Remove required in DevTools and submit the empty form. Then send the same request with curl to a Spring Boot endpoint that uses @Valid. Done when you can explain why the server still returns 400.
  8. Keyboard-only test. Navigate the whole profile page with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space. Fix the order or the focus if anything is skipped or invisible. Done when you never lose track of the focus.
  9. Audit and fix. Add title, description, favicon and Open Graph tags. Run Lighthouse (Accessibility, SEO, Best Practices) and the W3C validator. Done when all scores are 90+ and the validator is clean.
  10. Table from data. Write a table of 6 employees (name, department, salary) with a total in tfoot. Then write a small Spring Boot endpoint that returns the same data as JSON, and compare the two. Done when you can explain why one is presentation and the other is data.

Module 3·About 1.5 weeksMust

CSS

14 topics · about 1.5 h of reading

CSS turns plain HTML into a designed, responsive interface. It looks easy — a few colours and fonts — and then layout, specificity and "why will this not centre?" take the first week. The good news: CSS has a small number of core ideas (the cascade, the box model, Flexbox, Grid, positioning, media queries). Learn those properly and the rest is looking things up.

This module follows the order in which problems appear: how rules are written and which one wins, how every element is a box, how to size things, how to lay out rows (Flexbox) and grids (Grid), how to position and layer, how to adapt to phones, and how to animate. Then comes Tailwind CSS, the utility-first approach you will meet in many React projects. Module 2 gave you the HTML; in Module 5 you will apply these skills to React components.

  • Write rules with selectors and predict which rule wins using specificity and the cascade.
  • Explain the box model, box-sizing, margin collapsing and when to use each unit.
  • Build navbars, centred layouts, card rows, sidebars and sticky footers with Flexbox.
  • Build page layouts and responsive card grids with CSS Grid, and choose between Flexbox and Grid.
  • Use relative, absolute, fixed and sticky positioning and understand z-index stacking.
  • Make mobile-first, responsive pages with media queries, fluid images and clamp().
  • Add transitions and animations that perform well, and read Tailwind utility classes.
  • Organise CSS so it stays maintainable, and debug it in DevTools.

Adding CSS to a page and the anatomy of a rule

CSS is a list of rules, each a selector plus declarations in braces; add it with an external stylesheet linked in the head — inline styles and style tags exist but are for special cases.

Anatomy of a rule

/* selector   { property: value; } */
.card {
  background-color: white;     /* a declaration: property + value */
  padding: 1rem;
  border-radius: 8px;
}
  • The selector (.card) chooses which elements the rule applies to.
  • The declaration block is everything inside { }. Each declaration is property: value; — end every one with a semicolon.
  • A property is something you can style (color, margin); the value is what you set it to.
  • Comments are /* … */. There is no // comment in CSS.
  • An at-rule starts with @: @media, @keyframes, @font-face, @import, @layer.

CSS ignores what it does not understand. A misspelt property (colour: red) or an invalid value is silently dropped, and the rest of the rule still works — there is no error message. DevTools shows invalid declarations with a warning icon and a line through them.

Three ways to add CSS

WayWhereUse it for
External stylesheet<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css"> in the headAlmost everything. Cached by the browser, shared across pages, separate from HTML
<style> elementInside the headTiny demos, critical above-the-fold CSS, HTML emails
Inline style attribute<p style="color: red">Values computed by JavaScript (a progress bar width); quick tests
 
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/styles.css">
</head>

Inline styles have very high specificity (they beat any selector except !important) and cannot use media queries, hover states or pseudo-elements. That makes them hard to override and maintain. In React you will see style={{ width: "40%" }} for dynamic values; for everything else use classes.

An @import inside a CSS file loads another stylesheet, but it makes the browser download files one after the other (slow). In a Vite project you can import CSS from JavaScript (import "./styles.css") and the tool bundles it.

Where CSS fits in the page lifecycle

The browser downloads the HTML, finds the <link>, downloads the CSS, builds the CSSOM and only then paints (How the browser renders a page). Hence: keep the stylesheet in the head, keep it small, and split rarely used CSS out. A relative path in href is resolved against the page URL, so css/styles.css from /blog/post.html means /blog/css/styles.css — a classic cause of "my CSS does not load" (check the Network tab for a 404).

Rule: every declaration ends with a semicolon

A missing semicolon makes the browser merge that line with the next one, and both are dropped as invalid. This silent failure causes endless confusion; Prettier and the VS Code CSS validation catch it.

Conventions

  • One external stylesheet (or a few) linked in the head; no inline styles except for computed values.
