  • One declaration per line, two-space indent, a space after the colon, lowercase hex colours; class names lowercase with hyphens (.product-card).
  • Group related properties: layout, box, typography, colour, effects.

Edge cases

  • If two stylesheets set the same property with equal strength, the one linked later wins.
  • A stylesheet is cached. After editing, the browser may still use the old file; hard reload or "Disable cache" in DevTools. Vite adds a hash to file names in production to avoid this.
  • Web servers must send Content-Type: text/css; Spring Boot's static resource handler does this for files in static/.

Interview angle

  • "Inline vs internal vs external CSS?" — external is preferred: cacheable, reusable, separation of concerns.
  • "What happens with an invalid declaration?" — the browser ignores just that declaration, silently.

Selectors: choosing the elements to style

A selector describes which elements a rule applies to — by tag, class, id, attribute, relationship to other elements, state (pseudo-class) or a part of an element (pseudo-element).

Selectors are CSS's query language, comparable to a WHERE clause in SQL: they filter the DOM. The same selector syntax also works in JavaScript's document.querySelectorAll().

Basic selectors

SelectorExampleMatches
Type (element)pEvery <p>
Class.cardElements with class="card" (can be one of several classes)
ID#headerThe element with id="header"
Universal*Every element
Attribute[disabled], [type="email"]Has the attribute / has that exact value
Attribute (partial)[href^="https"], [href$=".pdf"], [class*="icon"]Starts with / ends with / contains
Groupingh1, h2, h3Any of them (the rule is shared)
Compoundbutton.primaryA button that also has class primary (no space)

Combinators: relationships

CombinatorExampleMatches
Descendant (space)nav aAny a anywhere inside a nav
Child >ul > liAn li that is a direct child of ul
Adjacent sibling +h2 + pThe p immediately after an h2
General sibling ~h2 ~ pEvery p after an h2, same parent

Remember the space matters: .card .title means a .title inside a .card, while .card.title means one element having both classes.

Pseudo-classes: states and positions

A pseudo-class starts with one colon and selects an element in a certain state or position.

Pseudo-classMatches
:hoverThe pointer is over the element
:focusThe element has keyboard focus
:focus-visibleFocus that should be shown visibly (keyboard use) — use for outlines
:activeWhile being pressed
:disabled, :checked, :requiredForm control states
:first-child, :last-childFirst or last among its siblings
:nth-child(n):nth-child(2), (odd), (even), (3n) every third, (n+4) from the fourth
:not(selector)Elements that do not match: li:not(.done)
:is(a, b), :where(a, b)Shorthand for lists: :is(h1, h2) a. :where adds zero specificity
:has(selector)An element that contains a match: .card:has(img) (the "parent selector"); supported in current browsers
:rootThe html element; used to declare CSS variables

Pseudo-elements: parts of an element

A pseudo-element uses two colons and styles a part of an element or adds generated content.

/* Add a decoration before each required label (content is mandatory) */
label.required::after {
  content: " *";
  color: #b00020;
}

input::placeholder {
  color: #6b7280;
}

p::first-line { font-weight: 600; }
::selection { background: #fde68a; }     /* text highlighted by the user */

::before and ::after insert a child box at the start or end of an element, and do nothing unless you set content (even content: ""). They are decorations — icons, quotes, badges — never real content, since screen readers may or may not read them and users cannot select the text.

Putting selectors to work

/* Reset link look in the nav, then show state */
nav a {
  color: inherit;
  text-decoration: none;
}
nav a:hover,
nav a:focus-visible {
  text-decoration: underline;
}

/* Zebra rows */
tbody tr:nth-child(even) { background: #f6f6f6; }

/* Space between list items, none after the last */
.tags li:not(:last-child) { margin-right: 0.5rem; }

/* External links get an arrow */
a[href^="http"]::after { content: " ↗"; }

/* A paragraph directly after a heading has no top margin */
h2 + p { margin-top: 0; }

You can test a selector quickly: type $$(".card > .title") in the DevTools Console to see which elements it finds.

Conventions

  • Style with classes. IDs are too strong (see specificity) and cannot repeat; reserve them for anchors and JavaScript hooks.
  • Avoid styling bare tags too deeply (div ul li a); long chains are fragile and slow to read. Two levels at most.
  • Name classes after what things are (.product-card), not how they look (.red-text).
  • Do not style by position in the HTML when a class would do — the markup will change.

Edge cases

  • Within a selector list, one invalid selector used to invalidate the whole rule: a:hover, b::unknown { } may apply to nothing. :is() and :where() forgive invalid items.
  • :nth-child(2) counts all siblings, regardless of type; p:nth-child(2) matches only if the second child is a p. Use :nth-of-type to count among the same tag.
  • :hover does not exist on touch screens in the same way (a tap simulates it and it may stick). Never hide essential content behind hover.
  • Class names are case-sensitive in standards mode; tag names are not.

Mistake: a space where there should be none

Wrong: looks for a .primary inside a button

button .primary { background: blue; }

Right: a button with the class primary

button.primary { background: blue; }

Interview angle

  • "Pseudo-class vs pseudo-element?" — a state or position (:hover) versus a part of an element (::before).
  • "Descendant vs child selector?" — space matches any depth, > only direct children.
  • "What does .a .b vs .a.b mean?" — inside versus same element.

Specificity, the cascade and inheritance

When several rules set the same property on one element, the browser picks the winner by importance and origin first, then specificity (inline, then ids, then classes, then tags), and finally by order — the later rule wins a tie.

"Why does my style not apply?" is the most common CSS question, and the answer is nearly always this article. The "C" in CSS stands for Cascading: the algorithm that decides, for every property of every element, which of the competing declarations wins. Think of it as conflict resolution, like Spring choosing between multiple beans (with @Primary and @Order) — except with a precise points system.

The order of decision

  1. Importance and origin. Declarations marked !important beat normal ones. Among normal ones, your author styles beat the browser's default styles (the "user agent" stylesheet that makes h1 big and links blue).
  2. Specificity. The more specific selector wins.
  3. Order of appearance. If still tied, the declaration that comes last in the source wins.

(Modern CSS also has @layer, which sits between importance and specificity: a later layer beats an earlier one regardless of specificity. Frameworks use it to let your styles override theirs easily; you only need to know it exists.)

Calculating specificity

Specificity is like a three-part score (IDs, classes, tags), compared left to right like a version number, not added as one decimal number. Inline styles sit above all three.

What countsColumnExamples
Inline style="…"Beats all selectors<p style="color:red">
ID selectors1st (hundreds)#nav
Classes, attribute selectors, pseudo-classes2nd (tens).card, [type="text"], :hover, :nth-child()
Type selectors, pseudo-elements3rd (ones)p, ::before
Universal *, combinators, :where()Nothing*, >, +

Worked examples (written as ID-class-tag):

p                      { }   /* 0-0-1 */
.card                  { }   /* 0-1-0 */
p.card                 { }   /* 0-1-1 */
nav ul li a            { }   /* 0-0-4 */
.nav a:hover           { }   /* 0-2-1  (.nav, :hover, a) */
#main .card p          { }   /* 1-1-1 */
#main                  { }   /* 1-0-0 */
:not(.a)               { }   /* 0-1-0  (:not counts its argument) */
:where(.a, .b)         { }   /* 0-0-0 */

Because the columns are compared in order, one class beats any number of tag selectors (0-1-0 beats 0-0-9), and one ID beats any number of classes. Now a real puzzle:

<p class="note" id="intro">Hello</p>
p          { color: red; }      /* 0-0-1 */
.note      { color: green; }    /* 0-1-0 */
p.note     { color: blue; }     /* 0-1-1 */
#intro     { color: purple; }   /* 1-0-0  <-- wins */
p.note     { color: orange; }   /* 0-1-1, but #intro still wins */

The text is purple. Remove the #intro rule and the last p.note (orange) wins over the blue one, because they tie on specificity and orange comes later.

!important

color: red !important; jumps over specificity. Only another !important with equal or higher specificity can beat it. It "works", which is the danger: the next developer needs an !important to override yours, and soon the stylesheet is a war. Avoid it. Acceptable uses: utility classes that must always win (Tailwind's ! modifier), and overriding third-party CSS you cannot edit. For ordinary cases, fix the specificity: lower the strong selector, or add a class.

Inheritance

Some properties are passed from parent to child automatically. If you set font-family on body, every paragraph uses it without any further rule.

  • Inherited by default (mostly text): color, font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height, text-align, visibility, cursor, list-style.
  • Not inherited (mostly boxes): margin, padding, border, background, width, height, display, position, overflow. If a border inherited, nesting would draw boxes inside boxes.

An inherited value is the weakest of all: any rule that directly targets the element beats it, whatever the specificity. This is why links stay blue after you set color on body — the browser's own a rule targets the link directly.

KeywordMeaningExample
inheritTake the parent's computed valuea { color: inherit; } — links look like surrounding text
initialUse the property's default from the CSS specdisplay: initial (becomes inline)
unsetinherit if the property is inherited, else initialall: unset on a button to remove all styling
revertGo back to the browser's default stylerevert undoes your own rules

currentColor is a related keyword: it equals the element's current color value, so a border or an SVG icon can follow the text colour: border: 1px solid currentColor;.

A debugging recipe: "my style does not apply"

  1. Inspect the element. In Styles, is your declaration there? If not, the selector is wrong or the CSS file did not load (Network tab, 404).
  2. Is it struck through? Another rule won. Scroll up in the Styles list to find the winning rule: it has a stronger selector, or comes later.
  3. Is there a warning icon? The property or value is invalid (typo, wrong unit).
  4. Is it greyed out and not struck through? The property has no effect here (for example width on an inline element, or top on a static element).
  5. Check Computed to see the final value and which rule supplied it.

Rule: specificity is calculated per selector, not per rule

In h1, .title { } the two selectors have different specificity (0-0-1 and 0-1-0); for an element matching both, the higher one is used. Order matters only when specificity is equal.

Conventions to keep specificity low and predictable

  • Style with single classes (0-1-0) so any later single class can override them.
  • Write general rules first (reset, base elements), then components, then utilities and overrides.
  • Do not use ID selectors for styling and do not chain more than two or three selectors.
  • To win over a rule, match its specificity and place yours later; do not escalate with !important.

Edge cases

  • Rules are applied per property. A losing rule still contributes the properties that the winner does not set. The cascade merges rules, not replaces them.
  • The order of :link, :visited, :hover, :active rules matters because they have equal specificity: remember LoVe HAte.
  • Order is by the position of the rule in the final combined CSS, so the order of your <link> tags (or imports) changes the result.
  • CSS-in-JS and component libraries inject styles at runtime; the injection order can change who wins. Check "Styles" in DevTools, not just the source.

Mistake: fighting specificity with ever longer selectors

Wrong: escalating

#page .content div.card p.text { color: red !important; }

Right: flat and simple

.card-text { color: red; }

Interview angle: "How does CSS decide which rule applies?"

  • Importance/origin → specificity (inline > ID > class/attribute/pseudo-class > tag) → source order.
  • Calculate a score for a given selector, e.g. #a .b p is 1-1-1.
  • Which properties inherit (text-related) and which do not (box-related)?
  • Why you avoid !important.

Colours, typography and CSS variables

Colours come as hex, rgb() or hsl() values; set font-family, font-size, line-height and font-weight on body so text inherits them; and define colours, spacing and fonts once as custom properties (--name) used with var().

Colour formats

FormatExampleNotes
Keywordtomato, transparent, currentColorAbout 140 named colours
Hex#1a56db, #fff, #1a56db80Red-green-blue in hex; 3-digit shorthand; 4th pair is opacity
rgb()rgb(26 86 219), rgb(26 86 219 / 50%)Channels 0–255; the older comma form rgba(26, 86, 219, 0.5) also works
hsl()hsl(220 79% 48%)Hue (0–360 degrees on a colour wheel), saturation, lightness. Easiest to adjust by hand

HSL is friendly: to make a hover colour, lower the lightness; to make a tint, raise it. The same hue keeps the shades consistent. Newer colour spaces like oklch() exist; you can ignore them for now. opacity: 0.5 fades the whole element and its children, while a transparent colour (rgb(0 0 0 / 50%)) fades only that colour — use it for overlays so the text on top stays solid.

Foreground colour is color; the fill behind is background-color; the box outline colour is in border. Check contrast (at least 4.5:1 for body text, see Accessibility): DevTools' colour picker shows the ratio.

Backgrounds and borders in brief

.hero {
  background: #0f172a url("images/hero.jpg") center / cover no-repeat;
  /* colour (fallback) + image + position / size + repeat */
}
.card {
  border: 1px solid #e5e7eb;
  border-radius: 12px;                         /* rounded corners; 50% makes a circle */
  box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.12);     /* x y blur colour */
}
.avatar { border-radius: 50%; object-fit: cover; }  /* crop an image without squashing */
.banner {
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1a56db, #7c3aed);
}

Typography

Set the base text once on body; everything inherits it.

body {
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif;
  font-size: 1rem;          /* 16px by default; respects the user's browser setting */
  line-height: 1.6;         /* unitless: 1.6 x the element's own font size */
  color: #1f2937;
}
h1, h2, h3 { line-height: 1.2; font-weight: 700; }
code { font-family: ui-monospace, "Cascadia Code", Consolas, monospace; }
p { max-width: 65ch; }      /* comfortable line length: about 65 characters */
font-family
A font stack: the browser uses the first installed font and falls back to the next. Always end with a generic family (sans-serif, serif, monospace). Quote names with spaces. system-ui uses the operating system's font: fast and familiar.
font-size
Use rem so text scales with the user's settings (Units). Do not set the root size to a fixed px.
font-weight
400 normal, 700 bold; keywords normal and bold. Variable fonts accept any value from 100 to 900.
line-height
Space between lines. Use a unitless number: 1.5–1.7 for body text, 1.1–1.3 for headings. With a unit like 24px, children inherit the fixed value, which clips big text.
Other
font-style: italic, text-align, text-decoration, text-transform: uppercase, letter-spacing, white-space, text-overflow: ellipsis (needs overflow: hidden; white-space: nowrap), and font as a shorthand.
Web fonts (brief)

To use a font that users do not have installed, load it. The easy route is Google Fonts: add its <link> and use the family name. Self-hosting gives better privacy and speed:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-var.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 100 900;        /* a variable font */
  font-display: swap;          /* show fallback text first, swap when loaded */
}
body { font-family: "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif; }

Use WOFF2, load only the weights you need (each adds download size), and keep a good fallback in the stack. Fonts for Hindi and other Indian scripts need the proper subset (Devanagari, Tamil…); otherwise the browser falls back to a system font for those characters.

CSS custom properties (variables)

A custom property is a value you name once and reuse everywhere. The name starts with two dashes; you read it with var(). Declare shared ones on :root.

:root {
  --color-primary: #1a56db;
  --color-text: #1f2937;
  --color-bg: #ffffff;
  --space: 1rem;
  --radius: 8px;
}

.button {
  background: var(--color-primary);
  padding: calc(var(--space) / 2) var(--space);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  color: var(--color-bg);
}

.card {
  padding: var(--space);
  color: var(--color-text, black);   /* second argument: fallback value */
}

Unlike Sass variables (compiled away), custom properties are live: they live in the browser, follow the cascade and inheritance, and can be changed by JavaScript or overridden inside any element. That makes theming easy.

:root {
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --text: #111827;
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --bg: #0b1020;
    --text: #e5e7eb;
  }
}

/* Or a manual switch: <html data-theme="dark"> */
:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --bg: #0b1020;
  --text: #e5e7eb;
}

body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }
document.documentElement.dataset.theme = "dark";             // switch theme
document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--space", "2rem"); // change one variable
getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue("--space"); // read it

Rule: a custom property name is case-sensitive and works only in values

--Color and --color are different. You cannot use a variable as a property name or inside a media-query condition. If a variable is undefined and has no fallback, the declaration becomes invalid at computed time and the property falls back to inherit/initial.

Conventions

  • Define design tokens (colours, spacing, radii, font sizes) as variables on :root with meaningful names (--color-primary, not --blue).
  • Set typography on body; use unitless line-height and rem font sizes.
  • Never use colour as the only signal, and keep text contrast at WCAG AA or better.

Edge cases

  • The shorthand font: 1rem/1.6 Inter, sans-serif resets everything not listed (weight, style) to defaults — easy to overwrite by accident. Order: style weight size/line-height family.
  • The #rrggbbaa and rgb(r g b / a) forms are supported in current browsers.
  • Fonts blocked by CORS (a font on another domain without the right header) fail silently; see the Console.

Interview angle

  • "What are CSS variables and how are they different from Sass variables?" — runtime, cascading and inheritable, changeable by JS; Sass variables are compile-time.
  • "Why unitless line-height?" — it scales with each element's own font size when inherited.

The box model, display and overflow

Every element is a rectangular box made of content, padding, border and margin; with box-sizing: border-box the width you set includes padding and border, which is why every project resets it.

The browser's layout engine thinks only in boxes. A paragraph, an image, a button, even a line of text inside a paragraph — all boxes. Layout is the art of sizing and placing boxes, so this is the most important concept in CSS. Think of a framed photo on a wall: the photo is the content, the white mat inside the frame is the padding, the frame is the border, and the gap to the next frame is the margin.

Content
The area for text or children. width and height set its size (by default).
Padding
Space between the content and the border. The element's background colour fills it. Negative values are not allowed.
Border
A line around the padding: border: 1px solid #ddd (width, style, colour). Without a style there is no border.
Margin
Space outside the border, separating the element from its neighbours. It is always transparent and may be negative. margin: 0 auto centres a block element that has a width.

Shorthands

.box {
  padding: 16px;                 /* all four sides */
  padding: 8px 16px;             /* vertical | horizontal */
  padding: 8px 16px 12px;        /* top | horizontal | bottom */
  padding: 8px 16px 12px 4px;    /* top | right | bottom | left (clockwise) */
  margin-inline: auto;           /* left and right (logical property) */
  margin-block: 2rem;            /* top and bottom */
  border-bottom: 2px solid currentColor;
}

Remember the clockwise order T-R-B-L ("trouble"). Logical properties (margin-inline, padding-block) follow the writing direction, so they also work for right-to-left languages.

box-sizing: the setting that decides what "width" means

By default (content-box), width sets only the content width; padding and border are added on top. So width: 300px with padding: 20px and border: 2px gives a box that is 344px wide (300 + 40 + 4). Add width: 100% to that and the box overflows its parent. With border-box, width includes padding and border, and the content shrinks to fit: the box is exactly 300px.

*,
*::before,
*::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}
width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 2pxcontent-box (default)border-box
Content width300px256px
Total visible width344px300px

Put this reset at the top of every stylesheet. Tailwind and Bootstrap include it. The sizes you write now match what you see — and percentages plus padding no longer overflow.

The display property

ValueBehaviour
blockNew line, full available width; width, height, margins all work (div, p)
inlineFlows within text; ignores width/height and vertical margin (span, a)
inline-blockFlows like text but accepts width, height and all margins (buttons, icons)
noneRemoved from the layout and from the accessibility tree
flex / inline-flexA flex container: children become flex items (Flexbox)
grid / inline-gridA grid container (Grid)
contentsThe element's own box disappears; its children take part in the parent's layout

Two different "hide" tools: display: none removes the element completely (no space, not read by screen readers); visibility: hidden hides it but keeps the space; opacity: 0 makes it invisible but it still takes space and can be clicked and focused.

width, height and max-width

  • A block element's default width is auto: it fills its parent. Do not write width: 100% on blocks — it is the default, and with content-box plus padding it overflows.
  • height: auto (the default) lets content decide. Fixing a height invites overflowing text; prefer min-height.
  • max-width is the key to fluid layouts: max-width: 1100px; margin-inline: auto; makes a centred column that is never wider than 1100px but shrinks on phones. min-width and min-height set lower limits.
  • Images: max-width: 100%; height: auto; keeps them inside the parent without distortion.

Overflow

When content is bigger than its box, it overflows. The overflow property decides what happens.

ValueResult
visible (default)Content spills outside the box
hiddenClipped; no scroll bar (also used to contain floats and rounded-corner images)
scrollAlways shows scroll bars
autoScroll bars only when needed — the usual choice

overflow-x and overflow-y control each axis. A horizontal scroll bar on the whole page on a phone is a bug: find the element that is too wide using DevTools (hover the elements) and fix it.

Margin collapsing

This surprises everyone once. Vertical margins of adjacent blocks collapse: when one block's bottom margin touches the next block's top margin, they do not add up — the larger one wins.

.a { margin-bottom: 30px; }
.b { margin-top: 20px; }
/* The gap between .a and .b is 30px, not 50px. */
  • A parent's top margin and its first child's top margin also merge, if nothing (padding, border, content) separates them — so the child's margin seems to "leak out" and push the parent down.
  • An empty block's own top and bottom margins collapse together.
  • Margins do not collapse in flex or grid containers, between floated or absolutely positioned elements, with inline-block boxes, or when a parent has padding, a border or overflow other than visible. Horizontal margins never collapse.

Many teams avoid the surprise by using margin in one direction only (for example only margin-bottom), or by spacing items with gap in flex/grid.

Seeing the box model

In DevTools, select an element and look at the box-model diagram in the Styles or Computed pane; hover each layer to highlight it on the page. Margins are shown orange, borders yellow, padding green, content blue.

Rule: start every stylesheet with the border-box reset

Without it, adding a padding or a border changes an element's total size and breaks layouts that were calculated with percentages.

Conventions

  • Use padding for space inside a component and margin (or gap) for space between components.
  • Use rem for padding and margin so spacing scales with text size.
  • Prefer max-width over fixed width for containers.

Edge cases

  • Percentage padding and margin are relative to the parent's width, even for top and bottom.
  • margin: auto centres horizontally only for blocks with a defined width, and does not centre vertically in normal flow (but does in flex and grid).
  • An inline element's vertical padding and border draw but do not push other lines away.
  • height: 100% works only if the parent has a definite height; use min-height: 100vh or flex instead.

Mistake: a mysterious horizontal scrollbar

Usually caused by width: 100% plus padding or border in a content-box element, by an image or table wider than the screen, or by 100vw (which includes the scrollbar width). Reset box-sizing, and find the culprit by deleting elements in DevTools until the scrollbar goes away.

Interview angle

  • "Explain the box model." — content, padding, border, margin; draw it.
  • "content-box vs border-box?" — what width includes; work out a 300px example.
  • "What is margin collapsing?" — adjacent vertical margins merge to the larger one; not in flex/grid.
  • "display: none vs visibility: hidden vs opacity: 0?"

CSS units: px, %, em, rem, vw, vh and more

Use rem for font sizes and spacing so they follow the user's settings, % and fr for flexible widths, vw/vh/dvh for viewport-relative sizes, px for hairlines, and calc(), min(), max() and clamp() to combine them.

A CSS length is a number plus a unit — 16px, 1.5rem, 50%. Zero needs no unit (margin: 0); any other number without a unit is invalid for lengths (but fine for line-height and flex). Units fall into two groups: absolute (fixed size) and relative (depends on something else).

UnitRelative toUse it for
pxA CSS pixel (fixed; 1/96 inch)Borders, shadows, thin lines, tiny fixed details
%The parent's matching value (width of parent, font size of parent…)Fluid widths: width: 50%
emThe element's own font size (for font-size itself: the parent's)Component-relative spacing, e.g. button padding that scales with the button's text
remThe root (html) font size, 16px by defaultFont sizes, margins, paddings, media queries
vw, vh1% of the viewport width / heightFull-screen sections, fluid type
dvh, svh, lvhDynamic / small / large viewport heightFixes mobile address-bar problems with vh
chWidth of the digit "0" in the current fontLine length: max-width: 65ch
frA share of free space in a gridgrid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr (Grid only)
deg, s, msAngle, timerotate(45deg), transition: 200ms

px vs rem — and why rem wins for text

The browser's default root font size is 16px, so 1rem = 16px, 1.5rem = 24px. Many people raise it in the browser settings for readability. Text sized in px ignores that setting; text sized in rem grows with it. That is an accessibility requirement, not a style choice. So size text and spacing in rem; keep html { font-size: 100% } (or leave it) rather than html { font-size: 16px }.

A once-popular trick, html { font-size: 62.5% } (so 1rem = 10px for easy sums), still respects the user's setting but needs you to restore the body size; many teams skip it and use a calculator or calc(). Convert rem to px by multiplying by 16.

em vs rem

.menu    { font-size: 1.2em; }   /* 1.2 x parent */
.menu li { font-size: 1.2em; }   /* 1.2 x 1.2 x parent = 1.44 x parent */

.menu    { font-size: 1.2rem; }  /* always 1.2 x root */
.menu li { font-size: 1.2rem; }  /* the same size: no surprise */

.btn { font-size: 1rem; padding: 0.5em 1em; }
/* padding follows this button's own font size: a bigger button gets more padding */

em in nested elements multiplies at each level, which is confusing for font sizes. Use rem for font sizes and em only where you want a value to follow the element's own text size.

Percentages

A percentage is always a share of something, and what depends on the property: width: 50% is half the parent's content width; height: 50% is half the parent's height (only if the parent's height is set); padding and margin use the parent's width; font-size: 120% uses the parent's font size; for an absolutely positioned element, left: 10% uses the containing block.

Viewport units

100vw is the full width and 100vh the full height of the window. Two traps:

  • 100vw includes the vertical scrollbar's width, so width: 100vw on a page with a scrollbar creates a horizontal scrollbar. Prefer width: 100% for page-wide blocks.
  • On mobile browsers, the address bar slides away while scrolling, so 100vh is taller than the visible area and the bottom of a full-screen section gets cut off. Use 100dvh (dynamic viewport height, current visible size) or 100svh (smallest). Provide 100vh first as a fallback for old browsers.
.hero {
  min-height: 100vh;     /* fallback */
  min-height: 100dvh;    /* modern browsers: the actually visible height */
}

calc(), min(), max(), clamp()

Math functions let you mix units that the browser can only resolve at layout time.

.sidebar { width: calc(100% - 280px); }       /* spaces around + - are required */
.hero    { height: calc(100vh - 4rem); }      /* full screen minus a 4rem header */

.container { width: min(100% - 2rem, 1100px); margin-inline: auto; }
/* the smaller of "full width minus gutters" and 1100px */

h1 { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.2rem + 2.5vw, 3rem); }
/* clamp(minimum, preferred, maximum): grows with the screen between 28px and 48px */

.panel { padding: max(1rem, 3vw); }           /* the larger of the two */

clamp(min, preferred, max) is the tool for fluid typography and spacing: no media queries needed. Always include a rem part in the preferred value (1.2rem + 2.5vw), not only vw, so zoom and browser font settings still work.

Which unit when?

NeedUse
Font sizesrem (or clamp() with rem)
Spacing (padding, margin, gap)rem
Page container widthmax-width in px, rem or ch, plus width: 100% / auto
Columns that share spacefr in Grid, flex in Flexbox, % rarely
Full-screen sectionsmin-height: 100dvh
Borders, shadows, dividerspx
Readable text linesmax-width: 65ch
Media-query breakpointsem or rem (follow the user's font setting) or px — be consistent

Rule: always write a unit for lengths (except 0)

margin: 10 is invalid and silently ignored (except in quirks mode, another reason for the doctype). Unitless values are valid only where the property expects a number: line-height: 1.5, flex: 1, opacity: 0.5, z-index: 10.

Convention: rem for type and space, px for hairlines, fr and clamp for flexible layout

Do not size text in px or with vw alone. Test by changing the browser's default font size to "Very large" and zooming to 200%.

Edge cases

  • Media queries using em/rem are based on the browser's default size, not your CSS html font size.
  • In calc(), + and - must have spaces (calc(100% -2rem) is invalid), while * and / do not need them.
  • A percentage height inside an auto-height parent behaves like auto.

Interview angle

  • "em vs rem?" — own/parent font size (compounds) versus root (predictable). Prefer rem.
  • "Why not 100vh on mobile?" — address-bar problem; use dvh.
  • "What does clamp(1rem, 2vw, 2rem) do?" — value between 1rem and 2rem following 2vw.

Flexbox: container and item properties

Flexbox lays out items in one direction (a row or a column) and lets you align them, space them and make them grow or shrink — you control the main axis with justify-content and the cross axis with align-items.

Flexbox (Flexible Box Layout) is the tool you will use every day: navbars, button groups, card rows, form rows, centring anything. It is made for one-dimensional layout — items along a single line (that may wrap onto more lines). Think of it as a smart row (or column) of boxes that shares leftover space and aligns itself. It replaced the old float hacks completely.

Turn it on

.toolbar {
  display: flex;      /* .toolbar is the flex container; its direct children are flex items */
}

Only the direct children become flex items; grandchildren are not affected (they can be flex containers themselves — nesting is normal). By default items sit in a row, stretch to the container's height, do not wrap, and shrink if they do not fit.

Main axis and cross axis

Everything in Flexbox depends on two axes. The main axis is the direction items flow; the cross axis is perpendicular. With flex-direction: row the main axis is horizontal; with column it turns vertical, and the roles of the properties swap.

Container properties

PropertyValuesWhat it does
displayflex, inline-flexCreates the flex container (block-level or inline-level)
flex-directionrow (default), row-reverse, column, column-reverseSets the main axis
flex-wrapnowrap (default), wrap, wrap-reverseWhether items move to a new line when there is no room
flex-flowrow wrapShorthand for direction + wrap
justify-contentflex-start, flex-end, center, space-between, space-around, space-evenlyDistributes free space along the main axis
align-itemsstretch (default), flex-start, flex-end, center, baselineAligns items along the cross axis (within one line)
align-contentSame as justify-content values, plus stretchSpaces the lines on the cross axis; only when there are several lines (wrap) and spare room
gap, row-gap, column-gapLengthSpace between items (not at the edges)

justify-content in pictures

space-between: the first item touches the start, the last touches the end, equal gaps between. space-around: equal space around every item (half-size gaps at the ends). space-evenly: all gaps, including the ends, are equal.

align-items in pictures

Item properties

These go on the children.

PropertyDefaultMeaning
flex-grow0Share of the extra space this item takes. 1 on all items = equal extra share
flex-shrink1How willing the item is to shrink when space is short. 0 = never shrink
flex-basisautoThe starting size along the main axis before growing or shrinking (like width in a row); auto uses width/content size
flex0 1 autoShorthand: grow shrink basis
align-selfautoOverrides the container's align-items for this one item
order0Visual order (lower first). Changes only the look, not the DOM or tab order — use sparingly

The flex shorthand

You writeIt meansUse for
flex: 11 1 0Equal shares: items split the whole space equally regardless of content
flex: auto1 1 autoStart from content size, then share the leftover
flex: none0 0 autoFixed: never grows or shrinks
flex: 0 0 200pxExactly 200pxA fixed-width sidebar
flex: 2 and flex: 1Grow 2 and 1A 2:1 split of the space

How the algorithm works: (1) every item starts at its flex-basis; (2) if the total is smaller than the container, the free space is shared in the ratio of the flex-grow values; (3) if the total is bigger, the overflow is taken from items in the ratio of flex-shrink times their basis. A worked example: a 900px container with three items of basis 100px and grow values 1, 1, 2 has 600px free; it is shared 150 / 150 / 300, so the widths are 250, 250 and 400.

.layout { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }
.layout .left  { flex: 1; }   /* 1 share */
.layout .right { flex: 2; }   /* 2 shares: twice as wide */

The minimum-size trap

A flex item cannot shrink below its content by default (min-width: auto). A long word, a wide image or a long line of code then overflows instead of shrinking. Fix with min-width: 0 on the item (and overflow-wrap: anywhere or overflow: hidden as needed). This is the cause of the common "my flex child will not shrink / text overflows" problem.

Auto margins

In a flex container, margin-left: auto on an item pushes it (and everything after it) to the far end — the standard way to put a logo on the left and a login button on the right in a navbar. margin: auto centres an item on both axes.

Rule: justify = main axis, align = cross axis

If justify-content seems to do nothing, check the direction. In flex-direction: column, justify-content is vertical. Also remember align-items needs spare cross-axis room to show an effect: a row container that is exactly as tall as its items cannot centre anything vertically — give it a height or min-height.

Conventions

  • Use gap for spacing between items instead of margins on the items.
  • Use flex: 1 to share space, flex: none for fixed-size items.
  • Write flex-wrap: wrap on rows that must work on small screens.
  • Use Flexbox for components and one-dimensional rows or columns; use Grid for two-dimensional page structure.

Edge cases

  • Floats, clear, vertical-align, and column-* properties have no effect on flex items. Margins of flex items do not collapse.
  • Absolutely positioned children of a flex container are taken out of the flex layout.
  • Children that are plain text nodes become anonymous flex items.
  • align-content does nothing on a single-line container (no wrap); align-items is what you need.
  • Images as flex items stretch to the cross size and distort; add align-self: flex-start or object-fit: cover.
  • With flex-basis and width both set, flex-basis wins (unless it is auto).

Mistake: putting flex properties on the wrong element

Wrong: the item has justify-content, the container has flex: 1

.card   { justify-content: center; }  /* no effect: card is not a flex container */
.nav    { flex: 1; }                   /* no effect: .nav is not a flex item */

Right: container properties on the parent, item properties on children

.nav       { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; }
.nav .logo { flex: 1; }

Interview angle

  • "Explain Flexbox." — one-dimensional layout; container and items; main vs cross axis.
  • "justify-content vs align-items?" — main versus cross axis.
  • "What does flex: 1 mean?" — flex: 1 1 0: grow, shrink, basis 0.
  • "flex-basis vs width?" — basis is the starting size along the main axis and wins over width in a flex item.

Common Flexbox layouts, ready to copy

Five layouts cover most daily needs: a navbar, centring anything, a wrapping card row, a sticky footer and a sidebar with content.

Learn these patterns by heart. In each, the HTML is short, and the CSS shows the flex idea that does the job. Try them in a scratch file and open the Flexbox overlay in DevTools (click the "flex" badge in Elements).

1. Navbar: logo left, links right

<header class="site-header">
  <a class="logo" href="/">MyShop</a>
  <nav>
    <ul class="nav-links">
      <li><a href="/products">Products</a></li>
      <li><a href="/cart">Cart</a></li>
      <li><a href="/login">Login</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
</header>
.site-header {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;   /* logo at one end, nav at the other */
  align-items: center;              /* vertically centred */
  padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
  background: #0f172a;
}
.nav-links {
  display: flex;                    /* the ul is a flex container too */
  gap: 1.5rem;
  list-style: none;                 /* remove bullets */
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
}
.site-header a { color: white; text-decoration: none; }

Two flex containers are nested: the header (logo vs nav) and the ul (the links in a row). A variation: put margin-left: auto on the nav and drop space-between to push everything after the logo to the right.

2. Centre anything, horizontally and vertically

.center-screen {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center;   /* horizontal */
  align-items: center;       /* vertical */
  min-height: 100dvh;        /* gives the container room to centre in */
}

/* Alternative with grid, shortest of all */
.center-grid { display: grid; place-items: center; min-height: 100dvh; }

This replaces the old tricks with negative margins and absolute positioning. The most common failure is the missing container height: without min-height, the container is only as tall as its content, so there is nothing to centre inside. Another is to forget that the centring properties go on the parent of the thing being centred.

3. A row of cards that wraps

.cards {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1rem;
}
.card {
  flex: 1 1 250px;          /* grow, shrink, start at 250px */
  border: 1px solid #e5e7eb;
  border-radius: 12px;
  padding: 1rem;
}

Each card wants to be at least 250px wide; when the row cannot fit another, the next card wraps and the cards on each line share the space. On a phone you get one card per line; on a laptop three or four. No media query. One catch: the last row's cards also stretch to fill the line, so a final single card becomes very wide. If you need uniform columns (a real grid), use CSS Grid. Alternatively cap the width with max-width: 400px.

4. Sticky footer: footer at the bottom even on short pages

<body>
  <header>…</header>
  <main>…short content…</main>
  <footer>…</footer>
</body>
body {
  min-height: 100dvh;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;     /* stack header, main, footer */
  margin: 0;
}
main {
  flex: 1;                    /* main takes all the free vertical space */
}

If the content is short, main grows and pushes the footer to the bottom of the screen; if the content is long, the page simply scrolls and the footer follows the content. (This is different from position: sticky, which keeps something fixed on screen while scrolling.)

5. Sidebar and content

<div class="layout">
  <aside class="sidebar">Menu</aside>
  <main class="content">Article text…</main>
</div>
.layout {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1.5rem;
  align-items: flex-start;    /* sidebar keeps its own height instead of stretching */
}
.sidebar {
  flex: 0 0 240px;            /* fixed 240px: no grow, no shrink */
}
.content {
  flex: 1;                    /* takes the rest */
  min-width: 0;               /* lets long code lines shrink instead of overflowing */
}

@media (max-width: 700px) {
  .layout { flex-direction: column; }   /* stack on phones */
}

6. Other quick patterns

/* Button with icon + text */
.btn { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem; }

/* Media object: image beside text */
.media { display: flex; gap: 1rem; align-items: flex-start; }
.media img { flex: none; width: 64px; height: 64px; border-radius: 50%; }

/* Equal-height cards with the button pinned to the bottom */
.card { display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.card .actions { margin-top: auto; }     /* pushes the actions down */

/* Tag chips that wrap */
.tags { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem; }

Rule: give the container room before you align

Vertical centring and bottom-pinning need a container taller than its content (min-height, a flex-column parent, or a parent with defined height). Otherwise there is no free space to distribute.

Convention: mobile-first flex

Start with a column (or a wrapping row) on small screens and switch to a row in a min-width media query, as shown in Responsive design.

Edge cases

  • An ul that is a flex container keeps its padding-left (the browser default) and bullets; reset them as in the navbar example.
  • Safari had bugs with gap in flexbox in very old versions; all current browsers support it.
  • The centred element's own margin still counts; margin: auto centres, margin-top offsets.

In real projects

React components often render a flex container with a few classes (className="flex items-center gap-4" in Tailwind). These patterns are exactly what those utility classes express; once you know them, reading Tailwind is trivial. Practise on Flexbox Froggy (flexboxfroggy.com) — see the Practice list.

Interview angle

  • "How do you centre a div?" — flex with justify-content and align-items: center (or grid place-items: center) plus a container height; also mention margin: auto for horizontal centring of a block with width.
  • "How do you make a sticky footer?" — flex column on body with min-height: 100dvh and flex: 1 on main.

CSS Grid: rows and columns together

Grid lays out items in two dimensions — you define columns and rows on the container (with fr, repeat() and minmax()) and the items fill or are placed into the cells; auto-fit with minmax() gives a responsive card grid with no media queries.

CSS Grid is the layout system for two dimensions: rows and columns at once. Where Flexbox lays items along one line and lets content decide, Grid lets you define the structure first (a table-like skeleton) and then put items into it. Use it for page layouts (header, sidebar, content, footer), dashboards, galleries and card grids.

A first grid

.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 1fr;   /* three columns: fixed, flexible, flexible */
  gap: 1rem;                              /* space between rows and columns */
}

Direct children are placed automatically, left to right, filling each row and then starting the next one. The number of rows follows from the number of items. The vocabulary:

Grid container / grid item
The element with display: grid and its direct children.
Grid line
The dividing lines, numbered from 1. Three columns have four vertical lines (1 to 4). Negative numbers count from the end: -1 is the last line.
Track
A row or column (the space between two lines).
Cell
One unit where a row and a column cross.
Area
A rectangle of one or more cells.

Defining tracks: fr, repeat() and minmax()

grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr;          /* shares: 25% / 50% / 25% of free space */
grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);       /* three equal columns */
grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 100px);     /* four fixed columns */
grid-template-columns: 250px 1fr;            /* sidebar + flexible content */
grid-template-columns: minmax(200px, 1fr) 3fr; /* at least 200px, else flexible */
grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;           /* header, stretchy middle, footer */
grid-auto-rows: minmax(100px, auto);         /* rows created automatically */
  • fr ("fraction") divides the free space left after fixed tracks and gaps: 1fr 2fr gives the second column twice the first. 1fr is really minmax(auto, 1fr), so a long word can still push the column wider than its share; use minmax(0, 1fr) to force an exact share.
  • repeat(count, size) avoids repeating yourself.
  • minmax(min, max) sets a range for a track.
  • Content-based keywords: auto (fit content, stretch if space is left), min-content (the narrowest the content can be), max-content (the widest it wants).

Implicit vs explicit grid

The tracks you declare with grid-template-* form the explicit grid. If there are more items than cells, the browser adds extra rows (or columns) on its own — the implicit grid. Control their size with grid-auto-rows and grid-auto-columns, and the filling order with grid-auto-flow (row by default, column, or dense to back-fill gaps).

Responsive card grid with no media queries

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

Read it aloud: "make as many columns as fit, each at least 250px wide, and share the leftover equally". On a 1,000px container you get three columns (3 × 250 = 750, the rest shared); on a 600px tablet two; on a 350px phone one. It is the single most useful Grid line. Unlike the Flexbox card row, all rows keep the same column widths.

auto-fill vs auto-fit

Both create as many tracks as fit. The difference shows when there are fewer items than tracks. auto-fill keeps the empty tracks, so three cards on a wide screen stay at their minimum-ish size, with empty columns on the right. auto-fit collapses the empty tracks to zero, so the existing cards stretch to fill the row. With many items, both look the same. Choose auto-fit when you want cards to stretch, auto-fill when you want a steady column rhythm.

A caution: minmax(250px, 1fr) overflows on screens narrower than 250px. For tiny screens use minmax(min(250px, 100%), 1fr).

Placing items: lines and span

.featured {
  grid-column: 1 / 3;        /* from line 1 to line 3 (spans two columns) */
  grid-row: 1 / 3;           /* spans two rows */
}
.wide    { grid-column: span 2; }       /* span two columns from wherever it lands */
.fullrow { grid-column: 1 / -1; }       /* from first to last line: the whole row */
.pinned  { grid-column: 3; grid-row: 2; }  /* a single cell */

grid-column: 1 / 3 is short for grid-column-start: 1; grid-column-end: 3. Items can overlap if you place them in the same cells; combine with z-index for layered designs.

Named areas: layout by drawing

For page layouts, grid-template-areas is the most readable way. You draw the layout with names:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header  header"
    "sidebar main"
    "footer  footer";
  min-height: 100dvh;
  gap: 1rem;
}
.page header  { grid-area: header; }
.page aside   { grid-area: sidebar; }
.page main    { grid-area: main; }
.page footer  { grid-area: footer; }

@media (max-width: 700px) {
  .page {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    grid-template-areas:
      "header"
      "main"
      "sidebar"
      "footer";
  }
}

Each string is a row; use a dot (.) for an empty cell. Areas must be rectangles. The responsive version just redraws the picture — a major advantage over Flexbox for page structure. (Rearranging a layout visually does not change the DOM order, so keep the HTML in a sensible reading order.)

Alignment in grid

PropertyOnDoes
justify-items, align-itemsContainerAlign all items inside their cells (inline/horizontal and block/vertical). Default stretch
place-itemsContainerShorthand: place-items: center centres in both directions
justify-content, align-contentContainerPlace the whole grid inside the container when the tracks are smaller than it
justify-self, align-self, place-selfItemAlign one item in its cell
gap, row-gap, column-gapContainerSpace between tracks

A dashboard example

.dashboard {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(12, 1fr);   /* a 12-column system like Bootstrap */
  gap: 1rem;
}
.kpi    { grid-column: span 3; }            /* four KPI tiles in a row */
.chart  { grid-column: span 8; }
.recent { grid-column: span 4; }

@media (max-width: 800px) {
  .kpi, .chart, .recent { grid-column: 1 / -1; }   /* each takes a full row */
}

Flexbox or Grid?

FlexboxGrid
DimensionsOne (row or column)Two (rows and columns)
Starts fromContent: items decide their size, the container fits themLayout: you define tracks, items fit in
Best forNavbars, toolbars, button rows, centring, small components, a row of unequal itemsPage layouts, galleries, dashboards, forms with aligned labels, anything with aligned rows and columns
WrappingWrapped lines are independent (items of different lines do not align)Columns stay aligned across rows
OverlapNeeds positioningNatural: place items in the same cell

A good rule: Grid for the page, Flexbox for the parts. Real pages use both — a grid for the page structure, flex rows inside the header, cards and buttons. If you find yourself fighting wrap behaviour or aligning columns across rows with Flexbox, switch to Grid. If you only need items in a line, Flexbox is simpler.

Subgrid (grid-template-columns: subgrid) lets nested grids align to the parent's tracks, useful for card content that must line up across cards; it is supported in current browsers.

Rule: only direct children are grid items

Like Flexbox, setting display: grid affects direct children only. Grandchildren need their own grid or flex container (or subgrid).

Conventions

  • Use gap instead of margins between items; use fr and minmax() instead of percentages (percentages plus a gap overflow).
  • Use repeat(auto-fit, minmax(…, 1fr)) for card grids, and grid-template-areas for page layouts.
  • Name areas after their purpose, matching the semantic elements.

Edge cases

  • Grid items have min-width: auto like flex items, so wide content stretches a 1fr column. Add min-width: 0 or use minmax(0, 1fr).
  • Items that are position: absolute inside a grid are positioned against the grid area if the container is positioned.
  • An unplaced item skips cells already occupied by explicit placements, which can create holes; grid-auto-flow: dense fills them at the cost of the visual order differing from the DOM.
  • Margins on grid items do not collapse.

Mistake: using percentages with gaps

Wrong: 3 × 33.33% + 2 gaps overflows

.grid { display: grid; gap: 1rem;
        grid-template-columns: 33.33% 33.33% 33.33%; }

Right: fr subtracts the gaps for you

.grid { display: grid; gap: 1rem;
        grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }

Interview angle

  • "Flexbox vs Grid?" — one-dimensional content-first versus two-dimensional layout-first; Grid for the page, Flexbox for components.
  • "What does repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)) do?" — responsive columns without media queries.
  • "What is fr?" — a fraction of the free space.
  • "auto-fit vs auto-fill?" — whether empty tracks collapse.

Positioning and stacking: relative, absolute, fixed, sticky and z-index

The position property takes an element out of or adjusts it within normal flow — absolute elements sit relative to the nearest positioned ancestor, fixed to the viewport, sticky switches between relative and fixed while scrolling, and z-index orders overlapping elements within stacking contexts.

Flexbox and Grid handle most layout now. position is for special cases: badges on cards, dropdown menus, modals, sticky headers, tooltips. You must understand it, because these are everywhere and the failure modes are confusing.

ValueIn normal flow?Positioned relative toTypical use
staticYes— (default; top/left/z-index are ignored)Normal elements
relativeYes (its original space stays)Its own normal positionSmall nudges; anchor for absolute children
absoluteNo (space removed)Nearest ancestor that is positioned (not static); else the page (initial containing block)Badges, icons in inputs, dropdowns, overlays
fixedNoThe viewportFixed headers, floating buttons, cookie banners
stickyYesNormal position until a scroll threshold, then sticks to its scroll containerSticky headers, table headings, sidebars

The offset properties top, right, bottom, left (and the shorthand inset) move a positioned element. inset: 0 means all four are 0.

relative

A relative element stays where it is in the flow, but top/left shift its drawing from that spot; the space it originally took is kept and other elements do not move. Its real power: it becomes the reference box for absolutely positioned children, even with no offsets at all.

absolute

An absolute element is removed from the flow (siblings act as if it is not there) and placed using its offsets inside its containing block: the padding box of the nearest ancestor with position other than static. If no ancestor is positioned, it uses the page itself — which is why an absolute badge "flies" to the top-left corner of the page when you forget to make the card relative.

.product-card {
  position: relative;          /* makes the card the anchor */
}
.product-card .badge {
  position: absolute;
  top: 0.5rem;
  right: 0.5rem;               /* 8px from the card's top-right corner */
  background: #dc2626;
  color: white;
  padding: 0.2rem 0.5rem;
  border-radius: 4px;
}

/* Cover the parent entirely: overlay */
.overlay { position: absolute; inset: 0; background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5); }

/* Centre an absolute element */
.modal {
  position: absolute;
  top: 50%;
  left: 50%;
  transform: translate(-50%, -50%);   /* shift back by half its own size */
}

Absolute elements do not take up space, so the parent can collapse in height, and they can overlap the content. A dropdown menu is the classic case: the wrapper is relative, the menu is absolute; top: 100%; left: 0.

fixed

A fixed element is positioned against the viewport and stays on screen when the page scrolls. Because it leaves the flow, other content slides under it; add padding or margin at the top of the page equal to the header height. A fixed element can be fooled into acting like absolute if an ancestor has a transform, filter or perspective (that ancestor becomes its containing block).

.top-bar {
  position: fixed;
  top: 0;
  left: 0;
  right: 0;                   /* full width */
  height: 3.5rem;
  z-index: 100;
}
body { padding-top: 3.5rem; } /* leave room so the content is not hidden */

.chat-button { position: fixed; bottom: 1rem; right: 1rem; }

sticky

Sticky is a hybrid: the element scrolls normally until it would pass a threshold you set with top (or another offset), and then it sticks — staying within its parent's bounds. Perfect for a table header or a section heading.

.site-header {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;                      /* required: without a threshold, nothing happens */
  background: white;
  z-index: 50;
}
thead th { position: sticky; top: 0; background: #f3f4f6; }
Why sticky "does not work"
  1. No threshold. You need at least one of top, bottom, left, right.
  2. An ancestor has overflow set (hidden, auto, scroll). Sticky sticks to the nearest ancestor that scrolls, and that ancestor does not scroll vertically. Check every parent in DevTools and remove the overflow.
  3. The parent is too short. A sticky element can move only inside its parent. If the parent is the same height as the element, there is nowhere to stick.
  4. A flex or grid parent stretches the item to the full height. Add align-self: flex-start to the sticky sidebar.
  5. No background, so content shows through, which looks like it is not working — add a background and z-index.

z-index and stacking contexts

When positioned elements overlap, z-index decides who is on top: a higher number is in front. It applies to positioned elements (anything except static) and to flex and grid items. Without it, later elements in the HTML paint over earlier ones.

The gotcha is that z-index is only comparable inside the same stacking context. A stacking context is like a separate deck of cards: the elements inside it are ordered among themselves, and the whole deck sits at one position among the cards of its parent. A new stacking context is created by: the root element; a positioned element with a z-index other than auto; position: fixed or sticky; opacity below 1; transform, filter, perspective, clip-path, mask; isolation: isolate; and flex or grid items with a z-index.

That is why "I set z-index: 9999 and it is still behind" happens: an ancestor created a context with a lower z-index. Fixes: move the element (render modals at the end of body, which is what React portals do), or remove the thing that created the context (often an accidental transform or opacity), or give the ancestor a higher z-index. In DevTools, the Layers view or an extension can show contexts.

Floats (legacy)

float: left was the old layout tool and is now used only to wrap text around an image. You will meet it in older code; replace it with Flexbox or Grid.

Rule: absolute needs a positioned parent

Whenever you write position: absolute on a child, decide which parent is the anchor and set position: relative on it. Make this a habit, and the "flying badge" bug disappears.

Conventions

  • Use Flexbox/Grid for layout; use positioning only for overlays, badges and sticky or fixed UI.
  • Keep a small, named scale of z-index values (CSS variables: --z-dropdown: 100; --z-modal: 1000) rather than random large numbers.
  • Always provide a background for sticky and fixed bars.

Edge cases

  • An absolute element with both left and right (and no width) stretches between them.
  • position: fixed misbehaves with iOS keyboards and mobile address bars; test on a device.
  • A sticky element inside a table works on th cells; thead and tr sticky support has varied. Use th.
  • Negative z-index can push an element behind its parent's background if the parent has none and creates no context.

Mistake: using position: absolute for page layout

Absolute elements do not affect each other or their parent's height, so everything breaks at another screen size or with longer text. Layout belongs to Flexbox and Grid.

Interview angle

  • "Explain the position values." — static, relative, absolute (nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (viewport), sticky (hybrid, needs an offset).
  • "Why doesn't my z-index work?" — stacking contexts; the element is not positioned; or an ancestor creates a lower context.
  • "Why doesn't sticky work?" — missing top, an ancestor with overflow, or a parent that is too short.

Responsive design: mobile-first, media queries and fluid layouts

Responsive design makes one page work on every screen: add the viewport meta tag, write the mobile layout first, add min-width media queries for larger screens, keep images fluid, and use clamp() and Grid auto-fit to reduce the number of breakpoints.

Most Indian users browse on phones, on screens from 360px to tablets and 1920px desktops. Responsive web design means a single codebase that adapts to all of them. It rests on three ideas: a flexible layout (percentages, Flexbox, Grid), flexible media (images that scale) and media queries (apply different CSS depending on the screen).

Step 1: the viewport meta tag

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

Without it, a phone shows your page at about 980px wide, zoomed out, and media queries never see a small width. This line goes in every page's head (see the boilerplate).

Step 2: write mobile-first

Mobile-first means your base CSS (no media query) is the phone layout; you then add @media (min-width: …) blocks that enhance the layout as the screen gets wider. This is simpler because a phone layout is usually a single column (the browser's natural flow), and the CSS the phone has to download and parse is the smallest.

/* Base: phone. One column, stacked. */
.layout { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }
.nav-links { display: none; }          /* hidden behind a menu button on phones */

/* Tablet and up */
@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
}

/* Desktop and up */
@media (min-width: 1024px) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr; }
  .nav-links { display: flex; gap: 1.5rem; }
}

The opposite, desktop-first, uses max-width queries to take features away for smaller screens. It works, but you end up undoing styles, and phones carry the heaviest CSS. Prefer min-width. Do not mix both styles in one stylesheet.

Media query syntax

@media (min-width: 768px) { … }                      /* width of 768px or more */
@media (max-width: 767.98px) { … }                   /* narrower than 768px */
@media (min-width: 600px) and (max-width: 900px) { … }
@media (orientation: landscape) { … }
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { … }            /* user chose dark mode */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { … }        /* user wants less animation */
@media (hover: hover) { a:hover { … } }              /* devices that can really hover */
@media print { nav { display: none; } }              /* styles for printing */
@media (width >= 768px) { … }                        /* modern range syntax, same meaning */

Breakpoints

A breakpoint is a width where the layout changes. Do not chase device models; set breakpoints where your content starts to look bad (drag the DevTools device toolbar wider until it breaks). As a starting point, the common values are:

Namemin-widthTypical device
Base (no query)0Phones, 360–480px wide
sm640pxLarge phones, landscape
md768pxTablets
lg1024pxSmall laptops
xl1280pxDesktops

(Tailwind's defaults are 640, 768, 1024, 1280 and 1536px; Bootstrap uses 576, 768, 992, 1200 and 1400px.) Keep to three or four, and define them as a team convention.

Flexible media

img, video, svg {
  max-width: 100%;      /* never wider than the parent */
  height: auto;         /* keep the proportions */
}
.thumb { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; object-fit: cover; width: 100%; }  /* uniform crops */

Use srcset to serve smaller image files to phones (Images). Wide tables get an overflow-x: auto wrapper.

Fewer breakpoints with modern tools

  • Grid auto-fit gives a column count that adapts to the width on its own (Grid).
  • Flex wrap with flex: 1 1 250px similarly (Flexbox layouts).
  • clamp() makes type and spacing fluid between a minimum and maximum:
h1      { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.2rem + 2.5vw, 3rem); }
section { padding-block: clamp(2rem, 6vw, 5rem); }
.container { width: min(100% - 2rem, 70rem); margin-inline: auto; }

Container queries (brief)

A media query looks at the screen. A container query looks at the width of the component's own container, so a card can switch between a stacked and a side-by-side layout depending on the space it gets, wherever you place it (a wide main area or a narrow sidebar). This suits reusable React components. It is supported in current browsers.

.card-wrapper { container-type: inline-size; }

.card { display: grid; gap: 0.5rem; }
@container (min-width: 480px) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 160px 1fr; }
}

Responsive navigation: the typical pattern

On phones the link list is hidden behind a button; on larger screens it shows inline. A no-JavaScript version can use a checkbox or the <details> element; in React you toggle a state variable and a class. Make sure the toggle is a real <button> with aria-expanded and aria-controls, and that the menu can be used with a keyboard (Accessibility).

Testing

  1. DevTools device toolbar (Ctrl+Shift+M): pick a phone, then drag the width through every size — not only the preset devices.
  2. Rotate to landscape. Zoom the browser to 200%. Increase the browser's default font size.
  3. Throttle the network to Slow 4G and check the loading experience.
  4. Open the page on a real phone on the same network (use your computer's IP address and Vite's --host option).
  5. Check there is no horizontal scrollbar at 320px width.

Rules

  • Always include the viewport meta tag.
  • Use min-width queries (mobile-first) consistently.
  • Never disable zoom; touch targets about 44 × 44 pixels.

Conventions

  • Set breakpoints from your content; keep them in one place (or use framework defaults); put each component's queries beside the component's CSS.
  • Do not hide important content on mobile; a smaller screen needs the same information, arranged differently.
  • Use relative units so text and spacing follow the user's settings.

Edge cases

  • Media queries cannot use CSS variables in the condition (@media (min-width: var(--md)) is invalid). Tailwind and Sass generate the values for you.
  • A max-width: 768px query and a min-width: 768px query both match at exactly 768px. Use 767.98px for the max, or the range syntax (width < 768px).
  • Hover-only features break on touch; use @media (hover: hover) and provide a tap alternative.
  • The DevTools emulator does not reproduce real mobile performance or the address-bar behaviour.

Mistakes

  • Forgetting the viewport meta tag, then wondering why media queries "do not work" on the phone.
  • Fixed pixel widths (width: 1200px) instead of max-width.
  • Designing only at 1920px and 375px; the in-between widths are where layouts break.

Interview angle

  • "What is responsive design?" — one codebase adapting to all screens via fluid layout, flexible media, media queries.
  • "Mobile-first vs desktop-first?" — base styles for small screens and min-width enhancements versus the reverse.
  • "How do you make images responsive?" — max-width: 100%; height: auto, srcset.
  • "How do you test?" — DevTools device mode, real devices, throttling.

Transitions, transforms and animations

A transition smoothly animates a property between two states (like normal and hover), transform moves, scales or rotates without disturbing layout, and @keyframes build multi-step animations — animate transform and opacity for smooth performance, and respect prefers-reduced-motion.

Small amounts of motion make an interface feel alive and explain changes (a menu sliding in, a button reacting). Too much is distracting and slow. CSS gives you three tools: transitions (from state A to state B), transforms (change shape or position visually) and keyframe animations (many steps, loops, no trigger needed).

Transitions

Put the transition on the element's base rule. When a listed property changes — because of :hover, :focus, a class toggled by JavaScript — the browser animates between the old and new values instead of jumping.

.button {
  background: #1a56db;
  transform: translateY(0);
  transition: background-color 200ms ease, transform 200ms ease;
}
.button:hover,
.button:focus-visible {
  background: #1e429f;
  transform: translateY(-2px);
}
PropertyMeaningExample
transition-propertyWhich properties animatebackground-color, transform, or all (avoid)
transition-durationHow long200ms, 0.3s
transition-timing-functionThe speed curveease (default), linear, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out, cubic-bezier(…)
transition-delayWait before starting100ms
transitionShorthand: property duration timing delayopacity 0.3s ease-out 0.1s

Good durations: 100–300ms for small UI feedback, up to 500ms for larger movements. ease-out (fast start, slow end) feels natural for things entering; ease-in for leaving. Not every property can animate: those with numeric or colour values can (width, opacity, color, transform), but display (none to block) cannot, and a transition from height: auto does not work. Fade with opacity and visibility, or animate max-height, or use the newer features if you need them.

Transforms

transform changes how an element is drawn without affecting the layout: neighbours do not move, and the element keeps its original space.

.a { transform: translate(20px, -10px); }  /* move x, y (% = of its own size) */
.b { transform: scale(1.1); }              /* grow 10%; scale(1, 0.5) squashes */
.c { transform: rotate(45deg); }           /* clockwise */
.d { transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.05) rotate(2deg); }  /* combine, in order */
.e { transform-origin: top left; }         /* the pivot point (default: centre) */

Order matters when combining: transforms apply right to left in terms of the coordinate system, so translate(100px) rotate(45deg) and rotate(45deg) translate(100px) end up in different places. The separate properties translate, scale and rotate also exist in current browsers and can be transitioned independently. Percentages in translate refer to the element's own size, which is why translate(-50%, -50%) centres an absolute element.

Keyframe animations

For motion that has several steps, loops or starts on its own (a loading spinner, a fade-in on page load), define the steps with @keyframes and attach them with animation.

@keyframes fade-in-up {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(16px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

.card {
  animation: fade-in-up 400ms ease-out both;
}

@keyframes spin {
  to { transform: rotate(360deg); }
}
.spinner {
  width: 2rem;
  height: 2rem;
  border: 3px solid #e5e7eb;
  border-top-color: #1a56db;
  border-radius: 50%;
  animation: spin 800ms linear infinite;
}

@keyframes pulse {
  0%, 100% { opacity: 1; }
  50%      { opacity: 0.4; }
}
.skeleton { animation: pulse 1.5s ease-in-out infinite; background: #e5e7eb; }
PropertyMeaning
animation-nameThe @keyframes to use
animation-durationLength of one cycle
animation-timing-functionSpeed curve (applied between each keyframe)
animation-delayWait before starting
animation-iteration-countNumber of times, or infinite
animation-directionnormal, reverse, alternate (back and forth)
animation-fill-modeboth keeps the first keyframe before the start (during the delay) and the last one after the end; without it the element snaps back
animation-play-staterunning or paused

Triggering by JavaScript is simple: add or remove a class (el.classList.add("is-open")) and let CSS do the animation. Listen to transitionend or animationend events if you must run code when it finishes.

Performance: animate transform and opacity

Remember the rendering pipeline (How the browser renders a page). Animating width, height, top, left or margin forces layout on every frame, which janks on cheap phones. Animating transform and opacity can be done on the GPU compositor with no layout and no repaint, and stays at 60 frames per second. So:

  • Move with transform: translate(), not left/top.
  • Resize with transform: scale() where possible, not width/height.
  • Fade with opacity.
  • Do not use transition: all; name the properties. It animates things you did not intend and can trigger layout.
  • The will-change: transform hint prepares the browser for an upcoming animation. Use it rarely and remove it afterwards; overuse wastes memory.

Check animation smoothness in DevTools → Performance, and the Rendering panel's "Paint flashing" option.

Respect reduced motion

Some people feel dizzy or ill from parallax, zooming and large movement (vestibular disorders), and some simply turn off animations in their operating system. The media query prefers-reduced-motion detects it. This is an accessibility requirement under WCAG.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

This blunt reset is one of the rare acceptable uses of !important. A subtler approach removes only large movement and keeps gentle fades. Also avoid anything that flashes more than three times per second.

Rule: put the transition on the base state, not only on :hover

If transition is only in :hover, the element animates when you enter but jumps back instantly when you leave, since the leaving state has no transition. Declare it in the normal rule so both directions animate.

Conventions

  • Keep UI motion short (150–300ms) and subtle; use one or two easing curves across the product.
  • Animate transform and opacity; list properties explicitly.
  • Always include a prefers-reduced-motion block; never convey information by motion alone.
  • Do the state change in CSS (classes), the logic in JavaScript.

Edge cases

  • Transitions do not run when an element is first inserted (no previous state) or when it goes from display: none; use a keyframe animation for entering elements, or the newer @starting-style and transition-behavior: allow-discrete where supported.
  • An element with a transform becomes a containing block for fixed descendants and a new stacking context (Positioning).
  • Hover-based transitions do not help on touch screens; also support :focus-visible.
  • Frameworks like React need the element to exist at both states to animate; libraries such as Framer Motion or React Transition Group help with enter and exit.

Interview angle

  • "Transition vs animation?" — transitions go between two states when a property changes; animations use keyframes, can loop and need no trigger.
  • "Which properties should you animate and why?" — transform, opacity: composited, no layout or paint.
  • "How do you handle users who dislike motion?" — prefers-reduced-motion.

Tailwind CSS and Bootstrap

Tailwind is a utility-first framework where you style by combining small single-purpose classes in the HTML (flex, p-4, md:grid-cols-3, hover:bg-blue-700), while Bootstrap supplies ready-made components and a 12-column grid — learn plain CSS first, then use whichever your team chose.

Writing every rule by hand is flexible but slow, and large teams need consistency. CSS frameworks give you a ready design system. You must know the CSS basics from this module first: Tailwind classes are nothing but short names for the properties you have just learned, and you cannot debug them without that knowledge. Two frameworks dominate: Tailwind (very common with React in startups and product companies) and Bootstrap (very common in service-company and older enterprise projects).

The utility-first idea

In traditional CSS you invent a class name (.card), then write its rules in another file. In Tailwind you compose the look directly from tiny classes, each doing one thing:

<div class="product-card">
  <h3 class="product-title">Masala Dosa Mix</h3>
  <button class="buy-button">Add to cart</button>
</div>
<div class="rounded-xl border border-gray-200 bg-white p-4 shadow-sm">
  <h3 class="text-lg font-semibold text-gray-900">Masala Dosa Mix</h3>
  <button class="mt-3 rounded-md bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 text-white
                 hover:bg-blue-700 focus-visible:outline-2">
    Add to cart
  </button>
</div>

No separate CSS file, no naming, no worry that changing .card breaks another page. The build tool scans your files and generates CSS only for the classes you used, so the final stylesheet is small. The cost: long class lists in the markup. In React you solve this by making a component (<ProductCard />) once and reusing it, so the long list appears in one place.

Setup with Vite (React)

$ npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react
$ cd my-app
$ npm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import tailwindcss from "@tailwindcss/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), tailwindcss()],
});
@import "tailwindcss";

Tailwind v4 vs v3

The setup above is Tailwind v4's CSS-first approach: one @import "tailwindcss" line and the Vite plugin, with no tailwind.config.js needed by default; customisation (colours, fonts) goes in CSS with @theme. Tailwind v3 projects, still common, use tailwind.config.js with a content list and the three @tailwind base/components/utilities directives, plus PostCSS. The utility class names are mostly the same, so what you learn here applies to both. Always follow the official installation guide at tailwindcss.com for your version.

Then import index.css in main.jsx and use classes in JSX with className. Install the "Tailwind CSS IntelliSense" extension in VS Code for autocomplete and hover previews.

Common utilities

The names are systematic. The spacing scale is in units of 0.25rem (4px): p-4 = 1rem = 16px.

AreaClassesEquivalent CSS
Spacingp-4, px-6, py-2, m-2, mt-4, mx-auto, gap-4, space-y-2padding, margin, gap
Sizingw-full, w-1/2, max-w-md, h-10, min-h-screenwidth, max-width, height
Flexflex, flex-col, items-center, justify-between, flex-wrap, flex-1display:flex and its properties
Gridgrid, grid-cols-3, col-span-2, gap-4display:grid, repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr))
Typographytext-lg, font-bold, text-center, leading-relaxed, tracking-wide, truncatefont-size, weight, align, line-height…
Coloursbg-blue-600, text-gray-700, border-red-500, bg-white/80background, color, border-color (the /80 sets opacity)
