Borders, effectsrounded-lg, border, shadow-md, opacity-50border-radius, border, box-shadow
Positionrelative, absolute, inset-0, top-2, sticky, z-10position and offsets
Displayhidden, block, inline-blockdisplay
Arbitrary valuesw-[340px], bg-[#1a56db], grid-cols-[200px_1fr]one-off values

Responsive and state prefixes

A prefix and a colon apply a utility only in a condition. Responsive prefixes are mobile-first min-width queries: an unprefixed class is the base; md: applies from 768px upwards.

<ul class="grid grid-cols-1 gap-4 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4">
  <li class="rounded-lg bg-white p-4 shadow">…</li>
</ul>

<nav class="flex flex-col gap-2 md:flex-row md:items-center md:gap-6">…</nav>
PrefixApplies when
sm: md: lg: xl: 2xl:Viewport at least 640 / 768 / 1024 / 1280 / 1536px
hover: focus: focus-visible: active: disabled:That state of the element
first: last: odd: even:Position among siblings
dark:Dark mode
group-hover:, peer-checked:When a parent marked group (or a sibling marked peer) is in that state
motion-reduce:The user prefers reduced motion

Prefixes stack: md:hover:bg-blue-700. Dark mode uses the dark: prefix: bg-white dark:bg-gray-900 text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100. By default it follows the operating system setting (prefers-color-scheme); to switch it with a button, you configure it to use a class or attribute on html (see the Tailwind docs for your version).

Tailwind pros and cons

Pros

  • Fast to build: no switching between files and no naming
  • Consistent spacing, colours and sizes from one design scale
  • Small production CSS, since unused classes are never generated
  • Changes are local: editing one element cannot break another
  • Responsive, state and dark variants are one prefix away

Cons

  • Long class strings; HTML is harder to scan
  • You must know CSS anyway; the learning curve is the class names
  • Needs a build step and tooling
  • Component reuse needs discipline (React components)
  • Different feel from "semantic" CSS; some teams dislike it

Bootstrap in brief

Bootstrap is a component library with a design: buttons, navbars, cards, modals, forms and a responsive 12-column grid, all styled out of the box. Add it with a CDN link or npm install bootstrap.

<div class="container">
  <div class="row g-3">
    <div class="col-12 col-md-6 col-lg-4">
      <div class="card">
        <div class="card-body">
          <h5 class="card-title">Masala Dosa Mix</h5>
          <a href="#" class="btn btn-primary">Add to cart</a>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
  • Grid: .container centres and limits width; .row is a flex row of 12 columns; .col-12 .col-md-6 .col-lg-4 mean full width on phones, half from 768px, a third from 992px. It is mobile-first like Tailwind.
  • Components: .btn .btn-primary, .navbar, .card, .modal, .alert, .form-control. Some need Bootstrap's JavaScript (modals, dropdowns, collapse) — in React use the React-Bootstrap library instead of the jQuery-era scripts.
  • Utilities exist too: d-flex, justify-content-between, mt-3, text-center, p-4.
  • Customise with Sass variables or CSS variables. Without that, every Bootstrap site looks like Bootstrap.

Plain CSS vs Tailwind vs Bootstrap

Plain CSSTailwindBootstrap
IdeaWrite your own rulesCompose utility classesUse prebuilt components
Design freedomTotalTotal, within a scaleLimited unless you customise
Speed to first screenSlowestFastFastest (looks decent at once)
Looks uniqueYesYesNeeds work
LearningThe foundationNeeds CSS + class namesNeeds CSS + component names
Common inEverywhere, small apps, design systemsReact/Next.js startups, product teamsEnterprise, service projects, admin panels

There are also component libraries built on these ideas — shadcn/ui and Headless UI (Tailwind based), Material UI and Ant Design (own styling) — that you will meet in React projects.

Rule: learn the CSS first

You cannot read items-center, col-span-2 or .row without knowing Flexbox and Grid. When a framework "does not work", the fix is almost always CSS knowledge: specificity, the box model, positioning contexts.

Conventions

  • With Tailwind: extract repeated class lists into React components (not into @apply), keep class order consistent (the official Prettier plugin sorts them), and use your theme's colours, not random hex values.
  • Never build class names by string concatenation like "bg-" + color + "-500": Tailwind scans the source as text and will not generate classes it cannot see written in full. Map to complete class names instead.
  • With Bootstrap: use its grid and components as documented; add your own CSS in a separate file loaded after Bootstrap rather than editing Bootstrap's files.

Edge cases

  • Tailwind's preflight (a CSS reset) removes default heading sizes, list bullets and margins — an h1 looks like plain text until you add classes.
  • Utility classes on the same element conflict by their order in the generated CSS, not in your class attribute: class="p-2 p-4" does not mean "p-4 wins" by position. Do not add both; compute one.
  • Bootstrap's old versions needed jQuery; Bootstrap 5 does not.

Interview angle

  • "What is utility-first CSS?" — style by composing small single-purpose classes in markup; consistent scale, small output.
  • "Tailwind vs Bootstrap?" — utilities versus prebuilt components; design freedom versus speed of a default look.
  • "How do you do responsive in Tailwind?" — mobile-first prefixes like md: and lg:.

Organising CSS and debugging it

Keep CSS maintainable with a small reset, a flat naming scheme such as BEM, low-specificity single-class selectors, variables for design tokens and one file per component — and debug problems in DevTools by checking the Styles, Computed and layout overlays.

CSS has no compiler, no types and no private scope. Everything is global, and the cascade connects it all. A stylesheet that grows without rules turns into a "append-only" mess that nobody dares to change. A few habits prevent that — much like the package structure and naming rules that keep a Java codebase healthy.

A small reset

Browsers apply their own default styles, differently from each other. A reset gives a consistent base. You do not need a heavy one; a few lines are enough:

*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

body {
  margin: 0;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
  color: var(--color-text, #1f2937);
}
img, video, svg { max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; }
button, input, select, textarea { font: inherit; }   /* forms use the page font */
h1, h2, h3, p { margin-block: 0 0.75em; }
a { color: inherit; }
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #1a56db; outline-offset: 2px; }

Well-known ready-made options are normalize.css (fixes browser differences but keeps the defaults), and "modern resets" such as Josh Comeau's or Andy Bell's. Tailwind ships its own (preflight); Bootstrap uses "Reboot".

Naming: BEM in brief

BEM (Block, Element, Modifier) is a naming convention that keeps selectors flat and self-explanatory.

  • Block: a standalone component — .card, .nav, .search-form.
  • Element: a part of the block — .card__title, .card__image (two underscores).
  • Modifier: a variant or state — .card--featured, .button--large (two hyphens).
<article class="card card--featured">
  <img class="card__image" src="dosa.jpg" alt="Masala dosa" width="400" height="300">
  <h3 class="card__title">Masala Dosa</h3>
  <a class="card__link button button--large" href="/menu/dosa">Order</a>
</article>
.card { border: 1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius: 12px; padding: 1rem; }
.card--featured { border-color: #f59e0b; }
.card__title { font-size: 1.25rem; margin: 0 0 0.5rem; }
.card__image { border-radius: 8px; }

Every selector is a single class (specificity 0-1-0), so nothing fights anything else and any later rule can override. The name tells you where it is used. You do not need strict BEM; the lesson is: one class per thing, flat selectors, meaningful names. In React with CSS Modules (Card.module.css), class names are made unique automatically, so you can write short names like .title per component.

Avoid deep selectors and over-qualification

Wrong: tied to the HTML structure

#sidebar div.widget ul li a.link { color: red; }
div.card h3 { margin: 0; }

Right: a class where you need it

.widget__link { color: red; }
.card__title { margin: 0; }

The long selector breaks the moment someone adds a wrapper div, is hard to override (high specificity) and slower to read. Rules of thumb: no IDs, no more than two or three parts, and do not qualify a class with a tag (div.card).

Structure of a project

css/
  base.css          reset, :root variables, body, typography
  layout.css        container, grid and page-level layouts
  components/
    button.css
    card.css
    navbar.css
  utilities.css     tiny helpers: .visually-hidden, .text-center
  styles.css        imports the above (or the build tool bundles them)

Order matters: base first, then layout, components, utilities last (so helpers win). In React projects you usually keep one CSS file (or module) beside each component, and a global file for the reset and variables. Use CSS custom properties for design tokens (Colours, typography and variables). Sass/SCSS adds nesting, partials and variables; native CSS now has nesting and variables too (& .child { } inside a rule), so you can often skip Sass in new projects.

Debugging CSS in DevTools

  1. Find it. Right-click → Inspect. Is the right element selected (maybe a child is covering it)?
  2. Read Styles. Your rule present? Struck through (lost the cascade)? A warning icon (invalid)? A greyed property (no effect in this context)?
  3. Check Computed. Final value and the winning rule. Filter by property name.
  4. Check the box model diagram for unexpected margin, padding or width, and the layout overlays for Flexbox and Grid (click the badge in the Elements tree).
  5. Toggle and edit live. Untick declarations to find the one causing the issue; change values; use :hov to force hover/focus states.
  6. Find overflow. Run in the Console: [...document.querySelectorAll("*")].filter(e => e.scrollWidth > document.documentElement.clientWidth) — it lists the elements that are wider than the page.
  7. Outline everything. Temporarily add * { outline: 1px solid red; } to see every box. (Outline takes no space, unlike border.)
  8. Isolate. Copy the HTML and CSS into a small file and remove things until the bug disappears.
Frequent causes and quick checks
SymptomCheck
Style does nothingCSS file loaded (Network 404)? Selector matches? Typo? Struck through?
Cannot centreIs the property on the parent? Does the container have height? Is the element inline?
width/margin ignoredInline element? Use block or inline-block
Absolute element in the wrong placeParent not position: relative
z-index ignoredElement static? Different stacking context?
Page wider than the screencontent-box, 100vw, a wide image/table, no min-width: 0 on a flex item
Works on desktop onlyViewport meta missing? Fixed widths? Hover-only?
Old CSS still showsCache: hard reload, "Disable cache"

Tooling worth adding

  • Prettier formats CSS automatically; Stylelint catches invalid properties, duplicates and overly specific selectors.
  • VS Code's built-in CSS validation and the CSS Peek / IntelliSense extensions.
  • The DevTools Coverage tab (Command menu → "Show Coverage") shows how much of your CSS is unused.

Rule: one component, one block of CSS, no reaching into others

A component's styles should not rely on its parent's class names or style other components' internals. When one block needs to change another, add a modifier class instead.

Conventions

  • Single-class selectors, kebab-case names, BEM or CSS Modules, no IDs, no !important.
  • Design tokens in variables; magic numbers explained with a comment.
  • Delete dead CSS (check Coverage) instead of piling overrides on top.

Edge cases

  • CSS Modules and CSS-in-JS rename classes at build time; in DevTools you will see names like Card_title__x7Gq2. That is normal.
  • Global resets and third-party library CSS can change your elements; check the order of the imports.
  • Native CSS nesting is supported in current browsers; check your target browsers before relying on it without a build step.

Mistake: adding more and more overrides instead of fixing the original rule

Each override raises the specificity bar; finally someone adds !important. Refactor the base rule so one clear rule applies, and delete the old ones.

Interview angle

  • "How do you keep CSS maintainable?" — flat single-class selectors, a naming scheme like BEM, variables, component files, no !important, a reset.
  • "How do you debug a CSS issue?" — DevTools Styles/Computed, box model, layout overlays, toggle declarations, isolate.

Interview questions — CSS

How does CSS decide which rule wins? How do you calculate specificity?

First importance and origin (!important, author over browser styles), then specificity, then source order — later wins a tie. Specificity is compared as ID count, then class/attribute/pseudo-class count, then type/pseudo-element count; inline styles beat all selectors. For example #nav .item a is 1-1-1 and beats .nav .item a.link at 0-3-1.

What is inheritance? Which properties inherit?

Some properties pass from parent to child automatically — mostly text ones such as color, font-family, font-size, line-height and text-align. Box properties such as margin, padding, border, background and width do not. inherit, initial, unset and revert control this explicitly.

Explain the box model and box-sizing.

Every element is a box of content, padding, border and margin. With content-box (the default) width is only the content, so padding and border add to the total. With border-box the width includes padding and border, which is predictable, so we reset it globally with *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }.

What is margin collapsing?

Adjacent vertical margins of block elements merge into one, with the size of the larger, rather than adding up. It also happens between a parent and its first or last child when nothing separates them. It does not happen in flex or grid containers or with padding/border/overflow on the parent. Using gap or margin in a single direction avoids surprises.

em vs rem vs px vs %?

px is fixed; rem is relative to the root font size (16px by default) and respects the user's browser setting; em is relative to the element's own (or parent's, for font-size) font size and compounds when nested; % depends on the property, usually the parent's size. Use rem for fonts and spacing, px for borders and shadows.

How do you centre a div horizontally and vertically?

Make the parent a flex container with justify-content: center; align-items: center; and give it a height (for example min-height: 100dvh). Or use display: grid; place-items: center. For horizontal-only, give a block a width and margin-inline: auto. An absolute alternative is top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%) inside a positioned parent.

Explain Flexbox: main axis, cross axis and flex: 1.

Flexbox lays out items in one dimension. The main axis follows flex-direction; the cross axis is perpendicular. justify-content distributes items along the main axis and align-items along the cross axis. flex: 1 is 1 1 0: the item may grow and shrink and starts from a zero basis, so items with flex: 1 share the space equally.

Flexbox vs Grid — when do you use which?

Flexbox is one-dimensional and content-driven: navbars, toolbars, rows of buttons, centring. Grid is two-dimensional and layout-driven: page structures, galleries and dashboards where rows and columns must align. Real pages use Grid for the overall layout and Flexbox inside components.

What does grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)) do?

It creates as many columns as fit in the container, each at least 250px and sharing the remaining space equally, so the grid adapts from one column on phones to several on desktops without media queries. auto-fit collapses empty tracks so existing items stretch; auto-fill keeps them.

Explain the position values.

static is the default flow. relative offsets from the normal position and is the anchor for absolute children. absolute leaves the flow and positions against the nearest positioned ancestor. fixed positions against the viewport. sticky behaves as relative until a scroll threshold (top), then sticks within its scroll container.

My z-index: 9999 does not work. Why?

Either the element is not positioned (static), or it sits inside a stacking context created by an ancestor (positioned with a z-index, or opacity below 1, transform, filter…). Z-index values only compete within the same stacking context, so the whole ancestor is stacked at its own level. Fix the ancestor, or move the element (a portal for modals).

Why might position: sticky not work?

No top (or other offset) is set; an ancestor has overflow hidden/auto/scroll, which becomes the scroll container; the parent is no taller than the element; or a flex/grid parent stretches the element. Fix the cause, for instance align-self: flex-start in a flex layout.

What is mobile-first design and how do you implement it?

You write the base CSS for small screens and add @media (min-width: …) blocks that enhance the layout for larger ones. It needs the viewport meta tag, fluid layouts (Flexbox, Grid, max-width), images with max-width: 100%, and relative units. It keeps the base CSS small and simple, and avoids undoing desktop styles on phones.

Transition vs animation? Which properties should you animate?

A transition animates between two states when a property changes; an animation uses @keyframes, can have many steps, loop and start without a trigger. Animate transform and opacity, which the browser can composite without layout or paint; avoid animating width, height, top or left. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.

Why use Tailwind (or not)? How does it differ from Bootstrap?

Tailwind provides small utility classes composed in markup — fast, consistent, small output, but long class lists and a build step. Bootstrap provides prebuilt styled components and a grid — fastest start, but sites look alike unless customised. Both need solid CSS knowledge and both are mobile-first.

Cheat sheet — CSS

  • Add CSS external <link rel="stylesheet"> in head (preferred); never rely on inline styles
  • Rule selector { property: value; } — end every line with a semicolon; invalid lines are ignored silently
  • Selectors p, .class, #id, [attr], a b, a > b, a + b, a ~ b, a, b
  • Pseudo :hover, :focus-visible, :nth-child(), :not(); ::before, ::after, ::placeholder
  • Specificity inline > ID > class/attribute/pseudo-class > tag; equal → later wins; avoid !important
  • Inherited color, font, line-height, text-align; not margin, padding, border, background, width
  • Variables --brand: #1a56db; on :root; use var(--brand, fallback)
  • Box model content + padding + border + margin; reset box-sizing: border-box
  • Margin collapse adjacent vertical margins merge; not in flex or grid
  • Units rem for type and space, px for borders, %/fr for fluid, dvh for mobile full height, ch for line length
  • Math calc(), min(), max(), clamp(min, preferred, max)
  • Flex container display:flex, flex-direction, justify-content (main), align-items (cross), flex-wrap, gap
  • Flex item flex: grow shrink basis; flex:1 equal shares; flex:none fixed; align-self; order
  • Flex gotchas container needs height to centre vertically; min-width: 0 to let items shrink
  • Centre flex: justify-content + align-items: center; grid: place-items: center
  • Grid grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr), gap, grid-column: span 2, grid-template-areas
  • Responsive grid repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr))
  • Flex vs Grid one dimension vs two; Grid for the page, Flexbox for the parts
  • Position relative (anchor), absolute (nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (viewport), sticky (needs top)
  • z-index works on positioned or flex/grid items; compared only within a stacking context
  • Responsive viewport meta + mobile-first min-width queries + max-width: 100% images
  • Breakpoints about 640 / 768 / 1024 / 1280px; choose them from the content
  • Motion animate transform and opacity; transition on the base rule; honour prefers-reduced-motion
  • Tailwind utility classes, md: responsive and hover: state prefixes, dark:; never build class names dynamically
  • Organise reset, single-class BEM names, tokens as variables, no IDs, shallow selectors

Practice — CSS

  1. Specificity quiz. Write five conflicting rules for one paragraph (a tag, a class, a tag with a class, an id, an inline style). Predict the colour, then check in DevTools (Styles shows what lost). Done when all five predictions are right and you can explain each score.
  2. Box model by hand. Make a 300px wide box with padding, border and margin, first with content-box, then border-box. Measure the box in DevTools and note the totals. Done when the numbers match your calculation (344px and 300px).
  3. Flexbox Froggy. Complete all levels of Flexbox Froggy (flexboxfroggy.com). Done when you can explain justify-content, align-items, flex-direction, order and align-self without notes.
  4. CSS Grid Garden. Complete all levels of Grid Garden (cssgridgarden.com). Done when you can write grid-column, grid-row and grid-area placements from memory.
  5. Five Flexbox layouts. Build from scratch, without copying: a navbar (logo left, links right), a centred login card on a full screen, a wrapping card row, a sticky footer, and a sidebar with content that stacks on phones. Done when each works at 320px and 1440px.
  6. Style the profile page (roadmap build). Take your semantic profile page from the HTML practice and style it with plain CSS only: reset, variables for colours and spacing, system font stack, a flex navbar, a sticky header, a hero section, a project cards grid with auto-fit, hover and focus states with transitions, a footer and a dark-mode variant with prefers-color-scheme. Done when Lighthouse gives 90+ for accessibility and the page works at 320px with no horizontal scroll.
  7. Responsive landing page (roadmap build). Pick a free design from Frontend Mentor (frontendmentor.io), a "newbie" or "junior" landing page challenge. Build it mobile-first with Flexbox and Grid: a header with a collapsing menu, hero, feature cards, testimonial and footer. Compare against the mobile and desktop previews at the specified widths. Done when it matches both previews and passes the keyboard-only test.
  8. Positioning lab. Build a product card with an absolutely positioned "Sale" badge, a sticky table header inside a scrolling container, and a modal overlay with a centred dialog using position: fixed. Then deliberately break it: remove position: relative from the card and put overflow: hidden on a parent of the sticky header; fix each in DevTools.
  9. Animate safely. Add a button hover transition, a card fade-in-up animation and a loading spinner. Then add the prefers-reduced-motion block and test it by turning on "reduce motion" in your operating system or in DevTools (Rendering panel). Done when the Performance panel shows no layout work during the animations.
  10. Rebuild with Tailwind. Create a Vite + React project, install Tailwind, and rebuild the product card and the navbar with utility classes only, including md: and hover: variants and dark mode. Done when the Tailwind version looks identical to your plain-CSS one and you can point to the CSS each class generates.
4

Module 4·About 3 weeks · the coreMust

JavaScript

25 topics · about 3 h of reading

JavaScript is the programming language of the browser. Every button that reacts, every form that checks your input before sending it, every list that updates without a page reload — that is JavaScript. React (Module 5) is a JavaScript library, and when your React app calls your Spring Boot API (Module 6) it does so with the JavaScript you learn here. This is the core module of the frontend page, so take your time with it.

As a Java developer you will find the syntax familiar: curly braces, if, for, class, try/catch. That familiarity is the trap. Under the same-looking syntax, JavaScript works very differently: values have types but variables do not, there is only one number type, functions are values, this changes with how you call a function, and all your code runs on one thread with an event loop. Every article in this module points out where JavaScript differs from Java.

  • Explain how JavaScript differs from Java and avoid the classic traps (==, coercion, this, floating-point numbers).
  • Write modern JavaScript: const/let, arrow functions, destructuring, spread, template literals and modules.
  • Transform data with map, filter, reduce and find instead of hand-written loops.
  • Build small apps with the DOM and events, without any framework.
  • Understand scope, closures, this, prototypes and the event loop well enough to answer "what does this print?" questions.
  • Call a REST API with fetch, handle every kind of error and send a JWT.
  • Use ES modules, npm and local storage the way real projects do.

Where JavaScript runs and how to add it to a page

JavaScript runs inside a JavaScript engine — built into every browser and into Node.js on servers; on a web page you load it with a <script> tag, normally with defer or type="module", and you watch it work in the browser console.

The language, the engine and the host

People use the word "JavaScript" for three different things. Keep them apart and many confusing errors start to make sense.

ECMAScript
The official language specification (ECMA-262), maintained by a committee called TC39. A new edition is published every year. ES2015 (also called ES6) was the big modern update — let, const, arrow functions, classes, modules, promises. Later editions are named by year (ES2016, ES2017 … ES2025 …). "Modern JavaScript" means ES2015 and later.
Engine
The program that executes JavaScript: V8 (Chrome, Edge, Node.js), SpiderMonkey (Firefox) and JavaScriptCore (Safari). An engine parses your source code, turns it into bytecode, interprets it, and compiles frequently used ("hot") functions to machine code with a JIT (just-in-time) compiler — the same idea as the JVM's HotSpot JIT.
Host environment
The program that embeds the engine and adds its own APIs. The browser adds the DOM (document), fetch, setTimeout, localStorage and many more. Node.js adds files, HTTP servers and process, but has no DOM.

This split explains real errors. document.querySelector() is not part of the JavaScript language; it is a browser API. Run it in Node.js and you get ReferenceError: document is not defined. In the same way, Node's require("fs") fails in a browser with ReferenceError: require is not defined. The language is the same; the host decides which extra objects exist.

One more fact clears up a common confusion: JavaScript has nothing to do with Java. It was created at Netscape in 1995, and the name was a marketing decision made while Java was popular. The two languages share C-style syntax and nothing else.

Is JavaScript compiled or interpreted?

Both, inside the engine. You never run a separate compile step like javac: the browser downloads your source code and the engine parses, interprets and JIT-compiles it on the spot. A syntax error is therefore found only when the file is loaded, and it stops that whole file from running. In real projects, tools such as Vite and TypeScript transform your code before it ships (bundling, minifying, removing types), but what the browser finally receives is still plain JavaScript source.

Adding JavaScript to a page

You attach JavaScript to an HTML page with the <script> element. You can write code inside the tag (an inline script) or point to a file with src (an external script). External files are the professional choice: the browser can cache them, and your HTML stays clean.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Order status</title>
  <!-- downloads in parallel, runs after the HTML is parsed -->
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
</head>
<body>
  <h1 id="status">Loading…</h1>
</body>
</html>
const heading = document.getElementById("status");
heading.textContent = "Order #1042 is out for delivery";
console.log("app.js ran after the HTML was parsed");

The attribute on the <script> tag decides when the code runs. This is one of the most common interview questions on the frontend.

TagDownloadWhen it runsOrder kept?Use for
<script src="a.js">Stops HTML parsingImmediately, then parsing continuesYesRarely — legacy pages
<script src="a.js" defer>In parallelAfter the whole HTML is parsed, before DOMContentLoadedYesNormal page scripts
<script src="a.js" async>In parallelAs soon as it arrives (pauses parsing)NoIndependent scripts (analytics)
<script type="module" src="main.js">In parallel, with its importsLike deferYesModern code with import/export

type="module" also changes how the code behaves: the file gets its own scope, it is in strict mode automatically, and it may use import and export. You will learn modules in ES modules.

Strict mode

Strict mode is a safer variant of JavaScript that turns several silent mistakes into real errors. You switch it on with the string "use strict"; as the very first statement of a script or a function. ES modules and class bodies are always strict, so in a Vite or React project you are in strict mode without writing anything.

"use strict";

function applyCoupon() {
  totl = 450; // typo for "total"
}
applyCoupon(); // ReferenceError: totl is not defined
// Without strict mode the typo silently creates a global variable "totl".

What strict mode changes:

  • Assigning to an undeclared variable throws ReferenceError instead of creating a global variable.
  • In a plain function call, this is undefined instead of the global object (window). See this.
  • Writing to a read-only property (a frozen object, a getter-only property) throws TypeError instead of failing silently.
  • Duplicate parameter names, the with statement and old octal literals like 010 become a SyntaxError.

The console: your first tool

Every browser has DevTools. In Chrome or Edge on Windows press F12 or Ctrl+Shift+J (on a Mac, Cmd+Option+J) to open the Console tab. The console does three jobs: it shows the output of console.log() (the JavaScript version of System.out.println), it shows errors in red with a link to the file and line, and it is a REPL — type any expression and press Enter to see the result. In Chrome, $0 in the console means "the element I selected in the Elements panel", which is handy for quick experiments.

Node.js gives you the same REPL in a terminal, and runs files with node:

console.log("Namaste from Node.js");
$ node hello.js
Namaste from Node.js
$ node
> 0.1 + 0.2
0.30000000000000004
> .exit

Rule: a script can only touch elements that already exist

A plain <script> in the <head> runs before the browser has parsed the <body>, so getElementById returns null. Use defer or type="module" (or put the script at the end of <body>, the old approach).

Wrong: runs before the body exists

<head>
  <script src="app.js"></script>
</head>
<!-- TypeError: Cannot set properties of null
     (setting 'textContent') -->

Right: waits until parsing is done

<head>
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
</head>
<!-- app.js runs after the whole
     document is parsed -->

Edge cases

  • defer and async only work on external scripts (with src). On an inline classic script they are ignored. Inline module scripts are deferred anyway.
  • Module scripts are fetched with CORS rules. If you open the HTML file by double-clicking it (a file:// URL), Chrome blocks the module with an error like "Access to script at 'file:///…/main.js' from origin 'null' has been blocked by CORS policy". Serve the folder with a local web server instead — the VS Code Live Server extension, npx serve ., or Vite.
  • Two async scripts can run in any order. Never use async for a script that depends on another script.

In real projects

In a React + Vite project you almost never write script tags yourself. The generated index.html contains one line — <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script> — and everything else is imported from that entry file. Vite then bundles the modules for production (see Node.js and npm).

Interview angle

  • "defer vs async?" Both download in parallel. defer runs after parsing, in document order; async runs as soon as the file arrives, in any order.
  • "Is JavaScript interpreted or compiled?" Engines like V8 interpret bytecode and JIT-compile hot code to machine code — no separate compile step.
  • "What is strict mode?" An opt-in safer mode (automatic in modules and classes): no accidental globals, this is undefined in plain calls, silent failures become errors.
  • "Can JavaScript run outside the browser?" Yes — Node.js runs it on servers and in build tools, but it has no DOM.

Further reading: the MDN JavaScript Guide is the best free reference for everything in this module.

JavaScript for Java developers: the big differences

JavaScript looks like Java but works differently: dynamic types, one number type, functions as values, objects without classes, a this that depends on the call, and one thread with an event loop instead of many threads.

Your Java knowledge helps — loops, conditions, objects, exceptions and clean code all carry over. But some Java habits produce bugs in JavaScript, and interviewers love to test exactly those. Read this table once now, and again at the end of the module; every row is explained in a later article.

TopicJavaJavaScript
TypingStatic: every variable has a declared type, checked by the compilerDynamic: values have types, variables do not; type errors appear at runtime (TypeScript adds static checking)
Running codejavac compiles to bytecode, the JVM runs itThe engine runs the source directly (with a JIT inside); no separate compile step
Numbersbyte, short, int, long, float, double; 7 / 2 is 3One number type (64-bit floating point) plus bigint; 7 / 2 is 3.5
TextString object plus a char typestring is a primitive; no char type; quotes '…', "…" or backticks
Equality== compares references; equals() compares content=== compares type and value (strings by content); == converts types first; objects always compare by reference
Missing valuesnull and NullPointerExceptionundefined (never set) and null (empty on purpose); TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
FunctionsMethods live inside classes; lambdas need a functional interfaceFunctions are values: store them, pass them, return them; no class needed
ObjectsEvery object comes from a classObject literals { } without any class; class is optional syntax over prototypes
thisAlways the current instanceDecided by how a function is called; arrow functions take it from outside
Visibilitypublic, protected, package-private, privateEverything is public except #private class fields; module scope hides the rest
OverloadingSame method name, different parameter listsNone — a second function with the same name replaces the first; use default and rest parameters
Interfaces, genericsYesNo (duck typing); TypeScript adds both
ExceptionsChecked and unchecked; one catch per typeAll unchecked; one catch block; you can throw any value
ConcurrencyMany threads, synchronized, executors, virtual threadsOne main thread plus an event loop; async work with promises and async/await; Web Workers for true parallel work
ModulesPackages, imports by class name, JPMSES modules: each file exports values and imports others by path
Build and librariesMaven/Gradle, pom.xml, Maven Centralnpm, package.json, the npm registry
Program startpublic static void mainThe file runs from top to bottom
SemicolonsRequiredOptional (automatic semicolon insertion), but write them or let a formatter do it

The differences in code

// 1. Types belong to values, not variables
let price = 499;
price = "₹499";               // allowed — no compile error
console.log(typeof price);    // "string"

// 2. One number type
console.log(7 / 2);           // 3.5 (Java int division gives 3)
console.log(Math.trunc(7 / 2)); // 3

// 3. Functions are values
const greet = (name) => `Hello, ${name}`;
const loud = (fn) => (name) => fn(name).toUpperCase();
console.log(loud(greet)("Asha")); // "HELLO, ASHA"

// 4. Objects without a class
const order = { id: 1042, items: 3, paid: true };
console.log(order.items);     // 3

// 5. A missing property is undefined, not a compile error
console.log(order.discount);  // undefined

// 6. Strings compare by content with ===
console.log("upi" === "UPI".toLowerCase()); // true (Java needs equals())

// 7. Missing arguments are undefined, extra ones are ignored
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
console.log(add(1));          // NaN  (1 + undefined)
console.log(add(1, 2, 3));    // 3
string
3.5
3
HELLO, ASHA
3
undefined
true
NaN
3

What stays the same

Plenty works exactly as you expect: if/else, for, while, do…while, break, continue, the ternary operator, ++ and +=, try/catch/finally, Math.max(), Math.floor(), Math.random(). Strings are immutable, objects live on a heap and are reached through references, and a garbage collector frees memory for you. switch works like Java's classic switch (with fall-through when you forget break), but it compares with ===, and there are no arrow-style case -> switch expressions.

Edge case: automatic semicolon insertion (ASI)

JavaScript inserts missing semicolons at line ends. Usually that is harmless, but a line break straight after return ends the statement:

function getUser() {
  return          // ASI inserts ";" here
  {
    name: "Asha"
  };
}
console.log(getUser()); // undefined

Always start the returned value on the same line as return: return {.

Common mistake: comparing arrays or objects with ===

Java developers expect value comparison, but === on objects compares references, and you cannot override it with an equals() method.

Wrong: compares references

const a = [1, 2, 3];
const b = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(a === b); // false
console.log(a == b);  // false

Right: compares the contents

const same = a.length === b.length &&
  a.every((x, i) => x === b[i]);
console.log(same); // true

Where TypeScript fits

TypeScript is JavaScript plus static types. You write .ts/.tsx files, the compiler checks types and removes them, and the browser runs the resulting JavaScript. Many React teams use it and it will feel closer to Java. Learn JavaScript first: TypeScript does not change how JavaScript runs — coercion, this and the event loop behave exactly as described in this module.

Interview angle: "How is JavaScript different from Java?"

  • Dynamically typed (variables have no fixed type) vs statically typed.
  • Prototype-based objects (classes are syntax on top) vs class-based.
  • Functions are first-class values; closures are everywhere.
  • Single-threaded with an event loop and non-blocking I/O vs multi-threaded.
  • One floating-point number type; null and undefined; type coercion with ==.
  • Runs in browsers (and Node.js), interpreted and JIT-compiled from source.

Values and types: primitives, objects and typeof

JavaScript has seven primitive types — string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol — and everything else is an object; variables have no type, only values do, and typeof tells you a value's type (with a few famous surprises).

A primitive is a simple, immutable value that is copied when you assign it. An object is a collection of properties that lives on the heap and is reached through a reference. Arrays, functions, dates, maps and plain { } objects are all objects. So the language has eight types in total: seven primitives plus object.

TypeExamplestypeof resultNotes
string"UPI", 'Pune', `Hi ${name}`"string"Immutable text, UTF-16; no char type
number42, 3.14, 1_000_000, NaN, Infinity"number"Always a 64-bit floating-point value (Java's double)
bigint9007199254740993n"bigint"Whole numbers of any size
booleantrue, false"boolean"
undefinedundefined"undefined""No value has been set"
nullnull"object" (!)"Empty on purpose"
symbolSymbol("id")"symbol"A unique value, used as a special object key
object{}, [], new Date(), functions"object" or "function"Everything that is not a primitive

number: one floating-point type for everything

Every JavaScript number is an IEEE 754 double-precision value — the same format as Java's double. There is no separate integer type. Integers are exact up to 253 − 1, and fractions behave like Java doubles, rounding errors included.

console.log(0.1 + 0.2);               // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);       // false
console.log(Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON); // true

console.log(7 / 2);                   // 3.5 — "/" never does integer division
console.log(Math.trunc(7 / 2));       // 3
console.log(-7 % 3);                  // -1 (sign follows the left side, as in Java)
console.log(2 ** 10);                 // 1024

console.log(1 / 0);                   // Infinity  (no ArithmeticException)
console.log(-1 / 0);                  // -Infinity
console.log(0 / 0);                   // NaN
console.log(Number("abc"));           // NaN
console.log(typeof NaN);              // "number"
console.log(NaN === NaN);             // false — NaN equals nothing, not even itself
console.log(Number.isNaN(0 / 0));     // true  — the correct way to test for NaN

console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER); // 9007199254740991 (2^53 - 1)
console.log(9007199254740993);        // 9007199254740992 — precision lost!
console.log(Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53)); // false

NaN ("Not a Number") is a special number value that means "this calculation failed". It spreads: any arithmetic with NaN gives NaN. Infinity appears when a result is too large or you divide by zero. Java throws ArithmeticException for integer division by zero; JavaScript just returns Infinity and carries on, so check your inputs.

Number literals can be written as 1_000_000 (underscores for readability), 0xff (hex), 0b1010 (binary), 0o17 (octal) or 1e6 (exponent).

In real projects: money and big IDs

  • Money. Never add rupees as fractions (0.1 + 0.2 problem). Keep amounts as integer paise, do integer maths, and format only for display. This is the JavaScript version of using BigDecimal or long paise in Java.
  • Big IDs from Java. A Java long can exceed 253. When Spring Boot sends {"id": 9007199254740993}, JSON.parse turns it into 9007199254740992 — a different ID. Send such IDs as strings (for example with Jackson's @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING) on the field).
const pricePaise = 49_900;          // ₹499.00 stored as an integer
const quantity = 3;
const totalPaise = pricePaise * quantity;   // 149700 — exact

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" });
console.log(inr.format(totalPaise / 100)); // ₹1,497.00
console.log(inr.format(12345678.5));       // ₹1,23,45,678.50 (lakh/crore grouping)

bigint: integers of any size

A bigint holds a whole number of any size, like Java's BigInteger — but with normal operators. Write it with an n suffix or create it with BigInt("…").

const big = 9007199254740993n;
console.log(big + 2n);               // 9007199254740995n
console.log(typeof big);             // "bigint"
console.log(7n / 2n);                // 3n — bigint division drops the fraction
console.log(BigInt("9007199254740993")); // 9007199254740993n — exact
console.log(BigInt(9007199254740993));   // 9007199254740992n — the number was already rounded
console.log(big + BigInt(1));        // 9007199254740994n
// big + 1  -> TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types, use explicit conversions

You cannot mix bigint and number in arithmetic, Math functions do not accept bigints, and JSON.stringify throws TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt. Use bigint only when you really need integers above 253.

string: immutable text

Strings can use single quotes, double quotes or backticks (template literals, see template literals). They are primitives, so === compares their content — no equals() needed. They are immutable: methods return new strings. length is a property, not a method, and counts UTF-16 code units, so an emoji like "😀" has length 2.

JavaScriptWhat it doesJava equivalent
s.lengthNumber of UTF-16 code unitss.length()
s[0], s.at(-1)First character, last characters.charAt(0)
s.toUpperCase(), s.trim()New upper-case / trimmed stringSame names
s.includes("pay")true if founds.contains("pay")
s.startsWith(), s.endsWith(), s.indexOf()Prefix, suffix, position (−1 if missing)Same names
s.slice(1, 4)Part from index 1 up to (not including) 4; negative indexes count from the ends.substring(1, 4)
s.split(",")Array of parts (a plain string separator, not a regex)s.split(",") (takes a regex)
s.replaceAll("-", " ")Replace every matchs.replace("-", " ")
"42".padStart(5, "0")"00042"String.format("%05d", 42)
a.localeCompare(b)Negative, zero or positive, language-awarea.compareTo(b)

undefined and null

JavaScript has two "no value" values. undefined means "nothing was ever put here": a declared variable without a value, a missing object property, a missing function argument, or the result of a function without return. null means "empty on purpose" — you, the programmer, assign it.

undefinednull
MeaningNot set / missingIntentionally empty
Who produces itThe engine, by defaultYour code
typeof"undefined""object" (a historic bug)
Number(x)NaN0
JSON.stringify({ a: x }){} — property dropped{"a":null}
Triggers a default parameter?YesNo

Spring Boot (Jackson) sends a missing Java value as null in JSON, so data from your API contains null; values you forgot to set in JavaScript are undefined. The check value == null (with two equals signs) is true for both — the one place where == is commonly accepted.

symbol

A symbol is a unique value: Symbol("id") === Symbol("id") is false. Symbols serve as object keys that can never clash with other keys. You will rarely create them yourself, but the language uses "well-known symbols" internally — for example Symbol.iterator is what makes arrays work with for…of.

typeof and its surprises

console.log(typeof "hi");            // "string"
console.log(typeof 42);              // "number"
console.log(typeof 42n);             // "bigint"
console.log(typeof true);            // "boolean"
console.log(typeof undefined);       // "undefined"
console.log(typeof Symbol("id"));    // "symbol"
console.log(typeof { a: 1 });        // "object"
console.log(typeof null);            // "object"   ← surprise 1
console.log(typeof [1, 2]);          // "object"   ← surprise 2
console.log(typeof function () {});  // "function" ← surprise 3 (functions are objects)
console.log(typeof class {});        // "function"
console.log(typeof notDeclaredAnywhere); // "undefined" — no ReferenceError

typeof null === "object" is a bug from the first JavaScript engine (values carried a type tag, and null's tag matched objects). Fixing it would break old websites, so it stays. Use the right tool for each check:

  • Is it null? → value === null
  • Is it null or undefined? → value == null or value ?? fallback
  • Is it an array? → Array.isArray(value)
  • Is it NaN? → Number.isNaN(value)
  • Is it a date, a map, an instance of your class? → value instanceof Date

Primitives are copied, objects are shared

Assignment copies a primitive's value. For objects, the variable holds a reference, and assignment copies the reference — exactly like Java. JavaScript is "pass by value" in the same sense as Java: for objects, the value passed is the reference.

Edge cases

  • Wrapper objects. "hi".toUpperCase() works because the engine briefly wraps the primitive in a String object, like Java autoboxing. Never write new String("hi") or new Number(5): they create objects, typeof says "object", and new String("a") === new String("a") is false.
  • Immutable strings. s[0] = "H" does nothing in sloppy mode and throws TypeError in strict mode. Build a new string instead: "H" + s.slice(1).
  • Negative zero. -0 exists. 0 === -0 is true, but Object.is(0, -0) is false and 1 / -0 is -Infinity.
  • typeof in the temporal dead zone. typeof x is safe for undeclared names, but throws ReferenceError if x is a let/const used before its declaration line (see let, const and var).

Common mistakes

Wrong: these checks never work

if (typeof items === "array") { }  // never true
if (result === NaN) { }            // never true
const total = 0.1 + 0.2;           // ₹0.30000000000000004

Right: the reliable checks

if (Array.isArray(items)) { }
if (Number.isNaN(result)) { }
const totalPaise = 10 + 20;        // 30 paise, exact

Interview angle

  • "Name the data types." Seven primitives (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol) plus object. Arrays and functions are objects.
  • "Why is 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3?" Numbers are binary floating point; 0.1 has no exact binary form — Java's double behaves the same. Compare with a tolerance or use integers.
  • "null vs undefined?" undefined = not set (engine default); null = intentionally empty (set by code). typeof null is "object" because of an old bug.
  • "What is NaN? How do you check it?" A number value for failed maths; it is not equal to itself, so use Number.isNaN().
  • "What is the largest safe integer?" Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER = 253 − 1 = 9007199254740991; beyond it use bigint or strings.

let, const and var: declaring variables

Use const by default, let when the variable must be reassigned, and never var: let and const are block-scoped and protected by the temporal dead zone, while var is function-scoped, can be re-declared and is silently hoisted as undefined.

JavaScript has three keywords for declaring variables. var is the original from 1995. let and const arrived in ES2015 to fix its problems. Modern code uses only let and const, but you must understand var because old code and interview questions are full of it.

varletconst
ScopeFunction (or global)Block { … }Block { … }
Before the declaration lineExists, value undefinedReferenceError (temporal dead zone)ReferenceError (temporal dead zone)
Re-declare in the same scopeAllowed, silentlySyntaxErrorSyntaxError
Re-assignYesYesNo — TypeError
Initial value requiredNoNoYes — SyntaxError: Missing initializer in const declaration
At the top level of a classic scriptBecomes a property of windowGlobal, but not on windowGlobal, but not on window

Block scope vs function scope

A block is any pair of curly braces: an if, a loop body, a try, or a bare { }. let and const live only inside the block where you declare them — the same rule as local variables in Java. var ignores blocks and belongs to the whole enclosing function.

function checkout(items) {
  if (items.length > 0) {
    var viaVar = "visible in the whole function";
    let viaLet = "visible only inside this if block";
  }
  console.log(viaVar);  // "visible in the whole function"
  console.log(viaLet);  // ReferenceError: viaLet is not defined
}
checkout(["Paneer Tikka"]);

The temporal dead zone (TDZ)

All three declarations are hoisted: before a scope runs, the engine registers every name declared in it. The difference is the starting value. A var starts as undefined. A let or const starts uninitialised, and touching it before its declaration line throws a ReferenceError. The stretch of code between the start of the scope and the declaration is called the temporal dead zone. It exists to catch bugs: reading a variable before it has a value is almost always a mistake.

console.log(orderId);      // undefined — var is hoisted with the value undefined
var orderId = 1042;

console.log(orderStatus);  // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'orderStatus' before initialization
let orderStatus = "PLACED";

Hoisting has its own article with output-prediction exercises: scope and hoisting.

Re-declaration

var count = 1;
var count = 2;    // allowed — silently replaces the first one (a classic source of bugs)

let total = 1;
let total = 2;    // SyntaxError: Identifier 'total' has already been declared

A SyntaxError is reported when the file is parsed, so none of the file runs — not even the lines above the error. Re-assigning (total = 2) is fine with let; only declaring the same name twice in one scope is an error. Declaring the same name in an inner block is allowed and shadows the outer variable.

const does not freeze objects

const means the binding cannot change: the name always points to the same value. If that value is an object or array, the object itself can still change. It is exactly Java's final on a reference variable.

const GST_RATE = 0.18;
// GST_RATE = 0.12;          // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

const cart = { items: [] };
cart.items.push("Vada Pav"); // fine — the object changes, the binding does not
cart.total = 40;             // fine
// cart = { items: [] };     // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

const city = Object.freeze({ name: "Pune" });
city.name = "Goa";           // TypeError in strict mode (modules); ignored otherwise
console.log(city.name);      // "Pune"

Object.freeze() makes an object's own properties read-only, but only one level deep: a frozen object's nested objects can still change. See objects for details.

Loops: let gives each iteration its own variable

In for (let i = 0; …), each iteration gets a fresh copy of i. This fixes the famous closure-in-a-loop bug (explained in closures). In a for…of loop you can use const, because each iteration creates a new binding: for (const item of items). A classic counting loop cannot use const: for (const i = 0; i < 3; i++) runs the body once and then throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable. at i++.

Naming rules and conventions

Rules: a name starts with a letter, _ or $, continues with letters, digits, _ or $, is case-sensitive, and cannot be a reserved word (class, const, function, new, this, default, delete …). The conventions are close to Java's:

WhatConventionExample
Variables, functions, methodscamelCaseorderTotal, calculateGst()
Classes and React componentsPascalCaseOrderService, CartItem
Fixed configuration valuesUPPER_SNAKE_CASEMAX_RETRIES, API_BASE_URL
Booleansis/has/can/should prefixisPaid, hasCoupon
Event handlershandle… or on…handleSubmit, onClose
"Private by agreement" (older code)Leading underscore_cache
File nameskebab-case or camelCase; components in PascalCaseapi-client.js, CartItem.jsx

Not every const is UPPER_CASE. Use capitals only for true constants that are known before the program runs (const MAX_RETRIES = 3). A const that holds a computed value is still camelCase: const total = calculateTotal(cart).

Convention: const first, let when needed, var never

Start every declaration with const. Change it to let only when you really reassign it (a counter, a value built in a loop). Seeing let then tells the reader "this changes later". ESLint enforces this with the rules prefer-const and no-var.

Java's var is not JavaScript's var

Java 10's var is local type inference: var list = new ArrayList<String>() still has a fixed, static type, and it follows normal block scope. JavaScript's var is the old function-scoped declaration with none of those guarantees. The closest JavaScript match for Java's var is let (or const for a final var).

Edge cases

  • No declaration at all. total = 10 without let/const creates a global variable in sloppy mode and throws ReferenceError: total is not defined in strict mode.
  • Globals in classic scripts. All classic <script> files on a page share one global scope, so two files declaring let user at the top level clash with a SyntaxError. Modules have their own scope and avoid this.
  • window properties. A top-level var name in a classic script overwrites window.name, which is a real browser property. Another reason to avoid var.

Common mistake: thinking const makes data immutable

Wrong: "it's const, so nobody can change it"

const ADMIN_ROLES = ["ADMIN", "OWNER"];
// some other code, far away:
ADMIN_ROLES.push("GUEST"); // works! security bug

Right: freeze shared constant data

const ADMIN_ROLES = Object.freeze(["ADMIN", "OWNER"]);
ADMIN_ROLES.push("GUEST");
// TypeError: Cannot add property 2,
// object is not extensible

Interview angle

  • "var vs let vs const?" Scope (function vs block), hoisting (undefined vs TDZ), re-declaration (allowed vs SyntaxError), re-assignment (const forbids it).
  • "What is the temporal dead zone?" The part of a scope before a let/const declaration runs; accessing the variable there throws ReferenceError.
  • "Does const make an object immutable?" No — it fixes the binding only. Use Object.freeze() (shallow) for the object.
  • "Are let and const hoisted?" Yes, they are hoisted but not initialised — that is exactly what creates the TDZ.

Operators, type coercion and truthy/falsy values

Always compare with ===; JavaScript silently converts types in ==, + and conditions, so know the six falsy values, use ?? for "missing" defaults, ?. for safe access, and convert input explicitly with Number().

Most operators look like Java's: + - * / %, ** (power), ++ --, && || !, ? :, and the compound forms like +=. The big difference is that JavaScript is happy to apply them to values of different types. It first converts ("coerces") the values and then continues, without any compile error. Type coercion means the automatic conversion of a value from one type to another. If you do not know the rules, you get bugs such as "5" + 3 giving "53". If you know the rules, you simply avoid the cases that confuse.

== vs ===

=== is strict equality: it returns true only when type and value are both the same, and it never converts anything. == is loose equality: if the types differ, it converts one or both sides first. In Java you never meet this, because the compiler stops you from comparing a String with an int. The rule for JavaScript is easy: use === and !== always. ESLint's eqeqeq rule enforces it.

Expression=====Why
5 == "5"truefalseThe string becomes a number
0 == ""truefalseBoth become 0
0 == "0"truefalseBoth become 0
"" == "0"falsefalseTwo strings: compared as text
false == "0"truefalseBoth become 0
null == undefinedtruefalseSpecial rule: they equal only each other
null == 0falsefalsenull equals only undefined
NaN == NaNfalsefalseNaN is never equal to anything
[] == falsetruefalse[] becomes "", then 0
[1] == 1truefalse[1] becomes "1", then 1
{} == {}falsefalseTwo different objects (references)

Do not memorise these rules. Memorise the habit: ===. The one accepted use of == is value == null, which is true for both null and undefined.

Truthy and falsy

In an if, a while, a ?: or with !, JavaScript does not need a boolean. Java would reject if (name); JavaScript converts the value to a boolean. A value that becomes false is falsy; every other value is truthy. There are exactly these falsy values:

Falsy valueType
falseboolean
0, -0number
0nbigint
"" (empty string)string
nullnull
undefinedundefined
NaNnumber

Everything else is truthy, including surprises: "0", "false", " ", [], {} and -1. An empty array is truthy, so if (items) does not test for "has items"; write if (items.length > 0). To convert explicitly, use Boolean(x) or the "double not" !!x.

+ with strings, and other conversions

The + operator does two jobs: addition and string joining. If either side is a string, the other side is converted to a string and the result is joined text. All other arithmetic operators (- * / %) convert both sides to numbers.

console.log("5" + 3);        // "53"   — string wins with +
console.log("5" - 3);        // 2      — "-" always means numbers
console.log("5" * "2");      // 10
console.log(1 + 2 + "3");    // "33"   — (1 + 2) first, then + "3"
console.log("1" + 2 + 3);    // "123"
console.log(true + 1);       // 2
console.log(null + 1);       // 1      — null becomes 0
console.log(undefined + 1);  // NaN    — undefined becomes NaN
console.log([] + {});        // "[object Object]"
console.log("abc" * 2);      // NaN
console.log(+"42");          // 42     — unary plus converts to number
console.log(`${5}${3}`);     // "53"   — template literal, explicit about joining

Convert explicitly

When a value comes from a form field, a URL or localStorage, it is always a string. Convert it on purpose.

CallBehaviourExamples
Number(x)Strict: the whole string must be a number, else NaN; empty string gives 0Number("42") → 42, Number("42px") → NaN, Number("") → 0
parseInt(s, 10)Reads leading digits, stops at the first bad character; always pass the radix 10parseInt("42px", 10) → 42, parseInt("3.9", 10) → 3
parseFloat(s)Same, with decimalsparseFloat("3.9kg") → 3.9
String(x), x.toString()To text (toString fails on null/undefined)String(null) → "null"
Boolean(x)TruthinessBoolean("0") → true
isNaN(x) (old)Converts to number first, then checks — gives odd answersisNaN("abc") → true, isNaN("") → false
Number.isNaN(x)True only for the value NaN, no conversionNumber.isNaN("abc") → false
 
const qtyText = "3";               // from an <input>
const qty = Number(qtyText);
if (Number.isNaN(qty) || qty <= 0) {
  console.log("Enter a valid quantity");
} else {
  console.log("Total:", qty * 499);    // Total: 1497
}

Logical operators return values, not booleans

&& and || short-circuit as in Java, but they return one of their operands, not true/false. a || b gives a if a is truthy, otherwise b. a && b gives a if a is falsy, otherwise b. That is why you see name || "Guest" for defaults.

?? (nullish coalescing) vs ||

The || default has a bug: it replaces every falsy value, including valid ones like 0, "" and false. The nullish coalescing operator ?? replaces only null and undefined.

const settings = { quantity: 0, coupon: "", notify: false };

console.log(settings.quantity || 1);     // 1     — wrong, 0 was a real value
console.log(settings.quantity ?? 1);     // 0     — right
console.log(settings.coupon ?? "NONE");  // ""
console.log(settings.notify ?? true);    // false
console.log(settings.missing ?? "n/a");  // "n/a"

Optional chaining ?. and logical assignment

Reading a property of undefined throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'city') — the JavaScript NullPointerException. The optional chaining operator ?. stops and returns undefined if the thing before it is null or undefined. Java's Optional.map(...) chain becomes one line.

const user = { name: "Asha", address: null, orders: [{ id: 1 }] };

console.log(user.address?.city);        // undefined (no TypeError)
console.log(user.orders?.[0]?.id);      // 1       — ?.[ ] for index access
console.log(user.sendEmail?.());        // undefined — ?.( ) calls only if it exists
console.log(user.address?.city ?? "Unknown city"); // "Unknown city"

// Logical assignment (ES2021)
let theme;
theme ??= "light";   // assign only if null/undefined
let retries = 0;
retries ||= 3;       // assign if falsy -> 3
let ready = true;
ready &&= false;     // assign only if truthy -> false

Rule: ?. guards the missing value, not a missing variable

a?.b is safe when a exists but is null/undefined. If a was never declared, you still get ReferenceError. Do not sprinkle ?. everywhere: it can hide a real bug that should have failed loudly.

Other operators worth knowing

  • typeof, instanceof, in ("id" in order tests a property), delete obj.key, and the comma-free void (rare).
  • Comparison < > <= >=: two strings are compared alphabetically by code unit ("10" < "9" is true); if one side is a number, the other becomes a number.
  • Bitwise operators exist (& | ^ ~ << >> >>>) and convert to 32-bit integers; you rarely need them.
  • Increment/decrement work as in Java; i++ on a string gives a number or NaN.

Edge cases

  • a ?? b || c without brackets is a SyntaxError: you cannot mix ?? with && or || unless you add parentheses.
  • Number(null) is 0 but Number(undefined) is NaN; Number(" 12 ") is 12 (spaces trimmed); Number("1,000") is NaN.
  • parseInt(0.0000005) is 5, because the number is first turned into the string "5e-7". Use Math.trunc() for numbers, parseInt only for strings.
  • ["1","2","3"].map(parseInt) gives [1, NaN, NaN], because map passes the index as the radix. Write .map(Number) or .map(s => parseInt(s, 10)).

Common mistake: using || for defaults and forgetting form values are strings

Wrong: drops 0, joins strings

const qty = input.value || 1;   // "0" is truthy, 0 is not
const total = input.value + 10; // "3" + 10 = "310"

Right: convert, then default

const qty = Number(input.value) ?? 1;
const total = Number(input.value) + 10; // 13

Interview angle

  • "== vs ===": strict compares type and value; loose converts first. Always use strict; the exception is x == null.
  • "List the falsy values." false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Empty arrays and objects are truthy.
  • "What is [] + [], 1 + "2", "3" - 1?" "", "12", 2.
  • "?? vs ||?" || replaces all falsy values, ?? only null and undefined.

Functions: declarations, expressions, arrows, defaults and rest

A function in JavaScript is a value you can store, pass and return; you can write it as a declaration, an expression or an arrow function, give parameters defaults, gather extra arguments with rest, and build behaviour by passing functions to higher-order functions.

In Java, code lives in methods inside classes, and passing behaviour needs a functional interface plus a lambda. In JavaScript, a function is an ordinary value, just like a number or a string. This is called having first-class functions. It is the idea behind map, filter, event handlers, promises and React hooks, so it deserves your full attention.

Three ways to write a function

// 1. Function declaration
function addGst(price) {
  return price * 1.18;
}

// 2. Function expression — a function value stored in a variable
const addGst2 = function (price) {
  return price * 1.18;
};

// 3. Arrow function (ES2015)
const addGst3 = (price) => price * 1.18;          // one expression: implicit return
const total = (price, qty) => {                   // block body: write "return"
  return price * qty;
};
const getUser = () => ({ id: 7, name: "Asha" });   // wrap an object literal in ( )

console.log(addGst(100));   // 118
console.log(total(499, 3)); // 1497
console.log(getUser());     // { id: 7, name: 'Asha' }
DeclarationExpressionArrow
Hoisted (callable before its line)Yes, fullyNo (variable rules apply)No
Own thisYes (depends on call)YesNo — uses this of the surrounding code
Own argumentsYesYesNo — use rest parameters
Can be used with newYesYesNo — TypeError: x is not a constructor
Best forTop-level named helpersRare todayCallbacks, short functions, React

Hoisting means a function declaration can be called above the line where it is written, but an arrow function stored in a const cannot: calling it early throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'total' before initialization. See scope and hoisting. The differences in this are explained in this.

Parameters are loose

JavaScript does not check the number of arguments. Missing parameters become undefined, extra arguments are ignored (but available through rest or arguments). There is no overloading: the second declaration of a name replaces the first. Use default and rest parameters instead.

function greet(name, greeting = "Hello") {   // default parameter
  return `${greeting}, ${name}!`;
}
console.log(greet("Asha"));           // "Hello, Asha!"
console.log(greet("Asha", "Namaste")); // "Namaste, Asha!"
console.log(greet("Asha", undefined)); // "Hello, Asha!" — undefined triggers the default
console.log(greet("Asha", null));      // "null, Asha!"  — null does not

// Rest parameter: collects the remaining arguments into a real array
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);
}
console.log(sum());           // 0
console.log(sum(10, 20, 30)); // 60

// Defaults can use earlier parameters and expressions
function createOrder(items, createdAt = new Date(), total = items.length * 100) {
  return { items, createdAt: createdAt.getFullYear(), total };
}
console.log(createOrder(["a", "b"])); // { items: [ 'a', 'b' ], createdAt: 2026, total: 200 }

A rest parameter (...numbers) must be last and is a real array, like Java's varargs int... numbers. The old arguments object (available in non-arrow functions) is array-like but has no map; prefer rest. To pass an array as separate arguments, use spread: Math.max(...prices) (see spread and rest).

A function with no return, or a bare return;, gives undefined. It returns one value only; to return several, return an object or array and destructure it.

Functions as values and higher-order functions

A callback is a function you pass to another function so that it is called later. A higher-order function is a function that takes functions as arguments or returns a function. map, filter, setTimeout and addEventListener are all higher-order functions.

const prices = [499, 1299, 250];

// A function that takes a function
function applyToAll(list, fn) {
  const result = [];
  for (const item of list) result.push(fn(item));
  return result;
}
console.log(applyToAll(prices, (p) => p * 0.9)); // [ 449.1, 1169.1, 225 ]

// A function that returns a function (a "function factory")
function discount(percent) {
  return (price) => price - (price * percent) / 100;
}
const diwali = discount(20);
console.log(diwali(1000)); // 800
console.log(typeof diwali); // "function"

// Functions have properties too
console.log(diwali.name, diwali.length); // "diwali" 1  (name, number of params)

Pass the function itself, not the result of calling it. setTimeout(sayHi, 1000) schedules a call; setTimeout(sayHi(), 1000) calls sayHi now and passes its return value (usually undefined). Brackets after the name mean "call now".

Pure functions and side effects

A pure function returns a result that depends only on its arguments and changes nothing outside itself (no changing a global, an argument, the DOM or the network). Pure functions are easy to test and to reason about, and React expects components to be pure. Prefer returning a new value over modifying the input.

// Impure: changes its argument
function addItemBad(cart, item) { cart.push(item); return cart; }

// Pure: returns a new array
const addItem = (cart, item) => [...cart, item];

const c1 = ["Rice"];
const c2 = addItem(c1, "Dal");
console.log(c1, c2); // [ 'Rice' ] [ 'Rice', 'Dal' ]

IIFE (briefly)

An IIFE (immediately invoked function expression) is a function that runs the moment it is defined: (function () { … })(); or (() => { … })();. It was the old way to make a private scope before modules and let existed. Today you meet it in old libraries and in one modern spot: an async IIFE, (async () => { await main(); })();, where top-level await is not available.

Other useful facts

  • Recursion works as in Java. Very deep recursion throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded (the JavaScript StackOverflowError).
  • Methods are just function-valued properties. The shorthand { total() { … } } is covered in objects.
  • Each function can have inner functions that remember the variables around them: a closure.
  • Naming: camelCase verbs for functions (calculateTotal), PascalCase for classes and React components.

Convention: when to use which form

  • Top-level, named, reusable functions: declaration (function formatPrice(p) {…}) or a const arrow — pick one style per project.
  • Callbacks and one-liners: arrow functions.
  • Object methods and class methods: method shorthand, not arrows (arrows have no own this).
  • Keep functions short and do one thing; limit parameters to three, then pass an options object: createUser({ name, role }).

Edge cases

  • Arrow function returning an object: () => { id: 1 } is a block with a label, so it returns undefined. Write () => ({ id: 1 }).
  • Default parameters are evaluated each call, so function f(list = []) gives a fresh array every time (unlike Python).
  • fn.length does not count parameters with defaults or rest.
  • Function declarations inside if blocks behave inconsistently in sloppy mode. Use a const arrow there.

Common mistake: calling instead of passing, and arrow methods

Wrong: calls the handler immediately

button.addEventListener("click", handleClick());
// handleClick runs now; its return value (undefined)
// is registered as the listener

Right: pass the function

button.addEventListener("click", handleClick);
button.addEventListener("click", () => handleClick(7));

Interview angle

  • "Declaration vs expression vs arrow?" Hoisting, own this and arguments, new-ability, and syntax.
  • "What is a higher-order function / callback?" Takes or returns a function; give map as an example.
  • "What are first-class functions?" Functions are values: assignable, passable, returnable.
  • "What is a pure function?" Same input, same output, no side effects.
  • "Does JavaScript support overloading?" No; the last definition wins. Use defaults, rest or an options object.

Scope, the scope chain and hoisting

Scope decides where a name is visible: global, function and block scopes are nested, a name is looked up from the inside outwards (the scope chain), and hoisting means declarations are registered before the code runs — var as undefined, functions fully, let/const in the temporal dead zone.

Scope is the region of code where a variable can be seen. Lexical scoping means the scope is decided by where you write the code, not by where you call it. You already know this from Java: a local variable is visible inside its block. JavaScript has the same idea with a few extra twists.

The three kinds of scope

  • Global scope — names declared at the top of a classic script (or on window). In an ES module the top level is the module scope, private to that file.
  • Function scope — parameters and everything declared inside a function. var belongs to this scope.
  • Block scope — a { } block, if, for, try. let, const and class belong to the block.

Scopes nest. When code uses a name, the engine looks in the current scope, then in the scope that contains it, and so on up to the global scope. This path is the scope chain. If the name is nowhere, you get ReferenceError: x is not defined. An inner variable with the same name shadows the outer one.

const platform = "web";             // module/global scope

function placeOrder() {
  const orderId = 1042;             // function scope
  if (orderId > 0) {
    const status = "PLACED";        // block scope
    console.log(platform, orderId, status); // found by walking up the chain
  }
  // console.log(status);           // ReferenceError — the block is gone
}

placeOrder(); // web 1042 PLACED

let x = "global";
function show() {
  let x = "local";                  // shadows the outer x
  console.log(x);
}
show();                // "local"
console.log(x);        // "global"

Lexical, not dynamic

A function sees the variables of the place where it was written, not the place where it is called. This is what makes closures work. Do not confuse it with this, which is decided at call time.

Hoisting

Hoisting is the behaviour that all declarations are processed before any code in the scope runs. It does not move your code; the engine simply knows the names in advance. What differs is the initial value:

DeclarationHoisted?Value before its line
function f() {}Yes, name and bodyThe working function — you can call it early
var x = 5Yes, the name onlyundefined (the assignment stays in place)
let x = 5, const x = 5Yes, but uninitialisedTemporal dead zone: ReferenceError
class A {}Like letTemporal dead zone
var f = function() {}, const f = () => {}Follows the variableundefined / TDZ — calling gives TypeError: f is not a function / ReferenceError

Output-prediction examples

These are favourite interview questions. Try to predict each answer before you read it.

// Puzzle 1
console.log(a);
var a = 10;
console.log(a);

// Puzzle 2
sayHi();
function sayHi() { console.log("hi"); }

// Puzzle 3
try {
  helloExpr();
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.name + ": " + e.message);
}
var helloExpr = function () { console.log("hello"); };

// Puzzle 4
try {
  console.log(b);
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.name + ": " + e.message);
}
let b = 5;

// Puzzle 5
var city = "Pune";
function where() {
  console.log(city);
  var city = "Goa";
}
where();
undefined
10
hi
TypeError: helloExpr is not a function
ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
undefined

Why: (1) the engine registers a as undefined first, assigns 10 later. (2) Function declarations are hoisted completely. (3) helloExpr exists but is still undefined, and calling undefined is a TypeError. (4) b is in the temporal dead zone. (5) The local var city is hoisted to the top of where and shadows the global one, so the function prints undefined, not "Pune". This last one surprises most people.

Global scope and window

In a classic script, a top-level var or function declaration becomes a property of window; let and const do not. Assigning to an undeclared name in sloppy mode creates an accidental global. Too many globals cause name clashes between scripts, one more reason to use modules and "use strict".

var oldStyle = 1;
let newStyle = 2;
console.log(window.oldStyle); // 1
console.log(window.newStyle); // undefined

function leak() {
  leaked = "oops";   // no declaration: sloppy mode creates window.leaked
}
leak();
console.log(leaked); // "oops" (in strict mode: ReferenceError inside leak)

Scope compared with Java

  • Java has block scope for locals, and a local cannot shadow another local in the same method. JavaScript lets an inner block shadow an outer variable of the same name.
  • Java has no hoisting of locals: using a variable before its declaration is a compile error. JavaScript catches it only at runtime (or silently gives undefined for var).
  • Java has no free-standing functions; JavaScript functions can be nested and capture variables from the enclosing function. Java lambdas can do the same only for effectively final variables — JavaScript functions can also change the captured variable.

Rule: declare at the top of the scope, use const/let

Declare variables before using them, in the smallest scope that works. Turn on ESLint's no-undef, no-use-before-define and no-var rules so the editor warns you about hoisting traps.

Edge cases

  • If a function declaration and a var share a name, the function wins until the var assignment runs.
  • Function parameters and the function's body var variables share a scope; let with the same name as a parameter is a SyntaxError.
  • catch (e) creates a block scope for e.
  • A switch has one shared block: let x in two cases clashes. Wrap each case body in { }.

Interview angle

  • "What is hoisting?" Declarations are registered before execution; var is undefined, functions are usable, let/const/class sit in the TDZ.
  • "What is the scope chain / lexical scope?" Name lookup walks outward through enclosing scopes as written in the source.
  • "What does Puzzle 5 print and why?" undefined, because var city is hoisted inside the function.
  • "What is an accidental global?" Assigning to an undeclared name in sloppy mode; strict mode throws.

Closures

A closure is a function together with the variables of the scope where it was created — the function keeps access to those variables even after the outer function has finished, which gives you private state, factories, memoization and the classic loop bug.

Take this small example. The function makeCounter finishes running, so you would expect its local variable count to be gone. It is not.

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;                 // local to makeCounter
