  return function () {           // inner function "closes over" count
    count++;
    return count;
  };
}

const counterA = makeCounter();
const counterB = makeCounter();   // a separate count

console.log(counterA()); // 1
console.log(counterA()); // 2
console.log(counterA()); // 3
console.log(counterB()); // 1  — its own private count
console.log(typeof count); // "undefined" — nobody outside can reach it

A closure is created every time a function is created. It consists of the function plus a hidden link to the lexical environment (the variables) where it was defined. The inner function does not copy count; it keeps a live reference to the variable itself. As long as the function can be reached, the variable stays in memory. Because every call to makeCounter() creates a new environment, counterA and counterB have separate counts.

Closure vs Java lambda

A Java lambda can capture only effectively final variables, so it can read a value but never change it. A JavaScript closure captures the variable itself and can update it. That is why the counter works in JavaScript, while in Java you would need an AtomicInteger or a one-element array.

Use 1: private state (encapsulation)

JavaScript objects have no private keyword outside classes (see classes for #private). Closures give you real privacy: nothing outside the function can touch the variable except through the functions you return.

function createWallet(initialPaise) {
  let balance = initialPaise;            // private

  return {
    deposit(amount) {
      if (amount <= 0) throw new Error("Amount must be positive");
      balance += amount;
    },
    withdraw(amount) {
      if (amount > balance) throw new Error("Insufficient balance");
      balance -= amount;
    },
    getBalance: () => balance,
  };
}

const wallet = createWallet(50_000);
wallet.deposit(10_000);
wallet.withdraw(5_000);
console.log(wallet.getBalance()); // 55000
console.log(wallet.balance);      // undefined — cannot be read or changed directly
wallet.withdraw(1_000_000);       // Error: Insufficient balance

Use 2: function factories

The discount(percent) example in functions is a closure: the returned function remembers percent. The same pattern gives you configured helpers such as makeLogger("orders") or createFormatter("en-IN").

Use 3: memoization (caching results)

Memoization stores the results of a slow pure function so that the same input is not computed twice. The cache lives in the closure.

function memoize(fn) {
  const cache = new Map();                 // private cache, one per memoized function
  return function (arg) {
    if (cache.has(arg)) {
      console.log("cache hit for", arg);
      return cache.get(arg);
    }
    const result = fn(arg);
    cache.set(arg, result);
    return result;
  };
}

const slowSquare = (n) => n * n;           // pretend this is expensive
const fastSquare = memoize(slowSquare);
console.log(fastSquare(12)); // 144
console.log(fastSquare(12)); // cache hit for 12, then 144

The same trick is behind useMemo and useCallback in React, and behind debouncing a search box (the timer id lives in a closure).

The classic loop bug: var vs let

A very common interview question. Three timers are created in a loop, each should print its own index.

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("var:", i), 0);
}
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("let:", j), 0);
}
var: 3
var: 3
var: 3
let: 0
let: 1
let: 2

With var there is only one i for the whole function. The three callbacks all close over the same variable, and they run later, after the loop has ended and i is 3. With let, every iteration gets its own fresh j, so each callback closes over a different variable. The old fix was an IIFE that copied i into a parameter; today you simply use let.

Closures in React hooks

Every render of a React component is a new function call, and the event handlers inside it close over the state values of that render. A handler that logs count after a delay shows the value from the moment the handler was created: this is the "stale closure" problem. It is a closure rule, not a React bug. You will meet it in Module 5.

Memory and closures

A closure keeps its whole environment reachable as long as the function is reachable. A long-lived function (for example an event listener on window) that closes over a huge array keeps the array in memory. Remove listeners you no longer need and do not capture big objects without a reason.

Edge cases

  • Closures capture variables, not values. If the variable changes before the function runs, the function sees the new value.
  • Two closures made in the same call share the same variables (deposit and getBalance above see one balance).
  • Every function in JavaScript is a closure; it only becomes noticeable when it outlives its outer function.

Common mistake: a shared variable captured in a loop

Wrong: every button alerts 3

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  buttons[i].onclick = () => alert(i);
}

Right: let makes one i per iteration

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  buttons[i].onclick = () => alert(i);
}

Interview angle

  • "What is a closure?" A function plus its lexical environment; it remembers outer variables after the outer function returns. Give the counter example.
  • "Why does the var loop print 3 three times?" One shared i, callbacks run after the loop. let creates one per iteration.
  • "Where do you use closures?" Private state, factories, memoization, debounce, event handlers, React hooks.
  • "Can closures cause memory leaks?" Yes, when long-lived functions hold large objects. Release references and listeners.

Arrays: creating, changing, looping and copying

A JavaScript array is a resizable list of any values (like an ArrayList<Object>); know which methods change the array and which return a new one, remember that sort() compares as strings, and copy with spread or structuredClone.

In Java you choose between a fixed-size array int[] and an ArrayList<T>. JavaScript has just one thing: the array. It grows and shrinks on its own, holds values of mixed types, and comes with dozens of built-in methods. It is an object, so typeof [] is "object"; test with Array.isArray(). Indexes start at 0, and arr.length is a property, not a method.

Creating arrays

const cart = ["Rice", "Dal", "Ghee"];        // literal — the normal way
const empty = [];
const mixed = [1, "two", true, null, { id: 4 }];   // allowed, but avoid it

console.log(cart.length);       // 3
console.log(cart[0], cart[2]);  // Rice Ghee
console.log(cart[10]);          // undefined — no ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
console.log(cart.at(-1));       // "Ghee" — negative index counts from the end

const zeros = new Array(3).fill(0);               // [0, 0, 0]
const range = Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i + 1);  // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
const letters = Array.from("abc");                // ["a", "b", "c"]
const fromSet = [...new Set([1, 2, 2, 3])];       // [1, 2, 3] — remove duplicates
console.log(Array.of(7));       // [7]  (new Array(7) would make 7 empty slots)

Reading a missing index gives undefined, and writing past the end grows the array and leaves empty holes: cart[5] = "Tea" makes length 6 with empty slots in between. Avoid this.

The method table

The most important question about an array method is: does it change the original array (mutating) or return a new one (non-mutating)? In React you must not mutate state, so this matters daily.

MethodWhat it doesChanges original?Returns
push(a, b) / pop()Add / remove at the endYesNew length / removed item
unshift(a) / shift()Add / remove at the start (slow on big arrays)YesNew length / removed item
splice(start, count, ...items)Remove and/or insert in the middleYesArray of removed items
sort(), reverse()Sort / reverse in placeYesThe same array
fill(v)Fill with a valueYesThe same array
slice(start, end)Copy a part (end not included)NoNew array
concat(other)Join arraysNoNew array
flat(depth), flatMap(fn)Flatten nested arraysNoNew array
join(", ")Make one stringNoString
includes(x), indexOf(x)Is it there? / where (−1 if not)Noboolean / number
at(i)Item at index, negative allowedNoItem
toSorted(), toReversed(), toSpliced(), with(i, v)Non-mutating versions (newer: ES2023, recent browsers and Node 20+)NoNew array
 
const items = ["Rice", "Dal"];
items.push("Ghee", "Salt");       // ["Rice","Dal","Ghee","Salt"]
console.log(items.pop());         // "Salt"
items.unshift("Atta");            // ["Atta","Rice","Dal","Ghee"]
items.shift();                    // removes "Atta"

// splice(start, deleteCount, ...insert)
items.splice(1, 1);               // removes "Dal"  -> ["Rice","Ghee"]
items.splice(1, 0, "Oil", "Tea"); // inserts        -> ["Rice","Oil","Tea","Ghee"]

const firstTwo = items.slice(0, 2);   // ["Rice","Oil"] — items unchanged
const last = items.slice(-1);         // ["Ghee"]
console.log(items.includes("Tea"));   // true
console.log(items.indexOf("Salt"));   // -1
console.log(items.join(" | "));       // Rice | Oil | Tea | Ghee
console.log([[1, 2], [3, [4]]].flat());    // [1, 2, 3, [4]]
console.log([[1, 2], [3, [4]]].flat(Infinity)); // [1, 2, 3, 4]
console.log(["a b", "c"].flatMap(s => s.split(" "))); // ["a","b","c"]

Note the pairs that confuse: slice (copies, safe) vs splice (edits, dangerous), and push (returns the new length, not the array).

sort() sorts as strings by default

Without a function, sort() converts items to strings and compares them in alphabetical (UTF-16) order. For numbers this is wrong. Pass a comparator: a function (a, b) that returns a negative number if a comes first, positive if b comes first, and 0 if equal. It works just like Java's Comparator.compare.

const marks = [100, 25, 9, 1000];
console.log(marks.sort());                 // [100, 1000, 25, 9]  — string order!

marks.sort((a, b) => a - b);               // ascending
console.log(marks);                        // [9, 25, 100, 1000]
marks.sort((a, b) => b - a);               // descending
console.log(marks);                        // [1000, 100, 25, 9]

const products = [
  { name: "Mouse", price: 499 },
  { name: "Cable", price: 199 },
  { name: "Bag",   price: 1299 },
];
products.sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price);          // by number
products.sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)); // by text, language-aware
console.log(products.map(p => p.name));   // ["Bag","Cable","Mouse"]

// Newer, keeps the original untouched
const sorted = products.toSorted((a, b) => b.price - a.price);

sort() is stable (equal items keep their order) in all current engines, and it changes the array in place. To keep the original, copy first: [...marks].sort(...) or use toSorted().

Looping: for, for...of, for...in, forEach

const cities = ["Pune", "Delhi", "Goa"];

for (let i = 0; i < cities.length; i++) console.log(i, cities[i]);  // classic

for (const city of cities) console.log(city);          // values — preferred

for (const [i, city] of cities.entries()) console.log(i, city);  // index + value

cities.forEach((city, i) => console.log(i, city));   // callback style

for (const key in cities) console.log(key);            // "0", "1", "2" — STRINGS
LoopGives youUse forWatch out
for (let i…)IndexWhen you need control, break, reverseOff-by-one
for…ofEach valueArrays, strings, Maps, SetsNot for plain objects (not iterable)
for…inEach enumerable key (as a string), including inherited onesPlain objects, rarelyNever use on arrays
forEachValue, index, arraySimple side effectsCannot break; ignores await (see async/await)

Copying: reference, shallow, deep

Like in Java, const b = a copies the reference: both names point to one array. To copy, use spread. A shallow copy copies the top level only; nested objects are still shared. A deep copy duplicates everything.

const a = [{ name: "Rice", qty: 1 }, { name: "Dal", qty: 2 }];

const same = a;              // same array
const shallow = [...a];      // new array, same item objects (also a.slice())
const deep = structuredClone(a);   // new array AND new item objects

shallow[0].qty = 99;         // changes the shared object
console.log(a[0].qty);       // 99 — the original changed!
console.log(deep[0].qty);    // 1  — unaffected

shallow.push({ name: "Tea", qty: 1 });
console.log(a.length, shallow.length); // 2 3 — the arrays are separate

structuredClone() (available in current browsers and Node 17+) copies plain data, dates, maps, sets and nested arrays; it throws DataCloneError for functions. The old trick JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) loses dates, undefined and functions (see objects and JSON).

Convention: do not mutate shared arrays

Prefer map, filter, spread and toSorted over push, splice and sort on data that other code also uses, especially React state. setItems([...items, newItem]) instead of items.push(newItem).

Edge cases

  • indexOf and includes compare with strict equality, so they cannot find an object by its content: [{a:1}].includes({a:1}) is false. Use some or find.
  • [1, 2, 3].includes(NaN) is false, but [NaN].includes(NaN) is true; indexOf(NaN) is always −1.
  • Setting arr.length = 0 empties the array; setting a smaller length cuts it.
  • new Array(3) makes holes, and map skips holes. Use Array.from({ length: 3 }) or .fill().
  • forEach over an empty array does nothing; reduce on an empty array without an initial value throws TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value.

Common mistake: default sort on numbers and mutating while sorting a copy

Wrong: string order, and edits state

const ranked = prices.sort();     // [100, 25, 9]...
// prices itself was reordered too

Right: comparator on a copy

const ranked = [...prices].sort((a, b) => a - b);
// or prices.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)

Interview angle

  • "slice vs splice?" slice returns a copy of a part; splice removes/inserts in place.
  • "Why does [10, 9, 1].sort() give [1, 10, 9]?" Default sort compares strings. Use (a, b) => a - b.
  • "for…in vs for…of?" keys vs values; for…of for arrays.
  • "Shallow vs deep copy?" Spread copies one level; structuredClone copies all levels.
  • "How do you check for an array?" Array.isArray(x).

map, filter, reduce, find and friends

Replace most hand-written loops with array methods: map transforms each item, filter keeps some, reduce folds the array into one value, find/some/every search, and you can chain them like Java streams — without any stream() or collect().

These methods take a callback and call it for every item. They are the daily tools of React code, where lists are turned into UI with map. If you know Java streams (stream().map().filter().collect()), you already know the ideas; in JavaScript the methods work directly on the array and return an array.

MethodCallback returnsResultJava stream
map(fn)The new itemNew array, same lengthmap
filter(fn)true to keepNew, shorter arrayfilter
reduce(fn, start)The next accumulatorAny single valuereduce / collect
find(fn)true for a matchFirst match or undefinedfilter().findFirst()
findIndex(fn)true for a matchIndex or −1—
findLast(fn)true for a matchLast match (newer)—
some(fn) / every(fn)booleanbooleananyMatch / allMatch
forEach(fn)nothing usedundefinedforEach

Callbacks receive up to three arguments: (item, index, array). Most of the time you write only the first.

map: transform every item

const cart = [
  { id: 1, name: "Paneer", price: 240, qty: 2, category: "dairy" },
  { id: 2, name: "Rice",   price: 650, qty: 1, category: "grocery" },
  { id: 3, name: "Curd",   price: 60,  qty: 4, category: "dairy" },
  { id: 4, name: "Atta",   price: 380, qty: 1, category: "grocery" },
];

const names = cart.map(item => item.name);
console.log(names);   // ["Paneer", "Rice", "Curd", "Atta"]

const lines = cart.map(({ name, price, qty }) => ({ name, lineTotal: price * qty }));
console.log(lines[0]); // { name: 'Paneer', lineTotal: 480 }

// In React you turn data into elements the same way:
// cart.map(item => <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>)

map always returns an array of the same length. If you do not use the returned array, you wanted forEach.

filter: keep what matches

const dairy = cart.filter(item => item.category === "dairy");
console.log(dairy.map(i => i.name));   // ["Paneer", "Curd"]

const expensive = cart.filter(i => i.price > 300);   // Rice and Atta
const cleaned = ["a", "", null, "b", undefined].filter(Boolean);  // ["a", "b"]
const withoutItem2 = cart.filter(i => i.id !== 2);     // "delete" without mutating

filter(i => i.id !== id) is the standard way to remove an item from a list in React state.

reduce: fold into one value

reduce goes through the array with an accumulator (the running result). Your callback receives (accumulator, item) and returns the next accumulator. The second argument is the starting value. Always pass it.

// Cart total
const total = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
console.log(total);   // 480 + 650 + 240 + 380 = 1750

// Count items per category
const countByCategory = cart.reduce((acc, i) => {
  acc[i.category] = (acc[i.category] ?? 0) + 1;
  return acc;
}, {});
console.log(countByCategory);   // { dairy: 2, grocery: 2 }

// Group items by category (like Collectors.groupingBy)
const grouped = cart.reduce((acc, i) => {
  (acc[i.category] ??= []).push(i.name);
  return acc;
}, {});
console.log(grouped);   // { dairy: [ 'Paneer', 'Curd' ], grocery: [ 'Rice', 'Atta' ] }

// Max price
const maxPrice = cart.reduce((m, i) => Math.max(m, i.price), 0);   // 650
// Newer: Object.groupBy(cart, i => i.category) does grouping directly (Node 21+, recent browsers)

Newer helpers

Object.groupBy(), toSorted() and findLast() exist in current browsers and recent Node versions, but not in old ones. Check MDN browser compatibility before relying on them in a project that supports older browsers.

find, findIndex, some, every

const rice = cart.find(i => i.name === "Rice");
console.log(rice?.price);                  // 650
console.log(cart.find(i => i.id === 99)); // undefined — no exception, check it
console.log(cart.findIndex(i => i.id === 3));   // 2
console.log(cart.some(i => i.qty > 3));         // true  — at least one
console.log(cart.every(i => i.price > 50));     // true  — all of them
console.log([].every(x => false), [].some(x => true)); // true false (empty array)

find returns the first match and stops. It returns the item itself (a reference, not a copy), so changing it changes the original array. filter(...)[0] does the same job but needlessly checks every item.

Chaining

Because map and filter return arrays, you can chain them. Read from top to bottom like a pipeline.

const dairyBill = cart
  .filter(i => i.category === "dairy")
  .map(i => i.price * i.qty)
  .reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0);
console.log(dairyBill);   // 480 + 240 = 720

const summary = cart
  .toSorted((a, b) => b.price - a.price)
  .slice(0, 2)
  .map(i => `${i.name}: ₹${i.price}`)
  .join(", ");
console.log(summary);     // Rice: ₹650, Atta: ₹380

Differences from Java streams: arrays are eager — each step builds a full intermediate array right away, while streams are lazy and process one element at a time. For typical UI data this does not matter. There is also no terminal operation to remember: the result is already an array.

Which one do I use?

  1. Need a new array of the same size with changed items? map.
  2. Need fewer items? filter.
  3. Need one value (total, object, map, string)? reduce (or a loop if it reads better).
  4. Need one item? find. Need yes/no? some or every.
  5. Need a side effect only (log, change the DOM)? forEach or for…of.

Edge cases

  • A map callback with a block body must return; forgetting it gives an array of undefined.
  • find compares nothing by itself: the callback must return a boolean. cart.find(i => i.id = 2) (assignment) is a bug that returns the first item.
  • These methods skip empty holes of sparse arrays and never wait for promises: arr.map(async x => …) returns an array of promises.
  • Changing the array inside a callback (pushing while iterating) leads to confusing results. Do not.

Common mistake: map for side effects, reduce without a start value

Wrong

cart.map(i => console.log(i.name));   // builds a useless array
[].reduce((a, b) => a + b);           // TypeError: Reduce of empty
                                      // array with no initial value

Right

cart.forEach(i => console.log(i.name));
[].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);        // 0

Interview angle

  • "map vs forEach?" map returns a new array; forEach returns undefined and is for side effects.
  • "Write a function that groups or totals with reduce." Show the cart total and grouping above; always pass the initial value.
  • "What does find return if nothing matches?" undefined (filter returns [], findIndex returns −1).
  • "Remove an item without mutating." list.filter(x => x.id !== id).
  • "Implement your own map." A loop that pushes fn(item, i, arr) into a result array.

Objects and JSON

A JavaScript object is a bag of key-value pairs you can create without a class; read it with dot or bracket access, loop with Object.keys/values/entries, and exchange it with servers as JSON using JSON.stringify and JSON.parse — remembering that functions, undefined and dates do not survive.

In Java, to hold a name and an age you first write a class. In JavaScript you write an object literal: curly braces with key: value pairs. The keys are strings (or symbols), the values can be anything, including functions and other objects. The same shape, written as text, is the format of nearly every web API, which is why objects and JSON go together.

const student = {
  name: "Asha",
  age: 21,
  skills: ["Java", "SQL"],
  address: { city: "Pune", pin: "411001" },
  greet() {                       // method shorthand
    return `Hi, I am ${this.name}`;
  },
};

console.log(student.name);            // dot access
console.log(student["age"]);          // bracket access: the key is a string
const field = "city";
console.log(student.address[field]);  // bracket access with a variable: "Pune"
console.log(student.greet());         // "Hi, I am Asha"
console.log(student.phone);           // undefined — missing key, no exception

student.email = "asha@example.com";   // add a property
student.age = 22;                     // change
delete student.skills;                // remove
console.log("age" in student);        // true
console.log(student.hasOwnProperty("name")); // true  (Object.hasOwn(student, "name") is newer)

Use dot access when you know the name; use brackets when the key is in a variable or contains characters like a dash (headers["Content-Type"]).

Shorthand and computed keys

const name = "Rice";
const price = 650;
const item = { name, price };                 // same as { name: name, price: price }
console.log(item);                             // { name: 'Rice', price: 650 }

const field2 = "qty";
const row = { [field2]: 3, [`${field2}Max`]: 10 };   // computed keys
console.log(row);                              // { qty: 3, qtyMax: 10 }

// Updating one field of a form: the pattern behind most React handlers
function updateField(form, key, value) {
  return { ...form, [key]: value };            // new object, one key changed
}
console.log(updateField({ name: "A", city: "X" }, "city", "Goa")); // { name: 'A', city: 'Goa' }

Looping over an object

const stock = { rice: 10, dal: 0, tea: 25 };

console.log(Object.keys(stock));     // ["rice", "dal", "tea"]
console.log(Object.values(stock));   // [10, 0, 25]
console.log(Object.entries(stock));  // [["rice",10], ["dal",0], ["tea",25]]

for (const [item, qty] of Object.entries(stock)) {
  console.log(`${item}: ${qty}`);
}
const inStock = Object.fromEntries(
  Object.entries(stock).filter(([, qty]) => qty > 0)
);
console.log(inStock);   // { rice: 10, tea: 25 }
console.log(Object.assign({}, stock, { dal: 5 })); // { rice: 10, dal: 5, tea: 25 }

Property order: integer-like keys first in ascending order, then the other keys in the order they were added. Do not depend on it for important logic.

Object.freeze and copying

Object.freeze(obj) makes the object's own properties read-only (shallow). Object.isFrozen(obj) checks. Copy an object with spread ({ ...obj }, shallow) or structuredClone(obj) (deep), as for arrays in arrays. Object.freeze on a const is how you make real constants, as shown in let, const and var.

Optional chaining on objects

Data from an API often has missing branches. order.customer?.address?.city ?? "Unknown" reads three levels without throwing (see operators).

JSON: the exchange format

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for data: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. It looks like a JavaScript object literal, but it is stricter: keys and strings must use double quotes, there are no comments, no trailing commas, and no functions or undefined. Spring Boot's Jackson produces and reads exactly this.

  • JSON.stringify(value) turns a value into a JSON string (like Jackson's writeValueAsString). JSON.stringify(value, null, 2) pretty-prints with 2 spaces.
  • JSON.parse(text) turns a JSON string into a value (like readValue). It throws SyntaxError on invalid JSON.
const order = {
  id: 1042,
  customer: "Asha",
  paid: true,
  note: undefined,                      // dropped
  total: NaN,                           // becomes null
  placedAt: new Date("2026-11-10T09:30:00Z"),   // becomes a string
  pay() { return true; },               // dropped
};

const text = JSON.stringify(order);
console.log(text);
// {"id":1042,"customer":"Asha","paid":true,"total":null,"placedAt":"2026-11-10T09:30:00.000Z"}

const back = JSON.parse(text);
console.log(typeof back.placedAt);   // "string" — not a Date any more
console.log(back.placedAt === order.placedAt); // false
console.log(new Date(back.placedAt).getFullYear()); // 2026

try {
  JSON.parse("{ 'id': 1 }");         // single quotes are invalid JSON
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.name);               // "SyntaxError"
}
console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: [1, 2] }, null, 2));
{
  "a": 1,
  "b": [
    1,
    2
  ]
}
JavaScript valueAfter stringify + parse
Function, undefined, symbol as property valueProperty removed (in an array: becomes null)
DateISO string (toJSON is called); you must convert back
NaN, Infinitynull
Map, Set{} — empty! Convert with [...map] first
BigIntTypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt
Circular referenceTypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON

A Map is not a plain object, but it is often the better data structure; see below.

Map and Set vs plain objects

Objects work as dictionaries for simple string keys, but Map is closer to Java's HashMap and Set to HashSet.

ObjectMap
Key typesStrings and symbols only (numbers become strings)Any value, even objects
SizeObject.keys(o).lengthmap.size
OrderMostly insertion order (integer keys first)Insertion order, guaranteed
Extra keysInherits toString etc.Clean
JSONWorks directlyNeeds conversion
Use forRecords with known fields; API dataDynamic lookups, caches, counting
 
const visits = new Map();
visits.set("home", 3).set("cart", 1);
visits.set("home", visits.get("home") + 1);
console.log(visits.get("home"), visits.has("pay"), visits.size); // 4 false 2
for (const [page, n] of visits) console.log(page, n);

const tags = new Set(["java", "js", "java"]);
console.log(tags.size);          // 2
console.log(tags.has("js"));     // true
console.log([...tags]);          // ["java", "js"]

Edge cases

  • Keys are always strings: { 1: "a" }[1] works because 1 becomes "1".
  • Methods written as arrow functions inside an object do not get this from the object (see this).
  • JSON.parse("") and JSON.parse(undefined) throw SyntaxError. When a Spring endpoint returns no body (204), calling response.json() fails the same way.
  • A key named __proto__ in data from the outside can be a security risk (prototype pollution); validate or use Map.

Common mistake: expecting objects to compare or copy by value

Wrong

const a = { id: 1 };
const b = a;           // same object
b.id = 2;
console.log(a.id);     // 2
console.log({ id: 1 } === { id: 1 }); // false

Right

const b = { ...a };    // copy
b.id = 2;
console.log(a.id);     // 1
const same = JSON.stringify(x) === JSON.stringify(y);
// quick compare for plain data; key order matters

Interview angle

  • "What does JSON.stringify drop?" Functions, undefined, symbols; it changes dates to strings, NaN to null, and throws for BigInt and cycles.
  • "Dot vs bracket notation?" Same result; brackets accept variables and unusual names.
  • "Object vs Map?" Map allows any key type, has size, and keeps insertion order.
  • "Is JSON the same as a JavaScript object?" No: JSON is text with strict rules; an object is an in-memory value.
  • "How do you iterate an object?" Object.entries() with for…of.

Destructuring, spread, rest and template literals

Destructuring unpacks arrays and objects into variables in one line, spread (...) copies or merges them, rest (...) gathers the remainder, and template literals (backticks) build strings with ${expression} — all four appear in every React file.

These four features are only syntax, but they make modern JavaScript short and readable. Java has no direct equivalent (records and string templates are the nearest ideas). The three-dot ... means two different things depending on position: spread when it expands something into pieces, rest when it collects pieces into one thing.

Object destructuring

Destructuring pulls values out of an object or array into separate variables. For objects you match by property name, using braces on the left side.

const user = {
  id: 7,
  name: "Asha",
  address: { city: "Pune", pin: "411001" },
  roles: ["USER", "ADMIN"],
};

const { name, id } = user;                 // name = "Asha", id = 7
const { name: fullName } = user;           // rename: variable fullName
const { phone = "not given" } = user;      // default when undefined
const { address: { city } } = user;        // nested: city = "Pune"
const { roles: [firstRole] } = user;       // object + array: "USER"
const { id: userId, ...others } = user;    // rest: others has name, address, roles

console.log(name, id, fullName, phone, city, firstRole);
// Asha 7 Asha not given Pune USER
console.log(Object.keys(others));          // [ 'name', 'address', 'roles' ]

If the value is null or undefined, destructuring throws TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'name' of 'user' as it is undefined. Give a default: const { name } = user ?? {}.

Array destructuring

For arrays you match by position, using square brackets.

const [first, second] = ["Rice", "Dal", "Ghee"];
const [, , third] = ["Rice", "Dal", "Ghee"];     // skip with commas
const [head, ...tail] = [1, 2, 3, 4];             // rest: tail = [2, 3, 4]
const [a = 10, b = 20] = [5];                     // a = 5, b = 20 (default)

let x = 1, y = 2;
[x, y] = [y, x];                                  // swap without a temp variable
console.log(first, second, third, head, tail, a, b, x, y);
// Rice Dal Ghee 1 [ 2, 3, 4 ] 5 20 2 1

// Functions that return pairs: React's useState returns an array
function minMax(list) { return [Math.min(...list), Math.max(...list)]; }
const [low, high] = minMax([4, 9, 2]);            // 2 9
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);            // React, Module 5

Destructuring in function parameters

This is how React components receive props, and it is a clean way to write "named arguments" in a language without them.

function printOrder({ id, items = [], paid = false }) {
  console.log(`#${id}: ${items.length} items, paid: ${paid}`);
}
printOrder({ id: 1042, items: ["a", "b"] });   // #1042: 2 items, paid: false

function createUser({ name, role = "USER", active = true } = {}) {
  return { name, role, active };               // "= {}" lets you call createUser()
}
console.log(createUser({ name: "Ravi" }));     // { name: 'Ravi', role: 'USER', active: true }

[["a", 1], ["b", 2]].forEach(([key, value]) => console.log(key, value));
// Destructure while looping: for (const { id, name } of users) { ... }

Spread: expand into pieces

const veg = ["Onion", "Tomato"];
const dairy = ["Milk"];
const all = [...veg, "Salt", ...dairy];        // [Onion, Tomato, Salt, Milk]
const copy = [...veg];                          // shallow copy

console.log(Math.max(...[4, 9, 2]));            // 9 — array becomes separate arguments

const defaults = { theme: "light", lang: "en", notify: true };
const mine = { lang: "hi", notify: false };
const settings = { ...defaults, ...mine };      // later keys win
console.log(settings);                          // { theme: 'light', lang: 'hi', notify: false }

// Immutable updates — the React way
const state = { user: { name: "Asha", city: "Pune" }, count: 1 };
const next = { ...state, user: { ...state.user, city: "Goa" }, count: state.count + 1 };
console.log(state.user.city, next.user.city);   // Pune Goa

console.log([..."हिंदी"].length, [..."abc"]);   // string spread; [ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]

Spread makes a shallow copy: nested objects are still shared, so update nested levels by spreading each level (as in the user line above). Spreading an object with the same key twice keeps the last one. Spread of null/undefined into an object is fine ({ ...null } is {}), but spread of null into an array or function call throws TypeError.

Rest: gather the remainder

Rest appears in a function's parameter list (function f(a, ...others)) and at the end of a destructuring pattern, as shown above. It always collects into a real array (or, for objects, a new object) and must be the last element.

WhereMeaningExample
Call or array/object literalSpread (expand)f(...args), [...a, ...b], { ...o }
Parameter list or destructuring patternRest (collect)function f(...args), const [h, ...t] = list

Template literals

A template literal uses backticks. It can span several lines, and ${...} inserts the result of any expression. It replaces Java's + joining, String.format and text blocks.

const name = "Asha";
const total = 1497;
console.log(`Hello ${name}, your total is ₹${total * 1.18}`);
// Hello Asha, your total is ₹1766.46
console.log(`Status: ${total > 1000 ? "FREE delivery" : "Delivery ₹40"}`);

const html = `
  <li class="item">
    <strong>${name}</strong>
  </li>`;                                // multi-line, keeps the line breaks
console.log(html.trim().split("\n").length);  // 3

console.log(`Price: ${total.toFixed(2)} \`INR\``);   // escape a backtick with \

// Tagged template (brief): a function called with the text parts and the values
function bold(strings, ...values) {
  return strings.reduce((out, s, i) => out + s + (values[i] !== undefined ? `*${values[i]}*` : ""), "");
}
console.log(bold`Order ${1042} for ${name}`);   // Order *1042* for *Asha*

Tagged templates are what libraries such as styled-components and GraphQL's gql use. You only need to recognise them.

Rule: never put user input into HTML templates unescaped

A template literal does not escape anything. If you build HTML with `<p>${comment}</p>` and assign it to innerHTML, a user comment containing a script tag becomes an attack (see the DOM). The same applies to SQL: never build SQL strings this way; use parameters.

Edge cases

  • Starting a statement with a destructuring pattern needs brackets: ({ a, b } = obj);, otherwise { is read as a block.
  • Defaults apply only for undefined, not null: const { x = 5 } = { x: null } gives null.
  • ${obj} calls toString(), giving "[object Object]"; use JSON.stringify(obj). A Symbol inside ${ } throws TypeError.
  • Rest in an object pattern copies only own enumerable properties.

Common mistake: mutating state instead of spreading

Wrong: edits the original

const updated = state;
updated.count = 5;          // state.count is 5 too
items.push(newItem);        // React will not re-render

Right: new object and array

const updated = { ...state, count: 5 };
const newItems = [...items, newItem];

Interview angle

  • "Spread vs rest?" Same ... symbol: spread expands, rest collects; position decides.
  • "How do you merge two objects?" { ...a, ...b }; the later wins. It is a shallow merge.
  • "Swap two variables without a temp?" [a, b] = [b, a].
  • "Destructure a nested object with a default and a rename." const { address: { city: town = "NA" } = {} } = user;

The DOM: selecting and changing elements

The DOM is the live tree of objects the browser builds from your HTML; with querySelector you find elements, with textContent, attributes, classList and createElement you change them, and you must never put user text into innerHTML (XSS).

When the browser loads HTML, it builds a tree of objects in memory: the DOM (Document Object Model). The <html> element is the root, <body> is a child, and so on. JavaScript gets this tree through the global document object. When your code changes a DOM object, the browser immediately updates what the user sees. The DOM is not part of the JavaScript language but a browser API (see where JavaScript runs). The HTML you wrote in Module 1 is the starting point; the DOM is what it becomes at runtime, and it can differ from the source after your script has changed it.

Selecting elements

Use querySelector with any CSS selector (the same selectors from Module 2). It returns the first match or null. querySelectorAll returns a NodeList of all matches (empty if none), which supports forEach and for…of; use [...list] or Array.from(list) to get map/filter.

const title = document.querySelector("h1");              // first h1
const form = document.querySelector("#login-form");      // by id
const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".card");        // all with class "card"
const firstItem = document.querySelector("ul.menu li:first-child");
const byId = document.getElementById("login-form");      // faster, id only, no "#"

console.log(cards.length);                 // 3
const names = [...cards].map(c => c.dataset.name);
console.log(document.querySelector(".nothing")); // null — check before using it

// Searching inside one element only
const firstCard = cards[0];
const price = firstCard.querySelector(".price");

// Walking the tree
console.log(price.parentElement === firstCard);   // true
console.log(firstCard.children.length, firstCard.nextElementSibling);
console.log(price.closest(".card") === firstCard); // closest ancestor matching a selector

The older getElementsByClassName and getElementsByTagName return live collections that update when the page changes; querySelectorAll returns a fixed snapshot. Prefer querySelector(All) for everything.

Reading and changing content

PropertyReads / writesHTML in the value is…Use for
textContentAll text inside, including hidden elementsTreated as plain text (safe)Showing any text, especially user data
innerTextVisible text only, aware of CSSPlain text (safe)Rare; slower
innerHTMLThe inner HTML as a stringParsed as HTML (dangerous)Only for your own fixed markup
valueThe current text of an <input>Plain textForm fields
 
const msg = document.querySelector("#message");
msg.textContent = "Order placed!";                // safe
console.log(msg.textContent);                     // "Order placed!"

const input = document.querySelector("#coupon");
console.log(input.value.trim());                  // what the user typed (a string)
input.value = "";                                 // clear the field

const userComment = '<img src=x onerror="alert(1)">';
msg.textContent = userComment;     // shows the tag as harmless text
msg.innerHTML = userComment;       // BROWSER BUILDS AN IMAGE; onerror runs your attacker's code

Danger: innerHTML with user data is an XSS hole

XSS (cross-site scripting) happens when an attacker's text is run as code in other users' browsers. Comments, names, search terms, URL parameters and API data can all contain it. The script can read localStorage, call your API with the user's token and more. See Module 6 for the security side.

Wrong: user text becomes HTML

list.innerHTML += `<li>${userText}</li>`;

Right: build elements, set textContent

const li = document.createElement("li");
li.textContent = userText;
list.append(li);

If you must show rich HTML from users, sanitise it with a library such as DOMPurify. React escapes text by default, which is a major reason people use it.

Attributes, dataset, classes and styles

const link = document.querySelector("a.docs");
link.getAttribute("href");              // "/docs" (as written in HTML)
link.setAttribute("target", "_blank");
link.removeAttribute("title");
link.hasAttribute("rel");               // false
link.href;                              // property: full URL "https://site.com/docs"

const btn = document.querySelector("#pay");
btn.disabled = true;                    // boolean attributes are properties
btn.dataset.orderId = "1042";           // sets data-order-id="1042"
console.log(btn.dataset.orderId);       // "1042" — always a string

btn.classList.add("loading");
btn.classList.remove("primary");
btn.classList.toggle("hidden");         // add if missing, remove if present
console.log(btn.classList.contains("loading")); // true

btn.style.backgroundColor = "tomato";   // inline style, camelCase names
btn.style.setProperty("--radius", "8px"); // CSS variables
// Prefer classes: define the look in CSS (Module 2), switch it with classList.

Names with dashes become camelCase in JavaScript: data-order-id → dataset.orderId, background-color → style.backgroundColor.

Creating, inserting, moving and removing

const list = document.querySelector("#cart");

const li = document.createElement("li");       // not on the page yet
li.textContent = "Paneer × 2";
li.classList.add("cart-item");
list.append(li);                               // add at the end
list.prepend(document.createElement("li"));    // at the start
li.before(document.createElement("hr"));       // before a sibling
li.after("plain text");                        // strings become text nodes

const clone = li.cloneNode(true);              // true = deep copy
li.remove();                                   // remove from the page
list.replaceChildren();                        // remove all children
list.replaceChildren(...["Rice", "Dal"].map(n => {
  const x = document.createElement("li"); x.textContent = n; return x;
}));

// Many insertions: build in a fragment, add once (one reflow)
const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();
for (const n of ["A", "B", "C"]) {
  const item = document.createElement("li");
  item.textContent = n;
  frag.append(item);
}
list.append(frag);

Changing the DOM many times in a loop is slow, because the browser may recalculate the layout each time. Batch the changes (fragment, or build one string of trusted markup). Frameworks like React exist partly to do this batching for you.

DOMContentLoaded and script placement

Your script can touch only elements that already exist. With defer or type="module" the DOM is ready when the script runs. If you cannot use those, wait for the event:

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {
  console.log("HTML parsed; images may still be loading");
});
window.addEventListener("load", () => console.log("everything loaded, images too"));

Edge cases and errors

  • TypeError: Cannot set properties of null (setting 'textContent'): the selector matched nothing (typo, wrong id, or script ran too early).
  • querySelector("#my id") or an id starting with a digit throws SyntaxError: '…' is not a valid selector; use getElementById or CSS.escape.
  • innerHTML += re-creates all existing children, which destroys their event listeners and input values.
  • NodeList has no map/filter; convert with spread first.
  • Each element is the same object everywhere: two querySelector calls for one element give === references.

In real projects

In React you almost never call querySelector: you describe the UI from state and React updates the DOM. Direct DOM code remains in small scripts, in non-React pages, in browser extensions and in the rare React escape hatch (useRef). Learning the DOM first shows you what React does for you.

Interview angle

  • "What is the DOM?" A tree of objects representing the page; the browser API through which JavaScript reads and changes it.
  • "textContent vs innerHTML?" Plain text (safe) vs parsed HTML (XSS risk with user data).
  • "querySelector vs getElementById?" Any CSS selector, first match or null; id only, slightly faster.
  • "NodeList vs array / live vs static?" Convert with spread; querySelectorAll is static.
  • "DOMContentLoaded vs load?" HTML parsed vs all resources loaded.

Events: listeners, bubbling, delegation and forms

An event is something that happens (click, input, submit); you react with addEventListener(type, handler), the event object describes it, events bubble up the tree so one listener on a parent can serve many children (delegation), and preventDefault() stops the browser default such as a form reload.

Browser programs are event-driven: you do not run top to bottom and finish; you register small functions and the browser calls them when the user clicks, types, scrolls, or when a timer or network response fires. A listener (or handler) is such a function. It is the same idea as a Swing ActionListener, without the interface.

const button = document.querySelector("#pay");

function handleClick(event) {
  console.log("clicked:", event.type, event.target.id);
}
button.addEventListener("click", handleClick);       // register
button.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("second listener")); // many allowed

button.removeEventListener("click", handleClick);    // needs the SAME function reference
button.addEventListener("click", () => {}, { once: true });  // run once, then auto-remove

Avoid the old styles button.onclick = fn (only one handler per event) and the HTML attribute onclick="…" (mixes code into markup).

Common events

EventFires whenNotes
clickMouse click, tap, Enter/Space on a buttonWorks for keyboard users on real buttons
inputValue of a field changes (every keystroke)Use for live search and validation
changeValue is committed (blur, select/checkbox changed)Good for dropdowns and checkboxes
submitA form is submitted (button or Enter)Listen on the form, not the button
keydown / keyupA key is pressed / releasedevent.key is "Enter", "Escape", "a"
focus / blurElement gains / loses focusDo not bubble; focusin/focusout do
mouseover, mouseoutPointer enters / leavesCSS :hover is often enough
scroll, resizeScrolling, window resizingFires very often — throttle
DOMContentLoadedHTML is parsedOn document

The event object

The browser passes an event object to your handler. The useful parts:

  • event.type — the event name, e.g. "click".
  • event.target — the element that was actually clicked (maybe a child of what you listened on).
  • event.currentTarget — the element the listener is attached to (always the same as the element you called addEventListener on).
  • event.key, event.shiftKey — for keyboard events; event.clientX/Y for the mouse.
  • event.preventDefault() — cancel the browser's default action (following a link, submitting a form).
  • event.stopPropagation() — stop the event from travelling to parent elements.

Bubbling and capturing

An event does not stay on the element where it happened. It travels in three phases: first capturing (from window down to the target), then the target itself, then bubbling (from the target back up to window). Listeners run in the bubbling phase by default, so a click on a button also triggers the click listeners on its parent div, then body, and so on. Pass { capture: true } as the third argument to listen during the capturing phase (rare).

// HTML: <div id="card"><button id="buy">Buy</button></div>
document.querySelector("#card").addEventListener("click", () => console.log("card"));
document.querySelector("#buy").addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  console.log("button");
  // e.stopPropagation();   // would hide the click from "card"
});
// Click the button:  button, then card

Use stopPropagation() sparingly: it breaks code (analytics, dropdowns that close on an outside click) which relies on seeing the event.

Event delegation

Event delegation means putting one listener on a parent and using event.target to find which child was clicked. It has three benefits: fewer listeners (one instead of a hundred), items added later work automatically, and removing items leaves no stale listeners. It is the standard pattern for lists and tables.

const list = document.querySelector("#cart");

list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const removeBtn = event.target.closest("button.remove");
  if (!removeBtn || !list.contains(removeBtn)) return;     // click was elsewhere

  const item = removeBtn.closest("li");
  console.log("removing", item.dataset.id);
  item.remove();
});

// Items added later also work — no new listener needed
const li = document.createElement("li");
li.dataset.id = "99";
li.innerHTML = '<span>Tea</span> <button class="remove">x</button>';   // fixed markup, no user data
list.append(li);

closest() matters: if the button contains an icon, event.target may be the icon, not the button. closest("button.remove") walks up from the target and finds the right element.

Forms

A form's default action on submit is to send a request and reload the page. A JavaScript app handles submit itself, calls event.preventDefault() and then works with the data. FormData reads all named fields at once.

// HTML:
// <form id="signup">
//   <input name="email" type="email" required>
//   <input name="age" type="number">
//   <p id="error"></p> <button>Join</button>
// </form>
const form = document.querySelector("#signup");
const error = document.querySelector("#error");

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();                       // stop the page reload
  const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
  console.log(data);                            // { email: 'a@b.in', age: '21' } — strings!

  const age = Number(data.age);
  if (!data.email.includes("@") || Number.isNaN(age) || age < 18) {
    error.textContent = "Enter a valid email and an age of 18 or more.";
    return;
  }
  error.textContent = "";
  console.log("send to server", { email: data.email, age });
  form.reset();
});

document.querySelector('input[name="email"]').addEventListener("input", (e) => {
  console.log("typing:", e.target.value);       // live
});

HTML5 validation attributes (required, type="email", min, pattern) run before the submit event; see Module 1. Always validate again on the server (Bean Validation in Spring Boot): browser checks are for user comfort only, not security.

Keyboard and debouncing

Typing into a live-search box fires input on every key. Sending one API call per key is wasteful. A debounce waits until the user pauses. It uses a closure for the timer id (see closures).

function debounce(fn, delayMs) {
  let timerId;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timerId);
    timerId = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), delayMs);
  };
}
const search = debounce((text) => console.log("searching for", text), 300);
document.querySelector("#q").addEventListener("input", (e) => search(e.target.value));

document.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => {
  if (e.key === "Escape") console.log("close the dialog");
  if (e.ctrlKey && e.key === "k") { e.preventDefault(); console.log("open search"); }
});

Rule: remove listeners you add to long-lived targets

A listener on window or document lives until you remove it, and keeps everything its closure uses in memory. Add it in setup and remove it in cleanup. In React, useEffect returns a cleanup function for exactly this.

Edge cases

  • this inside a normal-function handler is the element (currentTarget); inside an arrow function it is not. See this.
  • focus, blur and scroll do not bubble to parents (use focusin/focusout for delegation).
  • A <button> inside a form defaults to type="submit"; use type="button" for non-submit buttons.
  • Passive listeners: for touchstart/wheel the browser may ignore preventDefault() unless you say { passive: false }.
  • A checkbox's state is checked (boolean), not value.

Common mistake: forgetting preventDefault, and the wrong listener type

Wrong: page reloads, state lost

form.addEventListener("submit", () => {
  saveOrder();            // runs, then the page reloads
});
btn.addEventListener("click", save());  // called immediately

Right

form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  saveOrder();
});
btn.addEventListener("click", save);

Interview angle

  • "What is event bubbling? Capturing?" Events travel down then up the tree; listeners default to the bubbling phase.
  • "What is event delegation and why use it?" One parent listener + event.target/closest; fewer listeners, works for dynamic items.
  • "target vs currentTarget?" The element clicked vs the element the listener is on.
  • "preventDefault vs stopPropagation?" Cancel the default action vs stop the event travelling.
  • "Debounce vs throttle?" Run after a pause vs at most once per interval.

A complete example: a to-do list with the DOM

One page ties the DOM and events together: a form adds tasks, a delegated listener toggles and deletes them, and a single render() function draws the whole list from an array — the same "state in, UI out" idea that React uses.

This example uses no libraries. The important design choice is to keep the data in an array (the state) and to have one function that redraws the list from that array. Handlers change the array and call render(); they never patch the DOM by hand. That keeps data and screen from drifting apart. Saving the tasks to localStorage is added in Storage and in the practice exercises.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>To-do</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
  <script src="todo.js" defer></script>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>My tasks</h1>
    <form id="add-form">
      <input id="task-input" name="task" placeholder="What needs doing?"
             autocomplete="off" required>
      <button type="submit">Add</button>
    </form>
    <ul id="task-list"></ul>
    <p id="summary"></p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>
li { display: flex; gap: 0.5rem; align-items: center; padding: 0.4rem 0; }
li.done span { text-decoration: line-through; color: gray; }
li span { flex: 1; }
// ---- State: the single source of truth ----
let tasks = [
  { id: 1, text: "Learn closures", done: true },
  { id: 2, text: "Build the to-do app", done: false },
];
let nextId = 3;

// ---- Element references ----
const form = document.querySelector("#add-form");
const input = document.querySelector("#task-input");
const list = document.querySelector("#task-list");
const summary = document.querySelector("#summary");

// ---- Render: draw the list from the state ----
function render() {
  list.replaceChildren();                       // clear the old list

  for (const task of tasks) {
    const li = document.createElement("li");
    li.dataset.id = task.id;
    li.classList.toggle("done", task.done);

    const checkbox = document.createElement("input");
    checkbox.type = "checkbox";
    checkbox.checked = task.done;
    checkbox.setAttribute("aria-label", `Mark "${task.text}" as done`);

    const label = document.createElement("span");
    label.textContent = task.text;              // textContent: safe against XSS

    const remove = document.createElement("button");
    remove.type = "button";
    remove.className = "remove";
    remove.textContent = "Delete";

    li.append(checkbox, label, remove);
    list.append(li);
  }

  const left = tasks.filter(t => !t.done).length;
  summary.textContent = `${left} of ${tasks.length} tasks left`;
}

// ---- Actions: change the state, then render ----
function addTask(text) {
  tasks = [...tasks, { id: nextId++, text, done: false }];
  render();
}
function toggleTask(id) {
  tasks = tasks.map(t => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t));
  render();
}
function deleteTask(id) {
  tasks = tasks.filter(t => t.id !== id);
  render();
}

// ---- Events ----
form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const text = input.value.trim();
  if (text === "") return;                      // ignore blank tasks
  addTask(text);
  input.value = "";
  input.focus();
});

// One delegated listener for every checkbox and delete button
list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const li = event.target.closest("li");
  if (!li) return;
  const id = Number(li.dataset.id);             // dataset values are strings

  if (event.target.matches("input[type=checkbox]")) toggleTask(id);
  if (event.target.matches("button.remove")) deleteTask(id);
});

render();                                       // first draw
My tasks
[Add]
[x] Learn closures                [Delete]
[ ] Build the to-do app           [Delete]
1 of 2 tasks left

How it works, step by step

  1. The script is loaded with defer, so the form and list exist when the code runs.
  2. render() clears the list and creates one li per task. Text is set with textContent, so a task named <script> is shown as text and not run.
  3. Submitting the form calls preventDefault(), trims the text, adds a new task object to a new array, and redraws.
  4. The list has one click listener. event.target.closest("li") finds the row, dataset.id tells us which task, and matches() decides whether it was the checkbox or the Delete button.
  5. toggleTask and deleteTask create new arrays with map and filter instead of editing items in place.

From this to React

Look at what React will remove: the manual createElement code, the clearing and redrawing, and the element lookups. In React you write the tasks.map(...) part as JSX and call setTasks(...); React updates only the changed DOM nodes. The state array, the map/filter updates and the immutable style stay exactly the same. See Module 5.

Limits of this version

  • render() destroys and rebuilds every row; a text field being edited in a row would lose focus. Fine for a small list.
  • Ids come from a counter that restarts when the page reloads. With stored tasks, compute nextId from the maximum stored id.
  • Editing a task, filters (all/active/done) and drag-and-drop are good extensions: add them as exercises.

Interview angle

  • "Build a to-do list live." State array + render() + delegation + preventDefault; mention textContent for safety and immutability for easy testing.
  • "Why delegate?" New rows get handlers for free; one listener instead of many.
  • "Why does the id from dataset need Number()?" Dataset values are always strings, so "2" === 2 would fail.

The this keyword and how it is decided

In JavaScript this is not fixed to an object like in Java; it is decided by how a function is called — as a method (the object before the dot), as a plain function (undefined in strict mode), with new, with call/apply/bind — and arrow functions simply use the this of the code around them.

In Java, this always means the current instance, and you cannot lose it. In JavaScript a function does not belong to an object. Passing it somewhere else, or calling it differently, gives it a different this. This is the most common source of confusing bugs for Java developers, and a favourite interview topic. The good news: there are only a few rules. To find this, look at the call site, not at where the function was written (except for arrow functions).

The rules, in order of priority

  1. new call: new Cart() — this is the new object being created.
  2. Explicit binding: fn.call(obj), fn.apply(obj), fn.bind(obj)() — this is obj.
  3. Method call: obj.method() — this is obj, the thing left of the dot at call time.
  4. Plain call: fn() — this is undefined in strict mode (modules, classes) and window in sloppy mode.
  5. Arrow function: has no this of its own; it uses the this of the surrounding code where it was written, and none of the rules above can change it.
"use strict";
const cart = {
  owner: "Asha",
  show() { return this?.owner; },          // normal method
  showArrow: () => this?.owner,            // arrow: "this" of the module top level
};

console.log(cart.show());        // "Asha"       — method call, this = cart
console.log(cart.showArrow());   // undefined    — arrow ignores cart

const loose = cart.show;         // copy the function out of the object
console.log(loose());            // undefined    — plain call, this = undefined (strict)

function who() { return this?.name; }
console.log(who.call({ name: "Ravi" }));     // "Ravi"
console.log(who.apply({ name: "Meera" }));   // "Meera"
const bound = who.bind({ name: "Kabir" });
console.log(bound());                         // "Kabir"
console.log(bound.call({ name: "Other" }));   // "Kabir" — bind cannot be overridden
MethodWhen it runsArguments
fn.call(thisArg, a, b)ImmediatelyListed one by one
fn.apply(thisArg, [a, b])ImmediatelyIn an array
fn.bind(thisArg, a)Later — returns a new function with this fixedCan pre-fill the first arguments

Losing this: the classic bug

Passing a method as a callback passes only the function; the object before the dot is left behind. The caller (for example setTimeout) then makes a plain call.

"use strict";
class Timer {
  constructor() { this.seconds = 0; }
  tick() { this.seconds++; console.log(this.seconds); }
}
const t = new Timer();

setTimeout(t.tick, 0);                 // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
                                       // (reading 'seconds')   — this is undefined
setTimeout(() => t.tick(), 0);         // 1 — arrow calls it as a method
setTimeout(t.tick.bind(t), 0);         // 2 — bind fixes this

Three fixes: wrap the call in an arrow function (most common), use bind, or define the method as an arrow function class field, tick = () => { … }, so each instance keeps its own bound version (this is common in older React class components).

Arrow functions fix this inside callbacks

A normal function inside a method has its own this, which is not the method's. An arrow function inside the method uses the method's this.

"use strict";
const team = {
  name: "Backend",
  members: ["Asha", "Ravi"],
  listBad() {
    this.members.forEach(function (m) {
      console.log(this?.name, m);        // this is undefined here
    });
  },
  listGood() {
    this.members.forEach((m) => {
      console.log(this.name, m);         // arrow keeps the method's this
    });
  },
};
team.listBad();    // undefined Asha / undefined Ravi
team.listGood();   // Backend Asha / Backend Ravi

That is why the rule of thumb is: object and class methods are normal methods; callbacks inside them are arrows. Do not write an object method as an arrow (showArrow above), because it cannot see the object.

this in event handlers

For a normal-function handler, the browser calls it with this set to the element (same as event.currentTarget). In an arrow handler, this is the outer this (usually undefined in a module). Use event.currentTarget instead and the question disappears.

button.addEventListener("click", function () {
  console.log(this === button);              // true
});
button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  console.log(this === button);              // false
});
button.addEventListener("click", (e) => console.log(e.currentTarget === button)); // true

this at the top level and in functions called with new

At the top level of a module this is undefined; in a classic script it is window; in Node's CommonJS files it is module.exports. A function called with new acts as a constructor (see classes and prototypes); forgetting new then runs it as a plain call, where this is undefined in strict mode, and this.name = … throws TypeError.

Rule: ask "how was it called?"

Do not look at where a regular function is written; look at the call. a.b.fn() has this = a.b. fn() has no object. For arrow functions only, look at where they are written.

Edge cases

  • (obj.method)() keeps this; (0, obj.method)() and const f = obj.method; f() lose it.
  • call/apply/bind have no effect on the this of an arrow function.
  • In sloppy mode, call(null) makes this the global object; in strict mode it stays null.
  • Class bodies are always strict, so extracting a class method and calling it gives undefined, not window.

Common mistake: arrow function as an object or class method

Wrong: no access to the object

const counter = {
  count: 0,
  inc: () => { this.count++; }   // this is not counter
};

Right: method shorthand

const counter = {
  count: 0,
  inc() { this.count++; }
};

Interview angle

  • "What is this in JavaScript?" A value decided at call time: new > call/apply/bind > method call > plain call; arrows take it lexically.
  • "call vs apply vs bind?" Run now with listed args / run now with an array / return a new bound function.
  • "Why does setTimeout(obj.method, 0) fail?" The method is detached and called plainly; wrap in an arrow or bind.
  • "How are arrow functions different?" No own this, arguments or new.

Classes, prototypes and inheritance

The class keyword gives JavaScript a Java-like syntax (constructor, methods, static, getters, #private, extends/super), but underneath, objects inherit from other objects through the prototype chain — classes are just a cleaner way to set that up.

Since ES2015, JavaScript has a class syntax that looks very much like Java. It is popular in Node.js back ends and in custom error types. In modern React you write function components and rarely use classes, but interviews ask about them, and libraries use them. Remember one fact above all: a JavaScript class is not a blueprint that is copied into every object like in Java. It is a function that creates objects linked to a shared prototype object.

Classes

class BankAccount {
  #balance = 0;                       // private field (real privacy, # is part of the name)
  static bankName = "Desi Bank";      // static field: belongs to the class
  owner;                              // public field

  constructor(owner, openingPaise = 0) {
    this.owner = owner;
    this.#balance = openingPaise;
  }

  deposit(paise) {
    if (paise <= 0) throw new RangeError("Deposit must be positive");
    this.#balance += paise;
    return this;                      // allows chaining
  }

  get balance() { return this.#balance; }          // getter: used like a property
  set balance(v) { throw new Error("Use deposit()"); }

  static compare(a, b) { return a.balance - b.balance; }   // static method

  toString() { return `${this.owner}: ₹${this.#balance / 100}`; }
}

const acc = new BankAccount("Asha", 50_000);
acc.deposit(10_000).deposit(500);
console.log(acc.balance);             // 60500   (getter, no brackets)
console.log(`${acc}`);                // Asha: ₹605
console.log(BankAccount.bankName);    // "Desi Bank"
console.log(acc.#balance);            // SyntaxError — private outside the class
console.log(typeof BankAccount);      // "function" — a class is a function
BankAccount("x");                     // TypeError: Class constructor cannot be invoked without 'new'
FeatureJavaJavaScript
ConstructorNamed like the class; can overloadOne method named constructor; no overloading
FieldsDeclared with a type and a modifierDeclared (optional) or created with this.x = …
Privateprivate#name (enforced by the engine); an underscore name is only a convention
Staticstaticstatic — also static blocks
Getter/setterMethods like getBalance()get balance() looks like a property
Inheritanceextends, singleextends, single
Abstract classes, interfacesYesNone (TypeScript adds them)
Instance creationnewnew is required, else TypeError
Method overriding@OverrideJust define the same name in the subclass

Inheritance with extends and super

class Employee {
  constructor(name, salary) {
    this.name = name;
    this.salary = salary;
  }
  describe() { return `${this.name} earns ${this.salary}`; }
}

class Manager extends Employee {
  constructor(name, salary, reports) {
    super(name, salary);              // must come before using "this"
    this.reports = reports;
  }
  describe() {                        // overrides the parent method
    return `${super.describe()} and manages ${this.reports.length} people`;
  }
}

const m = new Manager("Meera", 150000, ["Asha", "Ravi"]);
console.log(m.describe());            // Meera earns 150000 and manages 2 people
console.log(m instanceof Manager, m instanceof Employee); // true true

If a subclass has a constructor, it must call super(...) before it touches this, otherwise: ReferenceError: Must call super constructor in derived class before accessing 'this'. Custom errors extend Error the same way (see error handling).

Prototypes: what is really happening

Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype (readable with Object.getPrototypeOf(obj); the old name is __proto__). When you read obj.prop, the engine looks at the object itself; if the property is missing, it follows the link to the prototype, then that object's prototype, and so on until null. This path is the prototype chain. It is how [1,2].map works: the array itself has no map, but Array.prototype has it.

// Before 2015: constructor function + prototype (what "class" compiles to conceptually)
function Animal(name) { this.name = name; }
Animal.prototype.speak = function () { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; };

const dog = new Animal("Tommy");
console.log(dog.speak());                                   // Tommy makes a sound
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === Animal.prototype); // true
console.log(dog.hasOwnProperty("speak"));                   // false — it lives on the prototype
console.log("speak" in dog);                                // true

// Object.create: make an object with a chosen prototype
const base = { greet() { return "hi " + this.name; } };
const child = Object.create(base);
child.name = "Asha";
console.log(child.greet());                                 // "hi Asha"

// Methods are shared: one copy for all instances
const d2 = new Animal("Bruno");
console.log(dog.speak === d2.speak);                        // true

Methods defined in a class body are placed on the prototype once and shared by all instances (memory efficient), while fields and this.x = … assignments are per instance. Arrow-function class fields (tick = () => …) are per instance, so each object gets its own copy.

Prototype vs Java classes

  • Java copies nothing at runtime: the class is fixed. In JavaScript you can add a method to a prototype at any time, and every existing object sees it. Do not modify built-in prototypes (Array.prototype.myMethod = …): it can break libraries.
  • Java has multiple interface inheritance; JavaScript has single prototype inheritance. For shared behaviour, use composition: call helper functions or put objects inside objects. Many JavaScript teams prefer composition over deep class hierarchies.
  • Plain objects need no class at all: { name: "Asha" } is the normal way to hold data.

Convention

  • Class names in PascalCase, one class per file, export default class or a named export.
  • Use #private for internals instead of an underscore name.
  • Prefer simple objects and functions; reach for a class when you need many instances with shared behaviour or custom Error types.

Edge cases

  • Classes are not hoisted like functions: using a class before its declaration gives ReferenceError (temporal dead zone).
  • A getter without a setter ignores writes in sloppy mode and throws TypeError in strict mode (class code is strict).
  • Methods are not bound: const f = acc.deposit; f(5) loses this (see this).
  • Private fields do not appear in Object.keys or JSON.stringify; getters on the prototype are not serialised either.
  • Instance fields are created before the constructor body in a base class but after super() in a subclass.

Common mistake: forgetting new, forgetting super

Wrong

const e = Employee("A", 100);   // TypeError: Class
                                // constructor cannot be
                                // invoked without 'new'
class M extends Employee {
  constructor() { this.x = 1; } // ReferenceError: super
}                               // must be called first

Right

const e = new Employee("A", 100);
class M extends Employee {
  constructor(n, s) {
    super(n, s);
    this.x = 1;
  }
}

Interview angle

  • "What is the prototype chain?" Each object links to a prototype; lookups walk the links up to null.
  • "Are JavaScript classes real classes?" They are syntax over constructor functions and prototypes; typeof Class is "function".
  • "What does new do?" Creates an empty object linked to the constructor's prototype, runs the constructor with this as that object, returns it.
  • "How do you make a private field?" #name in a class; closures for plain objects.
  • "hasOwnProperty vs in?" Own property only vs including the prototype chain.

The event loop: how single-threaded JavaScript does many things

JavaScript runs your code on one thread, one piece at a time; slow work (timers, network, clicks) is handed to the browser, and when it finishes the event loop moves its callback into a queue and runs it once the call stack is empty — microtasks (promises) always before the next macrotask (timers, events).

Java handles waiting with threads: one thread per request, or a thread pool. JavaScript has one main thread that runs all your code, and no synchronized, no race conditions between two lines of your code. Yet a page can wait for a 2-second API call and still respond to clicks. The trick is that your code never waits; it starts the job, gives the browser a callback, and moves on. This model is called non-blocking I/O, and it is the same idea Node.js uses on servers.

The parts

Call stack
The list of functions currently running, last in first out (same as the JVM stack). One function runs at a time; it must finish before the next starts.
Web APIs (the host)
Features supplied by the browser (or Node.js), not by the language: setTimeout, fetch, DOM events. They do their work outside the JavaScript thread, using the browser's own threads.
Task queue (macrotask queue)
Callbacks that are ready to run: a timer fired, a click happened, a message arrived. First in, first out.
Microtask queue
A higher-priority queue for promise callbacks (.then, catch, finally, code after await) and queueMicrotask().
Event loop
The loop that watches: when the call stack is empty, run all microtasks, then take one task from the task queue, run it, and repeat. The browser may redraw the screen between tasks.

The ordering puzzle

This is the most famous JavaScript interview question. Predict the output first.

console.log("1: script start");

setTimeout(() => console.log("2: setTimeout 0"), 0);

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log("3: promise 1"))
  .then(() => console.log("4: promise 2"));

queueMicrotask(() => console.log("5: microtask"));

(async () => {
  console.log("6: async function start");
  await null;
  console.log("7: after await");
})();

console.log("8: script end");
1: script start
6: async function start
8: script end
3: promise 1
5: microtask
7: after await
4: promise 2
2: setTimeout 0

Step by step:

  1. The script itself is one task. Synchronous lines run first, in order: 1, then the timer is handed to the browser, then the promise callback and the microtask are queued. The async function runs synchronously until its first await, so 6 prints, and the rest of the function is queued as a microtask. Finally 8 prints.
  2. The stack is empty. The loop now empties the microtask queue, in the order the callbacks were queued: 3: promise 1, 5: microtask, 7: after await. Running "promise 1" queues "promise 2" at the end of the same queue, so it runs next (4) before the loop leaves the microtask phase.
  3. Only now does the loop take the next macrotask: the timer callback, 2: setTimeout 0.

The rule to remember: synchronous code → all microtasks → next macrotask. setTimeout(fn, 0) does not mean "now": it means "after the current script and all promise work are done, and at least 0 ms later".

Blocking the loop

Because there is one thread, a long-running synchronous function freezes everything: no clicks, no scrolling, no timers. It also makes a timer late.

setTimeout(() => console.log("timer"), 100);

const start = Date.now();
while (Date.now() - start < 2000) { /* busy wait for 2 seconds */ }
console.log("loop finished");
// Output: "loop finished" after 2 s, then "timer" — about 2 s late.
// During those 2 seconds the page cannot be clicked.

Never run heavy loops, huge JSON.parse calls or big sorts on the main thread of a UI. Options: split the work into chunks with setTimeout, move it to a Web Worker (a real second thread with its own event loop; communication only by messages), or do it on the server. In Node.js, CPU-heavy work uses worker threads or a separate service.

Single thread vs Java threads

Java (servlet / Spring MVC)JavaScript (browser or Node.js)
Waiting for I/OThread blocks until done (virtual threads make it cheap)Never blocks; callback runs later
Parallel CPU workMany threadsWeb Workers / worker threads
Race conditions on shared dataYes: locks, synchronized, atomicsNot within one thread: code runs to completion
Long taskOccupies one threadFreezes the whole page or server
Async styleCompletableFuture, reactivePromises and async/await everywhere

"Run to completion" means a function that has started cannot be interrupted by another of your functions. But two async operations can interleave at await points, so logical race conditions still exist: two clicks may start two requests whose responses arrive in reverse order.

Rule: keep every task short

A task should finish in a few milliseconds. Anything that takes more than about 50 ms may be felt as a lag by the user. Start slow work with an async API and use its callback or promise.

Edge cases

  • An endless microtask chain (a promise callback that always queues another) starves the task queue: timers and clicks never run, and the page hangs.
  • Timers are not exact. setTimeout(fn, 100) means "no earlier than 100 ms"; browsers also slow timers in background tabs and clamp nested timers to at least about 4 ms.
  • Node.js has its own phases and also process.nextTick and setImmediate; the microtask-before-macrotask idea is the same, but details of the order differ from the browser.
  • alert(), confirm() and synchronous XHR block the thread. Avoid them.

Interview angle

  • "Explain the event loop." Single thread + call stack; async work goes to Web APIs; finished callbacks wait in queues; the loop runs microtasks, then one macrotask, when the stack is empty.
  • "Output of the script above?" Sync logs, then promise/microtask callbacks, then the timer. Explain microtask priority.
  • "Is JavaScript multi-threaded?" The language runs on one thread; the host uses threads underneath; Web Workers give extra threads.
  • "What happens if you run a 5-second loop?" The page freezes, no events or timers run until it finishes.

Callbacks and promises

A callback is a function you hand over to be called later, which leads to nested "callback hell"; a promise is an object that stands for a future value (pending, fulfilled or rejected) and lets you chain then, catch and finally in a flat line, or combine many with Promise.all.

Callbacks and callback hell

The first way to handle async work was the callback: pass a function that runs when the job is done. The convention in Node.js was "error first": callback(error, result).

function getUser(id, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => callback(null, { id, name: "Asha" }), 100);   // fake network
}
function getOrders(userId, callback) {
