  setTimeout(() => callback(null, [{ no: 1, amount: 499 }]), 100);
}
function getPayment(orderNo, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => callback(null, { status: "PAID" }), 100);
}

// Each step needs the previous result, so the code drifts to the right
getUser(7, (err, user) => {
  if (err) return console.error(err);
  getOrders(user.id, (err, orders) => {
    if (err) return console.error(err);
    getPayment(orders[0].no, (err, payment) => {
      if (err) return console.error(err);
      console.log(user.name, orders[0].amount, payment.status); // Asha 499 PAID
    });
  });
});

This staircase is called callback hell (or the pyramid of doom). Errors must be handled at every level, try/catch cannot catch an error thrown later in a callback, and the order of steps is hard to follow. Promises solve this.

What is a promise?

A promise is an object that represents the eventual result of an async operation. It is like a Java CompletableFuture, or a receipt for an order you placed: you do not have the food yet, but you can say what to do when it arrives. A promise is in exactly one of three states:

  • pending — the work is still running;
  • fulfilled — it finished with a value;
  • rejected — it failed with a reason (usually an Error).

Fulfilled and rejected together are called settled; a settled promise never changes again. Callbacks attached with then always run later, as microtasks (see the event loop), even if the promise is already settled.

Creating and using promises

// Creating one: wrap callback-style code (you rarely need this; fetch already returns promises)
function wait(ms) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}
function payUpi(amount) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      if (amount > 1000) reject(new Error("Daily limit exceeded"));
      else resolve({ txnId: "TX123", amount });
    }, 100);
  });
}

payUpi(500)
  .then((receipt) => console.log("Paid", receipt.txnId))   // Paid TX123
  .catch((err) => console.log("Failed:", err.message))
  .finally(() => console.log("done, hide the spinner"));

payUpi(5000)
  .then((receipt) => console.log("Paid", receipt.txnId))
  .catch((err) => console.log("Failed:", err.message))     // Failed: Daily limit exceeded
  .finally(() => console.log("done, hide the spinner"));
MethodRuns whenReturns
.then(onFulfilled, onRejected?)The promise fulfilsA new promise for the callback's result
.catch(onRejected)Rejected (or an earlier step threw)A new promise (fulfilled with the handler's result)
.finally(fn)Settled either way; gets no argumentA promise with the same outcome (unless fn throws)
Promise.resolve(x) / Promise.reject(e)—An already-settled promise

Chaining: the flat version

Every then returns a new promise. If your callback returns a plain value, the next then receives it. If it returns a promise, the chain waits for that promise and passes on its result. That is how the callback staircase becomes a straight line. An error thrown, or a rejected promise, skips ahead to the next catch.

const wait = (ms, value) => new Promise(res => setTimeout(() => res(value), ms));

const getUser = (id) => wait(100, { id, name: "Asha" });
const getOrders = (userId) => wait(100, [{ no: 1, amount: 499 }]);
const getPayment = (orderNo) => wait(100, { status: "PAID" });

getUser(7)
  .then((user) => getOrders(user.id))               // return a promise
  .then((orders) => getPayment(orders[0].no))
  .then((payment) => console.log(payment.status))    // PAID
  .catch((err) => console.error("Something failed", err))   // one handler for all steps
  .finally(() => console.log("end"));

Promise.resolve(1)
  .then((n) => n + 1)                 // returns a plain value
  .then((n) => { throw new Error("boom " + n); })
  .then(() => console.log("skipped"))   // skipped because of the throw
  .catch((e) => { console.log(e.message); return "recovered"; })   // boom 2
  .then((v) => console.log(v));        // recovered — catch returned a value, chain continues

Running promises together

FunctionFulfils whenRejects whenUse for
Promise.all([…])All fulfil — array of results in the original orderThe first one rejects (others keep running, results ignored)Independent calls where you need all
Promise.allSettled([…])All settle — array of {status, value|reason}NeverPartial success is fine
Promise.race([…])The first to settle (win or lose)If the first to settle rejectsTimeouts
Promise.any([…])The first to fulfilWhen all reject (AggregateError)Fastest mirror / fallback
 
const wait = (ms, v, fail) => new Promise((res, rej) =>
  setTimeout(() => (fail ? rej(new Error(v)) : res(v)), ms));

// All three run at the same time: total about 300 ms, not 600
Promise.all([wait(100, "user"), wait(300, "orders"), wait(200, "offers")])
  .then((results) => console.log(results));          // [ 'user', 'orders', 'offers' ]

Promise.allSettled([wait(100, "ok"), wait(100, "bad", true)])
  .then((r) => console.log(r));
// [ { status: 'fulfilled', value: 'ok' },
//   { status: 'rejected', reason: Error: bad } ]

Promise.race([wait(500, "slow API"), wait(100, "timeout!", true)])
  .catch((e) => console.log(e.message));             // timeout!

Promise.any([wait(300, "mirror A"), wait(100, "mirror B")])
  .then((v) => console.log(v));                      // mirror B

Rule: return the promise inside then, and always end with a catch

If you forget to return the inner promise, the next step runs immediately with undefined. A rejection that nobody handles triggers an "unhandled rejection": the browser logs Uncaught (in promise) in the console, and in Node.js the process exits with an error in recent versions. End chains with .catch, or use try/catch with await.

Edge cases

  • Exceptions thrown inside new Promise((resolve, reject) => …) or inside then become rejections; but an error thrown inside a setTimeout callback within the executor is not caught (call reject there).
  • resolve and reject work only once; later calls are ignored.
  • .then(a).catch(b) is not .then(a, b): with the second form, b does not see errors thrown in a.
  • A promise starts running when created, not when you call then. Creating the promises first and then Promise.all is how you get parallelism.

Common mistake: nesting promises like callbacks

Wrong: callback hell again

getUser(7).then((user) => {
  getOrders(user.id).then((orders) => {
    console.log(orders);
  });
});   // errors in the inner promise are lost

Right: return and flatten

getUser(7)
  .then((user) => getOrders(user.id))
  .then((orders) => console.log(orders))
  .catch(console.error);

Interview angle

  • "What is a promise? Its states?" Object for a future value: pending, fulfilled, rejected; settles once.
  • "What is callback hell and how do promises fix it?" Deep nesting with scattered error handling; chaining flattens it with a single catch.
  • "Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any?" Use the table above; mention fail-fast behaviour.
  • "What does then return?" A new promise, which allows chaining.
  • "Why do promise callbacks run before setTimeout?" Microtasks have priority over macrotasks.

async and await, timers and common mistakes

An async function always returns a promise, and await pauses it until a promise settles so asynchronous code reads like normal top-to-bottom code with try/catch; await sequentially when steps depend on each other, use Promise.all when they do not, and never await inside forEach.

async/await (ES2017) is syntax on top of promises. It removes the then chains and makes asynchronous code look synchronous, much like writing blocking Java code — but only the async function pauses; the rest of the program keeps running (see the event loop).

The two keywords

  • async function f() {} (or async () => {}) — always returns a promise. A returned value becomes the fulfilled value; a thrown error becomes a rejection.
  • await promise — only inside an async function (or at the top level of an ES module). It pauses the function, lets the event loop do other work, and resumes with the fulfilled value, or throws the rejection reason.
const wait = (ms, value) => new Promise(res => setTimeout(() => res(value), ms));
const getUser = (id) => wait(100, { id, name: "Asha" });
const getOrders = (userId) => wait(100, [{ no: 1, amount: 499 }]);
const getPayment = (orderNo) => wait(100, { status: "PAID" });

async function showOrderStatus(userId) {
  try {
    const user = await getUser(userId);            // pauses here, UI stays responsive
    const orders = await getOrders(user.id);
    const payment = await getPayment(orders[0].no);
    console.log(user.name, orders[0].amount, payment.status);
    return payment.status;                          // the returned promise fulfils with this
  } catch (err) {
    console.error("Could not load order:", err.message);
    throw err;                                      // rethrow if the caller should know
  } finally {
    console.log("hide spinner");
  }
}

showOrderStatus(7).then((s) => console.log("result:", s));
console.log("this prints first, the function is still waiting");
this prints first, the function is still waiting
Asha 499 PAID
hide spinner
result: PAID

Compare this with the callback pyramid and the then chain in callbacks and promises: the logic is the same, but now it is a straight line, and a single try/catch/finally covers every step like in Java. Note the difference: an await does not block the thread. Code after the call to showOrderStatus(7) ran first.

Sequential vs parallel

Each await waits for its promise before the next line starts. If the calls do not depend on each other, that wastes time.

async function sequential() {
  const t = Date.now();
  const user = await wait(300, "user");        // 300 ms
  const offers = await wait(300, "offers");    // another 300 ms
  console.log("sequential", Date.now() - t);   // ~600
}

async function parallel() {
  const t = Date.now();
  const [user, offers] = await Promise.all([wait(300, "user"), wait(300, "offers")]);
  console.log("parallel", Date.now() - t);     // ~300
}

async function parallelManually() {
  const userPromise = wait(300, "user");       // start both first
  const offersPromise = wait(300, "offers");
  const user = await userPromise;              // then wait
  const offers = await offersPromise;
}

Rule of thumb: depends on the previous result → sequential await; independent → Promise.all. A product page that loads details, reviews and recommendations should start all three at once.

Looping with await

const ids = [1, 2, 3];
const fetchOne = (id) => wait(100, `item ${id}`);

// One after another: ~300 ms (use when order or rate limits matter)
for (const id of ids) {
  const item = await fetchOne(id);
  console.log(item);
}

// All at once: ~100 ms
const items = await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchOne));
console.log(items);   // [ 'item 1', 'item 2', 'item 3' ]

// WRONG: forEach ignores the promises returned by its async callback
ids.forEach(async (id) => {
  const item = await fetchOne(id);
  console.log(item);
});
console.log("forEach finished");   // prints BEFORE any item is logged

forEach, map and filter do not wait for async callbacks. Use for…of with await to go one by one, or Promise.all(array.map(async …)) to go in parallel.

Timers: setTimeout and setInterval

Timers are Web APIs (also in Node.js). Both return an id that you pass to the matching clear… function. The delay is a minimum, not a promise (see the event loop).

const id = setTimeout(() => console.log("runs once after 1 s"), 1000);
clearTimeout(id);                     // cancelled — never runs

setTimeout((name) => console.log("hello", name), 500, "Asha");  // extra args are passed on

let seconds = 0;
const clock = setInterval(() => {
  seconds++;
  console.log("tick", seconds);
  if (seconds === 3) clearInterval(clock);   // stop it, or it runs forever
}, 1000);

// A promise-based sleep makes async code readable
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
async function retry(task, times = 3) {
  for (let i = 1; i <= times; i++) {
    try { return await task(); }
    catch (e) { console.log(`attempt ${i} failed`); await sleep(500 * i); }
  }
  throw new Error("All attempts failed");
}
  • setInterval does not wait for the previous run to finish; a slow callback can pile up. For polling, a setTimeout that re-schedules itself at the end of each run is safer.
  • Always clear intervals when the screen closes (in React, in the useEffect cleanup), or they keep running and leak memory.
  • requestAnimationFrame(fn) runs before the next screen repaint; use it for animations rather than a timer.

Common mistakes

Mistake 1: forgetting await

Wrong: user is a pending Promise

async function show() {
  const user = getUser(7);          // no await
  console.log(user.name);           // undefined
  console.log(user);                // Promise { <pending> }
}

Right

async function show() {
  const user = await getUser(7);
  console.log(user.name);           // "Asha"
}

Mistake 2: unhandled rejection, and awaiting without try/catch

Wrong: nobody catches the failure

button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  const data = await loadData();   // may reject
  render(data);
});
// Console: Uncaught (in promise) Error: ...

Right: handle it where the UI can react

button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  try {
    render(await loadData());
  } catch (err) {
    showError(err.message);
  }
});
  • Mistake 3: await inside forEach (shown above).
  • Mistake 4: awaiting in a loop when Promise.all would do — slow pages.
  • Mistake 5: await in a non-async function: SyntaxError: await is only valid in async functions and the top level bodies of modules.
  • Mistake 6: return somePromise inside try without await: the catch will not catch its rejection. Write return await somePromise there.
  • Mistake 7: making the executor of new Promise async, or wrapping an existing promise in new Promise needlessly.

Top-level await and async in React

In an ES module (type="module", Vite) you may write const config = await loadConfig(); at the top level. In React, the function you pass to useEffect must not be async; define an async function inside and call it. You will see this in Module 5.

Edge cases

  • An async function that throws before its first await still returns a rejected promise; it never throws synchronously to the caller.
  • await on a non-promise just wraps it: await 5 gives 5 (after a microtask delay).
  • With Promise.all, if one promise rejects the others still run to the end, but their results are dropped. Use allSettled to collect everything.
  • You cannot cancel a promise. To stop work such as a network request, use an AbortController (see fetch).

Interview angle

  • "What does an async function return?" Always a promise.
  • "Does await block the thread?" No; it suspends only that function and lets the event loop continue.
  • "How do you run two calls in parallel with await?" Start both, then await Promise.all([…]).
  • "Why doesn't await work in forEach?" forEach ignores the callback's returned promise; use for…of or Promise.all(map).
  • "setTimeout(fn, 0) vs a promise callback?" The promise runs first (microtask).
  • "setTimeout vs setInterval, and how do you stop them?" Once vs repeatedly; clearTimeout/clearInterval with the returned id.

fetch: calling a REST API from JavaScript

fetch(url, options) sends an HTTP request and returns a promise of a Response; it rejects only on network failure, so you must check response.ok yourself, then read the body with response.json() — wrap this in one reusable apiClient that adds the JWT header, a timeout and clear errors.

fetch is the browser's built-in way to make HTTP calls (also available in Node.js 18 and later). It is how your frontend talks to the Spring Boot REST API you built, so every call is one request/response from the HTTP you learned in Module 1. Fetch is promise-based, so you use it with async/await (see async and await). The older XMLHttpRequest is not used in new code; libraries like Axios wrap fetch-like behaviour, but plain fetch is enough for most projects.

A GET request

async function loadProducts() {
  const response = await fetch("http://localhost:8080/api/products");

  console.log(response.status);       // 200
  console.log(response.ok);           // true for status 200–299
  console.log(response.headers.get("Content-Type")); // "application/json"

  const products = await response.json();   // reads the body and parses the JSON — also a promise
  console.log(products);   // [ { id: 1, name: 'Mouse', price: 499 }, ... ]
  return products;
}
loadProducts();

Two awaits are needed: the first resolves when the headers arrive (the response object), the second when the body has been read and parsed. The body can be read only once; calling response.json() twice throws TypeError: body stream already read. Use response.clone() if you need two reads. Other readers: response.text(), response.blob() (files, images), response.formData().

fetch does NOT reject on 404 or 500

The promise rejects only when the request itself could not be completed: no network, DNS failure, CORS block, request aborted. An HTTP error such as 404, 401 or 500 is a successful fetch with response.ok === false. Java developers used to RestTemplate or WebClient throwing on 4xx/5xx are caught by this often. Always check response.ok.

Wrong: error body parsed as data

const res = await fetch("/api/products/999");
const product = await res.json();   // 404 JSON error
render(product);                    // renders "Not found" as a product

Right: check ok first

const res = await fetch("/api/products/999");
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
render(await res.json());

POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE with a JSON body

The second argument is an options object. For JSON you must set the method, the Content-Type header and a string body made with JSON.stringify. Without the header, Spring's @RequestBody answers 415 Unsupported Media Type.

const BASE = "http://localhost:8080/api";

async function createProduct(product) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/products`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(product),            // must be a string (or FormData, Blob)
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Create failed: ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();                           // 201 Created with the saved product
}

async function updateProduct(id, changes) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/products/${id}`, {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(changes),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Update failed: ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

async function deleteProduct(id) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/products/${id}`, { method: "DELETE" });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Delete failed: ${res.status}`);
  // a 204 No Content response has NO body: do not call res.json() here
}

await createProduct({ name: "Keyboard", price: 899 });
OptionMeaning
method"GET" (default), "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"
headersObject of request headers
bodyString (JSON), FormData, Blob, URLSearchParams; not allowed on GET
signalAn AbortSignal to cancel the request
credentials"omit", "same-origin" (default) or "include" to send cookies to another origin
cache, mode, redirectAdvanced controls; defaults are usually right

Query strings and URLs

Do not join query strings by hand: special characters (&, spaces, ₹) must be encoded. URLSearchParams does it for you.

const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: "mobile & cover", page: 2, size: 10 });
console.log(params.toString());   // q=mobile+%26+cover&page=2&size=10

const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/products?${params}`);

const url = new URL("/api/products", "http://localhost:8080");
url.searchParams.set("category", "phones");
console.log(url.href);            // http://localhost:8080/api/products?category=phones

Sending a JWT

After login, Spring Boot returns a JWT (JSON Web Token). Protected endpoints expect it in the Authorization header with the word Bearer and a space. A 401 means "not logged in or token expired"; a 403 means "logged in but not allowed". The backend side is explained on the Spring Boot page.

async function login(email, password) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/auth/login`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Invalid email or password");
  const { token } = await res.json();
  return token;                           // keep it in memory or storage; see "Storage"
}

async function loadMyOrders(token) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/orders/mine`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
  if (res.status === 401) throw new Error("Session expired, please log in again");
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

Timeouts and cancelling with AbortController

Fetch has no built-in timeout; a hung server would keep the request open for a very long time. An AbortController gives you a signal to pass to fetch; calling controller.abort() cancels the request, and the promise rejects with an error named AbortError. The same tool cancels outdated requests, for example when the user keeps typing in a search box or leaves a React screen.

async function fetchWithTimeout(url, options = {}, timeoutMs = 8000) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeoutMs);
  try {
    return await fetch(url, { ...options, signal: controller.signal });
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === "AbortError") throw new Error("Request timed out");
    throw err;
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);                      // always clean up the timer
  }
}

// Shorter, in newer browsers and Node 18+/20+: AbortSignal.timeout(8000)
const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/products`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(8000) });

Network errors vs HTTP errors

Handle the two kinds separately, because the user needs different messages.

SituationWhat fetch doesHow you see it
Server down, no internet, DNS failurePromise rejectsTypeError: Failed to fetch (Chrome) / NetworkError… (Firefox)
CORS blocked by the browserPromise rejects, response hiddenSame TypeError: Failed to fetch; the real reason is in the console
404, 401, 403, 500Promise fulfilsresponse.ok === false, response.status
200 but body is not JSONFulfils; json() rejectsSyntaxError: Unexpected token '<' … (often an HTML error page)
Timeout / cancelPromise rejectsAbortError / TimeoutError

CORS errors

If your React app runs on http://localhost:5173 and calls http://localhost:8080, the browser treats these as different origins and blocks the response unless the server allows it. The console shows "Access to fetch at '…' from origin '…' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header". The fix is on the server (Spring's @CrossOrigin or a global CORS configuration), or a Vite dev proxy. The request often reaches the server; the browser only refuses to let your code read the answer. JavaScript cannot "turn off" CORS. Full explanation in Module 6.

A reusable apiClient

Repeating headers, ok checks and JSON parsing in every call leads to bugs. Put them in one small module. This version adds the base URL, the JWT, JSON handling, a timeout and a custom error that carries the status code and the server's message.

const BASE_URL = "http://localhost:8080/api";

export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(status, message, body) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "ApiError";
    this.status = status;     // e.g. 404
    this.body = body;         // parsed error body from Spring, if any
  }
}

function getToken() {
  return localStorage.getItem("token");
}

async function request(path, { method = "GET", body, params, timeoutMs = 8000 } = {}) {
  const url = new URL(`${BASE_URL}${path}`);
  if (params) Object.entries(params).forEach(([k, v]) => url.searchParams.set(k, v));

  const headers = { Accept: "application/json" };
  const token = getToken();
  if (token) headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  if (body !== undefined) headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json";

  let response;
  try {
    response = await fetch(url, {
      method,
      headers,
      body: body !== undefined ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
    });
  } catch (err) {
    // network failure, CORS, timeout
    const msg = err.name === "TimeoutError" ? "The server took too long" : "Cannot reach the server";
    throw new ApiError(0, msg);
  }

  // 204 No Content, or any empty body
  const text = await response.text();
  const data = text ? safeJson(text) : null;

  if (!response.ok) {
    const message = data?.message ?? data?.error ?? `Request failed (${response.status})`;
    throw new ApiError(response.status, message, data);
  }
  return data;
}

function safeJson(text) {
  try { return JSON.parse(text); } catch { return text; }
}

export const api = {
  get: (path, params) => request(path, { params }),
  post: (path, body) => request(path, { method: "POST", body }),
  put: (path, body) => request(path, { method: "PUT", body }),
  del: (path) => request(path, { method: "DELETE" }),
};
import { api, ApiError } from "./apiClient.js";

try {
  const page = await api.get("/products", { category: "phones", page: 0 });
  console.log(page.length, "products");
  await api.post("/cart/items", { productId: 3, quantity: 2 });
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof ApiError && err.status === 401) {
    console.log("Please log in again");
  } else if (err instanceof ApiError) {
    console.log(`Error ${err.status}: ${err.message}`);
  } else {
    throw err;                              // a bug in our code: do not hide it
  }
}
12 products
Error 400: Quantity must be at least 1

In real projects

  • One apiClient (or an Axios instance with interceptors) is shared by all screens; on a 401 it clears the token and redirects to login.
  • React data libraries such as TanStack Query call your fetch functions and add caching, retries and loading states (Module 5).
  • Spring Boot returns errors as JSON (a message or ProblemDetail detail field), which the client turns into a readable message. Agree the shape with the backend team.
  • The base URL comes from an environment variable (in Vite, import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL), not hard-coded.

Edge cases

  • Do not set Content-Type yourself when the body is FormData: the browser adds the boundary.
  • Do not JSON.stringify a FormData or file; upload it as the body directly.
  • Sending cookies to another origin needs credentials: "include" and a matching server CORS setting.
  • Redirects are followed automatically; a login redirect may return an HTML page with status 200 — a reason json() sometimes fails.
  • A request with a custom header such as Authorization triggers a CORS preflight (an automatic OPTIONS request first). Your Spring Security config must allow it.

Interview angle

  • "Does fetch reject on a 404?" No. Only on network-level failures; check response.ok.
  • "How do you send JSON with fetch?" method, Content-Type: application/json header, JSON.stringify body.
  • "How do you send a JWT?" Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  • "How do you time out or cancel a request?" AbortController / AbortSignal.timeout().
  • "fetch vs Axios?" Axios rejects on HTTP errors, parses JSON automatically, has interceptors; fetch is built in with no dependency.
  • "What is CORS and where do you fix it?" Browser same-origin protection; fix with server headers.

ES modules: import and export

An ES module is a JavaScript file with its own private scope that shares only what it exports and takes what it needs with import; use named exports by default, one default export per file at most, and load the entry file with type="module".

Before modules, every script shared one global scope, and files depended on the order of the script tags. ES modules (ES2015) solve this and are the standard in browsers, in Vite and React projects, and in modern Node.js. The idea is like Java packages and imports, but at the file level: one file is one module; there is no package declaration and no class-per-file rule.

Named exports

export const GST_RATE = 0.18;

export function addGst(amount) {
  return amount * (1 + GST_RATE);
}

export const formatInr = (amount) =>
  new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(amount);

const secret = "not exported";      // private to this file
import { addGst, formatInr } from "./utils/price.js";   // names must match; braces required
import { GST_RATE as TAX } from "./utils/price.js";       // rename on import
import * as price from "./utils/price.js";                // everything in one namespace object

console.log(formatInr(addGst(1000)));   // ₹1,180.00
console.log(TAX);                       // 0.18
console.log(price.addGst(100));         // 118
console.log(Object.keys(price));        // [ 'GST_RATE', 'addGst', 'formatInr' ]

Default export

A module can have one default export. The importer chooses any name, with no braces. React components are usually exported by default.

// CartItem.js
export default function CartItem(props) { /* ... */ }

// elsewhere
import CartItem from "./CartItem.js";        // any local name works
import Item, { helper } from "./CartItem.js"; // default + named together
Named exportDefault export
Count per fileAny numberOne
Import syntaximport { a } fromimport a from
Rename on import{ a as b }Just use another name
Refactoring / auto-importSafer: the name is fixedNames can drift between files
Typical useUtilities, hooks, constantsOne main thing: a React component, a class

You can also re-export: export { addGst } from "./price.js"; and export * from "./price.js";, which is how an index.js file gathers a folder's exports ("barrel file").

Rules of modules

  • Module scope. Top-level variables are private to the file; no globals, no clash between files. Modules are always in strict mode and top-level this is undefined.
  • Run once. A module is executed the first time it is imported and then cached; all importers share the same instance (like a Spring singleton). A module-level let counter is therefore shared state.
  • Imports are live, read-only bindings, not copies. The importing file cannot assign to an imported name (TypeError: Assignment to constant variable), but sees later changes made inside the exporting module.
  • Static and hoisted. import lines must be at the top level (not inside if or functions), and run before the rest of the file. This lets tools do "tree shaking": removing unused exports from the final bundle.
  • The path. In the browser and in Node.js you write the file extension and a relative path starting with ./ or ../: "./price.js". Bundlers such as Vite let you leave the extension off for .js/.jsx files, but a bare name like "react" means a package from node_modules.
<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>
<!-- main.js can import others; they load automatically, in parallel -->

Dynamic import

import("./chart.js") loads a module on demand and returns a promise. Use it for code splitting: load a heavy page only when the user opens it. In React this is React.lazy(() => import("./Reports")).

button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  const { drawChart } = await import("./chart.js");   // downloaded only now
  drawChart(data);
});

CommonJS vs ES modules

Node.js started with its own system, CommonJS: const fs = require("fs") and module.exports = …. You will still see it in older code and config files. Modern Node.js runs ES modules when the file ends in .mjs or package.json contains "type": "module". Do not mix both styles in a file: require is not defined in ES module scope and Cannot use import statement outside a module are the two classic errors.

Edge cases

  • Circular imports (a imports b, b imports a) work only if the values are used later, not while the modules are loading; otherwise you see ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization.
  • Wrong braces are silent surprises: import { CartItem } for a default export gives SyntaxError: The requested module does not provide an export named 'CartItem'.
  • Opening a module page from file:// fails because of CORS; use a dev server (see where JavaScript runs).
  • Forgetting ./ in the path makes the browser treat it as a package name: Failed to resolve module specifier "utils/price.js".

Conventions

  • Prefer named exports for helpers; one default export per React component file, with the file name equal to the component name.
  • Keep one purpose per module; group by feature (cart/, orders/), not only by type.
  • Order imports: libraries first, then your own modules, then CSS.

Interview angle

  • "Named vs default export?" Many vs one; braces vs none; name fixed vs free.
  • "ES modules vs CommonJS?" Static import/export (tree-shakeable, async loading) vs dynamic require/module.exports (synchronous, Node).
  • "What is module scope?" Variables are private to the file unless exported.
  • "What is tree shaking / dynamic import?" Removing unused exports at build time; loading code on demand with import().

Node.js, npm and Vite basics

Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser and npm is its package manager (like Maven for Java): package.json lists your dependencies and scripts, npm install downloads them into node_modules, package-lock.json pins exact versions, and a bundler like Vite prepares your modules for the browser.

Real frontend projects use hundreds of libraries and build tools. They are all JavaScript packages, installed and run with npm (Node Package Manager), which comes with Node.js. Node uses the same V8 engine as Chrome (see where JavaScript runs). Install the LTS version from nodejs.org, then check:

$ node --version
v22.11.0
$ npm --version
10.9.0

(Your numbers will differ; use an LTS release.)

Maven vs npm

IdeaJava / MavenJavaScript / npm
Project filepom.xmlpackage.json
RepositoryMaven Centralnpm registry
Downloaded libraries~/.m2 (shared)node_modules/ inside each project (can be huge)
Exact versions fileDependency management / BOMpackage-lock.json
Installmvn installnpm install
Run a taskmvn testnpm run test / npm test
Test-only dependency<scope>test</scope>devDependencies

package.json

{
  "name": "shop-frontend",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build",
    "preview": "vite preview",
    "lint": "eslint ."
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "react": "^19.0.0",
    "react-dom": "^19.0.0"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "vite": "^6.0.0",
    "eslint": "^9.0.0"
  }
}
  • dependencies — packages your app needs at runtime (and that get bundled): React, a date library.
  • devDependencies — tools used only while building or testing: Vite, ESLint, Prettier, test libraries.
  • scripts — named commands. npm run dev runs the command under dev. start and test can be run without the word run.
  • "type": "module" tells Node that .js files are ES modules (see ES modules).
  • The versions in this file are examples; use the versions that npm installs for you.

Everyday commands

CommandWhat it does
npm init -yCreate a default package.json
npm install (or npm i)Install everything listed in package.json; updates the lock file if needed
npm install axiosAdd a dependency and save it to package.json
npm install -D vitestAdd a dev dependency
npm ciClean, exact install from the lock file; deletes node_modules first; fails if lock and package.json disagree. Use in CI and Docker builds.
npm uninstall axiosRemove a package
npm run devRun a script from package.json
npx vite --versionRun a package's command without installing it globally (it uses the local copy or downloads a temporary one)
npm outdated, npm auditShow old packages; scan for known vulnerabilities
npm create vite@latestStart a new project from the Vite template (React, Vue …)

Semantic versions: ^ and ~

Versions look like MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (for example 19.1.2): a major change may break your code, a minor adds features, a patch fixes bugs. Symbols in package.json say which updates are allowed:

WrittenAcceptsExample range for the entry
"^4.17.2"Same major: minor and patch updates≥ 4.17.2 and < 5.0.0
"~4.17.2"Same minor: patch updates only≥ 4.17.2 and < 4.18.0
"4.17.2"That exact version4.17.2

package-lock.json records the exact version of every package, including those that your packages depend on (transitive dependencies). Commit it to Git so every developer and the build server get identical code. Never commit node_modules: add it to .gitignore, and anyone can recreate it with npm ci.

What a bundler like Vite does

Browsers can load ES modules directly, but a real app has hundreds of files, JSX that browsers cannot read, and packages in node_modules. A bundler reads your entry file, follows every import, transforms JSX and TypeScript to plain JavaScript, removes unused code (tree shaking), minifies, splits the result into chunks and writes a few optimised files to dist/ that any web server (or the static folder of Spring Boot) can serve.

  • npm run dev starts the dev server (usually http://localhost:5173) with instant reload when you save a file.
  • npm run build creates the production files in dist/.
  • Environment variables for the browser must start with VITE_ in Vite (import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL), and are public: never put secrets in them.

Vite, JSX and React come together in Module 5.

Rule: every dependency is code you run

An npm package can run scripts at install time and a compromised or look-alike package (typosquatting) is a real attack path. Install packages you recognise, check download counts and maintainers, commit the lock file, run npm audit and use npm ci in pipelines.

Edge cases and common errors

  • npm ERR! code ERESOLVE: two packages need incompatible versions of a third (often React). Fix the versions rather than forcing with --force or --legacy-peer-deps.
  • 'vite' is not recognized / command not found: dependencies were not installed. Run npm install.
  • Error: Cannot find module 'x': package missing from package.json or node_modules deleted.
  • A global install (npm i -g) is for tools only; project dependencies stay local so every developer uses the same version.
  • Other managers (yarn, pnpm) use the same package.json with a different lock file. Use whatever the project already uses and never mix two in one repo.

Interview angle

  • "dependencies vs devDependencies?" Runtime libraries vs build/test tools.
  • "npm install vs npm ci?" Resolves and may update the lock file vs exact reproducible install from it.
  • "What does ^ mean?" Allow minor and patch updates, not major.
  • "Why commit package-lock.json but not node_modules?" Lock gives reproducible versions; node_modules is generated and huge.
  • "What does a bundler do?" Combines, transforms, tree-shakes and minifies modules into files for the browser.

Browser storage: localStorage, sessionStorage and cookies

localStorage keeps strings in the browser until you delete them, sessionStorage until the tab closes, and cookies travel to the server with every request; store objects with JSON.stringify/JSON.parse, and never keep secrets in storage because any script on the page (XSS) can read it.

The browser can keep small amounts of data on the user's device. The data belongs to one origin (scheme + host + port): http://localhost:5173 cannot read what http://localhost:3000 stored. This is client-side only; the Spring Boot server does not see it unless you send it. Typical uses: a theme choice, a half-written form, the items of a to-do list, a cart for a guest, a login token (with caution, below).

localStoragesessionStorageCookies
LifetimeUntil cleared by code or the userUntil the tab is closedUntil the expiry you set (or end of session)
Shared between tabsYes (same origin)No — each tab has its ownYes
Sent to the serverNoNoYes, with every matching request
Size (approximate)About 5 MB per originAbout 5 MBAbout 4 KB each
Readable by JavaScriptYesYesYes, unless HttpOnly
Set byJavaScriptJavaScriptServer (Set-Cookie) or JavaScript
APISynchronous key-valueSynchronous key-valueString in document.cookie (awkward)

The Storage API

Both storages have the same five methods. Keys and values are always strings: if you store a number or an object without converting it, you get text back.

localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
console.log(localStorage.getItem("theme"));       // "dark"
console.log(localStorage.getItem("nothing"));     // null — missing key
localStorage.removeItem("theme");
localStorage.clear();                              // delete everything for this origin
console.log(localStorage.length);                  // number of keys

localStorage.setItem("visits", 5);
console.log(typeof localStorage.getItem("visits")); // "string"
console.log(localStorage.getItem("visits") + 1);    // "51"  — not 6!
console.log(Number(localStorage.getItem("visits")) + 1); // 6

localStorage.setItem("user", { name: "Asha" });
console.log(localStorage.getItem("user"));          // "[object Object]" — data lost

sessionStorage.setItem("draft", "Dear team...");    // same methods, gone when the tab closes

Storing objects with JSON

Convert with JSON.stringify on the way in and JSON.parse on the way out (what survives is explained in objects and JSON). A small wrapper makes this safe: reading can return null, the stored text can be broken, and storage can be unavailable.

export const store = {
  get(key, fallback = null) {
    try {
      const raw = localStorage.getItem(key);
      return raw === null ? fallback : JSON.parse(raw);
    } catch {
      return fallback;           // corrupt JSON, or storage blocked
    }
  },
  set(key, value) {
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value));
      return true;
    } catch (err) {
      console.warn("Could not save", key, err.name);   // e.g. QuotaExceededError
      return false;
    }
  },
  remove(key) { localStorage.removeItem(key); },
};

store.set("cart", [{ id: 1, qty: 2 }]);
console.log(store.get("cart"));         // [ { id: 1, qty: 2 } ]
console.log(store.get("missing", []));  // []

// To-do app: load on start, save after every change
let tasks = store.get("tasks", []);
function saveTasks() { store.set("tasks", tasks); }

Other useful bits: the storage event (window.addEventListener("storage", e => …)) fires in other tabs when localStorage changes, which is handy for "logged out in one tab" behaviour. Object.keys(localStorage) lists the keys. Storage is synchronous, so do not store megabytes of data; for large data use IndexedDB.

Cookies in short

A cookie is a small piece of text the server sets with a Set-Cookie header; the browser sends it back automatically with every request to that site. Important flags the server sets: HttpOnly (JavaScript cannot read it, which blocks theft through XSS), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite=Lax|Strict|None (limits sending on cross-site requests, a defence against CSRF), Max-Age/Expires. Session logins in Spring Security use a cookie named JSESSIONID.

Security: what to store and what not

Never store secrets or sensitive personal data in web storage

Any script running on your page can read localStorage: an XSS bug, or a compromised npm package (see npm), can steal everything in it and send it to an attacker. Storage is not encrypted, and it is visible to the user in DevTools. Passwords, card numbers, Aadhaar or PAN numbers and API secrets do not belong there.

  • Safe: UI preferences, a draft, a cart of product ids, non-sensitive cached lists.
  • Debated: JWTs. Many tutorials store the access token in localStorage because it is easy; it is exposed to XSS. A more secure option is an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie set by the server, or a short-lived access token kept only in memory. Which one fits depends on the architecture; the trade-offs (XSS vs CSRF) are covered in Module 6. If you do use localStorage, keep tokens short-lived and prevent XSS (use textContent, escape output, set a Content-Security-Policy).
  • Always validate what you read back: the user can edit localStorage in DevTools. Never trust a stored role: "admin"; the server must check permissions on every request.

Edge cases

  • QuotaExceededError when the ~5 MB limit is hit; catch it in setItem.
  • In some private browsing modes or when the user blocks site data, access throws SecurityError; always wrap in try/catch if the feature is optional.
  • localStorage does not exist in Node.js (older versions) and in server-side rendering: guard with typeof window !== "undefined".
  • Values with a Date come back as strings; Map/Set come back as {}.
  • Because the data is shared across tabs, two tabs can overwrite each other's saved state.

Interview angle

  • "localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies?" Use the table: lifetime, size, sent to server, who sets it.
  • "Can you store an object in localStorage?" Only as a string: JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.
  • "Is it safe to store a JWT in localStorage?" It is readable by any script (XSS); an HttpOnly cookie is safer against XSS but needs CSRF protection. Explain the trade-off.
  • "What does HttpOnly do?" Hides the cookie from JavaScript.

Error handling and debugging

Use try/catch/finally and throw new Error() as in Java (but there are no checked exceptions, and you can throw anything), create custom errors by extending Error, and find bugs with the browser's console, breakpoints and the debugger statement.

try, catch, finally and throw

function parseQuantity(text) {
  const qty = Number(text);
  if (Number.isNaN(qty)) {
    throw new Error(`"${text}" is not a number`);      // like throw new IllegalArgumentException
  }
  if (qty <= 0) throw new RangeError("Quantity must be positive");
  return qty;
}

try {
  console.log(parseQuantity("3"));        // 3
  console.log(parseQuantity("abc"));      // throws
  console.log("never printed");
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name, "-", err.message);   // Error - "abc" is not a number
  console.log(err instanceof Error);          // true
  console.log(err.stack.split("\n")[0]);      // the stack trace text (non-standard but everywhere)
} finally {
  console.log("always runs, even after return or throw");
}

try { null.name; } catch { console.log("catch without a variable is allowed"); }

The semantics match Java: a thrown error unwinds the stack until a catch handles it; finally always runs. The differences:

  • There is one catch block per try; to react to different kinds, use instanceof or check err.name inside it.
  • All errors are unchecked; nothing forces you to catch. There is no throws clause.
  • You can throw any value (throw "oops"), but then you get no stack trace. Always throw Error objects.
  • try/catch catches only errors from code that runs inside it while it is running. It does not catch errors in a later callback (setTimeout) or an un-awaited promise; use await inside the try, or .catch() (see async and await).

Built-in error types

TypeTypical causeExample message
ReferenceErrorUsing a name that does not exist (or is in the TDZ)x is not defined
TypeErrorWrong type of value: calling a non-function, reading a property of undefined, assigning to constCannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name'), x is not a function
SyntaxErrorInvalid code or invalid JSONUnexpected token } in JSON at position 12
RangeErrorA value outside the allowed rangeMaximum call stack size exceeded, Invalid array length
URIError, EvalErrorRareURI malformed
AggregateErrorSeveral errors at once (Promise.any)All promises were rejected

The most common one in real life is TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'x'). It means the value before the dot is undefined: an API response with a different shape, a missing array item, an element not found. Read the message, find that line in the stack trace, and check what the value really is (see optional chaining).

Custom errors

Extend Error to give your errors a name and extra data. This is the JavaScript version of your own exception classes, and it is how the ApiError in fetch works.

class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(field, message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "ValidationError";
    this.field = field;
  }
}

class PaymentError extends Error {
  constructor(message, { cause, code } = {}) {
    super(message, { cause });      // "cause" chains the original error (ES2022)
    this.name = "PaymentError";
    this.code = code;
  }
}

function validateEmail(email) {
  if (!email.includes("@")) throw new ValidationError("email", "Enter a valid email");
}

try {
  validateEmail("asha.example.com");
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof ValidationError) {
    console.log(`Fix the ${err.field} field: ${err.message}`);   // Fix the email field: Enter a valid email
  } else {
    throw err;                      // unknown problem: rethrow, do not swallow
  }
}

try {
  try { JSON.parse("{bad"); }
  catch (e) { throw new PaymentError("Could not read gateway reply", { cause: e, code: "GW_PARSE" }); }
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.name, e.code, e.cause.name);    // PaymentError GW_PARSE SyntaxError
}

Where to catch

  • Catch where you can do something useful: show a message, retry, use a fallback value. Otherwise let it travel up.
  • Do not leave an empty catch {}: it hides bugs. At least log it with console.error(err).
  • Global safety nets log unexpected errors to a monitoring service (Sentry or similar): window.addEventListener("error", …) for runtime errors and window.addEventListener("unhandledrejection", …) for forgotten promise rejections. In React, error boundaries catch errors while rendering (see Module 5).
  • Show the user a friendly message; log the technical details. Never display raw stack traces on the page.
window.addEventListener("unhandledrejection", (event) => {
  console.error("Unhandled promise rejection:", event.reason);
  // sendToMonitoring(event.reason);
});

Debugging toolkit

console.log is fine for a quick look, but the console offers more:

MethodUse
console.log(), info(), warn(), error()Messages by severity; warnings are yellow, errors are red with a stack trace
console.table(array)Array of objects as a readable table
console.dir(obj)Browse an object (including DOM elements) as a tree
console.group() / groupEnd()Indented groups of logs
console.time("x") / timeEnd("x")Measure how long something takes
console.assert(cond, msg)Logs only if the condition is false
console.trace()Print the current call stack
 
const orders = [
  { id: 1, city: "Pune", total: 499 },
  { id: 2, city: "Goa", total: 1299 },
];
console.table(orders);
console.log({ orders });          // wrap in {} to print the variable name too
console.time("sum");
const sum = orders.reduce((s, o) => s + o.total, 0);
console.timeEnd("sum");           // sum: 0.05 ms
console.assert(sum > 5000, "Total too small:", sum);   // Assertion failed: Total too small: 1798
console.error(new Error("Payment failed"));
┌─────────┬────┬────────┬───────┐
│ (index) │ id │ city   │ total │
├─────────┼────┼────────┼───────┤
│ 0       │ 1  │ 'Pune' │ 499   │
│ 1       │ 2  │ 'Goa'  │ 1299  │
└─────────┴────┴────────┴───────┘

Browsers draw the table in a nicer grid; the characters differ a little between Node.js versions.

Breakpoints and the debugger statement

A breakpoint pauses the program on a line so you can look at the values, like in IntelliJ. In Chrome or Edge DevTools open Sources, find your file, and click the line number. Then:

  1. Trigger the code (click the button). Execution stops on that line.
  2. Read the Scope panel for local, closure and global variables, and the Call Stack panel to see who called this function.
  3. Step with Step over (F10), Step into (F11), Step out (Shift+F11) or Resume (F8).
  4. Add Watch expressions, or a conditional breakpoint (right-click the line number, "Add conditional breakpoint") to stop only when, for example, order.id === 7.

Writing the statement debugger; in your code does the same thing: if DevTools is open, execution pauses there. Remove it before committing. In VS Code you can debug Node.js scripts, and with a launch configuration also your browser app, using the same step buttons.

Other DevTools panels you will use daily: Elements (live DOM and CSS), Network (every fetch call with status, headers, payload and timing; the first place to look when an API call fails), Application (localStorage, cookies), and Performance. The React Developer Tools extension adds component inspection for Module 5.

A debugging routine that works

  1. Read the error message and the first line of the stack that is in your file.
  2. Check the Network tab: was the request sent, which status, what response body?
  3. Log or break just before the failing line and inspect real values (console.log({ user })).
  4. Reduce the problem: remove code until it works, then add it back.
  5. Fix the cause, not the symptom; add a test or a check so it cannot come back.

Edge cases

  • finally with return overrides a return/throw in try/catch, as in Java; avoid it.
  • A SyntaxError in a script file is not catchable inside that file: the file never runs. Only eval/JSON.parse can throw it at runtime.
  • A cross-origin script error is reported only as Script error. without details unless CORS headers are set.
  • Minified production code gives unreadable stack traces; build tools emit source maps that DevTools and monitoring tools use to map back to your source.
  • console.log(obj) shows the object as it is when you expand it, not when it was logged. To freeze a snapshot, log JSON.stringify(obj) or structuredClone(obj).

Common mistake: swallowing errors and throwing strings

Wrong: hides the bug, no stack

try {
  saveOrder(order);
} catch (e) {
  // nothing
}
throw "Payment failed";

Right: handle or rethrow an Error

try {
  saveOrder(order);
} catch (e) {
  console.error("saveOrder failed", e);
  showToast("Could not save the order");
}
throw new Error("Payment failed");

Interview angle

  • "How is error handling different from Java?" One catch, no checked exceptions, can throw any value, and async errors need promises or await.
  • "Will try/catch catch an error inside setTimeout?" No; the callback runs later outside the try. Put the try inside the callback.
  • "Name the error types." ReferenceError, TypeError, SyntaxError, RangeError.
  • "How do you debug a failing API call?" Network tab for status/response, console error, breakpoints in the handler.
  • "How do you create a custom error?" class X extends Error and set name.

Interview questions — JavaScript

How is JavaScript different from Java?

JavaScript is dynamically typed (values have types, variables do not), has one number type, treats functions as values, creates objects without classes (classes are syntax over prototypes), decides this at call time, and runs on a single thread with an event loop instead of many threads. It is interpreted and JIT-compiled from source by an engine such as V8. The two languages share only C-style syntax. See JavaScript for Java developers.

What is the difference between var, let and const?

var is function-scoped, hoisted as undefined, and can be re-declared. let and const are block-scoped, hoisted but unusable before the declaration (temporal dead zone, ReferenceError), and cannot be re-declared in the same scope. const also forbids re-assignment, but it does not freeze an object: const cart = []; cart.push(1) works. Use const by default, let when you must reassign, and never var.

What is the difference between == and ===? List the falsy values.

=== compares type and value with no conversion. == converts types first, which gives surprises such as 0 == "" and "0" == false both being true. Use ===; the only common exception is x == null to check for null or undefined. Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including [], {} and "0".

What does this print? console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3, typeof null, [] + [], "5" - 3, "5" + 3)

false object "" 2 "53". Numbers are binary floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. typeof null is "object" because of an old bug. Two empty arrays become empty strings and are joined. The - operator always converts to numbers; + joins when one side is a string.

What is hoisting? Predict the output of: console.log(a); var a = 1; console.log(b); let b = 2;

Declarations are registered before the code in their scope runs. var a exists with the value undefined, so the first line prints undefined. let b is hoisted but uninitialised, so the second console.log(b) throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization. Function declarations are hoisted completely and can be called early; function expressions and arrow functions follow their variable's rules. See scope and hoisting.

What is a closure? Why does a var loop with setTimeout print the same number?

A closure is a function plus the variables of the scope where it was created; it keeps using them after the outer function returns. Example: makeCounter returns a function that increments a private count. In for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)) all callbacks share one i, which is 3 when they run, so it prints 3 three times. With let each iteration has its own i, so it prints 0, 1, 2. Uses: private state, factories, memoization, debounce. See closures.

How is the value of this decided? How do arrow functions differ?

For normal functions, by the call: new gives the new object; call/apply/bind give the object you pass; obj.method() gives obj; a plain call gives undefined in strict mode (window in sloppy mode). Arrow functions have no own this; they use the this of the code where they are written, and this cannot be changed. That is why a detached method (setTimeout(obj.method)) loses this, and why an arrow function is a bad object method but a good callback inside a method.

map vs forEach vs filter vs reduce, and how do you sort numbers?

map returns a new array of the same length by transforming each item. filter returns a new array with the items that pass a test. reduce folds the array into one value using an accumulator (always give the start value). forEach returns nothing and is for side effects. sort() compares as strings by default, so numbers need a comparator: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b). sort changes the array in place; toSorted or [...arr].sort() does not.

const total = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
Shallow copy vs deep copy: how do you copy objects and arrays?

Assignment copies only the reference. Spread ([...a], { ...o }) and slice make a shallow copy: the top level is new, but nested objects are shared, so changing copy.address.city also changes the original. structuredClone(x) makes a deep copy of plain data, dates, maps and sets (it throws for functions). JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) is an older trick that loses functions, undefined and dates. In React you update nested state by spreading each level.

Explain the event loop. In what order does this print? console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4);

JavaScript runs on one thread with a call stack. Timers, network and events are handled by the host (Web APIs); when they finish their callback goes into a queue. When the stack is empty, the event loop runs all microtasks (promise callbacks), then takes one macrotask (timer, event). So the output is 1, 4, 3, 2: synchronous code first, then the promise callback, then the timer. See the event loop.

Promises vs async/await: what does an async function return, and how do you run calls in parallel?

A promise represents a future value (pending, fulfilled or rejected). async/await is syntax over promises: an async function always returns a promise, and await pauses only that function until the promise settles (it does not block the thread). Errors are handled with try/catch. Sequential awaits run one after another; for independent calls start them together: const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]). Promise.allSettled never rejects, race returns the first to settle, any the first to fulfil.

Does fetch reject on a 404 or 500? How do you handle errors, send JSON and a JWT?

No. The promise rejects only for network-level failures (offline, DNS, CORS, abort). An HTTP error is a normal response with response.ok === false, so you check response.ok or status and throw yourself. To send JSON: method, header Content-Type: application/json, and body: JSON.stringify(data). For a JWT: header Authorization: Bearer <token>. Add a timeout with AbortSignal.timeout() or an AbortController. See fetch.

textContent vs innerHTML, and what is event delegation?

textContent sets plain text, so it is safe. innerHTML parses its value as HTML, so putting user data in it allows XSS (for example an img tag with onerror). Use textContent or createElement. Event delegation puts one listener on a parent and uses event.target.closest(selector) to find which child was clicked; it needs fewer listeners and works for items added later because events bubble up the tree.

What are prototypes? Are JavaScript classes the same as Java classes?

Every object has a hidden link to a prototype object; reading a missing property walks the prototype chain up to null. Methods of a class live once on the prototype and are shared by all instances. The class keyword (constructor, extends, super, static, #private) is syntax over this; typeof a class is "function". Unlike Java there are no interfaces or abstract classes, no overloading, and a class is not a fixed blueprint (you can add to a prototype at runtime).

localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies, and is it safe to keep a JWT in localStorage?

localStorage lasts until cleared, sessionStorage until the tab closes; both are about 5 MB, string-only and never sent to the server. Cookies are about 4 KB and are sent with each request; the server can make them HttpOnly so scripts cannot read them. Store objects with JSON.stringify/parse. A JWT in localStorage can be stolen by any XSS bug or malicious package; an HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie avoids XSS theft but needs CSRF protection. Never store passwords or card data in web storage. See Module 6.

Cheat sheet — JavaScript

  • Declare const first, let if reassigned, never var; const freezes the binding, not the object.
  • Types string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol + object; typeof null is "object"; arrays: Array.isArray.
  • Numbers one 64-bit float; 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3; use integer paise; Number.isNaN; safe integer up to 253 − 1.
  • Equality always ===; objects compare by reference; x == null is the one OK use of ==.
  • Falsy false 0 -0 0n "" null undefined NaN; [] and {} are truthy.
  • Defaults a ?? b only for null/undefined; a || b for any falsy; obj?.x?.y safe access; x ??= 1.
  • Convert Number("42"), parseInt(s, 10), String(x), +"3"; form inputs are always strings.
  • Functions declaration (hoisted), expression, arrow (a) => a * 2; arrows have no own this/arguments; wrap object results in ( ).
  • Parameters defaults (a = 1), rest (...args), no overloading; pass the function, do not call it: onClick={fn}.
  • Scope block (let/const) vs function (var); lookup walks the scope chain; var hoists as undefined, let/const sit in the TDZ.
  • Closure a function remembers the variables where it was created; gives private state, factories, memoize; let in loops fixes the callback bug.
  • Arrays mutate: push pop shift unshift splice sort reverse; copy: slice concat map filter toSorted [...a].
  • sort default is string order; numbers need (a, b) => a - b.
  • Array methods map transform, filter keep, reduce(fn, start) fold, find first match, some/every yes/no; remove: filter(x => x.id !== id).
  • Objects { a, b } shorthand, [key] computed, Object.keys/values/entries, { ...o, k: v } immutable update, Object.freeze is shallow.
  • JSON JSON.stringify(v, null, 2) / JSON.parse(s); drops functions and undefined, dates become strings, throws on BigInt and cycles.
  • Destructuring const { a, b: x = 1 } = obj, const [h, ...t] = arr, swap [a, b] = [b, a]; spread expands, rest collects.
  • Templates `Hi ${name}`, multi-line; they do not escape HTML.
  • DOM querySelector(All), textContent (safe) not innerHTML (XSS), classList, dataset, createElement + append.
  • Events addEventListener; event.target vs currentTarget; bubbling; delegation with closest; preventDefault on form submit.
  • this new > call/apply/bind > obj.method() > plain call (undefined in strict); arrows use outer this.
  • Classes constructor, #private, static, get, extends + super(); syntax over prototypes; new is required.
  • Event loop sync code → all microtasks (promises, await) → one macrotask (timers, events); long loops freeze the page.
  • Promises pending/fulfilled/rejected; then returns a new promise; Promise.all fail-fast, allSettled never rejects, race, any.
  • async/await async returns a promise; await in try/catch; independent calls with Promise.all; never await in forEach.
  • fetch check response.ok; await res.json(); POST needs Content-Type + JSON.stringify; Authorization: Bearer; AbortSignal.timeout(ms).
  • Modules export named / export default one; import { a } from "./x.js"; type="module"; module scope is private.
  • npm package.json, npm install / npm ci / npm run dev, ^ minor+patch, ~ patch; commit the lock file, not node_modules.
  • Storage strings only: JSON.stringify/parse; localStorage persists, sessionStorage per tab; no secrets (XSS can read it).
  • Errors try/catch/finally, throw new Error(), class X extends Error; catch does not see later async errors; log with console.error.
  • Debug console (table, time, trace), breakpoints, debugger;, Network tab for API calls.

Practice — JavaScript

  1. Output prediction (30 minutes). Without running them, write down the output of the hoisting puzzles in scope and hoisting, the loop bug in closures and the ordering puzzle in the event loop. Then run them in the console. Done when all your predictions match, and you can explain every difference out loud.
  2. Array workout. Given a list of 10 products (id, name, price, category, qty) write one-line solutions: names of products over ₹500; the cart total; the most expensive product; items grouped by category with reduce; products sorted by price descending without changing the original; a list with one product removed by id. Done when no for loop is needed and the original array is never mutated (check with console.log).
  3. Closures and functions. Write makeCounter(step) with increment, reset and value that keep the count private; a memoize(fn) that logs "cache hit"; and a debounce(fn, ms). Done when counter.count is undefined, memoize logs the hit on the second call, and debounce runs once after a burst of five calls.
  4. To-do list saved in local storage (roadmap build). Start from the to-do example. Load tasks from localStorage on start, save after every add, toggle and delete, compute the next id from the highest stored id, and add a filter (All / Active / Done) plus a "Clear completed" button. Done when tasks survive a page reload, bad JSON in storage does not crash the page (wrap in try/catch), and a task named <b>hi</b> is displayed as text.
  5. Quiz app (roadmap build). Keep 8 questions in an array of objects (question, options, answerIndex). Show one question at a time with option buttons (use event delegation), mark the answer right or wrong, keep the score, show a final result with a "Play again" button, and store the best score in localStorage. Done when the whole flow works with only keyboard and mouse, with no global variables outside one module, and the best score stays after a reload.
  6. Calculator (roadmap build). Build a calculator with digit, operator, decimal point, clear and equals buttons, driven by one delegated click listener and data- attributes. Do not use eval. Handle division by zero (show "Cannot divide by 0"), repeated operators, and the 0.1 + 0.2 display (round to 10 decimal places). Add keyboard support with keydown. Done when 7 ÷ 2 shows 3.5, 0.1 + 0.2 shows 0.3 and no input crashes it.
  7. GitHub profile finder (roadmap build, async). A form takes a username and calls https://api.github.com/users/{username}, then shows avatar, name, bio, followers, public repos and the five most recently updated repositories from the /repos endpoint (load both with Promise.all). Show "Loading…" while waiting, a friendly message for 404 (user not found) and for network errors, disable the button during the request, and cancel the previous request with AbortController if the user searches again. Use textContent for all text. Done when every error path shows a message and the page never throws in the console. (A weather app with a public weather API is an equally good alternative.)
  8. Your own apiClient. Create apiClient.js (see fetch) as an ES module and use it against the Spring Boot REST API you built earlier: list, create, update and delete one resource, with a login that stores the JWT. Handle 401 by clearing the token and showing the login form. Done when each call works from a page served by a dev server (or Vite), CORS is configured on the Spring side, and you can show the failing request in the Network tab for a wrong password and for a stopped server and explain the difference.
  9. Review and explain. Without notes, answer the 13 questions in the interview article aloud in under two minutes each, then rebuild the event-delegation delete button from memory. Done when you can explain this, closures, the event loop and fetch error handling to someone who only knows Java.
