Module 5·About 3 weeksMust

React

17 topics · about 2.5 h of reading

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of small, reusable pieces called components. In Module 4 you changed the page by hand: find an element, set its text, add a class, remove a node. React turns that around. You describe what the screen should look like for the current data, and React works out which DOM changes are needed. When a Java full-stack job in India mentions a frontend, it almost always means React (often with TypeScript) talking to a Spring Boot REST API.

This module uses React 19 with Vite. It takes you from an empty folder to a multi-page app with forms, routing, shared state and server data. Module 6 then connects that app to your Spring Boot API, and Module 7 adds TypeScript, Next.js, state libraries and tests.

  • Create a React project with Vite and explain every file in it.
  • Write components with JSX and props, and keep them pure.
  • Manage state with useState and update objects and arrays without mutating them.
  • Handle events, render conditionally and render lists with correct keys.
  • Use useEffect correctly (dependencies, cleanup, data fetching, race conditions) and know when you do not need it.
  • Build forms with controlled inputs, validation and a proper submit flow.
  • Add pages with React Router, including nested layouts and a 404 page.
  • Share state by lifting it up or with Context, and extract your own custom hooks.
  • Fetch and cache server data with TanStack Query.
  • Debug with React DevTools and fix the most common React errors.

What React is and why it exists

React is a library for building user interfaces from components: you describe what the UI should look like for the current data, and React updates the real DOM to match every time that data changes.

The problem: keeping the DOM in sync by hand

In Module 4 you wrote imperative code: step-by-step instructions that change the page. That works for small pages. But every piece of data on screen now has two copies — one in your JavaScript variables and one in the DOM — and you must update both, every time, in every code path. Look at a tiny cart:

const items = [];
const list = document.querySelector('#cart-list');
const badge = document.querySelector('#cart-count');
const emptyMsg = document.querySelector('#empty');

function addItem(name) {
  items.push(name);
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = name;
  list.appendChild(li);
  badge.textContent = items.length;   // forget this line and the badge is wrong
  emptyMsg.hidden = items.length > 0; // forget this one and "Cart is empty" stays
}

// removeItem(), clearCart(), applyCoupon() ... each must repeat the same DOM updates

Add "remove", "change quantity" and "apply coupon" and you have many functions that must all remember to update the badge, the list, the empty message and the total. Miss one, and the screen shows "3 items" while the list has 4. This class of bug is exactly what React removes.

The React way: describe the result

React is declarative: you write what the UI should look like for a given state, not how to change it. When the state changes, React calls your component again and updates only the parts of the DOM that are different.

import { useState } from 'react';

function Cart() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([]);

  function addItem(name) {
    // Change the data. React re-renders and updates the DOM for you.
    setItems([...items, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), name }]);
  }

  return (
    <section>
      <h2>Cart ({items.length})</h2>
      {items.length === 0 ? <p>Cart is empty</p> : null}
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>)}
      </ul>
      <button onClick={() => addItem('Masala Dosa')}>Add dosa</button>
    </section>
  );
}

export default Cart;

There is no code that touches the badge or the empty message. The count, the list and the message are all calculated from items on every render, so they can never disagree.

AspectManual DOM (imperative)React (declarative)
You writeSteps: find node, change text, append childThe UI for the current state
Source of truthData and DOM, kept in sync by youOnly the data (state)
Adding a featureEvery code path must update every affected nodeChange the state; the UI follows
ReuseCopy HTML and selectorsReuse a component with different props
Typical bugScreen out of sync with dataWrong state shape or a misused effect

The core ideas

Component
A JavaScript function that returns a description of UI (written in JSX). You build pages by putting components inside components: App → Header, ProductList → ProductCard.
Props
The inputs a parent passes to a child component, like arguments to a function. Read-only.
State
Data a component remembers between renders, such as the text in a search box or the items in a cart. Changing state makes React re-render the component.
Render
React calling your component function to get the latest UI description. Rendering is not the same as touching the DOM.
One-way data flow
Data flows down the tree through props. A child never changes its parent's data directly; it calls a function the parent passed down (an event "flows up").
Reconciliation
React's process of comparing the new UI description with the previous one to find the minimum set of DOM changes.

How it works: render, reconcile, commit

  1. Trigger. Something calls a state setter (for example setItems). React schedules a render of that component.
  2. Render. React calls your component function again. It returns a new tree of React elements — plain JavaScript objects such as { type: 'h2', props: { children: ['Cart (', 2, ')'] } }.
  3. Reconcile (diff). React compares the new tree with the previous one and works out what changed.
  4. Commit. React applies only those differences to the real DOM — here, it changes one text node and appends one <li>.
  5. Paint and effects. The browser paints the screen, then React runs your effects (useEffect).

The virtual DOM in simple words

The tree of React elements is often called the virtual DOM: a lightweight copy of the UI made of plain objects. Creating objects is cheap; changing the real DOM is slower because the browser may have to recalculate layout and repaint. So React builds the cheap copy first, compares it with the last one, and then makes a small number of real DOM changes.

A perfect comparison of two arbitrary trees is expensive (the general algorithms are around O(n³)). React uses two simple assumptions to do it in roughly O(n):

  • Different type → new subtree. If a <div> becomes a <section>, or <LoginForm /> becomes <Dashboard /> at the same position, React throws away the old subtree (and its state) and builds a new one.
  • Same type → update in place. React keeps the DOM node or component instance and only updates the changed attributes or props. A component keeps its state.
  • Lists use keys. For children rendered from an array, the key prop tells React which item is which between renders (see Lists and keys).

Since React 16 the engine that does this work is called Fiber. It splits rendering into small units so React can pause, prioritise urgent updates (typing in an input) over less urgent ones (re-rendering a long list), and then continue. React 18 and 19 build their concurrent features, such as useTransition, on top of it.

Mistake: thinking "re-render" means "redraw the whole page"

A re-render is just React calling your function and comparing objects. If the output is the same, the DOM is not touched at all. Re-renders are normal and usually fast. Do not start adding optimisations (memo, useMemo) until you have measured a real slowdown.

A library, not a framework

React itself only handles the view: components, state and rendering. Routing, data fetching, form handling and global state are separate libraries you choose — this module uses React Router, TanStack Query and React Hook Form. Frameworks built on React, like Next.js (Module 7), make those choices for you and add server rendering.

ReactAngularVue
TypeUI library (from Meta)Full framework (from Google)Progressive framework (community)
MarkupJSX inside JavaScriptHTML templates with directivesHTML templates in single-file components
LanguageJavaScript or TypeScriptTypeScriptJavaScript or TypeScript
Built inComponents and state onlyRouter, forms, HTTP client, DICore plus official router and store
Data flowOne-wayOne-way plus two-way binding for formsOne-way plus v-model

Version note: React 19

React 19 has been the current major version since December 2024. Things you will meet in newer code: Actions for forms with useActionState and useFormStatus, useOptimistic, the use API for reading a promise or context, ref as a normal prop on function components (no forwardRef needed), rendering <MyContext value={…}> directly as a provider, and <title> / <meta> tags placed inside components. React 19 removed old APIs: ReactDOM.render (use createRoot), propTypes checks and defaultProps on function components, and string refs. React 19.2 (October 2025) added <Activity> and useEffectEvent.

Server Components and Server Functions are part of React 19, but they need a framework that supports them, such as Next.js. In a Vite single-page app, every component is a client component that runs in the browser.

In real projects

The common Java-shop setup is a React single-page application (SPA): Vite builds it into static files, a CDN or Nginx serves them, and the app calls a Spring Boot REST API with JSON and a JWT. Admin panels, internal dashboards, CRMs and banking back-office tools are mostly built this way. That is the setup this page teaches.

A Java way to think about it

A component is like a pure method View render(Props props, State state). Think of a Thymeleaf template that re-renders itself in the browser whenever its model changes — except React patches only the changed parts instead of reloading the page.

Interview: "What is the virtual DOM and how does React update the UI?"

  • Components return React elements — plain objects describing the UI (the virtual DOM).
  • On a state change, React re-renders the component and diffs the new tree with the old one (reconciliation), using element type and key as heuristics, which makes it about O(n).
  • It then commits only the differences to the real DOM; several state updates are batched into one render.
  • The virtual DOM is not "faster than the DOM". Its value is that you write simple declarative code and still get efficient, targeted updates.
  • Fiber (React 16+) lets React split and prioritise rendering work.

Create a React project with Vite

npm create vite@latest creates a React project in seconds, npm run dev starts a fast development server with instant updates, and npm run build produces optimised static files in dist/.

What Vite is

Vite (French for "quick", said "veet") is a build tool and development server. In development it serves your source files to the browser as native ES modules and transforms each file only when the browser asks for it, so the server starts almost instantly even for big apps. When you edit a file, Hot Module Replacement (HMR) swaps just that module in the running page; for React components this is called Fast Refresh and usually keeps the component's state. For production, Vite bundles, minifies and splits your code into a few optimised files.

You need Node.js (which includes npm, the package manager). Install a current LTS release from nodejs.org. Vite 7 needs Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+; newer Vite versions may need a newer Node, so check the Vite docs if the tool complains.

Create and run the project

  1. Open a terminal in the folder where you keep projects and run npm create vite@latest.
  2. Answer the prompts: a project name (for example employee-ui), the framework React, and the variant JavaScript (or TypeScript once you have read Module 7).
  3. Go into the folder and install dependencies: cd employee-ui, then npm install.
  4. Start the dev server with npm run dev and open http://localhost:5173.
  5. Edit src/App.jsx, save, and watch the browser update without a reload.
# Interactive: asks for the name, framework and variant
npm create vite@latest

# Or answer everything in one line (note the extra -- before --template)
npm create vite@latest employee-ui -- --template react      # JavaScript
npm create vite@latest employee-ui -- --template react-ts   # TypeScript

cd employee-ui
npm install
npm run dev
  VITE vX.Y.Z  ready in 350 ms

  ➜  Local:   http://localhost:5173/
  ➜  Network: use --host to expose
  ➜  press h + enter to show help

The project structure

index.html sits at the project root, not inside public/. Vite treats it as the entry point of your app. It contains one empty div and one script tag:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/vite.svg" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
    <title>employee-ui</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div id="root"></div>
    <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
  </body>
</html>

src/main.jsx is the JavaScript entry. It finds the #root element and tells React to render your App component inside it. Everything inside #root is now managed by React. Later you will wrap <App /> with providers here: the router, the TanStack Query client and the auth context.

import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import './index.css';
import App from './App.jsx';

// Find <div id="root"> and let React manage everything inside it
createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <App />
  </StrictMode>,
);

src/App.jsx is your root component. Replace the template's demo with something small of your own:

import { useState } from 'react';
import './App.css';

function App() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Employee UI</h1>
      <button onClick={() => setCount((c) => c + 1)}>
        Clicked {count} times
      </button>
    </main>
  );
}

export default App;

vite.config.js registers the React plugin (JSX transform and Fast Refresh). You will add the dev proxy here in Module 6 and the test settings in Module 7.

import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';

// https://vite.dev/config/
export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
});

package.json lists dependencies (react, react-dom) and dev dependencies (vite, @vitejs/plugin-react, ESLint packages), plus the scripts you run with npm run:

{
  "name": "employee-ui",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build",
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "preview": "vite preview"
  }
}

In the TypeScript template the build script is tsc -b && vite build: it type checks first, because Vite itself only strips types and does not check them.

Everyday npm commands

CommandWhat it doesMaven analogy
npm installInstalls everything listed in package.json into node_modules/Resolving dependencies
npm install axiosAdds a runtime dependencyAdding a <dependency>
npm install -D vitestAdds a development-only dependency<scope>test</scope>

StrictMode, and why things run twice in development

<StrictMode> in main.jsx turns on extra checks in development only. It renders nothing visible. It deliberately does some work twice to expose bugs early:

  • It calls each component function twice per render, to catch components that are not pure (for example, ones that change a global variable while rendering).
  • On mount, it runs every effect, then its cleanup, then the effect again (setup → cleanup → setup). If your effect has no proper cleanup, you will see the problem straight away instead of in production.
  • In React 19 it also runs ref callbacks twice on mount, and it warns about deprecated APIs.
useEffect(() => {
  console.log('connect');
  return () => console.log('disconnect');
}, []);
connect
disconnect
connect

This is why a fetch in an effect shows up twice in the Network tab during development. That is expected. The fix is never "remove StrictMode"; write the effect so that running it twice is harmless (a cleanup that aborts or ignores the first request — see Fetching data) or use TanStack Query. A production build runs everything once.

Rule: commit the lock file, never node_modules

Commit package.json and package-lock.json so every developer and the CI server install the same versions. Never commit node_modules/ or dist/; the template's .gitignore already excludes them.

Conventions

  • Files that contain JSX use the .jsx extension (.tsx in TypeScript). Vite's React setup expects that.
  • Component files are named in PascalCase, like the component: EmployeeList.jsx.
  • Keep main.jsx tiny: it only mounts the app and wraps it in providers.
  • Put your own code under src/; use public/ only for files that must keep their exact name and URL, such as robots.txt.

Edge cases

  • If port 5173 is busy, Vite picks the next free port (5174, 5175 …) and prints it. Set server.strictPort: true in vite.config.js if you would rather fail.
  • To open the dev server from your phone on the same Wi-Fi, run npm run dev -- --host and use the "Network" URL Vite prints.
  • Fast Refresh keeps state only when a file exports React components. Edit a file that also exports plain functions or constants and the page may fully reload instead.

Common mistakes

  • Double-clicking index.html to open it from disk (file://). You get a blank page. Always run npm run dev (or npm run preview for a build).
  • Running npm commands outside the project folder. npm complains that it cannot find package.json — cd into the project first.
  • Forgetting npm install after cloning a repository, then seeing "vite: not found" or "'vite' is not recognized".

Version note: Create React App is deprecated

Older tutorials use npx create-react-app and react-scripts start. The React team officially deprecated Create React App in February 2025. Do not start new projects with it; use Vite for a single-page app, or a framework such as Next.js when you need server rendering. Older environment variables like process.env.REACT_APP_API_URL become import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL in Vite (see Module 6).

Interview: "Why Vite? And why does my effect run twice?"

  • Vite serves native ES modules in development and transforms files on demand, so start-up and HMR stay fast as the app grows; for production it bundles, minifies and splits the code.
  • npm run build outputs static files in dist/ that any web server or CDN can serve.
  • Effects running twice is StrictMode in development: setup → cleanup → setup, to prove your cleanup works. It does not happen in production.

JSX: HTML-like markup inside JavaScript

JSX lets you write HTML-like markup in JavaScript files; it compiles to plain function calls that create React elements, so it follows JavaScript rules — className, camelCase attributes, one root element and {} for expressions.

What JSX really is

JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript. Browsers cannot run it, so Vite's React plugin compiles it into ordinary function calls before the code reaches the browser. Knowing this explains almost every JSX rule.

const greeting = <h1 className="title">Namaste, {user.name}!</h1>;
// Classic form (still valid, and what older code and interviews show)
const greeting = React.createElement('h1', { className: 'title' }, 'Namaste, ', user.name, '!');

// Modern "automatic runtime" (React 17+): same idea, a different helper,
// imported for you by the compiler
import { jsxs as _jsxs } from 'react/jsx-runtime';
const greeting2 = _jsxs('h1', { className: 'title', children: ['Namaste, ', user.name, '!'] });

The result is a React element: a plain object that describes what to show. It is not a DOM node.

{
  type: 'h1',
  props: { className: 'title', children: ['Namaste, ', 'Asha', '!'] },
  key: null,
  // ...a few internal fields
}

Because JSX becomes createElement(type, props, ...children), it must produce one value (hence one root), attributes are object keys (hence JavaScript property names like className), and anything inside {} must be an expression that produces a value.

The rules, compared with HTML

RuleHTML habit (wrong in JSX)JSX
One root elementReturning <h1> and <p> side by sideWrap them in <div> or a fragment <>…</>
Close every tag<br>, <img src="a.png"><br />, <img src="a.png" />
CSS classesclass="card"className="card"
Label targetfor="email"htmlFor="email"
camelCase attributestabindex, maxlength, readonly, autocompletetabIndex, maxLength, readOnly, autoComplete
Eventsonclick="save()"onClick={save} (a function, not a string)
Inline stylesstyle="color: red"style={{ color: 'red' }}
Comments<!-- note -->{/* note */}
ARIA and data attributesaria-label and data-id stay kebab-case in JSX too

Curly braces: JavaScript inside markup

Inside {} you can put any JavaScript expression — something that produces a value: a variable, a calculation, a function call, a ternary, array.map(…), a template literal, or more JSX. You cannot put a statement there: no if, for, switch or variable declarations. Do that work above the return.

function ProfileCard({ user }) {
  const initials = user.name
    .split(' ')
    .map((part) => part[0])
    .join('');
  const joined = new Date(user.joinedOn).toLocaleDateString('en-IN');

  return (
    <div className="card" data-user-id={user.id}>
      {/* Attribute values: quotes for fixed strings, braces for expressions */}
      <img src={user.avatarUrl} alt={`Photo of ${user.name}`} width={64} />
      <span className="avatar-fallback">{initials}</span>
      <h2>{user.name.toUpperCase()}</h2>
      <p>Joined on {joined}</p>
      <p>Experience: {user.years > 1 ? `${user.years} years` : 'Fresher'}</p>
      <label htmlFor="bio">Bio</label>
      <textarea id="bio" defaultValue={user.bio} maxLength={300} />
    </div>
  );
}

export default ProfileCard;

What happens to different values inside {}:

ValueWhat renders
String or numberAs text (strings are escaped automatically)
JSX elementThe element
ArrayEach item in order (give items a key)
true, false, null, undefinedNothing
0 and NaNThe text "0" and "NaN" (numbers are rendered)
A plain object or a DateError: "Objects are not valid as a React child"
A functionNothing, plus a warning "Functions are not valid as a React child"

Fragments: one root without an extra div

A component must return one element. When an extra <div> would break your layout (for example inside a table or a flex container), use a fragment. It groups children without adding a DOM node. The short form <>…</> cannot take attributes; when you need a key (in lists), write <Fragment key={…}>, imported from react.

function EmployeeCells({ employee }) {
  return (
    <>
      <td>{employee.name}</td>
      <td>{employee.department}</td>
    </>
  );
}

Style objects

The style prop takes a JavaScript object with camelCase property names. The double braces are not special syntax: the outer pair means "JavaScript expression", the inner pair is the object literal. A number becomes pixels for length properties (fontSize: 18 → 18px); unitless properties such as opacity, zIndex, flexGrow and lineHeight keep the plain number.

function ProgressBar({ percent }) {
  // Inline styles are best for values that change at runtime, like this width
  return (
    <div className="progress">
      <div
        className="progress-fill"
        style={{ width: `${percent}%`, backgroundColor: percent < 30 ? 'crimson' : 'seagreen' }}
      />
    </div>
  );
}

Multi-line JSX and the return trap

Wrap multi-line JSX in parentheses after return. If you put a line break right after return, JavaScript's automatic semicolon insertion ends the statement there and the function returns undefined — the component renders nothing.

Wrong: HTML habits and the return trap

function Badge() {
  return
    <span class="badge" style="color: green" onclick="alert('hi')">
      New
    </span>
}

Right: valid JSX

function Badge() {
  return (
    <span
      className="badge"
      style={{ color: 'green' }}
      onClick={() => alert('hi')}
    >
      New
    </span>
  );
}

Rules that break the build or the page

  • Return a single root (an element or a fragment).
  • Close every tag, including void ones: <input />, <img />, <br />. An unclosed tag is a compile error.
  • Only expressions inside {}. An if inside JSX is a syntax error.
  • style must be an object. A string gives the error "The style prop expects a mapping from style properties to values, not a string."

Edge cases and warnings

  • class= and onclick= still work in some cases but React warns: "Invalid DOM property class. Did you mean className?" and "Invalid event handler property onclick. Did you mean onClick?" Fix them.
  • Boolean attributes: <button disabled> means disabled={true}; disabled={false} removes the attribute. Writing disabled="false" passes a non-empty string, so React warns that this will not work as expected — use disabled={false}.
  • Dates and objects must be turned into strings first: {order.placedAt.toLocaleString()}, not {order.placedAt}.
  • Text in JSX is escaped, so {userComment} cannot inject HTML. That is built-in XSS protection. The escape hatch dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} turns it off — only use it with HTML you have sanitised (for example with the DOMPurify library).

Tip: converting existing HTML

When you paste HTML from a design or an old page, fix it in this order: class → className, for → htmlFor, close void tags, convert style strings to objects, turn onclick strings into functions, and replace HTML comments. Your editor and the React warnings in the console point to anything you missed.

Interview: "What is JSX? Can you write React without it?"

  • JSX is syntax sugar that compiles to React.createElement (or the modern jsx() helper) calls, which return plain objects called React elements.
  • Yes, React works without JSX — you would call createElement yourself — but JSX is far easier to read.
  • className and htmlFor exist because JSX attributes map to JavaScript DOM properties (element.className) and class / for are reserved words in JavaScript.
  • JSX escapes embedded values, which protects against XSS unless you use dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

Components and props

A component is a function that takes one object of props and returns JSX; props flow from parent to child, are read-only, and you build screens by composing small components.

Function components

A component is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and that returns JSX (or null to show nothing). You use it like an HTML tag: <EmployeeCard />. React treats lowercase tags (<div>) as built-in HTML elements and capitalised tags as your components. That is why <employeeCard /> fails: React looks for an HTML element called "employeecard".

Old code uses class components (class X extends React.Component). They still work but nobody writes them in new code. Everything in these notes uses function components and hooks.

function EmployeeCard({ name, role, salary, active = true }) {
  return (
    <article className="card">
      <h3>{name}</h3>
      <p>{role}</p>
      <p>₹{salary.toLocaleString('en-IN')} per month</p>
      {!active && <span className="badge">Inactive</span>}
    </article>
  );
}

export default EmployeeCard;
import EmployeeCard from './components/EmployeeCard.jsx';

function App() {
  return (
    <main>
      <EmployeeCard name="Asha Rao" role="Java Developer" salary={85000} />
      <EmployeeCard name="Vikram Nair" role="QA Engineer" salary={62000} active={false} />
    </main>
  );
}

export default App;

Props: the inputs of a component

Props (short for properties) are the attributes you write on the tag. React collects them into one object and passes it as the first argument of the function. Destructuring in the parameter list, as above, is the normal style.

  • Text can be passed with quotes: name="Asha". Everything else goes in braces: salary={85000}, active={false}, tags={['java', 'sql']}, onSave={handleSave}, user={user}.
  • A prop with no value, such as <Button disabled />, means true.
  • You can spread an object into props: <EmployeeCard {...employee} />. It is handy but hides which props a component needs, so use it sparingly.
  • Default values are normal JavaScript default parameters (active = true). The old Component.defaultProps is removed for function components in React 19.
  • Props can be anything: strings, numbers, objects, arrays, functions and even JSX.

Props are read-only

A component must never change its own props. Treat the props object like a Java record: it is a snapshot owned by the parent. If a child needs to change something, the parent passes a function as a prop, and the child calls it (the lifting state up pattern). This keeps data flowing in one direction — down — and events flowing up.

function DeleteButton({ onDelete }) {
  return <button onClick={onDelete}>Delete</button>;
}

function EmployeeRow({ employee, onRemove }) {
  return (
    <li>
      {employee.name}
      {/* The child calls back; the parent owns the data and decides what happens */}
      <DeleteButton onDelete={() => onRemove(employee.id)} />
    </li>
  );
}

Pure components

React expects a component to be pure while rendering: the same props and state in should give the same JSX out, and rendering must not change anything outside the component (no editing a global variable, no fetch, no Math.random() that changes the output, no writing to the DOM). Side effects belong in event handlers or in useEffect. StrictMode renders twice in development precisely to catch impure components.

children and composition

Whatever you put between the opening and closing tags arrives as the special prop children. This lets you build generic wrappers (cards, modals, layouts) that do not know what they contain.

function Card({ title, children, footer }) {
  return (
    <section className="card">
      <h2>{title}</h2>
      <div className="card-body">{children}</div>
      {footer && <div className="card-footer">{footer}</div>}
    </section>
  );
}

function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <Card title="Today's orders" footer={<a href="/orders">See all</a>}>
      <p>42 orders, ₹1,86,400 revenue</p>
    </Card>
  );
}

React prefers composition over inheritance. You never make SpecialCard extends Card. Instead you wrap, pass children, or pass JSX in props (as footer above). If you used the Decorator pattern in Java, this will feel familiar.

Prop drilling

Prop drilling means passing a prop through several layers of components that do not use it, only to deliver it to a deep child. One or two levels is fine. When the same value (the logged-in user, the theme) travels through five layers, use Context, or restructure with children so the middle layers never see the prop.

Folder structure that scales

Rules for components

  • Component names are PascalCase; the file has the same name; one main component per file, exported as default (or by name — be consistent).
  • Never define a component inside another component. Each render would create a new function, so React sees a "different type", destroys the subtree and loses its state.
  • Never modify props (props.items.push(x), props.user.name = 'x').
  • Components must be pure during render.

Conventions

  • Keep components small. If you cannot name what a component does in one phrase, or the file passes about 150 lines, split it.
  • Props that hold functions are named onSomething (onSave, onClose); the handler inside the parent is handleSomething.
  • Booleans read like questions: isOpen, hasError, disabled.
  • Pass the data a component needs, not a whole big object it barely uses, unless the object is the natural unit (an employee for an EmployeeCard).

Edge cases

  • key and ref are special. key is never delivered to your component as a prop. In React 19, ref is an ordinary prop on function components; in React 18 you needed forwardRef.
  • Destructuring undefined throws: function Row({ user }) then user.name gives "Cannot read properties of undefined" if the parent forgot to pass user. This is the most common error when data has not loaded yet — render a loading state first.
  • Passing a new object or array literal as a prop (style={{…}}, options={[1, 2]}) creates a new reference every render. That is harmless unless the child is wrapped in memo (see memo and useCallback).

Mistake: copying a prop into state

const [name, setName] = useState(props.name) reads the prop only on the first render. When the parent sends a new name, the child keeps showing the old one. Use the prop directly, or, if the component truly needs an editable copy, reset it by giving the component a key that changes when the source item changes.

Interview: "Props vs state?"

  • Props are inputs passed down by the parent and are read-only for the receiver. State is private memory owned by the component, changed through a setter, and it triggers a re-render.
  • When a parent re-renders, children get new props; state survives re-renders.
  • Data flows down as props; changes flow up by calling functions passed as props.
  • Avoid prop drilling with composition (children) or Context.

State with useState

useState gives a component memory: it returns the current value and a setter, state is a snapshot for each render, and you must replace objects and arrays instead of changing them.

Why a plain variable does not work

Local variables are thrown away every time the function runs, and changing one does not tell React to re-render. State fixes both problems: React stores the value outside your function, and calling the setter schedules a new render.

import { useState } from 'react';

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);   // [current value, setter]; 0 is the initial value

  return (
    <div>
      <p>You clicked {count} times</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Click me</button>
    </div>
  );
}

The syntax const [count, setCount] = useState(0) is array destructuring (from Module 4). The first item is the value in this render; the second is the setter. Name them x and setX. The initial value is used only on the first render. If computing it is expensive, pass a function and React calls it once: useState(() => readFromLocalStorage()) (a "lazy initial state").

State is a snapshot

This is the idea that causes the most confusion. In each render, count is a constant with one fixed value. Calling setCount(count + 1) does not change the variable in the running function; it asks React for a new render in which count has the new value.

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  function handleClick() {
    setCount(count + 1);   // asks for count = 1
    setCount(count + 1);   // still count is 0 in this snapshot: asks for count = 1 again
    setCount(count + 1);   // same
    console.log(count);    // prints 0, not 1
  }
  return <button onClick={handleClick}>Count: {count}</button>;
}
Console: 0
Button:  Count: 1   (not 3)

Functional updates

When the new value depends on the previous one, pass a function. React calls it with the latest pending value ("updater function"), so several updates in a row stack correctly.

function handleClick() {
  setCount((c) => c + 1);   // 0 -> 1
  setCount((c) => c + 1);   // 1 -> 2
  setCount((c) => c + 1);   // 2 -> 3
}   // one re-render, count is 3

Use the functional form whenever the next state is calculated from the old state — counters, toggles (setOpen(o => !o)), appending to a list — and always inside timers, async callbacks and effects, where the captured value may be stale.

Batching and when re-renders happen

React batches state updates: all set… calls inside one event handler are collected, then React renders once at the end. Since React 18 this also applies inside setTimeout, promises and native event handlers. Setting state to the same value (compared with Object.is) normally causes no visible work.

A component re-renders when its own state changes, when its parent re-renders (even if the props are the same, unless you use memo), or when a context it reads changes.

Updating objects and arrays immutably

React decides whether state changed by comparing references. If you mutate an object or array and pass the same reference to the setter, React sees "no change" and may skip the update. Always create a new object or array. You know the tools from Module 4: spread, map, filter.

GoalMutates (do not use)Immutable (use)
Add to arraypush, unshift[...items, newItem]
Remove from arrayspliceitems.filter(i => i.id !== id)
Update one itemitems[2].done = trueitems.map(i => i.id === id ? {...i, done: true} : i)
Sort or reversesort, reverse[...items].sort(...) or toSorted(...)
Update object fielduser.name = 'x'{...user, name: 'x'}
Nested objectuser.address.city = 'x'{...user, address: {...user.address, city: 'x'}}
 
import { useState } from 'react';

function TodoList() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState([
    { id: 1, text: 'Learn useState', done: false },
    { id: 2, text: 'Build the CRM UI', done: false },
  ]);

  function addTodo(text) {
    setTodos((prev) => [...prev, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), text, done: false }]);
  }
  function toggleTodo(id) {
    setTodos((prev) => prev.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)));
  }
  function removeTodo(id) {
    setTodos((prev) => prev.filter((t) => t.id !== id));
  }

  return (
    <ul>
      {todos.map((t) => (
        <li key={t.id}>
          <label>
            <input type="checkbox" checked={t.done} onChange={() => toggleTodo(t.id)} />
            {t.text}
          </label>
          <button onClick={() => removeTodo(t.id)}>Remove</button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

Wrong: mutation, no re-render

function toggleTodo(id) {
  const todo = todos.find((t) => t.id === id);
  todo.done = !todo.done;   // same array, same object
  setTodos(todos);          // same reference: React skips
}

Right: new array, new object

function toggleTodo(id) {
  setTodos(
    todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)),
  );
}

Spread makes a shallow copy: nested objects are still shared, so copy each level you change. For deeply nested state, flatten the shape or use the Immer library, which lets you write mutating-looking code that produces immutable updates (Redux Toolkit uses it too, see Module 7).

Derive values instead of storing them

If a value can be calculated from props or other state, calculate it during render. Do not store it in a second useState and sync the two — they will get out of step.

function Cart({ items }) {
  // No state for these: they are computed from items on every render
  const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
  const count = items.length;
  const isEmpty = count === 0;
  return <p>{isEmpty ? 'Cart is empty' : `${count} items, ₹${total}`}</p>;
}

Where should state live?

  • Keep state in the lowest component that needs it (a modal's open flag lives in the modal's parent, not in App).
  • If two siblings need the same state, move it to their closest common parent (lifting state up).
  • If many distant components need it (current user, theme), use Context.
  • Data that comes from the server is a different kind of state — see TanStack Query.
  • Filters and page numbers that should survive a refresh or be shareable belong in the URL (search params).

Resetting state

State belongs to a component's position in the tree. Same type in the same place keeps its state; a different type, or a different key, resets it. So <EmployeeForm key={employee.id} employee={employee} /> gives each employee a fresh form without any reset code.

Rules for state

  • Never change state directly. Always use the setter, and give it a new object or array.
  • Call useState at the top level of the component (rules of hooks), never in loops, conditions or event handlers.
  • Do not call a setter during render (outside special patterns): it causes "Too many re-renders".
  • Keep state minimal and avoid duplicate sources of truth.

Edge cases

  • setX(fn) treats a function argument as an updater. To store a function in state, wrap it: setHandler(() => myFunction).
  • Setting state right after await in a component that has already unmounted does nothing harmful in React 18+ (the old warning is gone), but the request is still wasted work.
  • State is lost when the component unmounts, and on a full page refresh. Persist what matters (token, theme) to localStorage, a cookie or the server.
  • Reading state right after setting it gives the old value; use the next render, or compute the new value in a local variable first and use that for both the setter and the follow-up work.

Interview: "Why is my state not updating immediately? Why not mutate state?"

  • State is a snapshot per render; the setter schedules a re-render with the new value, it does not change the variable in the running function.
  • Updates are batched; use the functional form when the new value depends on the old one.
  • React detects change by reference comparison, so mutated objects look unchanged and the UI does not update. Immutability also keeps history, memoisation and DevTools reliable.
  • Derive what you can; store the minimum.

Events and conditional rendering

Pass a function (not its result) to onClick, use &&, a ternary or an early return to show or hide UI, and beware the 0 && gotcha.

Handling events

React events are written in camelCase and take a function: onClick, onChange, onSubmit, onKeyDown, onMouseEnter, onFocus, onBlur. Under the hood React attaches one listener at the root and gives your handler a synthetic event: a wrapper with the same API as the browser event (target, preventDefault(), stopPropagation()) that works the same in every browser.

function SaveBar({ onSave }) {
  function handleClick(event) {          // named handler, receives the event
    console.log(event.type, event.target);
    onSave();
  }
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>
      <button onClick={() => onSave('draft')}>Save draft</button>   {/* inline arrow */}
    </>
  );
}

Wrong: calls the function during render

<button onClick={handleDelete(id)}>Delete</button>
<button onClick={handleClick()}>Go</button>

Right: pass a function to call later

<button onClick={() => handleDelete(id)}>Delete</button>
<button onClick={handleClick}>Go</button>

handleClick() runs the function while rendering and passes its return value (usually undefined) as the handler. If that function sets state, you get an infinite loop and "Too many re-renders". To pass an argument, wrap the call in an arrow function.

Rendering vs handling: when does your code run?

React separates two moments. Rendering is when React calls your component function to find out what the screen should look like; it must be pure and must not change anything. Event handling is when the user does something; this is where you are allowed to change things: set state, call an API, navigate. Most "why does my component loop?" bugs come from putting handler work into the render body. Think of the component function like a Java toString(): it describes, it does not act. Handlers are like controller methods: they act.

Two details about handlers and state, both covered in State with useState: a handler sees the state values from the render that created it (a snapshot), and React batches all setState calls inside one event into a single re-render. So setCount(count + 1) called three times adds only 1; use setCount((c) => c + 1) when the next value depends on the previous one.

How an event travels

A browser event goes through three phases: capture (from the root down to the target), target, and bubble (from the target back up to the root). React's onClick runs in the bubble phase; onClickCapture runs in the capture phase. Since React 17 the single listener is attached to the root container you passed to createRoot, not to document. React then calls the handlers of the clicked element and each of its parents, in order.

Common event patterns

  • preventDefault() stops the browser's default action: a form submit reloading the page, a link navigating. Always call it in onSubmit for React-controlled forms.
  • stopPropagation() stops the event bubbling to parent handlers — for example a delete button inside a clickable row.
  • event.target.value is the text of an input; event.target.checked is the state of a checkbox.
  • Events bubble: a click on a child also fires onClick on its parents. To handle the capture phase, use onClickCapture.
  • Prefer a real <button> or <a> over a clickable <div>; they work with the keyboard and screen readers.
function EmployeeRow({ employee, onOpen, onDelete }) {
  return (
    <li onClick={() => onOpen(employee.id)}>
      {employee.name}
      <button
        onClick={(e) => {
          e.stopPropagation();       // do not also fire the row's onClick
          onDelete(employee.id);
        }}
      >
        Delete
      </button>
    </li>
  );
}

Events you will use most

HandlerFires whenTypical use
onClickMouse click, tap, or Enter/Space on a buttonButtons, rows, menu items
onChangeEvery keystroke in an input; each change of a checkbox or selectControlled inputs
onSubmitA form is submitted (button or Enter key)Login, create and edit forms
onKeyDownA key is pressedEscape to close, shortcuts
onBlur / onFocusElement loses / gains focusValidate when the user leaves a field
onMouseEnterPointer enters the elementHover tooltips

A realistic form handler

A login form shows the usual pieces together: a controlled input, preventDefault, an async call, and state for the "submitting" and error cases. Forms are covered fully in Forms; here the point is where the work happens, which is in the handler.

function LoginForm({ onLoggedIn }) {
  const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
  const [password, setPassword] = useState('');
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  async function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();                    // no full page reload
    setSubmitting(true);
    setError(null);
    try {
      const res = await fetch('/api/auth/login', {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }),
      });
      if (!res.ok) {
        throw new Error(res.status === 401 ? 'Wrong email or password' : 'Server error');
      }
      onLoggedIn(await res.json());
    } catch (err) {
      setError(err.message);
    } finally {
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input type="email" value={email} onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)} />
      <input type="password" value={password} onChange={(e) => setPassword(e.target.value)} />
      {error && <p role="alert">{error}</p>}
      <button disabled={submitting}>{submitting ? 'Signing in…' : 'Login'}</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Conditional rendering

JSX has no if inside the markup, so you use ordinary JavaScript: an if before the return, the ternary operator, or logical &&. A component can also return null to render nothing. Inside JSX, null, undefined, true and false all render nothing, which is exactly why cond && <X /> works.

function OrderStatus({ order, isLoading, error }) {
  // 1. Early return: best for loading / error / empty screens
  if (isLoading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (error) return <p role="alert">Could not load: {error.message}</p>;
  if (!order) return null;               // render nothing

  // 2. Variable holding JSX
  let badge = null;
  if (order.status === 'DELIVERED') badge = <span>Delivered</span>;

  return (
    <div>
      {/* 3. Ternary: one thing or the other */}
      <p>{order.paid ? 'Paid' : 'Payment pending'}</p>
      {/* 4. &&: show something or nothing */}
      {order.items.length > 0 && <p>{order.items.length} items</p>}
      {badge}
    </div>
  );
}
TechniqueBest forWatch out for
Early returnLoading, error, empty, "not allowed" screensMust come after all hook calls
Ternary a ? b : cTwo alternatives inlineNesting gets unreadable fast
cond && <X />Show or nothingA numeric cond such as 0 is rendered
Variable / helper functionThree or more branchesName it clearly
switch in a functionRendering by status enumAdd a default branch

Mistake: the 0 && gotcha

{items.length && <List />} prints a literal 0 when the array is empty, because 0 && x evaluates to 0, and React renders numbers. Make the left side a real boolean: items.length > 0 && … or Boolean(items.length) && …. Strings are similar: an empty string renders nothing, but a number never does.

Rule: an early return must come after every hook

React identifies hooks by call order (see the rules of hooks). If you write if (!user) return null; and then call useState below it, the number of hooks changes between renders and React throws an error. Call all hooks first, then return early.

Hiding vs not rendering

When a condition is false, the element is not rendered, and any state inside that component is destroyed. To keep state while hiding (a half-filled tab), render it always and hide with CSS (hidden attribute or a class) or lift the state up (see Sharing state).

The reverse also matters. React keeps state for a component that stays at the same position in the tree with the same type. In {isAdmin ? <Form /> : <Form />} the two branches are the same component in the same place, so typed text survives the switch. If that is not what you want, give them different keys (see keys). Swapping <Form /> for <Other /> always resets the state.

Showing one of several states

A screen that loads data has at least four states: loading, error, empty and data. Handle them explicitly, in that order, with early returns. Missing the empty state is a very common review comment. Data from a Spring Boot endpoint that returns [] is a valid success, not an error; show a friendly "No employees yet" message with a button to add one.

const STATUS_LABEL = {
  PLACED: 'Order placed',
  SHIPPED: 'On the way',
  DELIVERED: 'Delivered',
  CANCELLED: 'Cancelled',
};

function StatusBadge({ status }) {
  const label = STATUS_LABEL[status] ?? 'Unknown status';   // safe default
  return <span className={`badge badge-${status.toLowerCase()}`}>{label}</span>;
}

A lookup object replaces a long if / else if chain, much like a Java switch on an enum or an EnumMap. The ?? fallback covers a value your backend adds later that the frontend does not know yet.

Conventions

  • Handler names: handleX inside the component, onX as a prop.
  • Keep inline arrows short. Move longer logic to a named function above the return.
  • Avoid nested ternaries in JSX; use early returns or small components instead.
  • Use a real <form> with onSubmit instead of an onClick on a button, so the Enter key works.
  • Disable the submit button while a request is in flight to stop double submits.

Edge cases

  • React 17+ attaches events at the root container, not document, so mixing React and native listeners behaves predictably. A native stopPropagation on document can no longer hide events from React; a native listener on a parent element that stops propagation can.
  • onChange in React fires on every keystroke (like the native input event), unlike the native change event that waits for blur.
  • Passing onClick={undefined} or null is fine: no handler is attached.
  • Since React 17 the synthetic event is no longer pooled, so reading event inside an await or setTimeout works. You may still prefer to copy the value first: const value = e.target.value;.
  • A disabled <button> does not fire onClick; a clickable <div> with aria-disabled still does, so check inside the handler.

In real projects

Delete flows use both ideas together: the button's handler calls DELETE /api/employees/{id}, and the row is rendered conditionally from the list in state, with a confirm step (window.confirm or a modal) before the call. Role-based buttons use the same && pattern; see Protected routes.

Interview: "What is the difference between onClick={fn} and onClick={fn()}?"

  • fn passes the function; React calls it on click. fn() calls it immediately during render and passes the result.
  • Use () => fn(arg) to pass arguments.
  • React wraps the browser event in a synthetic event, delegating at the root.
  • Follow-ups: why does count && <X /> show 0? (numbers are rendered), what is the difference between stopPropagation and preventDefault? (bubbling vs the browser's default action).

Rendering lists and keys

Turn an array into elements with map, and give each item a stable, unique key (usually the database id) so React can match items between renders.

map() in JSX

You render a list by mapping data to elements. filter and sort before map give you search and ordering; do them on a copy during render, not in state. This works like a Java stream pipeline: filter → sorted → map produces a new collection and leaves the source list alone. That is why you use toSorted (or [...list].sort()), because plain sort() changes the original array, which you must never do with props or state.

function EmployeeList({ employees, search }) {
  const visible = employees
    .filter((e) => e.name.toLowerCase().includes(search.toLowerCase()))
    .toSorted((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name));   // toSorted does not mutate

  if (visible.length === 0) return <p>No employees found.</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {visible.map((e) => (
        <li key={e.id}>
          {e.name} — {e.department}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

Version note: toSorted

toSorted, toReversed and with are newer array methods (ES2023) that return a copy. They exist in current browsers and in Node 20+. If you must support very old browsers, use [...employees].sort(compareFn).

A list from a Spring Boot API

The usual real case: load a list from your backend, keep it in state, and render it. A Spring Data Page response wraps the rows in content next to paging fields, so you map over page.content, not over the page object (see Pagination).

function EmployeeTable() {
  const [rows, setRows] = useState([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch('/api/employees?page=0&size=20')
      .then((r) => r.json())
      .then((page) => setRows(page.content));      // Spring Data Page: { content: [...] }
  }, []);

  function handleDelete(id) {
    setRows((prev) => prev.filter((e) => e.id !== id));   // new array, never splice
  }

  return (
    <table>
      <tbody>
        {rows.map((e) => (
          <EmployeeRow key={e.id} employee={e} onDelete={handleDelete} />
        ))}
      </tbody>
    </table>
  );
}

function EmployeeRow({ employee, onDelete }) {
  return (
    <tr>
      <td>{employee.name}</td>
      <td>{employee.department}</td>
      <td><button onClick={() => onDelete(employee.id)}>Delete</button></td>
    </tr>
  );
}

Notice the key is on <EmployeeRow> in the map, the outermost element of each item, not on the <tr> inside the row component.

Updating a list immutably

State must be replaced, not edited in place. React compares the old and new array by reference; push changes the same array, so React may skip the re-render. Use these patterns.

ActionWrong (mutates)Right (new array)
Addlist.push(x)[...list, x]
Removelist.splice(i, 1)list.filter((e) => e.id !== id)
Update onelist[i].name = 'A'list.map((e) => e.id === id ? { ...e, name: 'A' } : e)
Sortlist.sort(fn)list.toSorted(fn)

What the key is for

A key is a string or number that identifies an item among its siblings. When the list changes, React uses keys to decide which old element matches which new one: same key → same item (keep the DOM node and any component state, just update it); new key → new item; missing key → removed. Without keys React can only compare by position.

How reconciliation uses keys

Every render produces a new tree of elements. Reconciliation is the step where React compares the new tree with the previous one and works out the smallest set of DOM changes. It compares children one level at a time. For a list, it looks up each new child's key in the old children: if found and the type is the same, it reuses the existing instance (with its state and DOM node) and only updates changed props; if not found, it creates one; old keys that are no longer present are unmounted.

Rule: keys must be stable, unique among siblings, and not random

  • Use the record's id from your database (employee.id).
  • Uniqueness is only needed among siblings, not across the whole app.
  • The key goes on the outermost element returned by map, not on a child inside a component. In a fragment use <Fragment key={…}>.
  • Never use Math.random() or crypto.randomUUID() during render as a key; each render gives new keys, so every item is destroyed and rebuilt (inputs lose focus, state is lost). Generate ids once, when you create the item.

Why index keys break

key={index} removes the warning but ties identity to position. If an item is added at the top, removed from the middle, or the list is sorted, the index of each item changes. React then matches the wrong data to the wrong DOM node and component state.

// A list of rows, each with an uncontrolled input holding the user's typing
{todos.map((t, index) => (
  <li key={index}>                      {/* wrong */}
    {t.text} <input placeholder="note" />
  </li>
))}
// Type "urgent" in the first row's input, then delete the first todo.
// The input text "urgent" now sits in the row that used to be second:
// React kept DOM node 0 and just changed its label.

Wrong: index as key in a changing list

{todos.map((t, i) => (
  <TodoItem key={i} todo={t} />
))}

Right: the item's own id

{todos.map((t) => (
  <TodoItem key={t.id} todo={t} />
))}

Index keys are acceptable only when the list is static: never reordered, filtered, inserted into or deleted from, and items have no state. Even then, an id is better. If your data has no id (a list of plain strings that are unique), the string itself can be the key.

// Good: id from the API
employees.map((e) => <EmployeeCard key={e.id} {...e} />);

// Good: unique natural value
tags.map((tag) => <span key={tag}>{tag}</span>);

// Good: id assigned once when the item is created (not during render)
setTodos((prev) => [...prev, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), text }]);

// Avoid: index, unless the list is static
// Never: key={Math.random()}
Key choiceStable across renders?Safe for reorder/insert/delete?
Database id (e.id)YesYes: best choice
Unique natural value (tag name, email)YesYes, if truly unique
Id created once at creation timeYesYes
Array indexOnly while the list never changesNo
Math.random() in renderNo, new every renderNo: remounts everything

Nested lists and fragments

Keys only need to be unique among siblings, so an inner list can reuse ids used elsewhere. When one item must return several elements without a wrapper (two table rows, a term and its description), use the long form of the fragment, because the short <> cannot take a key.

import { Fragment } from 'react';

function DepartmentList({ departments }) {
  return (
    <dl>
      {departments.map((d) => (
        <Fragment key={d.id}>
          <dt>{d.name}</dt>
          {d.employees.map((e) => (
            <dd key={e.id}>{e.name}</dd>      {/* ids only need to be unique here */}
          ))}
        </Fragment>
      ))}
    </dl>
  );
}

Keys also reset state

A key is not only for lists. Changing the key of any component makes React treat it as a brand-new instance: old state is discarded. <Profile key={userId} /> is the clean way to reset a form when the user changes (see You might not need an effect).

The warning: "Each child in a list should have a unique key prop"

You rendered an array without keys, or the keys are duplicated, or you put the key on the wrong element (inside the child component instead of on the map result). Duplicate keys, such as two employees with the same id in test data, cause items to be duplicated or dropped on update. Check your data first.

Conventions

  • Extract the row into its own component (EmployeeRow) once it has more than a few lines; the map then stays one line.
  • Keep the list in state as an array of objects with ids; do not store an index.
  • Filter and sort in render (derived data) instead of keeping a second "visible" state.
  • Always handle the empty list, the loading state and the error state.

Edge cases

  • Keys are not passed as props. If the child needs the id, pass it separately (id={e.id}).
  • Ids from Spring Boot are numbers (Long) or strings (UUID); both work as keys. Be careful with composite data: if the id is not unique, combine fields (`${e.orderId}-${e.lineNo}`).
  • Rendering thousands of rows slows the page however good your keys are. Use pagination (see Module 6) or a virtualised list library such as TanStack Virtual.
  • A Java Long above 2^53 loses precision when parsed as a JavaScript number, so two different ids can become one key. Very large ids (for example snowflake ids) should be sent as strings from the API.
  • Keys of 0 and "0" are the same key (keys are compared as strings), so do not mix numbers and strings that look alike in one list.

In real projects

New records created in the browser before the server answers (optimistic add) have no database id yet. Give them a temporary client id (crypto.randomUUID() at creation), use it as the key, and replace the item with the saved one when the response arrives. If you swap the key at that moment, React remounts the row; keeping a separate stable clientId field avoids that flicker.

Interview: "Why do we need keys? Is index a good key?"

  • Keys identify items between renders so reconciliation can reuse, move or remove the right element and keep its state.
  • Use a stable unique id. Index keys are fine only for static lists; with reorder, insert or delete they mismatch state and DOM nodes and cause subtle bugs.
  • A random key every render forces a full remount of every item.
  • Changing the key of a component deliberately resets its state.
  • Follow-up: why is sort() on state a bug? It mutates the array that React compares by reference, so copy first.

useEffect: side effects and the dependency array

useEffect runs code after React has updated the screen, to synchronise your component with something outside React; the dependency array decides when it re-runs and the cleanup function undoes the previous run.

What an effect is for

Rendering must be pure, but real apps need to do things that are not pure: call an API, start a timer, subscribe to a WebSocket, change document.title, read the size of a DOM node. These are side effects. useEffect is the place for effects that happen because the component appeared or changed. Effects that happen because the user did something (clicked Save) belong in the event handler instead.

Think of an effect as: "after rendering, synchronise the outside world with the current props and state". It is not a lifecycle method like componentDidMount, even if it can imitate one.

import { useEffect } from 'react';

useEffect(() => {
  // setup: runs after the render is on screen
  return () => {
    // cleanup (optional): runs before the next setup and when the component unmounts
  };
}, [dep1, dep2]);   // dependency array

When does it run?

React renders your component, commits the changes to the DOM, lets the browser paint, and then runs effects. The dependency array controls re-runs:

Dependency arrayRunsTypical use
OmittedAfter every renderRare; almost always a mistake
[]Once after the first render (twice in dev StrictMode)Connect once, load initial data, add a global listener
[a, b]After the first render and whenever a or b changed (compared with Object.is)Fetch data for an id, re-subscribe to a room
 
function EmployeePage({ employee }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    document.title = `${employee.name} | HR Portal`;
  }, [employee.name]);                      // re-run only when the name changes

  return <h1>{employee.name}</h1>;
}

The dependency rule

Every reactive value the effect reads — props, state, and variables or functions declared inside the component — must be listed in the array. Do not lie to React to silence a warning. The react-hooks/exhaustive-deps ESLint rule (already in the Vite template) checks this. A missing dependency gives a stale closure: the effect keeps using old values from the render in which it was created (the closure idea from Module 4).

function Ticker() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => {
      console.log(count);            // always logs 0: closure from the first render
      setCount(count + 1);           // always sets 1
    }, 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, []);                            // count is missing

  return <p>{count}</p>;
}

Fix it by removing the dependency on count with a functional update (setCount(c => c + 1)), which makes the empty array correct, or by listing [count] (the interval is then recreated every second, which works but is wasteful).

Cleanup

The function you return is the cleanup. React calls it before running the effect again (with new values) and when the component unmounts. Use it for everything the effect started: timers, event listeners, subscriptions, WebSocket connections, in-flight requests.

function useWindowWidth() {
  const [width, setWidth] = useState(window.innerWidth);

  useEffect(() => {
    function onResize() {
      setWidth(window.innerWidth);
    }
    window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize);   // no leak
  }, []);

  return width;
}

Order for a change of [roomId]: render with the new value → cleanup of the previous effect (with the old values) → setup with the new values. In StrictMode development, React adds one extra setup → cleanup → setup on mount. If that breaks your component, your cleanup is incomplete; fix the effect.

Objects and functions as dependencies

React compares dependencies by reference. An object, array or function created inside the component is a new one on every render, so an effect depending on it runs after every render — and if that effect sets state, you get an infinite loop.

function Bad({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const options = { headers: { 'X-User': userId } };   // new object each render

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch('/api/me', options).then((r) => r.json()).then(setUser);
  }, [options]);     // changes every render -> fetch -> setUser -> render -> fetch ...
  return <p>{user?.name}</p>;
}

Fixes: depend on primitives (userId), move the object inside the effect, move constants outside the component, or memoise with useMemo / useCallback. The other classic infinite loop is an effect with no dependency array that sets state.

Rules for useEffect

  • List every reactive value the effect uses; never suppress the lint rule to "fix" a loop.
  • Return a cleanup for anything that needs one.
  • The effect function itself cannot be async (it would return a Promise instead of a cleanup function). Define an inner async function and call it.
  • Effects must be safe to run twice in development.
  • Do not use effects to respond to user actions; use event handlers.

Edge cases

  • Effects do not run during server rendering; they run only in the browser.
  • useLayoutEffect runs before the browser paints. Use it only to measure the DOM and adjust before the user sees a flicker; it blocks painting.
  • Refs and setters from useState/useReducer are stable and need not be listed (the linter knows), though listing them is harmless.
  • React 19.2 added useEffectEvent for reading the latest value inside an effect without making it a dependency (a chat room that logs the current theme but reconnects only when the room changes). It is new; many codebases do not use it yet.

Common mistakes

  • Empty array [] while the effect uses props or state (stale data, wrong request).
  • No array at all, plus setState in the effect: endless re-render loop.
  • Passing an async function directly to useEffect.
  • No cleanup for setInterval or addEventListener: duplicates pile up, and you see memory leaks and multiple handlers.
  • Putting state-changing logic in an effect that just reacts to another state change (see you might not need an effect).

Interview: "Explain useEffect and its dependency array"

  • It runs after render to synchronise with external systems; setup returns an optional cleanup.
  • No array: after every render. []: after mount only. [a]: when a changes.
  • Cleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount; use it for timers, listeners, subscriptions, aborting requests.
  • Missing dependencies cause stale closures; unstable object dependencies cause loops.
  • Runs twice on mount in StrictMode development to verify cleanup.

Fetching data with useEffect: loading, error and race conditions

A fetch in an effect needs three states (loading, error, data), a cleanup that aborts or ignores outdated responses, and a dependency array containing every input of the request.

The basic pattern

Fetching is the most common reason to write an effect. You need three pieces of state, because a request is not a single value: it starts, then ends with data or with an error. This uses the apiClient style from Module 4: check response.ok, because fetch only rejects on network failure, not on HTTP 404 or 500.

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

function EmployeeList() {
  const [employees, setEmployees] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    async function load() {
      try {
        setLoading(true);
        setError(null);
        const res = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/api/employees', {
          signal: controller.signal,
        });
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Server returned ${res.status}`);
        setEmployees(await res.json());
      } catch (err) {
        if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;   // cleanup aborted it: not a real error
        setError(err);
      } finally {
        if (!controller.signal.aborted) setLoading(false);
      }
    }
    load();

    return () => controller.abort();   // cancel the request on unmount / re-run
  }, []);

  if (loading) return <p>Loading employees…</p>;
  if (error) return <p role="alert">Something went wrong: {error.message}</p>;
  if (employees.length === 0) return <p>No employees yet.</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {employees.map((e) => <li key={e.id}>{e.name}</li>)}
    </ul>
  );
}

The race condition

Suppose a page shows employee details for an id from the URL. The user clicks employee 1, then quickly employee 2. Two requests are in flight. Network responses can arrive in any order. If the response for 1 arrives after the response for 2, the screen shows employee 1's data under employee 2's URL. This is a race condition, and it happens in real apps on slow mobile networks.

The cleanup function solves it. When id changes, React runs the cleanup of the old effect before starting the new one. Two options:

  • AbortController cancels the old request, so its promise rejects with an AbortError and never reaches setState. This also saves bandwidth.
  • An ignore flag lets the request finish but throws its result away. Use it when the library does not support abort.
function EmployeeDetails({ id }) {
  const [employee, setEmployee] = useState(null);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('loading');   // 'loading' | 'error' | 'success'

  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false;                 // belongs to THIS run of the effect
    setStatus('loading');

    fetch(`http://localhost:8080/api/employees/${id}`)
      .then((res) => {
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        return res.json();
      })
      .then((data) => {
        if (!ignore) {                  // only the latest effect run may set state
          setEmployee(data);
          setStatus('success');
        }
      })
      .catch(() => {
        if (!ignore) setStatus('error');
      });

    return () => {
      ignore = true;                    // this run is now outdated
    };
  }, [id]);                             // re-fetch when the id changes

  if (status === 'loading') return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (status === 'error') return <p role="alert">Could not load employee {id}.</p>;
  return <h2>{employee.name}</h2>;
}

Why this also fixes StrictMode's double effect in development: the first run's cleanup marks it as ignored (or aborts it), so only the second request updates the state. You may still see two requests in the Network tab; that is expected.

A status state instead of three booleans

Several separate booleans (loading, error, success) can contradict each other. One status string, or one state object, makes impossible combinations impossible. The same thinking leads to useReducer (see hooks toolbox) and to TanStack Query, which gives you exactly this.

Fetching on user action vs on mount

Use an effect to load data a screen needs to show. For data loaded because the user clicked something (search, refresh, submit), call the API directly in the event handler — no effect. And to keep UI responsive while typing in a search box, combine the effect with a debounce hook so you do not call the API on every keystroke.

SituationWhere to fetch
Screen opens and needs a list or detailsEffect (or better, TanStack Query)
Route param or filter changesEffect with that value in the dependency array
User clicks Save, Delete, SearchEvent handler
Many components need the same data, with cachingTanStack Query

Rule: every fetching effect needs a cleanup

Abort the request or set an ignore flag in the cleanup. Without it, fast navigation shows wrong data, and responses arriving after unmount waste work. Always check response.ok and always handle the error branch; an unhandled rejection leaves the user on a spinner forever.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to reset loading to true when the id changes, so the old employee shows while the new one loads.
  • Setting loading to false only on success; on an error the spinner stays.
  • Using async directly: useEffect(async () => {…}).
  • Reading data.name before data arrives: "Cannot read properties of null". Render the loading branch first, or use optional chaining.
  • Treating AbortError as a real error and showing it to the user.

In real projects

Hand-written fetch effects are fine for learning and for one or two small screens. In real codebases they are repeated in dozens of components, and each copy handles loading, errors, caching and refetching slightly differently. Teams usually switch to TanStack Query or at least a custom useFetch hook. In Module 6 the same calls go through an Axios instance with the JWT attached.

Interview: "How do you fetch data in React and avoid race conditions?"

  • Fetch in useEffect with the request inputs as dependencies; keep loading, error and data state.
  • Check res.ok since fetch does not reject on HTTP errors.
  • Return a cleanup that calls controller.abort() or sets an ignore flag, so an older response cannot overwrite a newer one.
  • Mention StrictMode's double effect and that libraries like TanStack Query handle caching, deduplication and cancellation for you.

You might not need an effect

Most "state that follows other state" bugs come from effects used where a plain calculation during render or an event handler is the right tool.

Why this matters

Effects are an escape hatch for talking to things outside React. When you use one only to move data between your own state variables, you add an extra render, risk showing stale values for a frame, and write code that is harder to follow. The React docs have a whole page on this (react.dev, "You Might Not Need an Effect"). Learn these patterns.

What an effect really costs

Remember the order of work from useEffect: React renders your component, commits the result to the DOM, the browser paints, and only then your effect runs. If the effect calls setState, React must render and commit again. So an effect that copies state costs two renders for every change, and for one frame the screen shows the old, inconsistent value (a "flicker"). With a chain of effects, each setting state for the next, you pay one extra render per link and the logic becomes very hard to follow. In development, Strict Mode also runs every effect twice (set up, clean up, set up) to expose missing cleanup, so careless effects show bugs earlier.

An easy test: is there an outside system involved? A WebSocket, a timer, the DOM, a browser API, a network request: yes, an effect may be right. Only your own props and state: probably not.

1. Derived state: calculate it during render

Wrong: effect copies data into state

const [employees, setEmployees] = useState([]);
const [search, setSearch] = useState('');
const [visible, setVisible] = useState([]);

useEffect(() => {
  setVisible(
    employees.filter((e) => e.name.includes(search)),
  );
}, [employees, search]);   // extra render, extra state

Right: derive while rendering

const [employees, setEmployees] = useState([]);
const [search, setSearch] = useState('');

const visible = employees.filter((e) =>
  e.name.includes(search),
);

If the calculation is truly expensive, wrap it in useMemo, not an effect.

The same applies to anything you can compute: a full name from first and last name, a cart total from the items, an "is the form valid" flag from the field values. Store the minimum (the raw fields); compute the rest. Storing both creates two sources of truth that can disagree.

function Cart({ items }) {
  // items: [{ id, name, priceInPaise, qty }] from your API
  const totalInPaise = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.priceInPaise * i.qty, 0);
  const itemCount = items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0);

  return <p>{itemCount} items — ₹{(totalInPaise / 100).toFixed(2)}</p>;
}

2. Responding to user actions: use the event handler

If something should happen because the user clicked, do it in the click handler. An effect cannot tell why state changed; it only sees that it did.

// Wrong: effect watches "submitted" and then posts
useEffect(() => {
  if (submitted) postEmployee(form);
}, [submitted]);

// Right: do the work where the event happens
async function handleSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  await postEmployee(form);
  showToast('Employee saved');
}

The effect version has a nasty extra problem: if form is in the dependency array, a later edit re-posts; if it is left out, the linter complains and you may post stale data. The handler has none of this, because it runs exactly once per click with the current values.

3. Resetting state when a prop changes: use a key

// Wrong: effect resets the form when the employee changes
useEffect(() => { setDraft(employee); }, [employee]);

// Right: a new key = a new component instance with fresh state
<EmployeeForm key={employee.id} employee={employee} />

With the effect, the form first renders with the old user's draft for one frame and then jumps to the new one. With the key, React throws the old instance away and mounts a new one, so the first render is already correct. See keys.

4. Notifying a parent: do it in the handler
