Do not call onChange(value) from an effect after setting local state. Call both the local setter and the parent's callback in the same event handler, or lift the state up so there is a single source of truth (see Sharing state).

// Wrong: parent is told one render late, by an effect
function Toggle({ onChange }) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false);
  useEffect(() => { onChange(on); }, [on, onChange]);
  return <button onClick={() => setOn(!on)}>{on ? 'ON' : 'OFF'}</button>;
}

// Right: update both in the handler (or make the parent own the state)
function Toggle({ onChange }) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false);
  function handleClick() {
    const next = !on;
    setOn(next);
    onChange(next);
  }
  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{on ? 'ON' : 'OFF'}</button>;
}

5. Adjusting some state when a prop changes

Sometimes only part of the state should reset when a prop changes (for example, clear the selected row when the list is replaced). The first choice is still to calculate it: store the selected id and derive the selected row with list.find(...); if the id is no longer in the list, you get undefined and no reset is needed. If you truly must store something from the previous render, React allows calling the component's own setState during render behind a condition (if (prevList !== list) { setPrevList(list); setSelected(null); }). It re-renders immediately without painting the stale value. Use it rarely; derive or use a key first.

6. Chains of effects

Avoid effects whose only job is to set state that triggers another effect (country → state → city dropdowns). Compute what you can, and put the real logic in the event handler that started the chain (handleCountryChange sets country and clears state and city together). Each hop in a chain is an extra render and a place for the values to go out of sync.

When an effect IS right

  • Synchronising with an external system: browser APIs, timers, WebSockets, a non-React widget.
  • Fetching data that a screen needs because it is displayed (ideally through a library).
  • Sending an analytics event because a page was shown.
  • Subscribing to an external store. For this, React provides useSyncExternalStore, which is safer than writing the subscription by hand; libraries such as Redux and Zustand use it.
You want to…Use
Compute a value from props or stateA variable in render (useMemo if slow)
Do something after a click or submitEvent handler
Reset state when an id changeskey on the component
Load server data for the screenTanStack Query (or an effect)
Connect to a WebSocket or add a window listeneruseEffect with cleanup
Measure a DOM node before paintuseLayoutEffect
Read a browser or third-party storeuseSyncExternalStore

Mistake: an effect that updates its own dependency

useEffect(() => { setCount(count + 1); }, [count]); loops forever: the effect changes count, which re-runs the effect. Similar loops happen when the effect sets an object or array that is also in its dependencies, because a new object is never equal to the old one. If you find yourself adding // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps to stop a loop, the effect is probably unnecessary.

Rule: every effect needs a clear external reason and a cleanup if it subscribes

Before writing useEffect, you should be able to name the outside system it synchronises with. If it starts something (listener, timer, connection, request), return a cleanup function that stops it. Dependencies must list every reactive value the effect reads.

Convention: a code-review question

Whenever you see useEffect(() => { setSomething(...) }, [other]), ask: "can something be calculated during render instead?" Usually it can.

Edge cases

  • Data fetching on mount is a legitimate effect, but it has traps (race conditions, double calls in Strict Mode); see fetching data, or avoid the problem with TanStack Query.
  • Do not use an effect to run code "once when the app starts" if the code is not about the component; module-level code (outside the component) or main.jsx is the place.
  • Initialising state from a prop is fine (useState(props.initial)) but later prop changes are ignored; that is why the key pattern exists.

Interview: "When should you NOT use useEffect?"

  • For derived data, for reacting to user events, for resetting state, for chains of effects that set state to trigger other effects.
  • Effects are for syncing with external systems; each unnecessary effect adds a render and a place for bugs.
  • Give one concrete example: filtering a list by search text is a variable in render, not useEffect plus a second state.
  • Mention the alternatives by name: render-time calculation, useMemo, event handlers, key, and a data library for server state.

useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer and the rules of hooks

useRef holds a value or DOM node without re-rendering, useMemo and useCallback cache a value or function between renders, useReducer organises complex state, and all hooks follow two strict rules.

useRef: a box that does not trigger renders

useRef(initial) returns an object { current: initial } that stays the same object for the whole life of the component. Changing ref.current does not cause a re-render. It has two uses.

1. Reaching a DOM element (focus an input, scroll to a row, measure size). Pass the ref to the element's ref prop; after the commit, ref.current is the DOM node.

import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

function SearchBox() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    inputRef.current.focus();          // DOM node is available after mount
  }, []);

  return <input ref={inputRef} placeholder="Search employees" />;
}

2. Keeping a mutable value between renders that is not part of the UI: a timer id, the previous value of a prop, a "has this run already" flag, the latest callback.

function Stopwatch() {
  const [seconds, setSeconds] = useState(0);
  const timerId = useRef(null);

  function start() {
    if (timerId.current) return;       // already running
    timerId.current = setInterval(() => setSeconds((s) => s + 1), 1000);
  }
  function stop() {
    clearInterval(timerId.current);
    timerId.current = null;
  }
  useEffect(() => stop, []);           // cleanup on unmount

  return (
    <div>
      <p>{seconds}s</p>
      <button onClick={start}>Start</button>
      <button onClick={stop}>Stop</button>
    </div>
  );
}

Rule: do not read or write ref.current during render

Refs are an escape hatch. Read and write them in event handlers and effects. If a value should appear on screen, it is state, not a ref. In React 19, ref is a normal prop for function components; in 18 you needed forwardRef to pass a ref to a child.

useMemo and useCallback: caching between renders

useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b]) remembers a calculated value and recalculates only when a dependency changes. useCallback(fn, [deps]) remembers a function (it is shorthand for useMemo(() => fn, [deps])). Because every render creates new objects and functions, these hooks give you stable references.

import { memo, useCallback, useMemo, useState } from 'react';

const EmployeeRow = memo(function EmployeeRow({ employee, onSelect }) {
  console.log('render row', employee.id);
  return <li onClick={() => onSelect(employee.id)}>{employee.name}</li>;
});

function EmployeeTable({ employees }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState(null);

  const visible = useMemo(
    () => employees.filter((e) => e.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase())),
    [employees, query],
  );
  const handleSelect = useCallback((id) => setSelectedId(id), []);

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      <p>Selected: {selectedId}</p>
      <ul>
        {visible.map((e) => (
          <EmployeeRow key={e.id} employee={e} onSelect={handleSelect} />
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}

React.memo(Component) makes a component skip re-rendering when its props are shallow-equal to last time. It only helps if the props are stable: without useCallback, onSelect would be a new function each render and memo would never skip. The three tools work as a team: memo + useCallback + useMemo.

When are they worth it?

  • A calculation is genuinely expensive (sorting or filtering thousands of rows, heavy maths) — measure first with the React DevTools Profiler.
  • A value is a dependency of an effect or another hook and must stay stable.
  • A function or object is passed to a memo-wrapped child, or into Context value.

Otherwise skip them. They cost memory and make code harder to read, and re-rendering is cheap. Do not wrap everything "just in case". The React Compiler (a build plugin that has reached a stable release) can add this memoisation automatically, which is one more reason not to hand-optimise early. Check the React docs before adopting it in a project.

useReducer: state with many transitions

When state has several related fields and many ways to change, or the next state depends on complex rules, useReducer puts all transitions in one pure function: (state, action) => newState. You dispatch actions such as { type: 'added', item }. Java developers: it is a small state machine, and the same idea as Redux (Module 7).

function cartReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'added': {
      const found = state.find((i) => i.id === action.item.id);
      if (found) {
        return state.map((i) => (i.id === found.id ? { ...i, qty: i.qty + 1 } : i));
      }
      return [...state, { ...action.item, qty: 1 }];
    }
    case 'removed':
      return state.filter((i) => i.id !== action.id);
    case 'cleared':
      return [];
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unknown action: ${action.type}`);
  }
}

function Cart() {
  const [cart, dispatch] = useReducer(cartReducer, []);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'added', item: { id: 1, name: 'Dosa' } })}>
        Add dosa
      </button>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'cleared' })}>Clear</button>
      <p>{cart.length} different items</p>
    </>
  );
}
useStateuseReducer
Best forIndependent, simple valuesRelated fields, many update types
Update logic livesIn event handlersIn one reducer (easy to unit test)
Passing updates downSeveral settersOne stable dispatch

The rules of hooks

Rule: two rules for every hook (anything named useSomething)

  1. Call hooks only at the top level. Not inside if, loops, nested functions, event handlers, or after an early return.
  2. Call hooks only from React function components or from other (custom) hooks, never from plain JavaScript functions.

Why? React does not know hook names. It remembers each component's hooks as an ordered list: "first useState, second useEffect…". On every render it expects the same calls in the same order. A conditional hook shifts the order and React hands back the wrong state. The ESLint plugin eslint-plugin-react-hooks catches both rules and is installed in the Vite template.

Wrong: hook after an early return

function Profile({ user }) {
  if (!user) return null;
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);   // skipped sometimes
  return <p>{user.name}</p>;
}

Right: hooks first, then conditions

function Profile({ user }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  if (!user) return null;
  return <p>{user.name}</p>;
}

The error you see: "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render" or "React has detected a change in the order of Hooks".

Other hooks you will meet

  • useContext (see Context), useId (stable unique ids for labels), useTransition and useDeferredValue (keep typing responsive while a heavy list updates), useSyncExternalStore (for library authors), useImperativeHandle (rare).
  • React 19: use, useActionState, useOptimistic, useFormStatus. use is not bound by the "no conditions" rule in the same way as other hooks; read the docs before using it.

Common mistakes

  • Wrapping everything in useMemo/useCallback with no measurement.
  • Using useMemo to guarantee something runs once; it is a performance hint, React may recompute.
  • Putting values that should render in a ref (the UI never updates).
  • Wrong dependency arrays in useCallback giving stale values.

Interview: "useMemo vs useCallback? Why the rules of hooks?"

  • useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function reference. Both depend on a dependency array and only help when stability matters (memo children, effect dependencies) or the work is expensive.
  • useRef persists a mutable value without re-rendering and holds DOM nodes.
  • Hooks are stored by call order, so they must run unconditionally at the top level, in components or custom hooks.
  • useReducer centralises complex transitions in a pure reducer.

Forms: controlled inputs and validation

In a controlled form, React state is the single source of truth for every input (value + onChange); you validate on submit, show errors next to fields, and disable the button while the request is running.

Controlled inputs

A controlled input gets its value from state and reports every change through onChange. The DOM input never holds its own truth; React does. That makes it easy to validate, format, clear or pre-fill the field. An uncontrolled input keeps its own value in the DOM and you read it later with a ref or FormData; it is simpler for tiny forms and is what libraries like React Hook Form use internally.

const [name, setName] = useState('');
const [role, setRole] = useState('DEVELOPER');
const [active, setActive] = useState(true);
const [shift, setShift] = useState('day');

// Text, number, email, password, textarea: value + onChange
<input value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />

// Select: value on the select, not "selected" on options
<select value={role} onChange={(e) => setRole(e.target.value)}>
  <option value="DEVELOPER">Developer</option>
  <option value="TESTER">Tester</option>
</select>

// Checkbox: checked + e.target.checked
<input type="checkbox" checked={active} onChange={(e) => setActive(e.target.checked)} />

// Radio group: checked is "does this one match the state?"
<input type="radio" name="shift" value="day"
       checked={shift === 'day'} onChange={(e) => setShift(e.target.value)} />
<input type="radio" name="shift" value="night"
       checked={shift === 'night'} onChange={(e) => setShift(e.target.value)} />

One state object and one handleChange

For forms with many fields, keep one object in state and give every input a name matching the key. One handler updates the right field using a computed property name [name].

import { useState } from 'react';

const empty = { name: '', email: '', salary: '', department: 'ENGINEERING', active: true };

function validate(values) {
  const errors = {};
  if (!values.name.trim()) errors.name = 'Name is required';
  if (!/^\S+@\S+\.\S+$/.test(values.email)) errors.email = 'Enter a valid email';
  const salary = Number(values.salary);
  if (!Number.isFinite(salary) || salary <= 0) errors.salary = 'Salary must be greater than 0';
  return errors;
}

function EmployeeForm({ initialValues = empty, onSubmit }) {
  const [values, setValues] = useState(initialValues);
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);
  const [submitError, setSubmitError] = useState(null);

  function handleChange(e) {
    const { name, type, value, checked } = e.target;
    setValues((prev) => ({ ...prev, [name]: type === 'checkbox' ? checked : value }));
  }

  async function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();                       // stop the page reload
    const found = validate(values);
    setErrors(found);
    if (Object.keys(found).length > 0) return;   // do not send invalid data

    setSubmitting(true);
    setSubmitError(null);
    try {
      await onSubmit({ ...values, salary: Number(values.salary) });
    } catch (err) {
      setSubmitError(err.message);
    } finally {
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit} noValidate>
      <label htmlFor="name">Name</label>
      <input id="name" name="name" value={values.name} onChange={handleChange}
             aria-invalid={Boolean(errors.name)} aria-describedby="name-error" />
      {errors.name && <p id="name-error" className="error">{errors.name}</p>}

      <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
      <input id="email" name="email" type="email" value={values.email}
             onChange={handleChange} />
      {errors.email && <p className="error">{errors.email}</p>}

      <label htmlFor="salary">Salary (₹ per month)</label>
      <input id="salary" name="salary" type="number" value={values.salary}
             onChange={handleChange} />
      {errors.salary && <p className="error">{errors.salary}</p>}

      <label>
        <input type="checkbox" name="active" checked={values.active} onChange={handleChange} />
        Active
      </label>

      {submitError && <p role="alert" className="error">{submitError}</p>}
      <button type="submit" disabled={submitting}>
        {submitting ? 'Saving…' : 'Save employee'}
      </button>
    </form>
  );
}

export default EmployeeForm;

Validation: when and where

  • On submit is the simplest and least annoying: validate all fields, show all errors.
  • On blur (when the user leaves a field) gives early feedback; track a touched object so you do not show errors on fields the user has not visited.
  • On every change suits password strength or availability hints, but shouting "invalid email" while the user is still typing is bad UX.
  • HTML attributes (required, minLength, pattern, type="email") give free browser validation. Use noValidate on the form when you show your own messages.
  • The server decides. Client validation is for convenience. Spring Boot's @Valid must check everything again, and the UI must display the server's field errors (see Module 6).

Edge cases that surprise people

  • value must never be undefined or null. React then treats the input as uncontrolled and later warns "A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled." Start with ''.
  • value without onChange makes a read-only input and a warning. Use readOnly or add the handler.
  • Number inputs return strings. Convert with Number() before sending JSON, or Spring will complain it cannot parse "85000" into a BigDecimal in some configurations (it usually coerces, but do not rely on it).
  • Date inputs return yyyy-MM-dd strings, which Jackson maps to LocalDate directly.
  • For file uploads use <input type="file" /> (always uncontrolled) and send FormData.
  • Every input needs a <label htmlFor> matching its id (or wrap the input in the label) for accessibility.

React Hook Form + Zod (the common library choice)

Hand-written forms get long. Most teams use React Hook Form (RHF), which tracks inputs without re-rendering on every keystroke, together with Zod, a schema library that defines the rules once and also gives you TypeScript types. The bridge is the @hookform/resolvers package. Install with npm install react-hook-form zod @hookform/resolvers.

import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form';
import { zodResolver } from '@hookform/resolvers/zod';
import { z } from 'zod';

const schema = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(1, 'Name is required'),
  email: z.string().email('Enter a valid email'),
  salary: z.coerce.number().positive('Salary must be greater than 0'),
});

function EmployeeFormRhf({ onSubmit }) {
  const {
    register,
    handleSubmit,
    setError,
    formState: { errors, isSubmitting },
  } = useForm({ resolver: zodResolver(schema) });

  async function submit(values) {
    try {
      await onSubmit(values);
    } catch (err) {
      setError('email', { message: 'This email is already registered' });  // server error
    }
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(submit)} noValidate>
      <input {...register('name')} placeholder="Name" />
      {errors.name && <p className="error">{errors.name.message}</p>}

      <input {...register('email')} placeholder="Email" />
      {errors.email && <p className="error">{errors.email.message}</p>}

      <input type="number" {...register('salary')} placeholder="Salary" />
      {errors.salary && <p className="error">{errors.salary.message}</p>}

      <button disabled={isSubmitting}>Save</button>
    </form>
  );
}

The API names above (register, handleSubmit, formState, setError, zodResolver) are stable across recent versions, but check the library docs for current details. Zod's Java parallel is Bean Validation: the schema is your @NotBlank, @Email and @Positive in one place.

Rules for forms

  • Always e.preventDefault() in onSubmit (or let RHF's handleSubmit do it).
  • Use a real <form> with a type="submit" button so Enter works. Buttons that are not submit buttons should say type="button".
  • Never trust client validation; the backend validates again.
  • Disable the submit button (or ignore clicks) while a request is running to prevent double submits.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting preventDefault: the page reloads and all state vanishes.
  • Writing onChange={setName(e.target.value)} (calling instead of passing).
  • Mutating the state object in handleChange (values[name] = value).
  • A button inside the form that should not submit but has no type="button".
  • Using defaultValue and value on the same input.

Interview: "Controlled vs uncontrolled components?"

  • Controlled: value lives in React state, changes come through onChange; easy validation and dependent fields, more re-renders.
  • Uncontrolled: DOM keeps the value, read through a ref or FormData; less code, fewer renders. File inputs are always uncontrolled.
  • Libraries such as React Hook Form use uncontrolled inputs with refs for speed.

Routing with React Router

React Router maps URL paths to components inside a single page: declare Routes, navigate with Link and useNavigate, read URL data with useParams and useSearchParams, and nest routes with Outlet.

Why a router?

A single-page app has one HTML file, but users expect different URLs for different screens: /employees, /employees/42, /login. They also expect the back button, bookmarks and shareable links to work. A client-side router watches the URL (using the browser History API), renders the matching component, and changes the address without a page reload. Install it with npm install react-router.

Version note: React Router v7

React Router v7 is the current major version. In v7 the package is react-router; the DOM pieces (BrowserRouter, Link, NavLink, …) are imported from react-router, and react-router-dom remains as a package that re-exports them for older projects. Older v6 code imports from react-router-dom. v7 can be used in two ways: the classic declarative mode shown here (BrowserRouter + Routes), a data mode with createBrowserRouter and loaders, and a framework mode (Remix merged into it). This module uses the declarative API because it is the same in v6 and v7. If your project's package.json says react-router-dom, use that import path.

Setup

import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { BrowserRouter } from 'react-router';
import App from './App.jsx';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <BrowserRouter>
      <App />
    </BrowserRouter>
  </StrictMode>,
);
import { Route, Routes } from 'react-router';
import Layout from './components/Layout.jsx';
import HomePage from './pages/HomePage.jsx';
import EmployeeListPage from './pages/EmployeeListPage.jsx';
import EmployeeDetailPage from './pages/EmployeeDetailPage.jsx';
import LoginPage from './pages/LoginPage.jsx';
import NotFoundPage from './pages/NotFoundPage.jsx';

function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/login" element={<LoginPage />} />

      {/* Layout route: renders the shared header, then the child route in its Outlet */}
      <Route element={<Layout />}>
        <Route index element={<HomePage />} />
        <Route path="employees" element={<EmployeeListPage />} />
        <Route path="employees/:id" element={<EmployeeDetailPage />} />
      </Route>

      <Route path="*" element={<NotFoundPage />} />   {/* 404: matches anything else */}
    </Routes>
  );
}

export default App;

Links and navigation

APIUse
<Link to="/employees">Navigate without a reload. Use instead of <a href> for internal links
<NavLink>Like Link, but knows if it is active; adds an active class (also accepts a function for className)
useNavigate()Navigate from code, e.g. after login or save: navigate('/employees'); navigate(-1) goes back
<Navigate to="/login" replace />Redirect while rendering (used in protected routes)
useParams()Read :id from the path: { id } = useParams() (always a string)
useSearchParams()Read and set the query string, like ?page=2&sort=name
useLocation()Current pathname, search and state
<Outlet />Where a layout route renders its matched child
 
import { NavLink, Outlet } from 'react-router';

function Layout() {
  return (
    <div>
      <header>
        <nav>
          <NavLink to="/" end>Home</NavLink>
          <NavLink to="/employees">Employees</NavLink>
        </nav>
      </header>
      <main>
        <Outlet />   {/* the matched child page appears here */}
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

export default Layout;
import { Link, useSearchParams } from 'react-router';

function EmployeeListPage() {
  const [searchParams, setSearchParams] = useSearchParams();
  const page = Number(searchParams.get('page') ?? 0);
  const q = searchParams.get('q') ?? '';

  // The URL is the state: refresh or share the link and you get the same view
  function nextPage() {
    setSearchParams({ q, page: String(page + 1) });
  }

  return (
    <section>
      <input value={q} onChange={(e) => setSearchParams({ q: e.target.value, page: '0' })} />
      {/* ...fetch /api/employees?q=...&page=... and render the list... */}
      <Link to="/employees/42">Open employee 42</Link>
      <button onClick={nextPage}>Next page</button>
    </section>
  );
}

export default EmployeeListPage;
import { useNavigate, useParams } from 'react-router';

function EmployeeDetailPage() {
  const { id } = useParams();        // "42" - a string; convert with Number(id) if needed
  const navigate = useNavigate();

  return (
    <section>
      <h1>Employee {id}</h1>
      <button onClick={() => navigate(-1)}>Back</button>
      <button onClick={() => navigate(`/employees/${id}/edit`)}>Edit</button>
    </section>
  );
}

export default EmployeeDetailPage;

Nested routes and the path rules

  • A route with no path but an element is a layout route: it wraps its children and shows them in <Outlet />.
  • index marks the default child of a parent path (the page at exactly / or /employees).
  • Child paths are relative to the parent: path="employees" then path=":id" gives /employees/:id. Do not start child paths with / unless you want an absolute path.
  • path="*" matches anything not matched elsewhere — your 404 page.
  • Router v6+ ranks routes by specificity, so the order you write them in does not matter.
  • <NavLink to="/" end> needs end so "Home" is not active on every page.

Rule: the server must also serve index.html for every path

Routing happens in the browser. If a user refreshes on /employees/42, the browser asks the web server for that path, and a plain static server returns 404. Vite's dev server already falls back to index.html. In production you must configure the same fallback (Netlify/Vercel rewrites, Nginx try_files, a Spring Boot forward controller) — see deployment in Module 6.

Conventions

  • Keep one component per route in src/pages/, named XxxPage; they fetch data and compose smaller components.
  • Put list filters, sort order and page numbers in search params so links are shareable.
  • Use replace when a redirect should not add a history entry (login redirect).
  • Link to routes with a helper or constants if paths repeat a lot.

Edge cases

  • useParams values are always strings ("42"), so id === 42 is false. This breaks strict comparisons with numeric ids.
  • The same page component rendered for /employees/1 and /employees/2 is not remounted when the id changes; state is kept, and your fetch effect must list id as a dependency.
  • Using <a href="/employees"> inside the app causes a full page reload and loses all state.
  • useNavigate must be called inside a component under the Router; calling it outside gives an error "useNavigate() may be used only in the context of a <Router> component".
  • Hash router (HashRouter, URLs like /#/employees) works without server rewrites but looks old; prefer BrowserRouter.

Interview: "How does client-side routing work?"

  • The router listens to URL changes via the History API (pushState, popstate), matches the path to a route, and renders its component without a page reload.
  • Dynamic segments (:id) come from useParams; query data from useSearchParams; layouts use nested routes with Outlet.
  • On refresh, the server must return index.html for all app paths (SPA fallback).

Sharing state: lifting state up and the Context API

When two components need the same state, move it to their closest common parent and pass it down; when many distant components need it, put it in a Context provider and read it with useContext.

Lifting state up

Each piece of state has one owner. If a sibling needs it too, you lift it up: the parent owns the state and passes the value (down) and a setter or handler (so children can ask for changes) as props. There is one source of truth, so the siblings can never disagree.

function EmployeesPage() {
  const [search, setSearch] = useState('');           // owned by the parent
  const [employees] = useState(initialEmployees);

  const visible = employees.filter((e) =>
    e.name.toLowerCase().includes(search.toLowerCase()),
  );

  return (
    <>
      <SearchBar value={search} onChange={setSearch} />     {/* writes the state */}
      <ResultCount count={visible.length} />               {/* reads derived data */}
      <EmployeeList employees={visible} />
    </>
  );
}

function SearchBar({ value, onChange }) {          // a controlled component
  return <input value={value} onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)} />;
}

How far up should you lift? To the closest common parent, and no further. Lifting too high makes that parent re-render (and re-render all its children) on every change, and passes props through components that do not care. A good habit: keep state as low as possible, and lift it only when a second component needs it. The opposite move also exists: if only one child uses a piece of state, push it down into that child.

Props, children and composition

Before reaching for Context, try composition. A component can accept children (or JSX in other props) so the page that owns the data builds the middle layers' content itself, and the middle layers never see the props.

// The Layout does not know about user at all
function Layout({ sidebar, children }) {
  return (
    <div className="layout">
      <aside>{sidebar}</aside>
      <main>{children}</main>
    </div>
  );
}

function DashboardPage({ user }) {
  return (
    <Layout sidebar={<UserCard user={user} />}>
      <Orders userId={user.id} />
    </Layout>
  );
}

The Context API

Lifting works until the value must pass through many layers (prop drilling). Context lets a component make a value available to everything below it without passing props. It has three steps: create the context, provide a value high in the tree, and read it anywhere below. Think of it like a Spring bean in the application context: you declare it once at the top and any component below "injects" it with useContext, though it only lives in the component tree, not globally.

import { createContext, useCallback, useContext, useMemo, useState } from 'react';

// 1. Create. The default is used only when there is no provider above.
const AuthContext = createContext(null);

// 2. Provide
export function AuthProvider({ children }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);       // { id, name, roles } or null

  const login = useCallback((userData) => setUser(userData), []);
  const logout = useCallback(() => setUser(null), []);

  // Memoise so consumers re-render only when something really changed
  const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, login, logout }), [user, login, logout]);

  return <AuthContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</AuthContext.Provider>;
}

// 3. Read, wrapped in a custom hook with a helpful error
export function useAuth() {
  const ctx = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (ctx === null) throw new Error('useAuth must be used inside an AuthProvider');
  return ctx;
}
// main.jsx: wrap the app once
<AuthProvider>
  <App />
</AuthProvider>

// Any component, any depth
function Header() {
  const { user, logout } = useAuth();
  return user ? <button onClick={logout}>Logout {user.name}</button> : null;
}

A realistic AuthProvider: restoring the session

A real provider also has to answer "is someone already logged in?" when the page loads. With a cookie-based session or a stored token you ask the backend (for example GET /api/auth/me in Spring Boot), and until the answer arrives the app does not know. That is why the context exposes an isLoading flag; protected routes use it so they do not redirect too early. The token flow itself is in JWT login end to end.

export function AuthProvider({ children }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(true);     // true until /me answers

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    fetch('/api/auth/me', { signal: controller.signal, credentials: 'include' })
      .then((res) => (res.ok ? res.json() : null))      // 401 = not logged in
      .then((me) => setUser(me))
      .catch(() => {})                                   // aborted or network error
      .finally(() => {
        if (!controller.signal.aborted) setIsLoading(false);
      });
    return () => controller.abort();
  }, []);

  const login = useCallback((me) => setUser(me), []);
  const logout = useCallback(() => setUser(null), []);

  const value = useMemo(
    () => ({ user, isLoading, login, logout }),
    [user, isLoading, login, logout],
  );
  return <AuthContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</AuthContext.Provider>;
}

Version note: React 19 and Context

In React 19 you can render the context itself as the provider: <AuthContext value={value}>…</AuthContext>. The <AuthContext.Provider> form still works and is what most existing code uses. The use(AuthContext) API can read a context too, but useContext is still the everyday choice.

What Context is good and bad at

When the provider's value changes, every component that reads that context re-renders, even if it only uses one field. Context has no selector mechanism. So it suits values that change rarely and are needed widely: the current user, theme, language, feature flags, the router. It is a poor fit for fast-changing data (mouse position, a form on every keystroke, large lists) or for server data (use TanStack Query). For big client state with frequent updates, look at Redux Toolkit or Zustand in Module 7.

How context re-renders work

Two different things can cause a re-render, and they are easy to mix up.

  • The provider's parent re-renders. If the provider component gets new props or its own state changes, it renders again. Its children prop is the same element objects as before (they were created by the component above), so React skips re-rendering those children. That is why wrapping children inside the provider is cheap, as in AuthProvider above.
  • The context value changes. React compares the new value with the old one using Object.is. If different, every component that called useContext for that context re-renders, skipping any memo in between.

This is why the object literal matters. value={{ user, login }} creates a new object each render of the provider, so the comparison always says "changed", and all consumers re-render even if user is the same. useMemo keeps the same object until a dependency changes.

Wrong: new value object every render

function ThemeProvider({ children }) {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
  return (
    <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>
      {children}
    </ThemeContext.Provider>
  );
}

Right: memoised value

function ThemeProvider({ children }) {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
  const value = useMemo(() => ({ theme, setTheme }), [theme]);
  return (
    <ThemeContext.Provider value={value}>
      {children}
    </ThemeContext.Provider>
  );
}

setTheme from useState is stable (same function every render), so it does not need to be in the dependency list. Functions you define yourself (like login) need useCallback to stay stable; see useMemo and useCallback.

Splitting a context

If some components only need to change a value (a "Logout" button) and others only read it, use two contexts so the writers do not re-render when the data changes. This is a common pattern for larger state.

const CartStateContext = createContext(null);
const CartActionsContext = createContext(null);

export function CartProvider({ children }) {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([]);

  const actions = useMemo(() => ({
    add: (item) => setItems((prev) => [...prev, item]),
    remove: (id) => setItems((prev) => prev.filter((i) => i.id !== id)),
    clear: () => setItems([]),
  }), []);                                  // setItems is stable, so never changes

  return (
    <CartActionsContext.Provider value={actions}>
      <CartStateContext.Provider value={items}>{children}</CartStateContext.Provider>
    </CartActionsContext.Provider>
  );
}
ApproachUse whenCost
PropsOne or two levelsDrilling if the tree grows
Lift state upSiblings share stateParent re-renders more
Composition (children)Avoid passing props through middle layersNeeds a restructure
ContextRarely changing global values (user, theme)All consumers re-render on change
State libraryLarge, frequently changing client stateAnother dependency
TanStack QueryServer dataAnother dependency, big win

Rule: a consumer must be below its provider

useContext reads the value of the nearest provider above the component in the tree. If there is none, it returns the default passed to createContext. Putting null as the default and throwing in your useXxx hook turns a silent bug into a clear error message. Providers can be nested; the inner one overrides the outer one for its subtree.

Conventions

  • One context per concern (AuthContext, ThemeContext); do not make one giant "AppContext".
  • Export a Provider component and a useXxx hook; do not export the raw context object.
  • Memoise the provider value (useMemo) when it is an object.
  • Split state and dispatch into two contexts if consumers mostly need only one.
  • Keep providers near the top (main.jsx), but put feature-specific ones around only that feature's routes.

Common mistakes

  • Passing a fresh object literal as value={{ user, login }} without memoising — every parent render re-renders all consumers.
  • Reading the context outside its provider and getting null or the default.
  • Putting all server data into context and hand-rolling cache invalidation.
  • Lifting state far higher than needed "just in case".
  • Keeping a copy of context data in local state (useState(user)); the copy goes stale when the context changes. Read it directly.
  • Storing a rapidly changing value (a text field's draft, the scroll position) in a global context, so half the app re-renders on every keystroke.

Edge cases

  • Context values are compared with Object.is; mutating an object in place and keeping the same reference will not notify consumers. Always create a new object or array.
  • Context does not cross separate React roots, and in tests you must wrap the component in the provider (a small renderWithProviders helper is normal).
  • React.memo on a consumer does not stop context-driven re-renders; the context update bypasses it.

In real projects

A typical Spring Boot + React app has an AuthProvider (current user and roles), maybe a ThemeProvider and a toast/notification provider. Everything that comes from your REST API (employees, orders) goes through TanStack Query instead, and form drafts stay local. That keeps the contexts small and rarely changing.

Interview: "Prop drilling, and how do you avoid it?"

  • Passing props through components that do not use them. Fix with composition, Context, or a state library.
  • Context re-renders all consumers when its value changes, so it is for low-frequency global values; use selectors (Zustand/Redux) for hot state.
  • Lifting state up: the closest common parent owns the state; children receive value and callbacks.
  • Why memoise the provider value? A new object each render makes Object.is see a change and re-renders every consumer.
  • Is Context a replacement for Redux? Not for frequent updates or complex logic; it only transports a value, it does not manage state by itself.

Custom hooks

A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks, so you can share stateful logic between components without sharing state.

Why and how

When two components need the same combination of useState, useEffect and helpers, extract it into a function. The hook must start with use (so React and the linter know the rules of hooks apply) and can call any hook. Each component that calls the hook gets its own copy of the state; hooks share logic, not data. Return what the component needs: a value, an array, or an object.

If you know Java, a custom hook is closest to a small reusable service class that you create per use, not a singleton: every new gives separate fields. The "fields" are the state and effects inside the hook, and the component that calls it owns them. Nothing is magic: when the hook's state changes, the component that called it re-renders, exactly as if you had written that useState directly in the component.

Extracting a hook step by step

  1. Spot repeated code: the same useState plus useEffect pair in two components.
  2. Cut it into a function named useSomething in src/hooks/.
  3. Turn the values that differ (a URL, a key, a delay) into parameters.
  4. Return the values and functions the component needs, and replace the old code with one call.

A first, tiny hook: useToggle

import { useCallback, useState } from 'react';

export function useToggle(initial = false) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(initial);
  const toggle = useCallback(() => setOn((v) => !v), []);   // stable function identity
  return [on, toggle, setOn];
}

// Use: const [open, toggleOpen] = useToggle();
//      <button onClick={toggleOpen}>{open ? 'Hide' : 'Show'} details</button>

useLocalStorage

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useLocalStorage(key, initialValue) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(() => {
    try {
      const stored = localStorage.getItem(key);
      return stored !== null ? JSON.parse(stored) : initialValue;
    } catch {
      return initialValue;       // blocked storage or invalid JSON
    }
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value));
    } catch {
      // storage full or disabled: ignore
    }
  }, [key, value]);

  return [value, setValue];      // same shape as useState
}

// Use: const [theme, setTheme] = useLocalStorage('theme', 'light');

Because it returns the real setValue from useState, the functional form also works: setTheme((t) => (t === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light')). The initial value is read once, using a function passed to useState (a lazy initialiser), so localStorage is not read on every render. Do not store tokens or secrets here; see the storage trade-offs in JWT login end to end.

useDebounce

Debouncing waits until the user stops typing before using the value, which avoids one API call per keystroke.

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useDebounce(value, delayMs = 400) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delayMs);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);       // typing again cancels the pending update
  }, [value, delayMs]);

  return debounced;
}
function EmployeeSearch() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  const query = useDebounce(text, 400);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!query) return;
    const controller = new AbortController();
    fetch(`/api/employees?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then((r) => r.json())
      .then(console.log)
      .catch(() => {});
    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [query]);          // runs when the debounced value changes, not on each keystroke

  return <input value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} />;
}

The input stays instant because text updates on every keystroke; only the debounced copy is delayed. A debounce hook returns a delayed value; a "debounced function" is a different tool. The server side matters too: your Spring Boot endpoint should still be efficient (an index on the searched column), because debouncing only reduces the number of calls.

useFetch

This hook bundles the loading / error / data pattern from fetching data, including the cleanup.

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useFetch(url) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ data: null, error: null, loading: true });

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    setState({ data: null, error: null, loading: true });

    fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then((res) => {
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        return res.json();
      })
      .then((data) => setState({ data, error: null, loading: false }))
      .catch((error) => {
        if (error.name !== 'AbortError') setState({ data: null, error, loading: false });
      });

    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [url]);

  return state;
}

// Use:
// const { data: employees, error, loading } = useFetch('/api/employees');

When url changes (a new page number, a different employee id) the cleanup aborts the old request, so a slow earlier response can never overwrite a newer one: this is the race condition from the fetching article, solved once inside the hook. Components that use it stay short:

function EmployeePage({ id }) {
  const { data: employee, error, loading } = useFetch(`/api/employees/${id}`);

  if (loading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (error) return <p role="alert">Could not load: {error.message}</p>;
  return <h2>{employee.name}</h2>;
}

A production-grade version needs caching, retries, deduplication and refetching — exactly what TanStack Query provides. Write useFetch once to understand the pattern, then prefer the library.

Hooks that wrap your domain

The most useful custom hooks in real projects are domain hooks like useEmployees(), useAuth() or useCart(). They hide where data comes from, so components stay small and you can change the implementation (hand-written fetch → TanStack Query) without touching them. This is the same idea as a Spring service interface: callers depend on the contract, not the implementation.

import { useCallback } from 'react';
import { useFetch } from './useFetch.js';

export function useEmployees(department) {
  const url = department
    ? `/api/employees?department=${encodeURIComponent(department)}`
    : '/api/employees';
  const { data, error, loading } = useFetch(url);

  const hasData = data !== null;
  return { employees: data ?? [], error, loading, hasData };
}

Custom hook vs similar tools

ToolUse it forHas its own state?
Custom hookReusing logic that uses hooks (state, effects, context)Yes, one copy per caller
Plain functionPure logic with no hooks (formatting, validation)No
ComponentReusing UI (markup plus logic)Yes, per instance
ContextSharing one value with many distant componentsOne shared value
Module-level variableRarely right; shared mutable data outside ReactShared, but not reactive

Rules for custom hooks

  • The name starts with use. Without it the linter cannot enforce the rules of hooks inside.
  • Call it only at the top level of a component or another hook: not inside loops, conditions, nested functions, or after an early return. React tracks hooks by call order, so the order must be the same on every render.
  • Call hooks only from React function components or other hooks, never from plain functions or class components.
  • Hooks share logic, not state: two components calling useFetch make two requests.
  • Do not create a hook that does nothing hook-like (no hook calls inside): a normal function is enough.

Conventions

  • One hook per file in src/hooks/, file name equals hook name (useDebounce.js).
  • Return an array for one or two values that callers will rename (like useState), and an object for three or more.
  • Accept simple parameters; for many options take one options object with defaults.
  • Keep a hook focused: "fetch", "debounce", "toggle". Compose small hooks into bigger domain hooks instead of writing one that does everything.

Mistakes

  • Expecting two components to share data just because they call the same hook. Each call has its own state; for shared state use Context, lifting, or a data library.
  • Passing an object or function created inline into the dependency array of the effect inside the hook (useFetch(url, { headers }) with a new headers object each render): the effect re-runs on every render and may loop. Memoise it, depend on its primitive fields, or accept primitives.
  • Forgetting the cleanup (abort, clearTimeout, remove listener) so a stale result or leaked timer arrives after the component has changed.
  • Calling the hook conditionally: if (id) { useFetch(...) } breaks the call order. Call it always and make the hook skip the work (for example, accept an enabled option or a null URL).

Edge cases

  • In development, Strict Mode runs effects twice, so useFetch may send two requests on mount. This is expected and only happens in development; the abort in the cleanup makes it harmless.
  • useLocalStorage reads the browser's storage, so it fails during server-side rendering where localStorage does not exist. In a Vite single-page app this does not matter, and the try / catch covers blocked storage.
  • Updates made in one browser tab do not reach useLocalStorage in another tab unless you also listen to the storage event.

Tip: test them too

Hooks can be tested with renderHook from React Testing Library (see Module 7). Keep logic in hooks and plain functions, and components become thin and easy to test.

Interview: "What is a custom hook and why use one?"

  • A function starting with use that composes built-in hooks to reuse stateful logic (fetching, forms, debouncing, local storage).
  • Each call has isolated state; hooks share logic only.
  • Benefits: no duplicated code, smaller components, testable logic, swap implementations behind a stable interface.
  • Be ready to write useDebounce or useLocalStorage on a whiteboard, and to state the two rules of hooks (top level only; only from components or hooks).
  • Follow-up: "Does a custom hook make two components share state?" No; use Context or lift the state.

TanStack Query for server data

TanStack Query manages server state for you: useQuery fetches and caches data by a query key with loading and error states, and useMutation sends changes and invalidates the cache so the UI refreshes.

Good to know

Server state is different

Data like "the list of employees" is not owned by your app. It lives on the server, can change without you knowing, can be shared by many screens, and can be out of date the moment you receive it. With useEffect you would have to build caching, deduplication, retries, background refresh, loading flags and invalidation yourself. TanStack Query (formerly React Query) does all of it. Install: npm install @tanstack/react-query. The current major version is v5; the examples use its object-style API.

Setup

import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';

const queryClient = new QueryClient({
  defaultOptions: {
    queries: {
      staleTime: 30_000,        // data counts as fresh for 30 s: no refetch in that window
      retry: 1,                 // retry failed requests once
    },
  },
});

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <App />
    </QueryClientProvider>
  </StrictMode>,
);

useQuery: reading data

You give useQuery a query key (an array that identifies the data) and a query function that returns a Promise (and throws on failure). The key is the cache key: same key, same cached data, shared by all components.

export async function fetchEmployees(page = 0) {
  const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:8080/api/employees?page=${page}&size=10`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);   // a thrown error becomes `error`
  return res.json();
}
import { keepPreviousData, useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { fetchEmployees } from './employeeApi.js';

function EmployeeListPage() {
  const [page, setPage] = useState(0);

  const { data, isPending, isError, error, isFetching } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['employees', { page }],         // changes with page -> new fetch, own cache entry
    queryFn: () => fetchEmployees(page),
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,         // keep showing old page while the next loads
  });

  if (isPending) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (isError) return <p role="alert">Error: {error.message}</p>;

  return (
    <>
      <ul>{data.content.map((e) => <li key={e.id}>{e.name}</li>)}</ul>
      {isFetching && <small>Updating…</small>}
      <button disabled={page === 0} onClick={() => setPage((p) => p - 1)}>Prev</button>
      <button disabled={data.last} onClick={() => setPage((p) => p + 1)}>Next</button>
    </>
  );
}

Compare this with the 30-line effect in fetching data: no loading state, no cleanup, no race conditions, and the result is cached. Key fields returned:

Field / optionMeaning
dataThe last successful result (or undefined)
isPendingNo data yet (first load)
isFetchingA request is running, including background refetches
isError / errorThe query function threw
refetch()Fetch again on demand
enabled: falseDo not run yet (e.g. wait until an id exists)
staleTimeHow long data is fresh. Default 0: always considered stale
gcTimeHow long unused cache stays in memory (default 5 minutes)

Fresh, stale and refetching

Cached data is fresh for staleTime, then stale. Showing stale data instantly while fetching a new copy in the background ("stale-while-revalidate") is the default behaviour. A stale query is refetched when a component mounts, the window regains focus, or the network reconnects. That is why your list refreshes when you come back to the tab. With staleTime: 0 (the default) this happens a lot; raise it for data that rarely changes.

Query keys

Keys are arrays, compared by value. Put everything the function depends on into the key, as you would with an effect's dependencies: ['employee', id], ['employees', { page, q }]. The key structure is hierarchical, so invalidating ['employees'] also matches ['employees', { page: 2 }].

useMutation: changing data

Writes (POST, PUT, DELETE) use useMutation. After a successful mutation you invalidate the affected queries, which marks them stale and refetches the ones on screen.

import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

async function createEmployee(newEmployee) {
  const res = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/api/employees', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(newEmployee),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

function AddEmployee() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();

  const mutation = useMutation({
    mutationFn: createEmployee,
    onSuccess: () => {
      queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['employees'] });   // list refetches
    },
  });

  return (
    <button
      disabled={mutation.isPending}
      onClick={() => mutation.mutate({ name: 'Meera Iyer', email: 'meera@corp.in' })}
    >
      {mutation.isPending ? 'Saving…' : 'Add employee'}
      {mutation.isError && <span role="alert"> Failed: {mutation.error.message}</span>}
    </button>
  );
}

Wrap it in custom hooks

import { useMutation, useQuery, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { createEmployee, fetchEmployee, fetchEmployees } from './employeeApi.js';

export const employeeKeys = {
  all: ['employees'],
  list: (page) => ['employees', { page }],
  detail: (id) => ['employee', id],
};

export function useEmployees(page) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: employeeKeys.list(page), queryFn: () => fetchEmployees(page) });
}

export function useEmployee(id) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: employeeKeys.detail(id),
    queryFn: () => fetchEmployee(id),
    enabled: Boolean(id),
  });
}

export function useCreateEmployee() {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: createEmployee,
    onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: employeeKeys.all }),
  });
}
Hand-written useEffectTanStack Query
Loading / error stateYou write it every timeBuilt in
Caching and sharingNone, or a custom contextAutomatic by query key
Duplicate requestsOne per componentDeduplicated
Race conditionsYour cleanupHandled
Refetch on focus, retriesManualConfigurable defaults
After a writeManually reloadinvalidateQueries
Optimistic updatesHardSupported through mutation callbacks

Rules

  • The query function must return a Promise and throw on HTTP errors. With fetch check res.ok; Axios already throws for 4xx/5xx.
  • Everything the request depends on goes in the query key.
  • Do not copy data into useState; read it from the query.
  • Use queries for reads and mutations for writes.

Edge cases

  • In v5, isLoading means "first fetch is running" (isFetching && isPending); isPending is "no data yet". In v4 the names were different (isLoading meant "no data"). Check which version tutorials use.
  • The default retry is 3 attempts with backoff. A 401 or 404 that retries three times just delays the error; set retry: false for those or handle them in one place.
  • Install the optional @tanstack/react-query-devtools to see the cache live.

In real projects

A common stack for a Spring Boot backend: Axios instance (Module 6) as the queryFn transport, TanStack Query for all GET/POST/PUT/DELETE calls, React Router for pages, Context only for auth and theme, and React Hook Form for forms.

Interview: "Why TanStack Query instead of useEffect and Redux?"

  • Server state is async, shared, cached and can go stale; it needs a cache layer, not just setState.
  • The query key identifies cached data; staleTime controls freshness; mutations plus invalidateQueries keep the UI in sync after writes.
  • It removes boilerplate and race conditions, and leaves Redux/Zustand for true client state.

React DevTools and common React errors

Use the React DevTools browser extension to inspect the component tree, props, state and renders, and learn to read the handful of error messages you will see every week.

React DevTools

Install the React Developer Tools extension for Chrome, Edge or Firefox. Open the browser DevTools; two new tabs appear:

  • Components: the component tree. Click a component to see its props, state, hooks and context on the right. You can edit state and props live, jump to the DOM node, and search by component name. Use it to answer "what value did this component really receive?".
  • Profiler: record an interaction, then see which components rendered, how long each took, and (with "Record why each component rendered" enabled in settings) why. Use it before adding memo/useMemo. The "Highlight updates when components render" option flashes every re-rendering component.

Combine it with the other DevTools tabs you know from Module 4: the Network tab for requests and the Console for errors. TanStack Query also has its own devtools panel.

Common errors and warnings

MessageCauseFix
Each child in a list should have a unique "key" propArray rendered without keys, or duplicate keysAdd key={item.id} on the outer element of map
Too many re-renders. React limits the number of renders to prevent an infinite loopA setter is called during render, e.g. onClick={setCount(1)}Pass a function: onClick={() => setCount(1)}
Cannot update a component while rendering a different componentA child calls a parent's setter during its renderMove the call into an event handler or useEffect
Objects are not valid as a React childRendering a plain object or Date: {user}Render a field: {user.name}, or format the date
Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')Using data before it loaded, or a wrong response shapeLoading branch first, optional chaining, check the Network tab
Invalid hook callHook called outside a component, in a condition, or two copies of React installedFollow the rules of hooks; run npm ls react
Rendered more hooks than during the previous renderA hook after a conditional returnMove all hooks above any return
A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlledInput value started as undefinedInitialise state to ''
Maximum update depth exceededAn effect sets state and has a bad dependency arrayFix dependencies; derive instead of syncing
X is not a function / X is not definedWrong import (default vs named), typo, or lowercase componentCheck the export style and the capitalisation
Warning: Invalid DOM property classHTML attribute in JSXUse className
Hydration failed (frameworks only)Server and client HTML differAvoid Date.now() or window in the first render

A debugging routine

  1. Read the first error in the Console and click the file and line in the stack trace; later errors are often a consequence.
  2. In the Components tab, check the props and state of the failing component. Is the value what you expected?
  3. In the Network tab, check the request URL, status, response body and headers. Is it a 404, a 401, a CORS failure, or the wrong JSON shape?
  4. Add console.log or a debugger statement; remember StrictMode runs renders twice in development, so logs appear doubled.
  5. Reduce the problem: comment out parts until it works, then add them back.

Tip: error boundaries

A rendering error in any component unmounts the whole tree and leaves a white page. An error boundary catches errors in its children and shows a fallback. It must be a class component, so most apps use the small react-error-boundary library: <ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Something broke</p>}>. Boundaries do not catch errors in event handlers or async code; handle those with try/catch.

Interview: "How do you debug a React app?"

  • Console error and stack trace first; React DevTools Components for props/state; Profiler for slow renders; Network tab for API problems.
  • Know the usual suspects: keys, too many re-renders, stale closures, undefined data before loading, wrong hook order.

Interview questions — React

What is React, and how is it different from a framework like Angular?

React is a library for building UIs from components. It handles rendering and state only; routing, forms, HTTP and global state come from separate libraries you choose. Angular is a full framework with its own router, forms, HTTP client and dependency injection, written in TypeScript. React is declarative: you describe the UI for the current state, and React updates the DOM.

What is the virtual DOM and how does reconciliation work?

Components return React elements, plain objects that describe the UI. After a state change React renders again, diffs the new tree with the previous one and commits only the differences to the real DOM. It assumes elements of different types produce different trees, and uses key to match list items, which gives roughly O(n) comparison. Several updates are batched into one render.

What is the difference between props and state?

Props are inputs from the parent and are read-only. State is data the component owns and changes through a setter, which triggers a re-render. State persists across renders; props change when the parent re-renders. Data flows down as props, and child-to-parent communication happens by calling functions passed as props.

Why must you not mutate state directly?

React detects changes by comparing references. If you mutate an array or object and pass the same reference to the setter, React sees no change and the UI is stale. Create a new value with spread, map or filter. Immutability also keeps DevTools, memoisation and time-travel debugging reliable.

After setCount(count + 1) three times in a handler, count only goes up by 1. Why, and how do you fix it?

State is a snapshot: in that render count is a constant, so all three calls schedule "count = old + 1". Use the functional form setCount(c => c + 1); React passes the latest pending value to each updater, and the result is +3 in one batched render.

Explain useEffect and its dependency array.

It runs after the render is committed, to synchronise with an external system. No array: after every render. []: once after mount. [a, b]: when a or b change. The returned cleanup runs before the next run and on unmount. List every reactive value you use, or you get stale closures. Unstable object or function dependencies cause extra runs or infinite loops.

How do you fetch data in a component and avoid race conditions?

Fetch inside useEffect with the inputs (such as id) in the dependency array. Keep loading, error and data state, and check res.ok. Return a cleanup that aborts with AbortController or sets an ignore flag so an older, slower response cannot overwrite a newer one. In real projects use TanStack Query.

Why do I see my effect (and API call) run twice in development?

StrictMode deliberately mounts, unmounts and mounts again in development to check that your effect has correct cleanup. It does not happen in production. Fix the effect rather than removing StrictMode.

Why do lists need keys? Is the array index a good key?

Keys let React match items between renders to reuse, move or remove the correct element and keep its state. Use a stable unique id. Index keys break when the list is reordered, filtered or has inserts or deletes, because state and DOM nodes attach to the wrong item. A random key per render recreates every item.

Controlled vs uncontrolled components?

A controlled input's value comes from state (value + onChange), so React is the source of truth and you can validate or transform on each change. An uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM; you read it with a ref or FormData. File inputs are always uncontrolled; React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs for performance.

What is prop drilling and how do you avoid it?

Passing props through intermediate components that do not need them. Avoid it with composition (pass children or JSX), with Context for rarely changing global values like the user or theme, or with a state library. Context re-renders all consumers when the value changes, so it is not for fast-changing data.

What are the rules of hooks, and why do they exist?

Call hooks only at the top level (not in conditions, loops or nested functions) and only in function components or custom hooks. React stores hook state in an ordered list per component, so the calls must happen in the same order every render. Breaking the rule gives "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render" or silently wrong state.

When would you use useMemo, useCallback and React.memo?

useMemo caches an expensive computed value; useCallback caches a function reference; React.memo skips re-rendering a component when its props are shallow-equal. Together they help when a memoised child receives stable props, or a value is an effect dependency. Measure with the Profiler first; unnecessary memoisation adds complexity without benefit.

Why TanStack Query instead of fetching in useEffect?

Server data needs caching, deduplication, background refetching, retries, loading and error states and invalidation after writes. TanStack Query provides these through query keys, staleTime, useQuery, useMutation and invalidateQueries, and removes race-condition boilerplate. Client-only state still belongs in useState or Context.

Cheat sheet — React

  • Create project npm create vite@latest → npm install → npm run dev (port 5173); npm run build → dist/
  • Component function with a Capital name returning JSX; one root or a fragment <>…</>
  • JSX attributes className, htmlFor, camelCase events, style={{ }}, comments {/* */}
  • Props read-only inputs; destructure with defaults; children for composition
  • useState [value, setValue]; state is a snapshot; use setX(x => …) when depending on the old value
  • Immutable updates add [...a, x], remove filter, change map + {...o, k: v}
  • Events onClick={fn} passes the function; () => fn(id) for arguments; e.preventDefault() in submit
  • Conditional early return, ternary, cond && <X />; never 0 &&
  • Lists items.map(i => <Row key={i.id} … />); stable unique keys, not random, not index
  • useEffect runs after render; no array = every render, [] = mount, [a] = when a changes; return a cleanup
  • Fetch in effect loading/error/data + res.ok + AbortController or ignore flag
  • Not an effect derived data → compute in render; user action → event handler; reset → key
  • useRef DOM node or mutable value, no re-render; useMemo value cache; useCallback function cache; useReducer complex state
  • Rules of hooks top level only; only in components or custom hooks
  • Forms controlled: value + onChange, one handler using name; disable submit while sending; server validates too
  • React Hook Form + Zod register, handleSubmit, zodResolver
  • Router BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link/NavLink, useNavigate, useParams (string), useSearchParams, Outlet, path="*" for 404
  • Lift state up closest common parent owns it; pass value + handler down
  • Context createContext → Provider with memoised value → useContext inside a useXxx hook; for rarely changing data
  • Custom hook name starts with use; shares logic, not state
  • TanStack Query useQuery({queryKey, queryFn}), useMutation + invalidateQueries, staleTime
  • Debug Console first error, DevTools Components/Profiler, Network tab

Practice — React

  1. Counter and toggles. Create a Vite React project. Build a counter with +, − and reset, using functional updates, and a button that shows/hides a panel. Done when clicking + three times in one handler adds 3 and no console warnings appear.
  2. Todo list. Add, toggle and delete todos stored in state with immutable updates, a filter (all/done/pending) derived during render, and ids as keys. Done when you can delete the first item without any text in other rows moving.
  3. Form with validation. Build a registration form (name, email, password, role select, terms checkbox) with controlled inputs, one handleChange, errors under each field and a disabled button while "submitting" (use a fake 1-second promise). Rebuild it with React Hook Form + Zod.
  4. Movie search or expense tracker. Pick one. Movie search: call a public movie API from an effect with a debounced search box, loading/error/empty states, AbortController and results as cards. Expense tracker: add/edit/delete expenses, totals by category derived in render, persisted with a useLocalStorage hook. Done when a fast typist never sees stale results.
  5. Add routing and Context. Extend that app with React Router: a list page, a detail page (/:id), a 404 page, a shared layout with NavLinks, and filters in search params. Add a ThemeContext (light/dark) and a favourites list in Context.
  6. Rebuild the Module 4 apps. Take your DOM and async apps from Module 4 (for example the weather or GitHub-user search) and rebuild them in React with routing. Compare how many lines handle "update the screen".
  7. Custom hooks. Write and use useFetch, useDebounce and useLocalStorage. Open StrictMode's double effect in the Network tab and prove your cleanup works.
  8. Switch to TanStack Query. Replace a hand-written fetch with useQuery, add a create form with useMutation and invalidateQueries. Done when the list updates after saving without a manual refetch.
  9. Break and debug on purpose. Trigger "Each child in a list should have a unique key", "Too many re-renders", and "Objects are not valid as a React child". Find each in the Console and fix it. Record a Profiler session and find one avoidable re-render.

Connecting React to your Spring Boot API

12 topics · about 2 h of reading

A React app on its own only shows data you typed into it. A real full-stack app talks to a backend: the browser loads your React files, then your JavaScript calls a Spring Boot REST API, which reads and writes PostgreSQL. This module is the glue between Module 5 and the Spring Boot work in Spring Boot · Module 4. Most real-world bugs for a new full-stack developer live here: a CORS error, a 401 on every request, a token that disappears on refresh, a validation message that never shows up.

You will build the whole path: an API client with the JWT attached, the CORS configuration on both sides, login and protected routes, forms that show backend errors, environment variables per environment, and a production build. Then you will put it all into one small project.

  • Draw the request path from browser to database and back.
  • Call your API with a configured Axios instance or a small fetch wrapper.
  • Explain CORS and preflight, read a CORS error, and fix it in Spring Boot or with the Vite proxy.
  • Implement JWT login with an AuthContext, restore the session on reload and handle expired tokens (401).
  • Build protected and role-based routes, and explain why the backend must still check roles.
  • Show loading, error, empty and paginated data, and map Spring's field errors onto form fields.
  • Use environment variables, build for production and deploy the static files.

The full-stack architecture and the request cycle

The browser downloads static React files once, then your JavaScript sends JSON requests to the Spring Boot API, which talks to PostgreSQL; the React app and the API are two separate programs, often on two different origins.

The pieces

  1. The page load. The user opens https://crm.example.com. A static host (Nginx, Vercel, Netlify, S3 + CDN) returns index.html and the JS and CSS files that npm run build produced. No Java runs here.
  2. React starts. The JavaScript runs in the browser, renders the first screen, and the router shows the page for the URL.
  3. API call. A component (or a query) calls https://api.example.com/api/employees with fetch or Axios, adding Authorization: Bearer <jwt>.
  4. Spring Boot. Security filters check the token, the controller calls the service, the repository runs SQL on PostgreSQL, and the result is serialised to JSON by Jackson.
  5. Response. The browser receives JSON, your code calls setState (or the query cache updates) and React re-renders.

Two origins, two deployments

In development you run two servers: Vite on http://localhost:5173 and Spring Boot on http://localhost:8080. These are different origins (different ports), and browsers apply the same-origin policy to scripts that call other origins. That is why CORS (next article) is the first thing that goes wrong. In production you choose between three layouts:

LayoutHowCORS needed?
Separate hostsUI on Vercel/Netlify/S3, API on its own domain or cloud serverYes
Reverse proxy, one domainNginx serves / from dist/ and forwards /api to Spring BootNo (same origin)
Bundled in the JARCopy dist/ into Spring Boot's static folderNo, but UI and API deploy together

The contract between the two sides

The frontend and backend agree on a contract: URLs, methods, JSON field names, status codes and the error format. Keep a short list of it (or an OpenAPI document from springdoc) and let the Java record DTOs drive the JavaScript object shapes. Typical mapping:

public record EmployeeResponse(Long id, String name, String email,
                               String department, BigDecimal salary, LocalDate joinedOn) {}
{
  "id": 7,
  "name": "Asha Rao",
  "email": "asha@corp.in",
  "department": "ENGINEERING",
  "salary": 85000.00,
  "joinedOn": "2024-06-03"
}

Things that trip people up in the JSON contract

  • Dates arrive as strings ("2024-06-03"). Convert with new Date(...) only when you need date maths or formatting.
  • Long ids above 253 lose precision in JavaScript numbers. Normal auto-increment ids are fine; send very large ids as strings.
  • BigDecimal becomes a JSON number; use integer paise or a string for money you calculate with.
  • Spring's default pagination response (Page) has content, totalElements, totalPages, number and size fields, plus flags such as first and last; the exact shape depends on your Spring Data version and whether you wrap it in your own DTO. Check the real response in the Network tab.

Conventions

  • Prefix all API routes with /api so a proxy or Nginx can tell them apart from frontend routes.
  • The frontend stores the API base URL in one place (an environment variable), never repeated in components.
  • All API calls go through one module (src/lib/apiClient.js). Components do not call fetch with full URLs.

Interview: "Walk me through what happens when a user opens the page and clicks Login"

  • Static files load from the host; React boots in the browser (SPA).
  • The login form POSTs credentials as JSON to the API (a cross-origin request, so CORS applies).
  • Spring Security authenticates, returns a JWT; the app stores it and attaches it to later requests.
  • Each API response is JSON that updates React state; the backend remains the authority for security and validation.

Calling your API: an Axios instance or a fetch wrapper

Create one configured HTTP client (base URL from an env variable, JSON headers, a request interceptor that adds the JWT, a response interceptor that handles 401) and use it everywhere; Axios gives this almost for free, and a 40-line fetch wrapper does the same.

Why a single client

Without one, every component repeats the base URL, the headers, the token, the res.ok check and the error parsing. One mistake or change then needs fifty edits. A central client makes four things happen automatically: the right base URL, the Authorization header, a consistent error shape, and one place to react to "401, token expired".

Axios

Axios is a popular HTTP client library. Install it with npm install axios. Compared with fetch, it parses JSON for you, throws on 4xx and 5xx responses, supports timeouts, and has interceptors: functions that run on every request or response.

import axios from 'axios';
import { tokenStore } from './tokenStore.js';

export const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,       // e.g. http://localhost:8080/api
  timeout: 10_000,                              // fail after 10 s instead of hanging
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
});

// Request interceptor: runs before every request
api.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = tokenStore.get();
  if (token) {
    config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }
  return config;
});

// Response interceptor: runs for every response
api.interceptors.response.use(
  (response) => response,                      // 2xx: pass through
