  (error) => {
    if (error.response?.status === 401 && !error.config.url.includes('/auth/')) {
      tokenStore.clear();                       // token invalid or expired
      window.dispatchEvent(new Event('auth:logout'));   // AuthContext listens for this
    }
    return Promise.reject(error);               // let the caller handle other errors
  },
);
import { api } from '../../lib/axios.js';

export const employeeApi = {
  list: (params) => api.get('/employees', { params }).then((r) => r.data),
  get: (id) => api.get(`/employees/${id}`).then((r) => r.data),
  create: (body) => api.post('/employees', body).then((r) => r.data),
  update: (id, body) => api.put(`/employees/${id}`, body).then((r) => r.data),
  remove: (id) => api.delete(`/employees/${id}`),
};

// employeeApi.list({ page: 0, size: 10, sort: 'name,asc' })
// -> GET /api/employees?page=0&size=10&sort=name%2Casc

Telling error kinds apart

An Axios error has different fields depending on what failed. This distinction decides what you show the user.

export function describeError(error) {
  if (error.response) {
    // The server answered with 4xx or 5xx
    const { status, data } = error.response;
    if (status === 401) return 'Your session has expired. Please log in again.';
    if (status === 403) return 'You do not have permission to do this.';
    if (status === 404) return 'Not found.';
    if (status >= 500) return 'Server error. Please try again later.';
    return data?.detail ?? data?.message ?? `Request failed (${status}).`;
  }
  if (error.request) {
    // The request was sent but no response arrived: server down, offline, or CORS blocked
    return 'Cannot reach the server. Check your connection.';
  }
  return error.message;                          // something broke before sending
}
KindAxios signTypical causeUI
Network errorerror.response is undefined; code ERR_NETWORKAPI down, offline, CORS block, wrong URL"Cannot reach server", retry button
Timeoutcode ECONNABORTEDSlow serverRetry message
4xxerror.response.status 400/401/403/404/409/422Your request is wrong or not allowedField errors, login redirect, "not found"
5xxstatus 500+Bug or outage in the backendGeneric error, log it

The same with fetch

fetch needs no library. The cost is that you write the wrapper yourself: it does not throw on HTTP errors, does not parse JSON automatically, has no built-in timeout, and has no interceptors. This wrapper adds all of them (this is the apiClient idea from Module 4, grown up).

import { tokenStore } from './tokenStore.js';

const BASE_URL = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;

export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(status, body) {
    super(body?.detail ?? body?.message ?? `HTTP ${status}`);
    this.status = status;
    this.body = body;            // keep the whole Spring ProblemDetail for field errors
  }
}

async function request(path, { method = 'GET', body, params, signal } = {}) {
  const url = new URL(BASE_URL + path, window.location.origin);
  if (params) Object.entries(params).forEach(([k, v]) => url.searchParams.set(k, v));

  const headers = { Accept: 'application/json' };
  if (body !== undefined) headers['Content-Type'] = 'application/json';
  const token = tokenStore.get();
  if (token) headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;

  const timeout = AbortSignal.timeout(10_000);   // built-in timeout signal
  const res = await fetch(url, {
    method,
    headers,
    body: body !== undefined ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
    signal: signal ? AbortSignal.any([signal, timeout]) : timeout,
  });

  if (res.status === 204) return null;           // No Content (typical for DELETE)
  const data = await res.json().catch(() => null);

  if (!res.ok) {
    if (res.status === 401 && !path.startsWith('/auth/')) {
      tokenStore.clear();
      window.dispatchEvent(new Event('auth:logout'));
    }
    throw new ApiError(res.status, data);
  }
  return data;
}

export const apiClient = {
  get: (path, opts) => request(path, opts),
  post: (path, body, opts) => request(path, { ...opts, method: 'POST', body }),
  put: (path, body, opts) => request(path, { ...opts, method: 'PUT', body }),
  delete: (path, opts) => request(path, { ...opts, method: 'DELETE' }),
};

Both versions expect a tiny token helper, shown here with an in-memory store. The JWT article explains where the token should live.

let accessToken = null;               // lives in memory only

export const tokenStore = {
  get: () => accessToken,
  set: (token) => { accessToken = token; },
  clear: () => { accessToken = null; },
};

Axios vs fetch

AspectAxiosfetch
Installationnpm install axios (adds bundle size)Built into browsers and Node 18+
JSON body and responseAutomaticManual JSON.stringify and res.json()
4xx / 5xxRejects the promiseResolves; you check res.ok
Timeouttimeout optionAbortSignal.timeout(ms)
InterceptorsBuilt inWrite a wrapper
Query paramsparams optionURLSearchParams manually
Upload / download progressSupportedUpload progress not available in the standard API
Cancel a requestsignal (AbortController) is supportedsignal

Which one should you pick?

Either is fine; consistency matters more. Many Spring Boot teams use Axios because interceptors make JWT handling short. If you use TanStack Query, both work as the queryFn. Do not mix them in the same project. The rest of this module uses Axios (api) in most examples and shows the fetch equivalent where it differs.

Common mistakes

  • Hard-coding http://localhost:8080 in components; it breaks in staging and production.
  • Treating fetch 404/500 as success because the promise resolved.
  • Redirecting to login on every 401, including the 401 of a wrong password on the login request, which clears the error message. Skip the interceptor for auth endpoints.
  • Logging the Authorization header or token to the console or an error tracker.
  • Sending Content-Type: application/json with a FormData body; leave the header off and let the browser set the multipart boundary.

Interview: "Axios vs fetch? What are interceptors?"

  • Both use promises. Axios adds automatic JSON, rejection on non-2xx, timeouts and interceptors; fetch is native and needs a wrapper for the same behaviour.
  • Interceptors are hooks on every request/response: add the bearer token on the way out; handle 401 (logout or refresh) on the way back.
  • Keep one configured client so base URL, auth and error handling live in one place.

CORS end to end: why the browser blocks your request and how to fix it

CORS is a browser rule: a page may read a response from another origin only if that server's headers allow it; fix it by allowing your frontend's origin in Spring Boot (or avoid it in development with the Vite proxy), and remember CORS does not protect your API.

The error you will meet first

You call http://localhost:8080/api/employees from a React app on http://localhost:5173. The API works in Postman, but the browser Console shows:

Access to XMLHttpRequest at 'http://localhost:8080/api/employees' from origin
'http://localhost:5173' has been blocked by CORS policy: No
'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.

Postman works because CORS is enforced by browsers, not by servers. Your Spring Boot code probably ran fine and returned data; the browser then refused to hand the response to your JavaScript.

What an origin is

An origin is the combination of scheme + host + port. Two URLs are the same origin only if all three match.

URL compared with http://localhost:5173Same origin?Why
http://localhost:5173/employeesYesOnly the path differs
http://localhost:8080/apiNoDifferent port
https://localhost:5173NoDifferent scheme
http://127.0.0.1:5173NoDifferent host name
https://api.crm.in vs https://app.crm.inNoDifferent host (subdomain)

The same-origin policy stops a script on one origin from reading data from another, so that a malicious page you visit cannot read your bank's pages using your logged-in session. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the controlled loophole: the server tells the browser, using response headers, which other origins may read its responses.

Simple requests and preflight

For some requests the browser just sends them with an Origin header and checks the response headers. For others, it first sends an OPTIONS "preflight" request to ask permission. A request needs preflight when it is not "simple": a method other than GET, HEAD or POST; or a Content-Type such as application/json; or a custom header such as Authorization. A JSON POST with a JWT therefore always triggers a preflight.

OPTIONS /api/employees HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080
Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type

HTTP/1.1 200
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET,POST,PUT,DELETE,OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization,content-type
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Max-Age: 3600
HeaderDirectionMeaning
OriginRequestWhich origin the calling page is on (set by the browser; you cannot change it)
Access-Control-Allow-OriginResponseThe allowed origin (or * for any, which cannot be combined with credentials)
Access-Control-Allow-MethodsResponse to preflightAllowed HTTP methods
Access-Control-Allow-HeadersResponse to preflightAllowed request headers (Authorization, Content-Type)
Access-Control-Allow-CredentialsResponsetrue lets cookies and HTTP auth be sent
Access-Control-Max-AgeResponse to preflightSeconds the browser may cache the preflight result
Access-Control-Expose-HeadersResponseExtra response headers JavaScript may read (such as Location)

The fix in Spring Boot

Option 1, without Spring Security: register CORS mappings in a WebMvcConfigurer.

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.CorsRegistry;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.WebMvcConfigurer;

@Configuration
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    private final String[] allowedOrigins;

    public WebConfig(@Value("${app.cors.allowed-origins}") String[] allowedOrigins) {
        this.allowedOrigins = allowedOrigins;
    }

    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
                .allowedOrigins(allowedOrigins)
                .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS")
                .allowedHeaders("Authorization", "Content-Type")
                .exposedHeaders("Location")
                .maxAge(3600);
    }
}
# application.properties (development)
app.cors.allowed-origins=http://localhost:5173

# application-prod.properties (override per environment)
app.cors.allowed-origins=https://crm.example.com

Option 2, with Spring Security (the case for any JWT API). The Security filter chain runs before Spring MVC, so a preflight request with no Authorization header would be rejected with 401 before MVC's CORS mapping is ever consulted. You must configure CORS in the security chain, using a CorsConfigurationSource bean.

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.web.cors.CorsConfiguration;
import org.springframework.web.cors.CorsConfigurationSource;
import org.springframework.web.cors.UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource;

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())          // uses the CorsConfigurationSource bean
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())             // OK for a stateless Bearer-token API
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.OPTIONS, "/**").permitAll()   // preflight
                .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated());
        // ... JWT filter, session policy STATELESS, etc. (see the Spring Boot page)
        return http.build();
    }

    @Bean
    CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource(
            @Value("${app.cors.allowed-origins}") List<String> origins) {
        CorsConfiguration config = new CorsConfiguration();
        config.setAllowedOrigins(origins);
        config.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
        config.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type"));
        config.setExposedHeaders(List.of("Location"));
        config.setAllowCredentials(true);            // needed only for cookie-based auth
        config.setMaxAge(3600L);

        UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
        source.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", config);
        return source;
    }
}

Rules of thumb for the Java side:

  • List the exact origins (scheme + host + port, no trailing slash). The origin http://localhost:5173/ with a trailing slash never matches.
  • allowedOrigins("*") together with allowCredentials(true) is rejected by Spring (and by browsers). With credentials you must name origins explicitly, or use allowedOriginPatterns.
  • Read origins from properties, so development, staging and production differ without code changes.
  • If Spring Security is present and you only added addCorsMappings, preflights fail with 401/403. Always use .cors(...) in the security chain.
  • A controller-level @CrossOrigin(origins = "...") exists for quick tests, but a central configuration is cleaner.

The Vite dev proxy: avoiding CORS in development

Instead of allowing another origin, make the browser think the API is on the same origin. Vite's dev server can forward requests: the browser calls http://localhost:5173/api/... (same origin, so no CORS), and Vite passes them on to Spring Boot on port 8080 server-to-server, where CORS does not apply.

import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  server: {
    proxy: {
      '/api': {
        target: 'http://localhost:8080',
        changeOrigin: true,        // sets the Host header to the target
      },
    },
  },
});
# With the proxy, use a relative base URL
VITE_API_URL=/api

The proxy works only with npm run dev; npm run build output has no proxy. In production use Nginx to proxy /api the same way (see deployment), or set the full API URL and configure CORS properly. Many teams do both: proxy in development, CORS or Nginx in production.

Reading a CORS problem in DevTools

  1. Open the Network tab. Find the failed request; a preflight shows as a separate OPTIONS line.
  2. If the OPTIONS response is 401/403/404, the server rejected the preflight (Spring Security not configured for CORS, or the path is not permitted).
  3. If it is 200 but the Console still complains, compare the response headers with the message: "origin not allowed" means a wrong or missing Allow-Origin; "header not allowed" means Allow-Headers misses Authorization or Content-Type; "method not allowed" means Allow-Methods misses PUT or DELETE.
  4. Test the API without the browser (Postman, curl). If it works there, the problem is CORS, not your controller.

Edge cases

  • A 500 error from the controller can also look like a CORS error: error responses created before the CORS filter applies may lack the headers, and the browser reports only "CORS". Check the server log and the Network tab response.
  • A wrong URL or the server not running also gives "Failed to fetch" / ERR_NETWORK, with no HTTP status. Do not assume CORS every time.
  • Cookies across origins need withCredentials: true (Axios) or credentials: 'include' (fetch) on the client and Allow-Credentials: true plus an explicit origin on the server, and SameSite/Secure cookie settings that allow cross-site use.
  • Multiple CORS configurations (a @CrossOrigin, a gateway, and Nginx all adding headers) can produce duplicate Access-Control-Allow-Origin values, which browsers reject. Configure CORS in exactly one layer.

CORS is not security for your API

CORS only tells browsers what scripts may read. curl, Postman, scripts and other servers ignore it completely, so anyone can still call your API. Real protection is authentication, authorisation and validation on the server (Spring Security). Allow your real frontend origins only, and never reflect any origin back automatically.

Interview: "What is CORS? What is a preflight? How did you fix it?"

  • Origin = scheme + host + port. Browsers block scripts from reading cross-origin responses unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin (same-origin policy plus CORS).
  • Non-simple requests (JSON, Authorization, PUT/DELETE) trigger an OPTIONS preflight asking for allowed methods and headers.
  • Spring fix: CorsConfigurationSource bean plus .cors() in the security chain (or addCorsMappings without Security); origins from properties.
  • In dev, the Vite proxy removes the need. CORS is browser-only and is not an API security mechanism.

JWT login end to end: storing the token and handling 401

The login form POSTs credentials, Spring Boot returns a JWT, the app keeps it (best: in memory, with a refresh token in an httpOnly cookie), attaches it as Authorization: Bearer to every request, and reacts to 401 by refreshing or logging out.

The flow

The backend side (generating and verifying the JWT, the security filter) is covered in Spring Boot · Module 4. Here is the frontend's half of the same conversation.

  1. Login request. Send { email, password } over HTTPS to a public endpoint such as POST /api/auth/login.
  2. Token response. The backend returns the JWT (and user info: id, name, roles). A JWT is a signed string of three base64 parts: header, payload (claims such as sub, roles, exp) and signature. The payload is readable by anyone, so never put secrets in it.
  3. Store. Keep the token somewhere the next requests can read it (see the trade-offs below).
  4. Attach. A request interceptor adds Authorization: Bearer <token> to each call.
  5. Verify. Spring's JWT filter checks the signature and expiry on each request (the server stays stateless).
  6. Expiry. When exp passes, the API answers 401. The client either gets a new token with a refresh token, or sends the user back to the login page.

Where to store the token

This is a security decision, and a favourite interview question. The two attacks to know: XSS (cross-site scripting: attacker JavaScript runs on your page and can read anything JavaScript can read) and CSRF (cross-site request forgery: another site makes the browser send a request that carries your cookies automatically).

StorageXSS riskCSRF riskSurvives reload?
localStorageHigh: any script can read the tokenNone (not sent automatically)Yes
sessionStorageHigh, same as aboveNonePer tab only
JavaScript memory (a variable)Lower: the token is not in a place scripts can scrape later, but running malicious code can still use itNoneNo; needs a refresh to restore
httpOnly cookieJavaScript cannot read it, so it cannot be stolen by XSS (it can still be used by injected code to make requests)Yes: you need SameSite and/or CSRF tokensYes

The recommended pattern

  • Keep the short-lived access token (say 15 minutes) in memory.
  • Keep a long-lived refresh token in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, scoped to the refresh endpoint (POST /api/auth/refresh).
  • On page load, call the refresh endpoint: if the cookie is valid you get a new access token and the session is restored. A reload therefore does not log the user out.
  • Use CSRF protection on the refresh endpoint (SameSite=Strict/Lax plus a check) since it relies on a cookie.

localStorage is simple and very common in tutorials and small projects, and many employers accept it, but you should be able to explain its XSS weakness. For learning projects it is acceptable; say so honestly in an interview.

Backend endpoints the frontend expects

EndpointRequestResponse
POST /api/auth/login{ email, password }200 { accessToken, user } (+ Set-Cookie refresh)
POST /api/auth/refreshCookie only200 { accessToken, user } or 401
POST /api/auth/logoutCookie204 and the cookie cleared
GET /api/meBearer token200 { id, name, email, roles }
 
public record LoginRequest(@NotBlank @Email String email, @NotBlank String password) {}
public record UserDto(Long id, String name, String email, List<String> roles) {}
public record AuthResponse(String accessToken, UserDto user) {}

@PostMapping("/api/auth/login")
public AuthResponse login(@Valid @RequestBody LoginRequest request) {
    // authenticate, then: String jwt = jwtService.generate(user);
    return new AuthResponse(jwt, userDto);
}

AuthContext: login, logout and the current user

The Context pattern fits auth well: the user changes rarely and many components need it. The provider exposes user, isLoading, login and logout, and restores the session when the app starts.

import { createContext, useCallback, useContext, useEffect, useMemo, useState } from 'react';
import { api } from '../lib/axios.js';
import { tokenStore } from '../lib/tokenStore.js';

const AuthContext = createContext(null);

export function AuthProvider({ children }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(true);    // true until we know if a session exists

  // Restore the session on page load: the refresh cookie gives us a new access token
  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false;
    api.post('/auth/refresh', null, { withCredentials: true })
      .then(({ data }) => {
        if (ignore) return;
        tokenStore.set(data.accessToken);
        setUser(data.user);
      })
      .catch(() => { /* no valid session: user stays null */ })
      .finally(() => { if (!ignore) setIsLoading(false); });
    return () => { ignore = true; };
  }, []);

  // The 401 interceptor fires this event when the token is rejected
  useEffect(() => {
    const onForcedLogout = () => setUser(null);
    window.addEventListener('auth:logout', onForcedLogout);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('auth:logout', onForcedLogout);
  }, []);

  const login = useCallback(async (email, password) => {
    const { data } = await api.post('/auth/login', { email, password }, { withCredentials: true });
    tokenStore.set(data.accessToken);
    setUser(data.user);
    return data.user;
  }, []);

  const logout = useCallback(async () => {
    try {
      await api.post('/auth/logout', null, { withCredentials: true });
    } finally {
      tokenStore.clear();
      setUser(null);
    }
  }, []);

  const value = useMemo(
    () => ({ user, isLoading, isAuthenticated: user !== null, login, logout }),
    [user, isLoading, login, logout],
  );
  return <AuthContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</AuthContext.Provider>;
}

export function useAuth() {
  const ctx = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useAuth must be used inside AuthProvider');
  return ctx;
}

The simpler variant, with localStorage and no refresh cookie, replaces the first effect with reading the stored token and calling GET /api/me to load the user:

const KEY = 'access_token';

export const tokenStore = {
  get: () => localStorage.getItem(KEY),
  set: (token) => localStorage.setItem(KEY, token),
  clear: () => localStorage.removeItem(KEY),
};

// In AuthProvider's restore effect:
//   if (!tokenStore.get()) { setIsLoading(false); return; }
//   api.get('/me').then(({ data }) => setUser(data)).catch(() => tokenStore.clear())
//      .finally(() => setIsLoading(false));

The login page

import { useState } from 'react';
import { Navigate, useLocation, useNavigate } from 'react-router';
import { useAuth } from '../context/AuthContext.jsx';
import { describeError } from '../lib/errors.js';

function LoginPage() {
  const { login, isAuthenticated } = useAuth();
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const location = useLocation();
  const from = location.state?.from?.pathname ?? '/employees';   // where the user wanted to go

  const [form, setForm] = useState({ email: '', password: '' });
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);

  if (isAuthenticated) return <Navigate to={from} replace />;

  async function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    setSubmitting(true);
    setError(null);
    try {
      await login(form.email, form.password);
      navigate(from, { replace: true });             // do not leave /login in history
    } catch (err) {
      setError(err.response?.status === 401 ? 'Wrong email or password' : describeError(err));
    } finally {
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <h1>Login</h1>
      <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
      <input id="email" type="email" autoComplete="username" required value={form.email}
             onChange={(e) => setForm({ ...form, email: e.target.value })} />
      <label htmlFor="password">Password</label>
      <input id="password" type="password" autoComplete="current-password" required
             value={form.password}
             onChange={(e) => setForm({ ...form, password: e.target.value })} />
      {error && <p role="alert" className="error">{error}</p>}
      <button disabled={submitting}>{submitting ? 'Signing in…' : 'Login'}</button>
    </form>
  );
}

export default LoginPage;

Handling 401 and 403

StatusMeaningFrontend reaction
401 UnauthorizedNot authenticated: no token, bad token, expired tokenRefresh the token once and retry; if that fails, clear the session and go to /login
403 ForbiddenAuthenticated but not allowedShow "You do not have access"; do not log out

To refresh and retry transparently, extend the response interceptor. Share one refresh promise so that ten simultaneous 401 responses trigger only one refresh call.

let refreshPromise = null;

api.interceptors.response.use(
  (res) => res,
  async (error) => {
    const original = error.config;
    const isAuthCall = original?.url?.includes('/auth/');

    if (error.response?.status === 401 && !original._retry && !isAuthCall) {
      original._retry = true;                           // retry each request only once
      try {
        refreshPromise ??= api.post('/auth/refresh', null, { withCredentials: true })
          .then(({ data }) => { tokenStore.set(data.accessToken); return data.accessToken; })
          .finally(() => { refreshPromise = null; });
        const newToken = await refreshPromise;
        original.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${newToken}`;
        return api(original);                           // repeat the failed request
      } catch {
        tokenStore.clear();
        window.dispatchEvent(new Event('auth:logout'));
      }
    }
    return Promise.reject(error);
  },
);

Rules

  • Use HTTPS in production; a JWT sent over HTTP can be stolen on the network.
  • Keep access tokens short-lived. A JWT cannot be revoked before exp unless the server keeps a deny list.
  • Never put passwords, personal data or secrets in the JWT payload; it is only encoded, not encrypted.
  • Never trust client-side checks of the JWT (decoding exp or roles) for security; they are for convenience. The server verifies every request.
  • Do not log tokens. Never commit real tokens to Git.

Common mistakes

  • Sending the token as Authorization: token or Bearer: token. The format is Authorization: Bearer <token> with a space.
  • Calling the app logged out after refresh because the token lived only in a variable and there is no refresh step.
  • Handling 401 on the login request itself (redirect loop or lost message).
  • A refresh interceptor that retries forever; use a _retry flag and exclude auth endpoints.
  • Forgetting withCredentials / CORS credentials settings when using cookies, so the browser silently drops the cookie.

Interview: "Explain the JWT login flow and where you store the token"

  • Login POST → server verifies the password → returns signed JWT → client sends it as a Bearer header → server verifies the signature and expiry on every request (stateless).
  • localStorage: easy but XSS-readable. httpOnly cookie: safe from XSS theft but needs CSRF defence. Best practice: access token in memory plus refresh token in an httpOnly cookie.
  • 401 means not authenticated (refresh or re-login); 403 means authenticated but forbidden.
  • On reload, restore the session by calling refresh (or /me with a stored token).

Protected routes and role-based UI

A RequireAuth route wrapper redirects anonymous users to /login and remembers where they wanted to go; role checks hide UI and pages from the wrong users, but only the backend can truly enforce access.

The idea: three layers of access control

"Who can see what" is decided in three places, and each has a different job. The browser layers exist for a good user experience; only the last one is security.

LayerExamplePurposeTrusted?
Route guardRequireAuth around /employeesSend anonymous users to loginNo (UX only)
UI hidingHasRole around a Delete buttonDo not show actions that will failNo (UX only)
API authorisation@PreAuthorize, 401/403Actually protect data and actionsYes

RequireAuth

A protected route renders its page only for a logged-in user. The component checks the auth context (see the AuthContext); while the session is still being restored on page load it shows a loading state (otherwise a logged-in user would be bounced to the login page on every refresh); if there is no user it redirects with <Navigate>, saving the current location in route state so that the login page can send the user back afterwards.

import { Navigate, Outlet, useLocation } from 'react-router';
import { useAuth } from '../context/AuthContext.jsx';

function RequireAuth({ roles }) {
  const { user, isLoading } = useAuth();
  const location = useLocation();

  if (isLoading) return <p>Checking your session…</p>;          // do not redirect too early

  if (!user) {
    // Remember the page they wanted; replace so Back does not return to a blocked page
    return <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location }} />;
  }

  if (roles && !roles.some((r) => user.roles.includes(r))) {
    return <Navigate to="/forbidden" replace />;                // logged in, wrong role
  }

  return <Outlet />;                                            // render the child routes
}

export default RequireAuth;
function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/login" element={<LoginPage />} />
      <Route path="/forbidden" element={<ForbiddenPage />} />

      {/* Every route inside needs a logged-in user */}
      <Route element={<RequireAuth />}>
        <Route element={<Layout />}>
          <Route index element={<DashboardPage />} />
          <Route path="employees" element={<EmployeeListPage />} />
          <Route path="employees/:id" element={<EmployeeDetailPage />} />
        </Route>
      </Route>

      {/* Only ADMIN users */}
      <Route element={<RequireAuth roles={['ADMIN']} />}>
        <Route element={<Layout />}>
          <Route path="admin/users" element={<UserAdminPage />} />
        </Route>
      </Route>

      <Route path="*" element={<NotFoundPage />} />
    </Routes>
  );
}

Because RequireAuth renders an <Outlet />, it works as a layout route (a route with no path): one guard protects a whole group of pages. This is cleaner than wrapping each page in its own guard component. The guard is also a normal component, so it re-renders whenever the auth context changes; when the user logs out, it redirects by itself, with no extra code.

Sending the user back after login

The guard saved state.from. The login page reads it with useLocation, and after a successful login navigates to that path instead of always going to the dashboard. It also redirects away if the user is already signed in.

import { Navigate, useLocation, useNavigate } from 'react-router';
import { useAuth } from '../context/AuthContext.jsx';

function LoginPage() {
  const { user, login } = useAuth();
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const location = useLocation();

  // Same-app path only; fall back to the home page
  const from = location.state?.from?.pathname ?? '/';

  if (user) return <Navigate to={from} replace />;       // already signed in

  async function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const form = new FormData(e.currentTarget);
    const res = await fetch('/api/auth/login', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(Object.fromEntries(form)),
      credentials: 'include',
    });
    if (res.ok) {
      login(await res.json());                 // sets the user in AuthContext
      navigate(from, { replace: true });       // back to /employees/7
    }
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input name="email" type="email" required />
      <input name="password" type="password" required />
      <button>Login</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Roles in the UI

Hide buttons and menu items the user cannot use. A small helper keeps the check readable:

import { useAuth } from '../context/AuthContext.jsx';

export function useHasRole(...roles) {
  const { user } = useAuth();
  return Boolean(user) && roles.some((r) => user.roles.includes(r));
}

export function HasRole({ roles, children, fallback = null }) {
  const allowed = useHasRole(...roles);
  return allowed ? children : fallback;
}

// Use
// <HasRole roles={['ADMIN', 'HR']}><button onClick={onDelete}>Delete</button></HasRole>

The same hook can build a menu from a list, so the sidebar and the route table never disagree:

const NAV = [
  { to: '/employees', label: 'Employees', roles: ['USER', 'HR', 'ADMIN'] },
  { to: '/payroll', label: 'Payroll', roles: ['HR', 'ADMIN'] },
  { to: '/admin/users', label: 'Users', roles: ['ADMIN'] },
];

function Sidebar() {
  const { user } = useAuth();
  const items = NAV.filter((n) => n.roles.some((r) => user.roles.includes(r)));
  return (
    <nav>
      {items.map((n) => (
        <NavLink key={n.to} to={n.to}>{n.label}</NavLink>
      ))}
    </nav>
  );
}

Rule: frontend checks are for experience, the backend enforces security

Everything in the browser can be changed by the user: they can edit JavaScript, flip user.roles in DevTools, or call your API with curl. A hidden delete button does not stop DELETE /api/employees/7. Every endpoint must check authentication and authorisation itself — @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") or requestMatchers rules in Spring Security (Spring Boot · Module 4). The server must answer 403 for a forbidden call, and the UI should handle that 403 gracefully.

Wrong: the role check exists only in React

@DeleteMapping("/api/employees/{id}")
public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    employeeService.delete(id);      // any logged-in user, or anyone with curl, can call this
}

Right: the server checks the role too

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
@DeleteMapping("/api/employees/{id}")
public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    employeeService.delete(id);      // others get 403 Forbidden
}

Handling 401 and 403 in the UI

The two status codes mean different things, and your Axios interceptor or fetch wrapper (see Calling your API) should treat them differently.

StatusMeaningUI reaction
401 UnauthorizedNot logged in, or the token expiredClear the user in context; the guard redirects to login
403 ForbiddenLogged in, but not allowedShow "You do not have access" or a toast; keep the user logged in

Mistake: trusting a role stored in the browser

Reading the role from localStorage (localStorage.getItem('role')) and deciding access from it is the most common beginner error. The user can type localStorage.setItem('role', 'ADMIN') and see the admin pages. Take the roles from the server response (/me or the decoded token), and remember that even those only change what is shown. Another version: decoding the JWT in the browser and trusting its roles claim for anything beyond display. The backend verifies the signature; the browser cannot.

Role names must match the backend

Spring's hasRole('ADMIN') checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN. Decide whether your /me response sends ADMIN or ROLE_ADMIN and be consistent in the frontend comparisons. A typo here causes "I am admin but see nothing". Keep the role names in one constants file (roles.js) instead of repeating string literals.

Conventions

  • Use a layout route with <Outlet /> for guards instead of wrapping every page.
  • Keep user, isLoading, login, logout in one AuthContext and expose it through a useAuth hook.
  • Check permissions rather than raw roles when the rules grow (can('employee:delete') instead of roles.includes('ADMIN')), so changing which role may do what touches one place.
  • Always give a 403 page and a 404 page their own routes.

Edge cases

  • Flash of login: skipping the isLoading branch redirects logged-in users to the login page for a moment (or permanently) on every refresh.
  • Deep links: a user opening /employees/7 while logged out should land on login, then come back to /employees/7; that is what state.from does. Only use same-app paths from the state, never a full URL from a query string, to avoid open-redirect bugs.
  • When the token expires while the user is on a page, the interceptor fires logout, the context sets user to null, and RequireAuth re-renders into the redirect — you get this for free with the event pattern.
  • Multiple tabs: logging out in one tab does not update the others unless you listen to the storage event or use BroadcastChannel.
  • Redirecting an already logged-in user away from /login (as in the login page above) avoids showing the form to signed-in users.
  • Roles can change on the server while the user is logged in. Re-fetch /me after important actions or on a timer; a stale role in the UI is harmless for security (the API still decides) but confusing.
  • A route guard hides a page only after the JavaScript bundle is downloaded. The code of an admin page is still visible to anyone who opens the files, so never put secrets or hidden endpoints' keys in it.

In real projects

A common setup: Spring Security issues a JWT or session cookie at login; /api/auth/me returns { id, name, roles }; AuthProvider calls it once on load; a single RequireAuth layout wraps all private pages and another with roles wraps admin pages; buttons use HasRole. Tests then check the important part separately: that the API returns 401 and 403 correctly without any React in front of it.

Interview: "How do you implement protected routes? Is hiding a button enough?"

  • A wrapper/layout route reads auth state; shows a loader while restoring the session; redirects with <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from }} /> if anonymous; renders <Outlet /> otherwise. Role checks add an allowed-roles prop.
  • Not enough: the client is untrusted. The API must enforce authentication and roles on every endpoint (401/403), and the UI only mirrors that for usability.
  • Explain 401 vs 403, and why the loading state avoids a redirect flash.
  • Where does the role come from, and can the user fake it? It comes from the server; the user can fake what the browser shows, never what the server allows.

Loading and error states: network vs 4xx vs 5xx, spinners, toasts

Every API call can be loading, succeeded, empty or failed; a good UI shows a clear face for each, tells a network failure apart from a 4xx (your request was wrong) and a 5xx (the server broke), and never leaves the user staring at a spinner or a blank page.

The states of one request

When a component asks the Spring Boot API for data, the screen is in one of four situations. Beginners code only the happy one. Real apps handle all four:

  • Loading: the request is in flight. Show a spinner or a skeleton.
  • Error: the request failed. Say what happened and offer a way forward (retry, go back, log in again).
  • Empty: the request worked but the list has zero items. This is not an error. Show "No employees yet" and a button to add one.
  • Data: the normal screen.

Not all errors are the same

The first question is: did the server answer at all? With Axios, a failed call throws an error. If the server answered with a status such as 404 or 500, error.response exists. If the request never got an answer (server down, no internet, CORS block, timeout), error.response is undefined. That single check splits "network problem" from "server answered with a problem".

KindWhat it meansWhat the user should seeRetry?
Network / timeout (no response)Server down, offline, DNS, CORS block, timeout"Cannot reach the server. Check your connection." + Retry buttonYes
400 / 422Your data failed validationField errors next to inputs (see next article)Fix input first
401Not logged in or token expiredHandled by the interceptor: refresh or go to login (JWT flow)After login
403Logged in but not allowed"You do not have access to this."No
404Resource does not exist (deleted, wrong id)"Employee not found" page with a link back to the listNo
409Conflict, for example duplicate emailMessage on the conflicting fieldFix input first
429Too many requests"Slow down, try again in a moment."Later
5xxBug or outage on the server"Something went wrong on our side." + Retry; never show a stack traceYes, a few times

Why the difference matters: retrying a 404 or a 400 is pointless because the same request will fail the same way. Retrying a network blip or a 503 often works. Showing "Server error" when the user simply lost Wi-Fi sends them to the wrong place.

One place to classify errors

Do not scatter err.response?.status === 404 checks across components. Write one helper that turns any thrown value into a small object the UI understands.

import axios from 'axios';

const fail = (kind, status, message, retryable) => ({ kind, status, message, retryable });

export function classifyError(err) {
  if (axios.isCancel(err)) {
    return { kind: 'canceled', status: null, message: '', retryable: false };
  }
  if (!err.response) {                       // the server never answered
    const timeout = err.code === 'ECONNABORTED' || err.code === 'ETIMEDOUT';
    return {
      kind: timeout ? 'timeout' : 'network',
      status: null,
      message: timeout
        ? 'The server took too long to respond. Please try again.'
        : 'Cannot reach the server. Check your internet connection.',
      retryable: true,
    };
  }

  const { status, data } = err.response;
  // Spring Boot ProblemDetail has "detail"; fall back to "message"
  const serverText = typeof data?.detail === 'string' ? data.detail : data?.message;

  if (status === 401) return fail('auth', status, 'Please log in again.', false);
  if (status === 403) return fail('forbidden', status, 'You do not have access to this.', false);
  if (status === 404) return fail('not-found', status, serverText ?? 'Not found.', false);
  if (status === 429) return fail('rate-limit', status, 'Too many requests. Try again soon.', true);
  if (status >= 500) {
    return fail('server', status, 'Something went wrong on our side. Please try again.', true);
  }
  return fail('client', status, serverText ?? 'The request was not accepted.', false);
}

// Short text for banners and toasts
export function describeError(err) {
  return classifyError(err).message;
}

Rule: never show raw server internals

For 5xx responses show your own friendly sentence, not err.message or the response body. Raw text such as "Request failed with status code 500" is meaningless to users, and a leaked stack trace or SQL message helps attackers. Log the details to the console (or an error-tracking tool) instead. Spring Boot should not send stack traces in production responses either.

The loading state, by hand

This is the pattern from the useEffect articles in Module 5, now with a real API call. Three pieces of state and a finally that always clears the loading flag.

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import { api } from '../lib/axios.js';
import { classifyError } from '../lib/errors.js';

function EmployeeListSimple() {
  const [employees, setEmployees] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);
  const [attempt, setAttempt] = useState(0);            // bump to retry

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    setLoading(true);
    setError(null);
    api.get('/employees', { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(({ data }) => setEmployees(data.content))
      .catch((err) => {
        const info = classifyError(err);
        if (info.kind !== 'canceled') setError(info);
      })
      .finally(() => {
        if (!controller.signal.aborted) setLoading(false);
      });
    return () => controller.abort();                   // cleanup: cancel the old request
  }, [attempt]);

  if (loading) return <p>Loading employees…</p>;
  if (error) {
    return (
      <div role="alert">
        <p>{error.message}</p>
        {error.retryable && <button onClick={() => setAttempt((n) => n + 1)}>Try again</button>}
      </div>
    );
  }
  if (employees.length === 0) return <p>No employees yet.</p>;
  return <ul>{employees.map((e) => <li key={e.id}>{e.name}</li>)}</ul>;
}

export default EmployeeListSimple;

This works, but you need the same 25 lines on every page. That is why most teams use TanStack Query (Module 5), which keeps these states for you.

The same with TanStack Query

import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { api } from '../lib/axios.js';
import { QueryState } from '../components/QueryState.jsx';

function EmployeeListQuery() {
  const query = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['employees'],
    queryFn: async () => (await api.get('/employees')).data,
  });

  return (
    <QueryState query={query} isEmpty={query.data?.content.length === 0}>
      <ul>{query.data?.content.map((e) => <li key={e.id}>{e.name}</li>)}</ul>
    </QueryState>
  );
}
import { classifyError } from '../lib/errors.js';
import { Spinner } from './Spinner.jsx';

export function QueryState({ query, isEmpty, emptyMessage = 'Nothing here yet.', skeleton, children }) {
  if (query.isPending) return skeleton ?? <Spinner />;
  if (query.isError) {
    const info = classifyError(query.error);
    return (
      <div role="alert" className="error-box">
        <p>{info.message}</p>
        {info.retryable && <button onClick={() => query.refetch()}>Try again</button>}
      </div>
    );
  }
  if (isEmpty) return <p className="empty">{emptyMessage}</p>;
  return children;
}

Two flags to tell apart: isPending is true only when there is no data yet (first load), while isFetching is true whenever a request runs, including a background refresh. Use isPending for the big spinner and isFetching for a small "refreshing…" indicator, otherwise the screen flashes every time the user returns to the tab.

TanStack Query version names

In TanStack Query v5 the first-load flag is isPending and mutations use isPending too. Older v4 code and many older tutorials use isLoading for this. If a tutorial's code behaves differently, check which major version it targets.

Retries: do not retry what cannot succeed

TanStack Query retries a failed query a few times by default, which is good for network blips and bad for a 404 (the user waits several seconds for a result that will never change). Give it a function that retries only when it makes sense:

import { QueryCache, QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import toast from 'react-hot-toast';
import { classifyError } from './lib/errors.js';

export const queryClient = new QueryClient({
  defaultOptions: {
    queries: {
      staleTime: 30_000,
      retry: (failureCount, error) => classifyError(error).retryable && failureCount < 2,
    },
  },
  queryCache: new QueryCache({
    // Runs once per failed query. Only toast for background refreshes: when data is on screen
    // already, the user would otherwise never learn the refresh failed.
    onError: (error, query) => {
      if (query.state.data !== undefined) toast.error(classifyError(error).message);
    },
  }),
});

Spinners, skeletons and button states

PatternUse it forNotes
SpinnerShort waits of unknown length, small areas, buttonsAdd role="status" and a visually hidden "Loading" text for screen readers
SkeletonPage or list first loadGrey placeholder shapes that match the final layout; avoids layout jump
Disabled button + labelSubmit, delete, any write actionPrevents double submission: "Saving…"
Keep old data visiblePagination, search, refetchDim the table instead of replacing it with a spinner (keepPreviousData)
 
export function SkeletonRows({ rows = 5 }) {
  return (
    <div aria-busy="true" aria-label="Loading employees">
      {Array.from({ length: rows }, (_, i) => (
        <div key={i} className="skeleton skeleton-row" />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}
.skeleton {
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, #e5e7eb 25%, #f3f4f6 37%, #e5e7eb 63%);
  background-size: 400% 100%;
  animation: shimmer 1.4s ease infinite;
  border-radius: 4px;
}
.skeleton-row { height: 2.5rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
@keyframes shimmer {
  0% { background-position: 100% 50%; }
  100% { background-position: 0 50%; }
}

For write actions, disable the button while the request runs. Without this, an impatient user double-clicks "Create" and your API creates two employees.

const mutation = useMutation({ mutationFn: createEmployee });

<button type="submit" disabled={mutation.isPending}>
  {mutation.isPending ? 'Saving…' : 'Save employee'}
</button>

Toasts

A toast is a small message that appears for a few seconds in a corner and then goes away. Use toasts for results of actions that do not have a natural place on the page: "Employee deleted", "Saved", "Could not delete: server error". Do not use them for form validation (errors belong next to the field) or for failures the user must act on (use a visible banner). react-hot-toast and sonner are two popular small libraries; the example below uses react-hot-toast.

// main.jsx: render the container once
import { Toaster } from 'react-hot-toast';
// <Toaster position="top-right" /> next to <App />

// anywhere:
import toast from 'react-hot-toast';

const remove = useMutation({
  mutationFn: (id) => api.delete(`/employees/${id}`),
  onSuccess: () => {
    toast.success('Employee deleted');
    queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['employees'] });
  },
  onError: (err) => toast.error(describeError(err)),
});

Error boundaries: a different kind of error

A bug in a component, such as reading user.name when user is null, throws during rendering and, left alone, blanks the whole page. An error boundary is a component that catches errors thrown while its children render and shows a fallback instead. It does not catch errors in event handlers, async code or fetch/Axios failures; those you handle with try/catch and the patterns above. React supports boundaries only as class components, so most projects use the small react-error-boundary package and wrap the app (or each route) once.

Common mistakes

  • Swallowing errors: .catch(() => {}) or only console.log(err). The user sees an empty list and thinks there is no data.
  • Forgetting finally: setLoading(false) only in .then, so a failed call leaves the spinner forever.
  • Treating empty as error (or the reverse): an empty array is a success.
  • Rendering error.message directly (Axios text like "Network Error").
  • Trusting a 200 status for everything: some APIs return 200 with an error body. Your own Spring Boot API should use proper status codes, and the frontend should rely on them.
  • Toast spam: a toast for every failed refetch plus a banner plus a log. Pick one place per error.

Edge cases

  • A 204 No Content response (typical for DELETE) has no body; data is empty. Do not call data.id on it.
  • A CORS block looks like a network error in JavaScript (no response). Open the Network tab and the console to tell them apart: see CORS.
  • A request cancelled by AbortController throws too; classify it as canceled and show nothing.
  • If the API gateway or Nginx answers with an HTML error page (502, 504), data is a string, not JSON. Read data?.detail safely, as above.

Interview: "How do you handle errors from an API call in React?"

  • Model the states: loading, error, empty, data. Use try/catch/finally or a query library so loading always ends.
  • Separate network errors (no response), 4xx (client; show message or field errors) and 5xx (server; friendly message, retry). Do not retry 4xx.
  • Centralise: an Axios interceptor for 401, one error classifier, a shared QueryState component, toasts for action results, an error boundary for render crashes.

Showing backend validation errors on form fields (ProblemDetail)

When Spring Boot rejects a form with 400, send back a ProblemDetail that includes a field-to-message map; the React form reads that map and shows each message under the right input, so the server stays the single source of truth for rules.

Why the server's validation must reach the screen

Client-side checks (required, a regex, "password at least 8 characters") give instant feedback, but they are only a convenience: anyone can bypass the browser and call your API with curl. The backend therefore validates again with Bean Validation (@NotBlank, @Email, @Positive and so on; see Spring Boot · Module 2). Some rules also exist only on the server, such as "this email is already registered". The frontend must show those messages properly instead of a vague "Request failed".

What Spring Boot sends back

ProblemDetail is Spring's class for the standard error format of RFC 7807 (later RFC 9457), sent with the media type application/problem+json. The standard members are type, title, status, detail and instance. You can add your own members; Spring writes them at the top level of the JSON. The code below returns the field errors in an errors member.

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleValidation(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
        Map<String, String> errors = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().forEach(fe ->
                errors.putIfAbsent(fe.getField(), fe.getDefaultMessage()));

        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
                HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "One or more fields are invalid");
        pd.setTitle("Validation failed");
        pd.setProperty("errors", errors);
        return pd;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(DuplicateEmailException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleDuplicate(DuplicateEmailException ex) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, ex.getMessage());
        pd.setTitle("Duplicate email");
        pd.setProperty("errors", Map.of("email", "This email is already registered"));
        return pd;
    }
}
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "One or more fields are invalid",
  "instance": "/api/employees",
  "errors": {
    "email": "must be a well-formed email address",
    "salary": "must be greater than 0"
  }
}

ProblemDetail in Spring Boot 3.x and 4.x

ProblemDetail arrived with Spring Framework 6 (Boot 3) and is the same idea in Framework 7 (Boot 4). Extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler makes Spring's own MVC exceptions (bad JSON, wrong method, missing parameter) come back as problem details; if you extend it, override handleMethodArgumentNotValid instead of adding a second @ExceptionHandler for the same exception (two handlers for the same exception cause an ambiguity error at startup). Boot also has a property to switch problem details on for the default handling; check the reference for your exact version. The errors member is a convention of this project, not part of the standard, so agree on it with the backend developer (probably you).

Reading the response in React

Add a helper next to classifyError that returns a plain object from field name to message. It returns an empty object when the error is not a field error, so callers can fall back to a general message.

// { email: 'must be a well-formed email address', salary: '...' }
export function getFieldErrors(err) {
  const errors = err?.response?.data?.errors;
  if (errors && typeof errors === 'object' && !Array.isArray(errors)) return errors;
  return {};
}

export function hasFieldErrors(err) {
  return Object.keys(getFieldErrors(err)).length > 0;
}

A reusable field component

Put the label, the input and the error message in one component so every form shows errors the same, accessible way. aria-invalid and aria-describedby let screen readers announce the message with the field.

import { useId } from 'react';

export function TextField({ label, name, error, ...inputProps }) {
  const id = useId();
  const errorId = `${id}-error`;
  return (
    <div className="field">
      <label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label>
      <input
        id={id}
        name={name}
        aria-invalid={error ? 'true' : undefined}
        aria-describedby={error ? errorId : undefined}
        {...inputProps}
      />
      {error && <p id={errorId} className="field-error">{error}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

The form: client rules, then server rules

import { useState } from 'react';
import { TextField } from './TextField.jsx';
import { describeError, getFieldErrors, hasFieldErrors } from '../lib/errors.js';

const EMPTY = { name: '', email: '', department: '', salary: '' };

function validateClient(values) {
  const errors = {};
  if (!values.name.trim()) errors.name = 'Name is required';
  if (!/^\S+@\S+\.\S+$/.test(values.email)) errors.email = 'Enter a valid email';
  if (!(Number(values.salary) > 0)) errors.salary = 'Salary must be greater than 0';
  return errors;
}

export function EmployeeForm({ initial = EMPTY, onSubmit, submitLabel = 'Save' }) {
  const [values, setValues] = useState(initial);
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});          // field name -> message
  const [formError, setFormError] = useState(null);  // message not tied to a field
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);

  function handleChange(e) {
    const { name, value } = e.target;
    setValues((v) => ({ ...v, [name]: value }));
    setErrors((prev) => ({ ...prev, [name]: undefined }));  // clear this field's error on typing
  }

  async function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const clientErrors = validateClient(values);
    setErrors(clientErrors);
    setFormError(null);
    if (Object.keys(clientErrors).length > 0) return;     // do not call the API

    setSubmitting(true);
    try {
      await onSubmit({ ...values, salary: Number(values.salary) });
    } catch (err) {
      if (hasFieldErrors(err)) setErrors(getFieldErrors(err));  // server said which fields
      else setFormError(describeError(err));                    // network, 5xx, ...
    } finally {
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit} noValidate>
      {formError && <p role="alert" className="form-error">{formError}</p>}
      <TextField label="Name" name="name" value={values.name}
                 onChange={handleChange} error={errors.name} />
      <TextField label="Email" name="email" type="email" value={values.email}
                 onChange={handleChange} error={errors.email} />
      <TextField label="Department" name="department" value={values.department}
                 onChange={handleChange} error={errors.department} />
      <TextField label="Salary" name="salary" type="number" value={values.salary}
                 onChange={handleChange} error={errors.salary} />
      <button type="submit" disabled={submitting}>
        {submitting ? 'Saving…' : submitLabel}
      </button>
    </form>
  );
}

Notes on the choices: noValidate switches off the browser's own bubbles so that your messages are the only ones; the field name must be exactly the Java record component name (email, not emailAddress), because the server's keys come from fe.getField(); and the submit handler throws errors up to onSubmit's caller so the form decides how to show them.

The same with React Hook Form

If you use React Hook Form (Module 5), server errors are pushed into the form with setError. The field then behaves exactly like one that failed client validation.

const { register, handleSubmit, setError, formState: { errors, isSubmitting } } = useForm();

const onSubmit = async (values) => {
  try {
    await createEmployee(values);
  } catch (err) {
    const fieldErrors = getFieldErrors(err);
    Object.entries(fieldErrors).forEach(([field, message]) => {
      setError(field, { type: 'server', message });
    });
    if (Object.keys(fieldErrors).length === 0) {
      setError('root.server', { message: describeError(err) });
    }
  }
};

Conventions

  • Show client-side errors on submit (and on blur), then clear each field's error as soon as the user edits it.
  • Keep the user's input. Never reset the form after a failed submit.
  • Move focus to the first invalid field or to the error summary so keyboard and screen-reader users find it.
  • Duplicate rules (client and server) only for fast feedback. The server is the authority.
  • Use the status code to decide the kind of error: 400 or 409 with errors means "show on fields"; anything else means "show a general message".

Edge cases

  • Nested and list fields: Spring reports address.city or items[0].quantity as the field path. Your form must use the same keys, or map them.
  • Class-level rules (for example "end date after start date") produce object errors, not field errors. Put them under a key such as global or return them in detail and show them as the form error.
  • Several rules fail on one field (blank and too short): the handler above keeps the first with putIfAbsent. Return a list per field if you want to show all.
  • Malformed JSON or wrong types (a string in a number field) make Spring throw HttpMessageNotReadableException, a 400 without field errors. Your form falls back to the general message.
  • Messages are English by default. For other languages use message bundles on the server or map error codes to text on the client.

Common mistakes

  • Showing only err.message ("Request failed with status code 400") and losing the server's field errors.
  • Form field names that differ from the DTO property names, so messages never match an input.
  • Not clearing old server errors when the user retypes, so a stale red message stays.
  • Returning 200 with { success: false } instead of 400. Use real status codes.
  • Validating only in the browser and assuming it is safe.

Interview: "How do you display backend validation errors?"

  • Backend: @Valid on the request body, a @RestControllerAdvice turns MethodArgumentNotValidException into a 400 ProblemDetail with a field-to-message map.
  • Frontend: in the catch block, read error.response.data.errors, store it in state keyed by field name and render each message beside its input; fall back to a general message for other failures.
  • Both sides validate: the client for speed, the server for safety.

Pagination UI and optimistic updates

Ask Spring Data for one page at a time with page and size parameters, keep the current page in the URL, render controls from the response's totals, and use optimistic updates only for quick, low-risk actions you can roll back.

Why paginate

A table with 50,000 rows must not be sent to the browser in one response. It is slow to download, heavy to render and wasteful in the database. Pagination returns a small slice (a page) per request. Spring Data supports this directly with Pageable (see Spring Boot · Module 3).

The backend contract

Spring MVC turns the query string ?page=0&size=10&sort=name,asc into a Pageable. Page numbers start at 0. The repository returns a Page<T>, which knows the content and the totals.

public record PageResponse<T>(List<T> content, int page, int size,
                              long totalElements, int totalPages) {
    public static <T> PageResponse<T> from(Page<T> p) {
        return new PageResponse<>(p.getContent(), p.getNumber(), p.getSize(),
                p.getTotalElements(), p.getTotalPages());
    }
}

@GetMapping("/api/employees")
public PageResponse<EmployeeDto> list(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "") String q,
                                      @PageableDefault(size = 10, sort = "name") Pageable pageable) {
    return PageResponse.from(employeeService.search(q, pageable).map(EmployeeDto::from));
}
{
  "content": [
    { "id": 3, "name": "Meera Iyer", "email": "meera@acme.in", "department": "HR", "salary": 62000 },
    { "id": 4, "name": "Rohan Das", "email": "rohan@acme.in", "department": "IT", "salary": 71000 }
  ],
  "page": 1,
  "size": 2,
  "totalElements": 9,
  "totalPages": 5
}

Serialising Page directly

If a controller returns a Spring Data Page object itself, the JSON contains many fields (pageable, sort, first, last, numberOfElements…). Newer Spring Data versions warn about serialising the default implementation directly and offer a DTO-style output with the totals nested under a page object. Because the shape can differ between versions and settings, a small PageResponse record of your own, as above, gives the frontend a stable contract. Always look at the real JSON in the Network tab before writing the TypeScript or JavaScript that reads it.

Page state belongs in the URL

If the current page lives only in useState, a refresh sends the user back to page 1, the Back button leaves the list, and nobody can share "page 3 of the IT department". Store page, size and search text in the query string with useSearchParams from React Router. The URL becomes the single source of truth, and the query key follows from it.

import { keepPreviousData, useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useSearchParams } from 'react-router';
import { api } from '../lib/axios.js';

export function useEmployeeParams() {
  const [searchParams, setSearchParams] = useSearchParams();
  const page = Math.max(0, Number(searchParams.get('page') ?? 0) || 0);
  const q = searchParams.get('q') ?? '';

  function update(changes) {
    const next = new URLSearchParams(searchParams);
    Object.entries(changes).forEach(([key, value]) => {
      if (value === '' || value === null || value === undefined) next.delete(key);
      else next.set(key, String(value));
    });
    setSearchParams(next);
  }
  return { page, q, update };
}

export function useEmployees({ page, q, size = 10 }) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: ['employees', { page, q, size }],        // a new key per page = cached per page
    queryFn: async ({ signal }) => {
      const { data } = await api.get('/employees', { params: { page, size, q }, signal });
      return data;
    },
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,                  // keep showing the old page while loading
  });
}

Because the page is part of the query key, going to page 2 and back to page 1 shows page 1 instantly from the cache. keepPreviousData keeps the old rows on screen while the next page loads, so the table does not flash empty. While that happens query.isPlaceholderData is true; use it to dim the table and disable the "Next" button.

The pagination component

Build it from page (0-based) and totalPages only. Show the user a 1-based number, because people do not read "page 0".

export function Pagination({ page, totalPages, onChange, disabled = false }) {
  if (totalPages <= 1) return null;                      // nothing to page through
  const isFirst = page === 0;
  const isLast = page >= totalPages - 1;

  return (
    <nav aria-label="Pagination" className="pagination">
      <button onClick={() => onChange(page - 1)} disabled={disabled || isFirst}>
        Previous
      </button>
      <span>Page {page + 1} of {totalPages}</span>
      <button onClick={() => onChange(page + 1)} disabled={disabled || isLast}>
        Next
      </button>
    </nav>
  );
}

// In the list page:
// <Pagination page={data.page} totalPages={data.totalPages}
//             disabled={query.isPlaceholderData} onChange={(p) => update({ page: p })} />

Edge cases in pagination

  • Off-by-one: the API is 0-based, the UI is 1-based. Convert in exactly one place.
  • Search resets the page: when the search text changes, set page back to 0, or you may ask for page 7 of a result that has only 2 pages.
  • Last item deleted: after deleting the only row on the last page, the page you are on no longer exists (an empty content with totalPages smaller than page + 1). Move to totalPages - 1.
  • Sorting: send sort=field,direction. Whitelist sortable fields on the server; Spring Data throws PropertyReferenceException for an unknown property, which becomes a 500 unless you handle it.
  • Zero results: totalPages is 0. Show the empty state, not "Page 1 of 0".
  • Data changes between pages: with offset paging, if someone adds a row while you read, an item can appear twice or be skipped. Large, fast-changing feeds use cursor (keyset) paging instead.

Pages, "load more" and infinite scroll

StyleGood forTrade-off
Numbered pagesAdmin tables, search results, anything the user wants to return toNeeds total count (an extra COUNT query on big tables)
"Load more" buttonFeeds, comment listsPage grows in the DOM; position is lost on refresh unless you store it
Infinite scrollSocial-style feedsHard to reach the footer, harder accessibility; TanStack Query offers useInfiniteQuery

Optimistic updates (briefly)

Normally a UI action waits for the server: click "Done", wait 300 ms, the checkbox changes. An optimistic update changes the screen immediately, as if the request already succeeded, sends the request in the background, and rolls back if it fails. It makes quick actions feel instant. With TanStack Query the recipe is: stop in-flight refetches, save the old data, write the new data into the cache, undo on error, and always refetch at the end so the cache matches the server.

const queryClient = useQueryClient();

const remove = useMutation({
  mutationFn: (id) => api.delete(`/employees/${id}`),

  onMutate: async (id) => {
    await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['employees'] });   // avoid overwrite by a refetch
    const snapshots = queryClient.getQueriesData({ queryKey: ['employees'] });
    queryClient.setQueriesData({ queryKey: ['employees'] }, (old) =>
      old ? { ...old, content: old.content.filter((e) => e.id !== id) } : old);
    return { snapshots };                                          // passed to onError as context
  },

  onError: (err, id, context) => {
    context?.snapshots.forEach(([key, data]) => queryClient.setQueryData(key, data));
    toast.error('Could not delete. The employee is back in the list.');
  },

  onSettled: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['employees'] }),
});

When optimistic updates are a bad idea

  • When the server decides the result: new rows need a server-generated id, prices are recalculated, stock may be insufficient.
  • For money, bookings and anything irreversible. A UPI payment must show "processing", then the real outcome; never "success" first.
  • When failures are common. Constant rollbacks feel worse than a short wait.

Good candidates: toggling a favourite, marking a task done, reordering, deleting a draft.

Common mistakes

  • Keeping the page number in state only, so refresh and Back break.
  • Putting the page outside the query key, so every page shows the cached first page.
  • Optimistic updates without rollback, leaving the UI lying after a failure.
  • Forgetting invalidateQueries in onSettled, so the cache drifts from the server.
  • Fetching all rows and paging in JavaScript. That defeats the purpose.

Interview: "How would you build a paginated table against a Spring Boot API?"

  • Backend takes Pageable (0-based page, size, sort) and returns content plus totalElements and totalPages.
  • Frontend keeps page and search in the URL, uses them in the query key, keeps the previous page visible while the next loads, and builds controls from the totals.
  • Mention the edge cases: reset page on search, page beyond the end after deletes, sort whitelist, and offset vs cursor paging for huge or live data.

Environment variables in Vite and the production build

Vite reads .env files and exposes only variables that start with VITE_ as import.meta.env.VITE_…, baked into the JavaScript at build time; npm run build produces a static dist folder, and nothing in it can be secret.

Why the API URL must not be hard-coded

On your laptop the API is at http://localhost:8080/api. In production it is https://api.acme.in/api, and on a staging server it is something else again. If you type the URL into your code, you must edit code for every environment and you will one day ship localhost to production. An environment variable is a named setting that lives outside the code and changes per environment. The code only says "use whatever VITE_API_URL is".

The .env files

Vite loads these files from the project root (the folder with package.json):

FileLoaded whenCommit to Git?
.envAlwaysYes, if it holds only harmless defaults
.env.localAlways; your personal overridesNo (git-ignored)
.env.developmentMode development (npm run dev)Yes
.env.productionMode production (npm run build)Yes
.env.[mode].localThat mode only; local overridesNo (git-ignored)

A mode is a name for the situation. vite (dev server) runs in development, vite build runs in production, and you can invent your own: vite build --mode staging loads .env.staging. When the same variable is in several files, the more specific file wins (.env.production.local beats .env.production, which beats .env.local, which beats .env), and a variable already set in the shell or by the hosting platform beats all files. The Vite project template already puts *.local in .gitignore.

VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8080/api
VITE_APP_NAME=Employee Manager (dev)
VITE_API_URL=https://api.acme.in/api
VITE_APP_NAME=Employee Manager

Using them in code

Vite does not use Node's process.env in browser code. It gives you import.meta.env:

const apiUrl = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;     // 'http://localhost:8080/api' in dev
const appName = import.meta.env.VITE_APP_NAME;

// Built-in values, always present:
import.meta.env.MODE;        // 'development' | 'production' | your custom mode
import.meta.env.DEV;         // true when running npm run dev
import.meta.env.PROD;        // true in the production build
import.meta.env.BASE_URL;    // the base path the app is served from ('/' by default)

if (import.meta.env.DEV) {
  console.log('Calling API at', apiUrl);        // dev-only logging
}

Rules

  • Only variables starting with VITE_ are exposed to your code. A variable called API_URL is undefined in the browser. The prefix is a safety net so that a stray server variable is not leaked by accident.
  • Values are always strings. VITE_ENABLE_X=false gives the string "false", which is truthy. Compare explicitly: import.meta.env.VITE_ENABLE_X === 'true'.
  • Values are replaced at build time. Vite copies the text into the bundle. Changing the variable on the server later does nothing until you build again.
  • Restart npm run dev after editing a .env file; the dev server reads them at start-up.

Never put secrets in frontend environment variables

A VITE_ variable ends up as plain text inside dist/assets/*.js. Anyone can open DevTools, search the bundle and read it. The prefix does not hide anything; it only decides what is included.

  • Fine in the frontend: the API base URL, an app name, a feature flag, a publishable key that is designed to be public (Stripe publishable key, a Google Maps key restricted to your domain).
  • Never: database passwords, the JWT signing secret, a Stripe secret key, cloud access keys, anything that grants power. Those live only in the Spring Boot backend (environment variables or a secrets manager), and the frontend asks the backend to act for it.

If you ever committed a secret, treat it as leaked and rotate it. Removing it from Git history is not enough.

Typing the variables (TypeScript projects)

/// <reference types="vite/client" />

interface ImportMetaEnv {
  readonly VITE_API_URL: string;
  readonly VITE_APP_NAME: string;
}

interface ImportMeta {
  readonly env: ImportMetaEnv;
}

Fail early when a variable is missing

A missing VITE_API_URL produces confusing errors later ("requests go to undefined/employees"). Check once at start-up:

function required(name) {
  const value = import.meta.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`Missing environment variable ${name}. Check your .env files.`);
  return value;
}

export const config = {
  apiUrl: required('VITE_API_URL'),
  appName: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_NAME ?? 'Employee Manager',
};

npm run build and the dist folder

The Vite template's package.json has these scripts:

CommandWhat it does
npm run devStarts the dev server with hot module replacement. Not optimised; for development only.
npm run buildCreates the production bundle in dist/ (runs vite build; the TypeScript template runs the type check first).
npm run previewServes the built dist/ locally to check it. Not a production server.
npm run lintRuns ESLint, if the template includes it. The build does not run it for you.

During the build, Vite starts at index.html and follows every import to produce optimised files. The browser cannot run your JSX or your hundreds of small modules efficiently, so the build does these jobs:

  • Compiles JSX (and TypeScript) to plain JavaScript.
  • Bundles modules into a few files and tree-shakes unused exports.
  • Minifies JavaScript and CSS (short names, no spaces).
  • Splits code where you use dynamic import() (for example lazy-loaded routes), so users download a page's code only when they visit it.
  • Hashes file names (index-3f9a2c1b.js) so that a new release has new names and browsers never use a stale cached file.
  • Replaces import.meta.env.VITE_* with the real values.
$ npm run build
vite building for production...
✓ 112 modules transformed.
dist/index.html                   0.46 kB
dist/assets/index-DiwrgTda.css    3.21 kB │ gzip:  1.18 kB
dist/assets/index-BMq1r0Qv.js   236.40 kB │ gzip: 76.02 kB
✓ built in 1.84s

The numbers above are only an illustration; your version and sizes will differ.

dist/
├── index.html            ← the only HTML file; loads the hashed scripts
├── favicon.svg           ← copied from public/
└── assets/
    ├── index-BMq1r0Qv.js     ← your app + libraries
    └── index-DiwrgTda.css

dist is just static files: no Node.js is needed to run them. Never commit it to Git (it is in .gitignore); the hosting platform or your CI pipeline builds it.

Other settings you will meet

  • base in vite.config.js: set it (for example base: '/hr/') when the app lives under a sub-path such as https://acme.in/hr/. React Router then needs the same value as basename. Most apps use the default /.
