  • Source maps (build.sourcemap) are off by default. They map minified code back to your source for debugging; upload them to an error tracker rather than serving them publicly if your code is sensitive.
  • One build per environment. Because values are baked in, a staging build and a production build are different artefacts. If you need one image for all environments, load a /config.json at start-up instead (a runtime config) and keep the build generic.

Check the production build before deploying

Run npm run build and npm run preview, then click through the app. Some bugs only appear in production: wrong environment variable, a missing SPA fallback, a case-sensitive import that worked on Windows but breaks on Linux (./Header.jsx vs ./header.jsx). Also open the Network tab and confirm that requests go to the production API URL, not localhost.

Edge cases

  • If you set a variable in the hosting dashboard after the first deploy, you must trigger a new build for it to take effect.
  • An absolute http:// API URL called from an https:// page is blocked by the browser as mixed content. Production APIs must use HTTPS.
  • A blank white page after deploy with a console error about a .js file usually means the server returned index.html for a missing asset or the base path is wrong.

Interview: "How do you configure a React app for different environments?"

  • .env.development and .env.production, variables prefixed with VITE_, read with import.meta.env; set in the host's dashboard or CI for real deployments.
  • They are compiled into the bundle, so they are public: only non-secret configuration belongs there. Secrets stay on the backend.
  • Changing a value needs a rebuild; for run-time changes use a config file fetched at start-up.

Deploying the React app: Vercel, Netlify, Nginx or Spring Boot

A built React app is a folder of static files, so any static host can serve it; the one thing to configure is the SPA fallback (unknown paths return index.html), and the choice between a separate host or Spring Boot's own static folder is a trade-off between convenience and simplicity.

What you are deploying

After npm run build the dist folder contains one HTML page and some hashed JavaScript and CSS (see the previous article). All the "pages" of your app, such as /login and /employees/7, are drawn by JavaScript in the browser using the History API. To the web server, they do not exist as files.

The SPA fallback problem

Open https://app.acme.in/, click around to /employees/7: works, because React Router changes the URL without asking the server. Now press F5. The browser asks the server for the path /employees/7. There is no such file, so a plain static server answers 404. The same happens when a user opens a bookmark or a shared link.

The fix is a fallback rule (also called a rewrite): for any path that is not a real file, return index.html with status 200. React then starts, reads the URL and shows the right page. Every hosting option below needs this rule in its own syntax.

Your four main options

OptionEffortSame origin as API?Best for
Vercel or NetlifyVery lowNo, so you need CORSPortfolio projects, startups, preview deploys per pull request
Nginx (VM or Docker)MediumYes, if Nginx also proxies /apiCompany servers, Docker/Kubernetes setups
Spring Boot static folderLowYesSmall internal apps, one deployable JAR
Object storage + CDN (S3 + CloudFront and similar)MediumNoProduction on a cloud provider (see DevOps · Module 5)

Option 1: Vercel

  1. Push the React project to GitHub (Git · Module 2).
  2. In Vercel, import the repository. It detects Vite; the build command is npm run build and the output directory is dist.
  3. Under the project's environment-variable settings add VITE_API_URL with your production API URL.
  4. Add the SPA rewrite below, commit, and push. Every push deploys; every pull request gets its own preview URL.
{
  "rewrites": [{ "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" }]
}

Files that exist (such as the JavaScript assets) are served first; the rewrite applies to paths that do not match a file.

Option 2: Netlify

The flow is the same: connect the repository, build command npm run build, publish directory dist, set VITE_API_URL. For the fallback, put a _redirects file in the public/ folder (Vite copies it into dist/), or use netlify.toml:

/*    /index.html   200
[build]
  command = "npm run build"
  publish = "dist"

[[redirects]]
  from = "/*"
  to = "/index.html"
  status = 200

The status 200 matters: it means "serve this content, keep the URL". A 301/302 would change the URL in the address bar.

Cross-origin deployment: what changes

On Vercel or Netlify the app is at https://employee-app.vercel.app while the API is elsewhere, so every call is cross-origin. Three things follow:

  • CORS: add the exact deployed origin to your Spring Boot allowed origins, with no trailing slash and the right scheme (CORS in Spring Boot). Use an environment variable on the backend, not a hard-coded list.
  • HTTPS on both sides, or the browser blocks the calls as mixed content.
  • Cookies: if the refresh token is an httpOnly cookie (JWT flow), a cookie set by api.acme.in for a page on another site is a third-party cookie. It needs SameSite=None; Secure, and browsers increasingly restrict such cookies. The robust design is to serve the app and the API under the same parent domain (app.acme.in and api.acme.in count as the same site) or behind one origin, as in the next options.

Option 3: Nginx

Nginx is a fast web server and reverse proxy (DevOps · Module 2). One Nginx can serve the React files and forward /api to Spring Boot. The browser sees one origin, so there is no CORS at all, and the app can call the relative URL /api.

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name app.acme.in;

    root /usr/share/nginx/html;
    index index.html;

    gzip on;
    gzip_types text/css application/javascript application/json image/svg+xml;

    # Hashed assets never change: cache for a year
    location /assets/ {
        expires 1y;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
    }

    # The HTML entry point must always be revalidated, or users keep an old app
    location = /index.html {
        add_header Cache-Control "no-cache";
    }

    # Forward API calls to Spring Boot
    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://backend:8080;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }

    # SPA fallback: real file, real folder, otherwise index.html
    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
    }
}

In Docker, a two-stage build compiles with Node and ships only the static files in a small Nginx image (DevOps · Module 3):

FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
ARG VITE_API_URL=/api
ENV VITE_API_URL=$VITE_API_URL
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
EXPOSE 80

The build argument is how the variable reaches Vite, because it is read at build time, not when the container starts.

Option 4: Spring Boot's static folder

Spring Boot serves files from src/main/resources/static (on the classpath at /static) without any configuration. Copy the contents of dist there, build the JAR, and one process serves both the API and the UI. Use VITE_API_URL=/api.

employee-api/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/
    ├── java/in/acme/employee/...
    └── resources/
        ├── application.yml
        └── static/            ← contents of the React dist/ folder
            ├── index.html
            └── assets/...

Spring only returns files that exist, so a refresh on /employees/7 gives 404 here too. Add the fallback by teaching the resource handler to return index.html for unknown paths. Controllers are matched first, so real /api/** endpoints keep working.

import java.io.IOException;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.core.io.ClassPathResource;
import org.springframework.core.io.Resource;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.ResourceHandlerRegistry;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.WebMvcConfigurer;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.resource.PathResourceResolver;

@Configuration
public class SpaWebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void addResourceHandlers(ResourceHandlerRegistry registry) {
        registry.addResourceHandler("/**")
                .addResourceLocations("classpath:/static/")
                .resourceChain(true)
                .addResolver(new PathResourceResolver() {
                    @Override
                    protected Resource getResource(String resourcePath, Resource location)
                            throws IOException {
                        Resource requested = location.createRelative(resourcePath);
                        return requested.exists() && requested.isReadable()
                                ? requested
                                : new ClassPathResource("/static/index.html");
                    }
                });
    }
}

If Spring Security is on, permit the static files and the SPA paths (permitAll for /, /index.html, /assets/** and the frontend routes), while /api/** stays protected; the frontend's own RequireAuth handles the login redirect. Many teams automate "build React, copy into the JAR" in the Maven or Gradle build with a frontend plugin, or in the CI pipeline (DevOps · Module 4).

Pros of serving from Spring Boot

  • One artefact, one server, one URL. Easy to demo and to run on a single VM.
  • Same origin: no CORS configuration, simple cookies.
  • No extra hosting account or cost.

Cons

  • A frontend-only change needs a rebuild and redeploy of the whole backend.
  • The Java server serves static files less efficiently than a CDN or Nginx; no global edge caching.
  • Frontend and backend release together, and you cannot scale or cache them separately.
  • Unknown paths (including mistyped /api/... URLs) can fall through to index.html unless you restrict the fallback.

Which should you choose?

  • Learning, portfolio, interview demo: Vercel or Netlify for the UI and any Java host for the API. It shows you can handle CORS and environment variables.
  • Company with Docker/Kubernetes: Nginx image (or a CDN) for the UI, a separate Spring Boot container, a reverse proxy in front of both.
  • Small internal tool, one team: Spring Boot static is the least moving parts.

Pre-deploy checklist

  • VITE_API_URL set for production; build run after setting it.
  • API reachable over HTTPS; allowed origins on the backend include the deployed UI origin.
  • SPA fallback configured and tested by refreshing a deep link.
  • A route for path="*" (404 page) exists in the app.
  • Hashed assets cached for long, index.html not cached (or revalidated).
  • No secrets or .env.local committed.

Common mistakes

  • Refresh gives 404 on any non-root page: the fallback rule is missing.
  • The deployed app calls http://localhost:8080: the variable was not set before the build.
  • CORS error only in production: the allowed origin has a trailing slash, uses http instead of https, or is the old preview URL.
  • Redirect rule with status 301 instead of 200 (Netlify) so the URL changes.
  • Serving npm run dev or npm run preview as the production server.
  • Case-sensitive file name errors that only break on a Linux build server.

Interview: "Your React app shows 404 when you refresh /employees/7 in production. Why?"

  • The route exists only in client-side JavaScript. On refresh the browser asks the server for that path; the server has no such file.
  • Configure a fallback to index.html with status 200: try_files in Nginx, a rewrite on Vercel, _redirects on Netlify, a resource resolver in Spring Boot.
  • Add the trade-offs: separate hosting needs CORS and HTTPS but deploys the UI independently; bundling in Spring Boot is simplest but couples releases.

Mini project: Employee Manager UI — contract, folders and app shell

The project is a React app with JWT login, protected routes and a paginated list/create/edit/delete screen for one resource (employees) against your Spring Boot API; this article fixes the API contract, the folder structure and the wiring files, and the next article builds the pages.

What you build and why this project

Almost every business application is "log in, see a table, add a row, change it, delete it". If you can build this one resource cleanly, you can build most screens of a real project. The project uses everything from Modules 5 and 6: routing, forms, Context, TanStack Query, Axios with interceptors, CORS, JWT, error handling and environment variables. It is also the frontend of Project 3 in the roadmap (see Practice).

The API contract

Agree on the contract before writing screens. This table is what the React app expects from your Spring Boot application (the controller code is in Spring Boot · Module 2; authentication is in Module 4).

EndpointBody / paramsSuccessErrors the UI handles
POST /api/auth/loginemail, password200 + accessToken, user401 wrong credentials
GET /api/employeespage, size, q200 + PageResponse401, 5xx
GET /api/employees/{id}-200 + Employee404
POST /api/employeesname, email, department, salary201 + Employee400 field errors, 409 duplicate email
PUT /api/employees/{id}same as create200 + Employee400, 404, 409
DELETE /api/employees/{id}-204403 (not ADMIN), 404
 
public record EmployeeRequest(
        @NotBlank String name,
        @NotBlank @Email String email,
        @NotBlank String department,
        @NotNull @Positive BigDecimal salary) {}

public record EmployeeDto(Long id, String name, String email, String department,
                          BigDecimal salary) {}

// Controller outline (bodies omitted)
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/employees")
class EmployeeController {
    @GetMapping
    PageResponse<EmployeeDto> list(String q, Pageable pageable) { /* ... */ }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    EmployeeDto get(@PathVariable Long id) { /* 404 if missing */ }

    @PostMapping
    ResponseEntity<EmployeeDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody EmployeeRequest r) { /* 201 */ }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    EmployeeDto update(@PathVariable Long id, @Valid @RequestBody EmployeeRequest r) { /* ... */ }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable Long id) { /* 204 */ }
}

The validation error body (errors map) and the PageResponse record are the ones from validation errors and pagination. CORS is set up as in CORS in Spring Boot: allow the Vite origin http://localhost:5173 with the headers Authorization and Content-Type.

Create the project

$ npm create vite@latest employee-ui -- --template react
$ cd employee-ui
$ npm install
$ npm install react-router axios @tanstack/react-query react-hot-toast
$ npm run dev

Then create .env.development with VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8080/api (see environment variables). If your tutorial or company uses react-router-dom, the code is the same; only the import path differs.

Folder structure

Files marked "built earlier" were written in the previous articles; this article does not repeat them. The rule behind the layout: a page is one route; a component is reused by several pages; a hook wraps server data; lib has no React in it (except Context). For bigger projects, group by feature instead (features/employees/…); the idea is the same.

The only file that knows the URLs: employeeApi.js

Components never call api.get('/employees') directly. A small module owns every URL and returns plain data, so a changed endpoint is a one-file edit and tests can mock one module.

import { api } from './axios.js';

export const employeeApi = {
  async list({ page = 0, size = 10, q = '' }, signal) {
    const { data } = await api.get('/employees', {
      params: { page, size, q: q || undefined },         // undefined params are not sent
      signal,
    });
    return data;                                          // PageResponse
  },

  async get(id, signal) {
    const { data } = await api.get(`/employees/${id}`, { signal });
    return data;
  },

  async create(body) {
    const { data } = await api.post('/employees', body);
    return data;
  },

  async update(id, body) {
    const { data } = await api.put(`/employees/${id}`, body);
    return data;
  },

  async remove(id) {
    await api.delete(`/employees/${id}`);                 // 204: no body to return
  },
};

The useEmployees hook from the pagination article now calls employeeApi.list({ page, q, size }, signal) inside its queryFn instead of api.get. Keep it in the same file as the hooks below.

The query hooks

import {
  keepPreviousData, useMutation, useQuery, useQueryClient,
} from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { employeeApi } from '../lib/employeeApi.js';

// Query keys in one place: a typo in a key is a classic cache bug
export const keys = {
  list: (params) => ['employees', params],
  all: ['employees'],
  one: (id) => ['employee', String(id)],
};

export function useEmployees({ page, q, size = 10 }) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: keys.list({ page, q, size }),
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => employeeApi.list({ page, q, size }, signal),
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
  });
}

export function useEmployee(id) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: keys.one(id),
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => employeeApi.get(id, signal),
  });
}

export function useCreateEmployee() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: employeeApi.create,
    onSuccess: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: keys.all }),
  });
}

export function useUpdateEmployee() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: ({ id, body }) => employeeApi.update(id, body),
    onSuccess: (saved, { id }) => {
      queryClient.setQueryData(keys.one(id), saved);             // detail page is fresh at once
      queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: keys.all });     // lists refetch
    },
  });
}

export function useDeleteEmployee() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: employeeApi.remove,
    onSuccess: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: keys.all }),
  });
}

Why invalidateQueries: after a write, the cached lists are out of date. Invalidating the ['employees'] prefix marks every cached page of the list stale and refetches the ones on screen. The single-employee key is ['employee', id] (singular), so it is not matched by that prefix; the update hook sets it directly.

main.jsx: providers in the right order

import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { BrowserRouter } from 'react-router';
import { QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { Toaster } from 'react-hot-toast';
import App from './App.jsx';
import { AuthProvider } from './context/AuthContext.jsx';
import { queryClient } from './lib/queryClient.js';
import './index.css';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <BrowserRouter>
        <AuthProvider>
          <App />
          <Toaster position="top-right" />
        </AuthProvider>
      </BrowserRouter>
    </QueryClientProvider>
  </StrictMode>,
);

src/lib/queryClient.js is the QueryClient with the retry rule and the global QueryCache error toast from the error-states article, moved into its own file and exported. The order matters: AuthProvider may call the API, so it sits inside the places that provide what it needs; RequireAuth uses router hooks, so BrowserRouter must be above App.

App.jsx and Layout.jsx

import { Navigate, Route, Routes } from 'react-router';
import RequireAuth from './components/RequireAuth.jsx';
import Layout from './components/Layout.jsx';
import LoginPage from './pages/LoginPage.jsx';
import EmployeeListPage from './pages/EmployeeListPage.jsx';
import EmployeeCreatePage from './pages/EmployeeCreatePage.jsx';
import EmployeeEditPage from './pages/EmployeeEditPage.jsx';
import ForbiddenPage from './pages/ForbiddenPage.jsx';
import NotFoundPage from './pages/NotFoundPage.jsx';

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/login" element={<LoginPage />} />
      <Route path="/forbidden" element={<ForbiddenPage />} />

      <Route element={<RequireAuth />}>
        <Route element={<Layout />}>
          <Route index element={<Navigate to="/employees" replace />} />
          <Route path="employees" element={<EmployeeListPage />} />
          <Route element={<RequireAuth roles={['ADMIN', 'HR']} />}>
            <Route path="employees/new" element={<EmployeeCreatePage />} />
            <Route path="employees/:id/edit" element={<EmployeeEditPage />} />
          </Route>
        </Route>
      </Route>

      <Route path="*" element={<NotFoundPage />} />
    </Routes>
  );
}
import { NavLink, Outlet } from 'react-router';
import { useAuth } from '../context/AuthContext.jsx';

export default function Layout() {
  const { user, logout } = useAuth();
  return (
    <div className="app">
      <header className="topbar">
        <strong>Employee Manager</strong>
        <nav>
          <NavLink to="/employees">Employees</NavLink>
        </nav>
        <span className="spacer" />
        <span>{user.name} ({user.roles.join(', ')})</span>
        <button onClick={logout}>Log out</button>
      </header>
      <main>
        <Outlet />
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

Conventions used in this project

  • One module owns the API URLs; pages never build URLs.
  • Server data lives in TanStack Query, not in useState or Context. Context holds only the logged-in user.
  • Every list page has the four states: loading, error, empty, data.
  • URL is state: page and search text are in the query string; the edit page's id is in the path.
  • Roles are shown as the backend sends them (ADMIN); routes and buttons use the same strings.

Common mistakes when wiring the app

  • Two nested BrowserRouter components, or AuthProvider above the router when it needs router hooks.
  • Placing /employees/new after /employees/:id logic that would treat new as an id. React Router ranks static segments higher, but the habit of checking the order is still useful.
  • Fetching in components with useEffect and also in hooks, so the same data loads twice.
  • Forgetting that useParams() returns strings: id is "7", not 7.

Mini project: list, create, edit and delete pages — and debugging it

The list page combines search, pagination, role-based buttons and delete; the create and edit pages reuse one form that shows server validation errors; a short debugging table maps common symptoms to causes, and a checklist tells you when the project is done.

The list page

This page uses almost everything: URL state for page and search, the query hook, the QueryState wrapper, the pagination control, a role-aware delete button and a mutation with a toast.

import { useState } from 'react';
import { Link } from 'react-router';
import toast from 'react-hot-toast';
import { useEmployeeParams } from '../hooks/useEmployeeParams.js';
import { useDeleteEmployee, useEmployees } from '../hooks/employeeHooks.js';
import { QueryState } from '../components/QueryState.jsx';
import { Pagination } from '../components/Pagination.jsx';
import { SkeletonRows } from '../components/SkeletonRows.jsx';
import { HasRole } from '../components/HasRole.jsx';
import { describeError } from '../lib/errors.js';

export default function EmployeeListPage() {
  const { page, q, update } = useEmployeeParams();
  const query = useEmployees({ page, q });
  const remove = useDeleteEmployee();
  const [search, setSearch] = useState(q);

  function handleSearch(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    update({ q: search.trim(), page: 0 });               // a new search starts at page 0
  }

  function handleDelete(employee) {
    if (!window.confirm(`Delete ${employee.name}?`)) return;
    remove.mutate(employee.id, {
      onSuccess: () => {
        toast.success(`${employee.name} deleted`);
        const onlyRowOnPage = query.data.content.length === 1;
        if (onlyRowOnPage && page > 0) update({ page: page - 1 });
      },
      onError: (err) => toast.error(describeError(err)),
    });
  }

  const rows = query.data?.content ?? [];

  return (
    <section>
      <div className="toolbar">
        <h1>Employees</h1>
        <form onSubmit={handleSearch} role="search">
          <input value={search} onChange={(e) => setSearch(e.target.value)}
                 placeholder="Search name or email" aria-label="Search employees" />
          <button>Search</button>
        </form>
        <HasRole roles={['ADMIN', 'HR']}>
          <Link to="/employees/new" className="button">Add employee</Link>
        </HasRole>
      </div>

      <QueryState query={query} isEmpty={rows.length === 0}
                  skeleton={<SkeletonRows />}
                  emptyMessage={q ? `No employees match "${q}".` : 'No employees yet.'}>
        <table className={query.isPlaceholderData ? 'dim' : undefined}>
          <thead>
            <tr>
              <th>Name</th><th>Email</th><th>Department</th>
              <th>Salary</th><th></th>
            </tr>
          </thead>
          <tbody>
            {rows.map((e) => (
              <tr key={e.id}>
                <td>{e.name}</td>
                <td>{e.email}</td>
                <td>{e.department}</td>
                <td>₹{Number(e.salary).toLocaleString('en-IN')}</td>
                <td>
                  <HasRole roles={['ADMIN', 'HR']}>
                    <Link to={`/employees/${e.id}/edit`}>Edit</Link>
                  </HasRole>
                  <HasRole roles={['ADMIN']}>
                    <button onClick={() => handleDelete(e)}
                            disabled={remove.isPending && remove.variables === e.id}>
                      Delete
                    </button>
                  </HasRole>
                </td>
              </tr>
            ))}
          </tbody>
        </table>
        <Pagination page={query.data?.page ?? 0} totalPages={query.data?.totalPages ?? 0}
                    disabled={query.isPlaceholderData}
                    onChange={(p) => update({ page: p })} />
      </QueryState>
    </section>
  );
}

Two small files complete it: useEmployeeParams is the URL-state hook from the pagination article saved as src/hooks/useEmployeeParams.js, and SkeletonRows is the skeleton component from the error-states article. A salary shown with toLocaleString('en-IN') gives Indian digit grouping (for example 1,25,000).

Create and edit pages share one form

EmployeeForm takes initial values and an async onSubmit. It already handles client rules, server field errors and the disabled button. The two pages only decide what to call.

import { useNavigate } from 'react-router';
import toast from 'react-hot-toast';
import { EmployeeForm } from '../components/EmployeeForm.jsx';
import { useCreateEmployee } from '../hooks/employeeHooks.js';

export default function EmployeeCreatePage() {
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const create = useCreateEmployee();

  async function handleSubmit(values) {
    await create.mutateAsync(values);          // throws on 400/409: the form shows the errors
    toast.success('Employee created');
    navigate('/employees');
  }

  return (
    <section>
      <h1>Add employee</h1>
      <EmployeeForm onSubmit={handleSubmit} submitLabel="Create" />
    </section>
  );
}
import { Link, useNavigate, useParams } from 'react-router';
import toast from 'react-hot-toast';
import { EmployeeForm } from '../components/EmployeeForm.jsx';
import { QueryState } from '../components/QueryState.jsx';
import { useEmployee, useUpdateEmployee } from '../hooks/employeeHooks.js';

export default function EmployeeEditPage() {
  const { id } = useParams();                   // a string such as "7"
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const query = useEmployee(id);
  const update = useUpdateEmployee();

  async function handleSubmit(values) {
    await update.mutateAsync({ id, body: values });
    toast.success('Employee updated');
    navigate('/employees');
  }

  const employee = query.data;

  return (
    <section>
      <h1>Edit employee</h1>
      <QueryState query={query}>
        {employee && (
          <EmployeeForm
            key={employee.id}                   // new employee loaded = fresh form state
            initial={{
              name: employee.name,
              email: employee.email,
              department: employee.department,
              salary: String(employee.salary),
            }}
            onSubmit={handleSubmit}
            submitLabel="Save changes"
          />
        )}
      </QueryState>
      <Link to="/employees">Back to the list</Link>
    </section>
  );
}

The form copies initial into its own state once, when it first renders. That is why the edit page renders the form only after the data has loaded (inside QueryState), and why it passes a key: with the key, loading a different employee mounts a fresh form. If you rendered the form first with empty values and passed the data later, the inputs would stay empty, which is a very common bug.

Try the whole flow

  1. Start PostgreSQL and the Spring Boot API (port 8080), then npm run dev (port 5173).
  2. Open /employees while logged out. You must land on /login.
  3. Log in with a wrong password: a clear message, no redirect loop. Log in correctly: you return to /employees.
  4. Add an employee with an empty name and a bad email: client messages appear without a request. Fix them and submit an email that already exists: the server's 409 message appears under the email field.
  5. Create a valid employee, see the toast and the new row. Edit it. Delete it as ADMIN; log in as a normal user and check that the Delete button is hidden and that DELETE from curl gives 403.
  6. Stop the Spring Boot app and reload: you see the "cannot reach the server" message with a retry button, not a white page.
  7. Wait for the token to expire (or shorten it to one minute in application.yml) and click around: the interceptor refreshes, or sends you to the login page.
  8. Run npm run build and npm run preview; repeat steps 2 to 5 against the built app.

Debugging with the Network tab

Open DevTools (F12) and the Network tab, filter by Fetch/XHR. Click a request and read four things: the status code, the request headers (is there Authorization: Bearer …?), the request payload (are the field names right?) and the response body (what did Spring say?). The Console tab shows CORS errors in red.

SymptomLikely causeWhere to look / fix
Console: "blocked by CORS policy"Origin not allowed, or the preflight (OPTIONS) was rejected by Spring SecurityNetwork tab: failed OPTIONS request. Fix the CORS bean; see CORS
Every API call is 401Token missing or malformed header; token expired; backend filter orderRequest headers: Authorization: Bearer <token> with a space
Request goes to /employees on port 5173 (404)baseURL empty because the env variable is missing or misspelledRestart npm run dev; the name must start with VITE_
Field errors never showForm field names differ from DTO names, or the response has no errorsCompare the response JSON keys with the input names
400 with "JSON parse error"Sending a string where the DTO expects a number, or bad JSONRequest payload: convert salary with Number()
List is empty but the database has rowsReading data instead of data.content, or page out of rangeResponse body shape; page param
Page works, refresh logs me outToken only in memory and no refresh/restore stepJWT flow: restore on load
Create works but list does not updateNo invalidateQueries, or a different query keyCompare keys in the hooks file; TanStack Query devtools
Edit form shows empty inputsForm rendered before data loaded, no keyRender the form inside QueryState

Reproduce an API problem outside React

If something fails, copy the request from the Network tab (right-click, Copy as cURL) and run it in a terminal or Postman. If curl works but the browser fails, the problem is browser-specific: CORS, cookies or headers. If curl fails too, the bug is in the backend. This one habit saves hours.

Edge cases to test

  • Open /employees/9999/edit (a missing id): the page shows the 404 message and a link back; it does not crash.
  • Double-click Create quickly: the button disables and only one employee is created.
  • Delete the last row on the last page: the list moves to the previous page.
  • Change the search while on page 3: the page resets to 0.
  • Salary of 0, negative, or letters: client and server both reject.
  • A normal user opens /employees/new by typing the URL: redirected to /forbidden by the route, and a direct API call is also rejected.

How a real team would extend this

  • Replace hand-written forms with React Hook Form and Zod schemas; keep the server-error mapping.
  • Add TypeScript (Module 7) so a renamed DTO field breaks the build, not the user.
  • Add tests for the form and the list with Vitest and MSW (testing).
  • Deploy: the UI on Vercel or in an Nginx container, the API in Docker (deployment), a pipeline on every push (DevOps · Module 4).

Interview: "Walk me through the React app you built against your Spring Boot API"

  • Architecture: Vite SPA, Axios instance with interceptors, JWT in memory plus refresh cookie (or localStorage in a simple version), React Router with a guard, TanStack Query for server state.
  • Features: login, protected routes, CRUD, pagination in the URL, role-based UI, backend validation errors on fields, loading/error/empty states, toasts.
  • Hard parts you solved: CORS and preflight, 401 refresh with a single shared promise, cache invalidation after writes, the SPA fallback on deploy.
  • Honest limits: client roles are cosmetic; the backend enforces security.

Interview questions — Connecting React to your Spring Boot API

Why does the browser block my React app's request to the Spring Boot API, and how do you fix it?

The browser enforces the same-origin policy. An origin is scheme + host + port, so http://localhost:5173 (React) and http://localhost:8080 (Spring) are different origins. The browser lets the page send the request but hides the response unless the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin for that origin. This is CORS.

Fix it on the server: configure allowed origins, methods and headers in Spring Boot (a CorsConfigurationSource bean with Spring Security, or addCorsMappings without). In development you can also use the Vite proxy (server.proxy) so the browser sees one origin. The fix is never in React code.

What is a preflight request?

For "non-simple" requests (methods like PUT or DELETE, a JSON Content-Type, or an Authorization header) the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking "may I send this?", with headers such as Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers. The server must answer with matching Access-Control-Allow-Methods and -Headers. Only then does the browser send the real request. A common bug: Spring Security rejects the OPTIONS request with 401 because CORS is not enabled in the security filter chain.

Is CORS a security feature of your API?

No. CORS protects the user's browser from other sites reading responses with the user's credentials. It does not stop curl, Postman or a script on a server from calling your API. Your API still needs authentication, authorisation and validation on every endpoint.

fetch or Axios: which would you use and why?

Both work. fetch is built into the browser and needs no dependency, but it does not reject on 4xx/5xx (you check response.ok), you call response.json() yourself, and there are no interceptors or default timeout. Axios adds a base URL, automatic JSON, rejection on non-2xx, interceptors (perfect for adding the token and handling 401), cancellation and timeouts. Many teams choose Axios for apps with auth; a small fetch wrapper gives the same features if you want zero dependencies.

Explain the JWT login flow in a React and Spring Boot app.

The login form POSTs email and password to /api/auth/login. Spring verifies the password hash and returns a signed JWT (and user info). The app keeps the token and an Axios request interceptor adds Authorization: Bearer <token> to every call. Spring's filter verifies signature and expiry on each request, so the server stays stateless. When the token expires the API returns 401; the app uses a refresh token to get a new access token and retries, or logs the user out and redirects to /login. On page reload the session is restored by the refresh call (or by reading the stored token and calling /me).

Where should the token be stored: localStorage, sessionStorage, memory or a cookie?

localStorage and sessionStorage are readable by any JavaScript on the page, so an XSS bug lets an attacker steal the token. An httpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, but it is sent automatically, so you must defend against CSRF (SameSite, CSRF token). A common best practice: the short-lived access token in memory, the long-lived refresh token in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. localStorage is acceptable for learning projects if you can explain the risk.

What is the difference between 401 and 403, and how does the frontend react to each?

401 means "not authenticated": no, invalid or expired credentials. The client refreshes the token or sends the user to login. 403 means "authenticated but not allowed". The client shows an "access denied" message and keeps the session. Redirecting to login on a 403 is a bug that loops the user.

How do you implement protected routes? Is hiding a button enough?

A layout route (RequireAuth) reads the auth context. While the session is being restored it shows a loader; if there is no user it returns <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location }} /> so login can send the user back; otherwise it renders <Outlet />. Roles are an extra check. Hiding buttons is not security: users can edit the client or call the API directly, so every endpoint must enforce authentication and roles (@PreAuthorize, request matchers).

How do you handle loading and error states for an API call?

Model four states: loading, error, empty and data. With useEffect that means three pieces of state and finally to end loading; with TanStack Query you get isPending, isError and data. Classify errors: no response (network or timeout; retry), 4xx (user or request problem; no retry, show field errors or a message), 5xx (server problem; friendly message and retry). Disable submit buttons while a request runs, use skeletons for first loads, and use toasts for action results.

The backend returns validation errors. How do they get onto the form fields?

Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException for an invalid @Valid body. A @RestControllerAdvice converts it to a 400 ProblemDetail that includes an errors map of field name to message. In the React catch block you read error.response.data.errors, store it in state and render each message under the input with the same name. With React Hook Form you call setError(field, …). Field names must match the DTO property names.

How do you build pagination in the UI with Spring Data?

The API accepts page (0-based), size and sort and returns the content plus totalElements and totalPages. The UI keeps the page in the URL (useSearchParams), puts it in the TanStack Query key, uses keepPreviousData so the table does not flash, and draws Previous/Next from totalPages. Reset to page 0 when the search changes and move back a page if the last row of the last page is deleted.

What happens to environment variables in a Vite build? Can you store an API key there?

Only variables prefixed with VITE_ are exposed, through import.meta.env, and their values are copied into the JavaScript at build time. So the bundle contains them in plain text and anyone can read them. Use them for the API URL and other public configuration, never for secrets such as database passwords, JWT secrets or secret API keys. Changing a value needs a rebuild.

After deploying, refreshing /employees/7 shows 404. Why, and what is the fix?

React Router changes the URL in the browser only. On refresh the server is asked for the path /employees/7 and has no file for it. Configure a fallback that returns index.html with status 200 for unknown paths: try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html in Nginx, a rewrite in vercel.json, a /* /index.html 200 line in Netlify's _redirects, or a resource resolver in Spring Boot.

Separate hosting (Vercel) or Spring Boot's static folder: how do you decide?

Separate hosting deploys the UI independently, gives CDN speed and preview URLs, but is cross-origin, so you need CORS, HTTPS and careful cookie settings. Bundling the build into Spring Boot's static folder gives one artefact and one origin (no CORS), which is simple for small internal tools, but couples frontend and backend releases and serves static files less efficiently. Nginx in front of both gives one origin and separate deployables.

How would you debug "the request fails only from the browser, but works in Postman"?

That points to something browser-specific. Open the Network tab and look at the failing request and its OPTIONS preflight, and the Console for a CORS message. Check the origin allowed on the server (exact scheme, host, port, no trailing slash), that Authorization is in the allowed headers, and that Spring Security lets OPTIONS through. If cookies are involved, check withCredentials, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, a specific (not *) origin and the cookie's SameSite and Secure flags.

Cheat sheet — Connecting React to your Spring Boot API

  • Architecture browser → React (static files) → Spring Boot REST API → PostgreSQL; JSON over HTTP.
  • Origin scheme + host + port; :5173 and :8080 are different origins.
  • CORS server-side permission for cross-origin reads; send Access-Control-Allow-Origin; not API security.
  • Preflight automatic OPTIONS before PUT/DELETE/JSON/Authorization requests.
  • Spring CORS CorsConfigurationSource bean + http.cors(...) with Security; addCorsMappings without.
  • Vite proxy server.proxy forwards /api to :8080 in dev, so no CORS locally.
  • Axios instance baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, timeout, JSON by default.
  • Request interceptor adds Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  • Response interceptor on 401 refresh once (_retry, shared promise) or log out.
  • fetch does not reject on 4xx/5xx; check response.ok, call .json().
  • JWT storage memory + httpOnly refresh cookie (best); localStorage (simple, XSS-readable).
  • 401 vs 403 not authenticated (refresh/login) vs not allowed (show message, stay logged in).
  • RequireAuth loader while restoring, Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from }}, else Outlet.
  • Frontend roles cosmetic only; the backend enforces with @PreAuthorize.
  • Four UI states loading, error, empty, data. isPending vs isFetching.
  • Error kinds no response = network/timeout; 4xx = fix request; 5xx = retry later.
  • ProblemDetail RFC 7807 JSON: type, title, status, detail, instance + your extras (errors).
  • Field errors errors[name] under the input with the same name; clear on change.
  • Pagination ?page=0&size=10&sort=name,asc; 0-based; page in the URL and the query key.
  • Optimistic update change cache at once, roll back on error, refetch in onSettled; not for payments.
  • Vite env .env, .env.development, .env.production; only VITE_*; strings; build-time.
  • No secrets everything in the bundle is public.
  • Build npm run build → dist/ (static, hashed files); npm run preview to check it.
  • SPA fallback unknown path → index.html with 200 (Nginx, Vercel, Netlify, Spring resolver).
  • Debugging Network tab: status, request headers, payload, response body, OPTIONS; copy as cURL.

Practice — Connecting React to your Spring Boot API

  1. Break and fix CORS (easy). Run a Vite app and a Spring Boot endpoint without any CORS settings and call it with fetch. Read the console error and the failed request in the Network tab. Then fix it with a CORS configuration, and again with the Vite proxy. Done when you can say which header was missing and which approach you used.
  2. Axios instance (easy). Create lib/axios.js with a baseURL from VITE_API_URL, a request interceptor that adds the Bearer token and a response interceptor that clears the session on 401. Done when a wrong token sends you to the login page.
  3. Rebuild a DOM/async app in React (easy to medium). Take the movie search or expense tracker you built with plain JavaScript in Module 4 and rebuild it in React with routing (list page, detail page), Context for shared state (favourites or theme) and loading and error states. Done when it has no manual DOM code and a refresh on the detail URL works in npm run preview.
  4. Login and protected routes (medium). Add AuthContext, LoginPage and RequireAuth with return-to-original-page. Done when opening a protected URL logged out redirects to login and back, and a page reload keeps you logged in.
  5. CRUD with backend validation (medium). Build list, create, edit and delete for one resource of your own (books, expenses, students). Show server validation errors beside the fields, including a 409 for a duplicate. Done when a bad submit never shows a generic error and a double-click creates one record.
  6. Pagination and search (medium). Add page, size and search to the list, stored in the URL, with keepPreviousData. Done when Back/refresh/share keep the same page and deleting the last row of the last page moves you back one page.
  7. Project 3 frontend (hard). Build a React UI for your Spring Boot API from Project 3: JWT login, protected pages, role-based buttons, forms that show backend validation errors, and pagination. Done when you can log in to your own API, see protected data, and a normal user cannot delete (hidden button and 403 from the API).
  8. Error handling pass (medium). Test the four states on every page: stop the backend, return 500 from a controller, return 404 for a bad id, return an empty list. Done when each case shows the right message, and 4xx errors are not retried.
  9. Deploy it (hard). Set production env variables, run npm run build, and deploy the UI to Vercel or Netlify (with the SPA rewrite) and the API somewhere reachable over HTTPS, or serve the build from an Nginx container with a proxy to the API. Done when a deployed deep link survives refresh and login works with the production CORS settings.
  10. Debug drill (medium). Ask a friend (or yourself with a git stash) to introduce three bugs: a wrong allowed origin, a missing VITE_ prefix, and a mismatched form field name. Find each using only the Network tab and console. Done when you can name the symptom, the tab and the fix for each in under five minutes.
