Module 7·LaterLater

Later, for full-stack roles

7 topics · about 1 h of reading

This module covers what job listings for full-stack roles ask for after "React and REST": TypeScript, Next.js, a state library for bigger apps, and automated tests for the frontend. You do not need these to build your first project, which is why the module is marked Later. You do need them soon after: most companies write their React code in TypeScript, many use Next.js, and almost every team expects tests.

As a Java developer you have an advantage with TypeScript. You already think in types, interfaces and generics, and your Spring Boot DTOs (records) map almost one-to-one to TypeScript interfaces. The module builds on the Employee Manager from Module 6: the same API, now typed, state-managed and tested.

After this module you will be able to:

  • Write TypeScript with unions, generics and narrowing, and know when unknown beats any.
  • Type React props, state, events, context and API responses that mirror your Java records.
  • Turn on strict mode and read the common compiler errors.
  • Explain what Next.js adds and decide between Next.js and a Vite SPA with a Spring Boot backend.
  • Choose between Context, TanStack Query, Redux Toolkit and Zustand for a given kind of state.
  • Write component tests with Vitest and React Testing Library, mock the API with MSW, and describe end-to-end tests with Playwright.
  • Plan what to learn next for a full-stack career.

TypeScript basics: types, unions, interfaces, generics, narrowing

TypeScript is JavaScript plus a static type system that is checked before the code runs and then erased; learn the basic types, unions, interface vs type, generics and narrowing, and you can read and write most TypeScript in React projects.

What it is and why teams use it

JavaScript decides types while the program runs. If you write employee.nmae (a typo), nothing warns you; the user sees undefined or a crash. TypeScript (TS) adds type annotations to JavaScript. A tool called the type checker (tsc, or your editor) reads your code, reports mistakes at once, and then the types are erased: the browser runs plain JavaScript. Every valid JavaScript program is also valid TypeScript, so you can adopt it gradually.

What you get: autocomplete for every property, safe renaming and refactoring, errors for typos and wrong argument types, null-safety, and types that document your API data. For a Java developer, this is the feeling of working with an IDE and a compiler again.

Vite does not type-check

When you create a project with npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts, Vite only strips the types (fast), it does not check them. Type errors appear in your editor and when you run the check script; the template's build script runs tsc first so that a build fails on type errors. Files are named .ts and .tsx (TSX = TypeScript with JSX).

Basic types and inference

const name: string = 'Asha';
const age: number = 29;               // one number type: no int/long/double
const active: boolean = true;
const nothing: null = null;
let maybe: undefined = undefined;
const big: bigint = 9007199254740993n; // for integers beyond 2^53

// Inference: the compiler works out the type, so you usually do NOT annotate
const city = 'Pune';                  // type is the literal 'Pune' (const)
let count = 0;                        // type is number
count = 'five';                       // Error: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'

// Arrays
const ids: number[] = [1, 2, 3];
const names: Array<string> = ['Asha', 'Ravi'];   // same thing; number[] is more common

// Tuple: fixed length, known type at each position
const point: [number, number] = [18.52, 73.85];
const entry: [string, number] = ['salary', 50000];

// Objects
const employee: { id: number; name: string; email?: string } = { id: 1, name: 'Asha' };

Annotate the places the compiler cannot infer: function parameters, function return types of public functions, and empty initial values (const items: Employee[] = []). Let it infer the rest.

Functions

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}

// Arrow function, optional parameter (?) and default value
const greet = (name: string, greeting = 'Hello', suffix?: string): string =>
  `${greeting}, ${name}${suffix ?? ''}`;

// void: returns nothing useful
function log(message: string): void {
  console.log(message);
}

// A function type, used for callbacks
type Predicate<T> = (item: T) => boolean;

add(1, '2');          // Error: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to 'number'
add(1);               // Error: Expected 2 arguments, but got 1

Union and literal types

A union type says "this or that": string | null. A literal type is one exact value. Together they replace most uses of Java enums and make states precise. Java has no direct equivalent of a union (sealed interfaces come closest).

type Role = 'ADMIN' | 'HR' | 'USER';           // a union of string literals
type Id = number | string;
let selected: Employee | null = null;           // "maybe an employee"

function canDelete(role: Role): boolean {
  return role === 'ADMIN';
}
canDelete('ADMIN');
canDelete('admin');    // Error: Argument of type '"admin"' is not assignable to type 'Role'

// A discriminated union: each case has a common "tag" property
type LoadState =
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'error'; message: string }
  | { status: 'success'; data: Employee[] };

interface vs type

Both describe the shape of an object. Pick one style per project; both are fine.

interface Employee {
  readonly id: number;        // cannot be reassigned after creation
  name: string;
  email: string;
  phone?: string;             // optional: string | undefined
}

interface Manager extends Employee {   // inheritance
  reports: Employee[];
}

type EmployeeDraft = Omit<Employee, 'id'>;       // a type alias built from another type
type Status = 'active' | 'on-leave' | 'resigned';   // aliases can name unions; interfaces cannot

const e: Employee = { id: 1, name: 'Asha', email: 'asha@acme.in' };
e.id = 2;   // Error: Cannot assign to 'id' because it is a read-only property
interfacetype
Object shapesYesYes
Unions, tuples, primitives, function typesNo (functions: call signatures only)Yes
ExtendingextendsIntersection A & B
Declaration merging (same name declared twice is combined)YesNo (error)
Typical usePublic object shapes, DTOs, props, class contractsUnions, utility combinations

Generics

Generics let you write one type or function that works for many types, exactly as in Java. The syntax is the same: angle brackets. Your API already returns a generic page.

function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}
const a = first([1, 2, 3]);          // a: number | undefined (T inferred as number)
const b = first(['x', 'y']);         // b: string | undefined

// Generic interface: the same shape for Page<Employee>, Page<Department>, ...
interface Page<T> {
  content: T[];
  page: number;
  size: number;
  totalElements: number;
  totalPages: number;
}

// Constraint: T must have an id (like <T extends HasId> in Java)
interface HasId { id: number }
function indexById<T extends HasId>(items: T[]): Record<number, T> {
  const result: Record<number, T> = {};
  for (const item of items) result[item.id] = item;
  return result;
}

// Default type parameter
interface ApiResult<T = unknown> { data: T; status: number }

Narrowing

Narrowing means the compiler follows your checks and gives a more precise type inside each branch. This is how you safely use a union.

function show(value: string | number | null): string {
  if (value === null) return 'none';                // value: string | number
  if (typeof value === 'string') return value.toUpperCase();   // value: string
  return value.toFixed(2);                          // value: number
}

// 'in' and instanceof
function describe(x: Employee | Error): string {
  if (x instanceof Error) return x.message;         // narrowed to Error
  return x.name;                                    // narrowed to Employee
}

// Discriminated union + exhaustive check
function render(state: LoadState): string {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'loading': return 'Loading…';
    case 'error': return state.message;                       // state has message here
    case 'success': return `${state.data.length} employees`;  // state has data here
    default: {
      const unreachable: never = state;   // compile error if a new status is added and not handled
      return unreachable;
    }
  }
}

// Your own check: a type guard (the return type "x is ..." tells the compiler)
function isApiError(x: unknown): x is { message: string } {
  return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'message' in x;
}

any vs unknown vs never

TypeMeaningSafe?
any"Turn off checking for this value." Anything goes in, anything can be done with it.No. It spreads: one any silently removes safety from everything it touches.
unknown"I do not know the type yet." Anything can go in, but you must narrow before use.Yes. Use it for data from outside (JSON, catch errors).
neverA value that cannot exist (a function that always throws; an impossible branch).Used for exhaustive checks.
 
function parse(json: string): unknown {
  return JSON.parse(json);                 // JSON.parse returns any; we hide that behind unknown
}

const value = parse('{"name":"Asha"}');
value.name;                                // Error: 'value' is of type 'unknown'
if (typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && 'name' in value) {
  console.log(value.name);                 // OK after narrowing
}

try {
  riskyCall();
} catch (err) {                            // err is unknown in strict mode
  if (err instanceof Error) console.log(err.message);
}

Two escape hatches you will see: a type assertion (value as Employee) tells the compiler "trust me", and the non-null assertion (user!.name) says "this is not null". Neither checks anything at run time. Use them rarely, and only when you know something the compiler cannot.

Utility types you will use daily

UtilityResultExample use
Partial<T>All properties optionalPATCH payloads, form drafts
Required<T>All properties requiredAfter defaults are applied
Readonly<T>All properties read-onlyImmutable state
Pick<T, 'a' | 'b'>Only the named propertiesList rows: Pick<Employee, 'id' | 'name'>
Omit<T, 'id'>Everything except the named onesCreate request without the id
Record<K, V>Object with keys K and values VField errors: Record<string, string>
ReturnType<typeof fn>The return type of a functionTypes derived from functions

Rules

  • Types exist only at compile time. They are erased, so you cannot use a type in a value position (if (x instanceof Employee) fails when Employee is an interface) and the compiler cannot check data that arrives at run time, such as an API response.
  • Optional phone?: string means the property may be missing, and its type includes undefined. Java's null maps to string | null.
  • A readonly property is only enforced by the compiler; it does not freeze the object at run time.

Conventions

  • Types and interfaces in PascalCase without an I prefix (Employee, not IEmployee).
  • Prefer string-literal unions over TypeScript's enum keyword: simpler, and they match the JSON strings your Java enums produce.
  • Let inference work; annotate function boundaries (parameters, exported return types).
  • Prefer unknown to any; if you must use any, leave a comment saying why.
  • Prefer discriminated unions to several optional fields that are "only set in some cases".

Common mistakes

  • Sprinkling any or as to make red lines go away. The error was telling you something.
  • Believing the types describe the real API response. If the backend sends a different shape, your code compiles and still crashes. Validate at the boundary when it matters (next article).
  • Comparing against types at run time (typeof x === 'Employee' is never true; the typeof results are only 'string', 'number', 'object' and a few more).
  • Forgetting that arrays and objects are still mutable even when typed as constants (const only stops reassignment).

Interview: "Why TypeScript, and what is the difference between any and unknown?"

  • Static types catch typos and wrong calls before run time, give autocomplete and safe refactoring, and document data shapes. Types are erased, so there is no run-time cost and no run-time checking.
  • any disables checking; unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow before using it.
  • interface vs type: both describe objects; type also names unions and tuples, interface supports declaration merging and extends.
  • Narrowing with typeof, instanceof, in, equality and discriminated unions.

TypeScript with React and your API: props, state, events and DTO types

Type props with an interface, give useState a type when the initial value does not say it, use React's event types for handlers, and write TypeScript interfaces that mirror your Java records so a renamed backend field becomes a compile error in the frontend.

Props, children and callbacks

A component is a function; its props are its parameter. Describe them with an interface. Use ReactNode for anything React can render (text, elements, arrays, null) and plain function types for callbacks.

import type { ReactNode } from 'react';
import type { Employee } from '../types/employee';

interface EmployeeCardProps {
  employee: Employee;
  highlight?: boolean;                       // optional prop
  onDelete: (id: number) => void;            // callback prop
  children?: ReactNode;                      // anything nested inside the component
}

export function EmployeeCard({ employee, highlight = false, onDelete, children }: EmployeeCardProps) {
  return (
    <article className={highlight ? 'card highlight' : 'card'}>
      <h3>{employee.name}</h3>
      <p>{employee.email}</p>
      {children}
      <button onClick={() => onDelete(employee.id)}>Delete</button>
    </article>
  );
}

// Usage: a missing or wrongly typed prop is a compile error
// <EmployeeCard employee={e} onDelete={(id) => remove(id)} />
// <EmployeeCard employee={e} />              // Error: Property 'onDelete' is missing

Most projects type props like this and let the return type be inferred. You will also see React.FC<Props>; it is not needed and many style guides avoid it. import type imports a name that exists only as a type; it is erased and makes that fact clear.

State

// Inferred from the initial value
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);              // number
const [query, setQuery] = useState('');             // string

// When the initial value does not tell the whole story, pass the type
const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);
const [rows, setRows] = useState<Employee[]>([]);       // without it: never[]
const [errors, setErrors] = useState<Record<string, string>>({});

// State that is a discriminated union
type Request =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'error'; message: string };
const [request, setRequest] = useState<Request>({ status: 'idle' });

// Refs: the DOM element type, null at first
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
inputRef.current?.focus();

Events

React wraps browser events. Its types take the element as a generic argument: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>, MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>. When you write the handler inline the compiler infers the type for you; annotate only when the handler is a separate function.

import type { ChangeEvent, FormEvent } from 'react';

interface FormValues { name: string; email: string; department: string }

function EmployeeFormTs({ onSave }: { onSave: (values: FormValues) => Promise<void> }) {
  const [values, setValues] = useState<FormValues>({ name: '', email: '', department: '' });

  function handleChange(e: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement | HTMLSelectElement>) {
    const { name, value } = e.target;
    setValues((prev) => ({ ...prev, [name]: value }));
  }

  async function handleSubmit(e: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
    e.preventDefault();
    await onSave(values);
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input name="name" value={values.name} onChange={handleChange} />
      <input name="email" value={values.email} onChange={handleChange} />
      <select name="department" value={values.department} onChange={handleChange}>
        <option value="">Choose…</option>
        <option value="IT">IT</option>
      </select>
      <button type="submit">Save</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Context with types

import { createContext, useContext } from 'react';

export type Role = 'ADMIN' | 'HR' | 'USER';

export interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  roles: Role[];
}

interface AuthContextValue {
  user: User | null;
  isLoading: boolean;
  login: (email: string, password: string) => Promise<User>;
  logout: () => Promise<void>;
}

const AuthContext = createContext<AuthContextValue | null>(null);   // null = "no provider"

export function useAuth(): AuthContextValue {
  const ctx = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (ctx === null) throw new Error('useAuth must be used inside AuthProvider');
  return ctx;               // narrowed: no null checks needed in every component
}

DTO types that mirror your Java records

The biggest win for a full-stack developer: write each Java DTO's TypeScript twin. Jackson turns a record into a JSON object with the same property names, so the interface has the same names.

public record EmployeeDto(Long id, String name, String email, String department,
                          BigDecimal salary, LocalDate joinedOn, Status status) {}

public enum Status { ACTIVE, ON_LEAVE, RESIGNED }

public record EmployeeRequest(String name, String email, String department, BigDecimal salary) {}
export type Status = 'ACTIVE' | 'ON_LEAVE' | 'RESIGNED';     // Java enum names as JSON strings

export interface Employee {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  department: string;
  salary: number;            // BigDecimal -> number (see the table: precision caveat)
  joinedOn: string;          // LocalDate -> "2026-04-01" (ISO string, not a Date)
  status: Status;
}

export type EmployeeRequest = Omit<Employee, 'id' | 'joinedOn' | 'status'>;

export interface Page<T> {
  content: T[];
  page: number;
  size: number;
  totalElements: number;
  totalPages: number;
}
Java typeJSONTypeScriptWatch out
int, long, doublenumbernumberA long above 253 loses precision in JavaScript; send it as a string
BigDecimalnumber (default)number or stringMoney: calculate on the server; show with Intl.NumberFormat
StringstringstringAny reference can be null in Java: use string | null if it can be
boolean / Booleantrue/falsebooleanBoxed Boolean can be null
LocalDate, Instant, LocalDateTimeISO string (with Spring Boot's default Jackson settings)stringConvert with new Date(...) only when needed
enumname stringstring-literal unionKeep the union in sync with the enum
List<T>, Set<T>arrayT[]Sets lose uniqueness in JSON
Map<String, V>objectRecord<string, V>
Optional<T> / nullable fieldvalue or nullT | nullWhether a null field is sent or omitted depends on Jackson settings

Typed API calls and hooks

import { api } from './axios';
import type { Employee, EmployeeRequest, Page } from '../types/employee';

export const employeeApi = {
  async list(params: { page: number; size: number; q?: string },
             signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<Page<Employee>> {
    const { data } = await api.get<Page<Employee>>('/employees', { params, signal });
    return data;                                   // typed as Page<Employee>
  },
  async create(body: EmployeeRequest): Promise<Employee> {
    const { data } = await api.post<Employee>('/employees', body);
    return data;
  },
};

// src/hooks/employeeHooks.ts: the generics are inferred from the queryFn
export function useEmployees(page: number, q: string) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: ['employees', { page, q }],
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => employeeApi.list({ page, size: 10, q }, signal),
  });
}
// const { data } = useEmployees(0, '');   data: Page<Employee> | undefined
// data.content[0].nmae                    Error: Property 'nmae' does not exist

Errors from Axios are unknown in a catch block. Narrow them with isAxiosError:

import { isAxiosError } from 'axios';

export function getFieldErrors(err: unknown): Record<string, string> {
  if (isAxiosError(err)) {
    const errors = err.response?.data?.errors;     // data is any here: narrow before trusting it
    if (errors && typeof errors === 'object') return errors as Record<string, string>;
  }
  return {};
}

Types are not run-time checks

api.get<Employee> does not verify anything. It tells the compiler "believe me". If the backend renames department to dept, your code still compiles and employee.department is undefined at run time. Three ways to close the gap:

  • Generate the types from the backend. Add the springdoc OpenAPI documentation to Spring Boot and generate the TypeScript types from it with a tool such as openapi-typescript. A backend change then shows up as a frontend compile error.
  • Validate at the boundary with Zod. A schema checks the data when it arrives and the type is derived from the schema.
  • Contract tests and integration tests on the API (Spring Boot · Module 5).
import { z } from 'zod';

export const employeeSchema = z.object({
  id: z.number(),
  name: z.string(),
  email: z.string(),
  department: z.string(),
  salary: z.number(),
});

export type Employee = z.infer<typeof employeeSchema>;

// In the API function:
const { data } = await api.get('/employees/1');
const employee = employeeSchema.parse(data);   // throws if the shape is wrong

Common mistakes

  • useState([]) without a type: the state is never[] and every setRows(data) is an error. Write useState<Employee[]>([]).
  • Typing an event as any or React.ChangeEvent without the element (e.target.value then is not found). Use ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>.
  • Using the DTO type for form state: forms hold strings (a salary input is a string until you convert it), so the form values often need their own type.
  • Using Date in the interface for a LocalDate: JSON gives you a string.
  • Copying the whole Java entity (with lazy relations and passwords) instead of the DTO your controller actually returns.

Edge cases

  • useParams() values are string | undefined. Convert and check: const id = Number(params.id) and handle Number.isNaN(id).
  • The type of document.getElementById('root') is HTMLElement | null; the Vite template uses ! because index.html always has it.
  • An index access such as rows[0] is typed as Employee although the array may be empty. The option noUncheckedIndexedAccess (not part of strict) makes it Employee | undefined.

Interview: "How do you type API responses in a React and Spring Boot project?"

  • Interfaces that mirror the DTO records; generics such as Page<T>; api.get<Page<Employee>>; separate request and response types (Omit<Employee, 'id'>).
  • Say honestly that types are erased: use generated types from OpenAPI and/or Zod validation so the types match the real JSON.
  • Map Java types: LocalDate to string, enums to string unions, BigDecimal to number (watch precision), nullable to T | null.

tsconfig strict mode, common errors, and TypeScript vs Java

Keep "strict": true in tsconfig, learn to read the five or six error messages you will see every day, and use your Java experience: TypeScript's types are structural and erased, while Java's are nominal and present at run time.

The project files

The Vite react-ts template generates TypeScript configuration files (recent templates split them: one for the app code in src, one for the Vite config). The options that matter are the same in all of them. The listing shows the important ones; open your generated file and compare, because the template changes between Vite versions.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "lib": ["ES2022", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"],
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "strict": true,
    "noUnusedLocals": true,
    "noUnusedParameters": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
  • jsx: "react-jsx": compile JSX without importing React in every file.
  • noEmit: tsc only checks; Vite produces the output.
  • moduleResolution: "bundler": resolve imports the way Vite does.
  • skipLibCheck: do not type-check the .d.ts files inside node_modules (faster, avoids errors in libraries you do not control).

What strict mode turns on

"strict": true is a switch for a group of checks. Always start new projects with it; adding it to an old project later produces hundreds of errors.

Flag (part of strict)What it catches
strictNullChecksnull and undefined are separate types: no more "cannot read properties of undefined" surprises. The most valuable flag.
noImplicitAnyA parameter or variable whose type cannot be inferred must be typed, not silently any
strictFunctionTypesSafer assignment of callbacks
strictPropertyInitializationClass properties must be set in the constructor
useUnknownInCatchVariablesThe err in catch is unknown, not any
noImplicitThis, alwaysStrict, strictBindCallApplySmaller correctness checks

Errors you will meet every day

Message (shortened)MeaningUsual fix
Type 'X' is not assignable to type 'Y'A value of the wrong type is usedFix the value, or widen the target type if the design allows it
'x' is possibly 'undefined' (or 'null')You use a value that may be missingCheck first (if (x), x?.name, x ?? default)
Property 'p' does not exist on type 'T'Typo, or the type is not narrowedFix the name, or narrow the union
Parameter 'x' implicitly has an 'any' typeMissing annotation under noImplicitAnyAdd a type
Argument of type 'string | undefined' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'Value from useParams or Map.get may be missingHandle undefined before calling
Cannot find module './x' or its type declarationsWrong path, missing package typesFix the path; install the types package if the library has none
'T' refers to a value, but is being used as a typeMixed up typeof and typesUse typeof value to get a type from a value

Migrating a JavaScript project step by step

  1. Add TypeScript and a tsconfig; allow JavaScript (allowJs) so old files keep working.
  2. Rename files one at a time from .jsx to .tsx, starting with the leaves (utilities, small components).
  3. Add the DTO interfaces first; they give the biggest benefit.
  4. Keep strict on for new files. Fix, do not suppress.

TypeScript vs Java typing

The similarities help you learn quickly; the differences are where interview questions and bugs come from.

TopicJavaTypeScript
Typing styleNominal: a class is compatible only if it declares implements or extendsStructural: any object with the right properties fits ("duck typing" checked at compile time)
Types at run timePresent: instanceof, reflection, class objectsErased: only JavaScript remains
GenericsErased too, but classes remainErased completely; generics are only for checking
NullAny reference may be null (Optional, annotations help)With strictNullChecks, null/undefined must appear in the type
Numbersint, long, double, BigDecimalOne number (64-bit float) plus bigint
UnionsNo direct form; sealed interfaces + recordsFirst-class: A | B, with narrowing
EnumsReal classes with methodsString-literal unions preferred (the enum keyword exists)
Immutabilityfinal (enforced), recordsconst, readonly (compile-time only)
Inferencevar for locals onlyPervasive: variables, returns, generics
BuildCompile to bytecode; the compiler is mandatoryTranspile to JavaScript; browsers do not know TS
InterfacesMust be implemented explicitlyDescribe shapes; objects satisfy them automatically
 
interface Named { name: string }

function hello(x: Named): string { return `Hi ${x.name}`; }

const employee = { id: 1, name: 'Asha', email: 'asha@acme.in' };
hello(employee);              // OK: it has a name; no "implements Named" needed

class Dog { constructor(public name: string) {} }
hello(new Dog('Tommy'));      // also OK, unrelated class, same shape

Edge case: excess property checks

A fresh object literal with an extra property is rejected (hello({ name: 'A', age: 3 }) errors: "Object literal may only specify known properties"), but the same object stored in a variable first is accepted. The first check catches typos; the second follows structural rules.

Interview: "How is TypeScript's type system different from Java's?"

  • Structural vs nominal; erased at compile time vs available through reflection.
  • Unions, literal types, narrowing and inference are central in TS. Java has sealed types and pattern matching for similar ideas.
  • strict mode, and in particular strictNullChecks, gives null-safety that Java does not have by default.
  • No run-time guarantees: validate external data (Zod, generated types).

Next.js: what it adds and when to choose it over a Vite SPA

Next.js is a React framework that adds file-based routing, rendering on the server (SSR, static generation, Server Components), API routes and a production server; choose it when SEO, first-load speed or a backend-for-frontend layer matter, and stay with a Vite SPA plus Spring Boot for logged-in dashboards and internal tools.

React is a library, Next.js is a framework

React alone draws components. It does not give you routing, a way to render on the server, a build setup or a deployment story; with Vite you add React Router and the rest yourself. Next.js (made by Vercel) is a framework built on React that includes those pieces and makes the choices for you. The React team itself recommends using a framework for new full-stack React apps.

The problem with a pure SPA

A Vite single-page app sends an almost empty index.html and a large JavaScript bundle. The browser downloads the JavaScript, runs React, calls your API, and only then shows content. This is client-side rendering (CSR). Consequences:

  • The first meaningful content appears late, especially on slow phones and networks.
  • Search engines and link previews (WhatsApp, LinkedIn) see an empty page unless they run JavaScript. Big search engines do run it, but less reliably and more slowly, and social-preview bots usually do not.
  • Every page waits for a second round trip (the API call after the JavaScript loads).

For an employee dashboard behind a login, none of this matters: nobody indexes it and users wait once. For a public product catalogue, a blog or a marketing site, it matters a lot.

Rendering modes

ModeWhere and when HTML is madeGood for
CSR (Vite SPA)In the browser, after JavaScript loadsDashboards, admin tools, apps behind login
SSR (server-side rendering)On the server for every requestPersonalised or frequently changing public pages
SSG (static generation)Once at build timeBlogs, docs, marketing pages
ISR (incremental static regeneration)Static pages that are re-generated in the background after a set timeProduct pages that change now and then

With SSR or SSG the browser receives ready-made HTML, so content shows quickly and crawlers see it. React then hydrates the page: it attaches event handlers to the existing HTML so it becomes interactive.

What Next.js gives you

File-based routing
Folders under app/ are URLs. app/employees/page.tsx is /employees. A folder named [id] is a dynamic segment.
Layouts
layout.tsx wraps all pages in a folder (navigation bar, footer) and is not re-created when you move between those pages. loading.tsx and error.tsx give loading and error screens by naming convention.
Server Components
In the App Router, components run on the server by default. They can be async, fetch data directly, and send no JavaScript for themselves to the browser.
Client Components
Files that start with 'use client' run in the browser too and can use state, effects and event handlers.
Route handlers
A route.ts file defines an HTTP endpoint (GET, POST…) inside the Next.js app, a small backend-for-frontend.
Server Actions
Functions marked to run on the server and called from forms or components.
Built-ins
next/link (client navigation with prefetching), next/image (image optimisation), font loading, metadata for SEO tags.
app/
├── layout.tsx              root layout: <html>, <body>, navigation
├── page.tsx                /
├── employees/
│   ├── page.tsx            /employees           (Server Component)
│   ├── loading.tsx         shown while the page loads
│   ├── error.tsx           shown when the page throws   (Client Component)
│   ├── EmployeeFilter.tsx  'use client': search box with state
│   └── [id]/
│       └── page.tsx        /employees/7
└── api/
    └── health/
        └── route.ts        GET /api/health

import EmployeeFilter from './EmployeeFilter';

interface Employee { id: number; name: string; department: string }
interface Page<T> { content: T[]; totalPages: number }

export default async function EmployeesPage() {
  // Runs on the server. API_URL is a server-only variable: it never reaches the browser.
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/api/employees?page=0&size=10`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Could not load employees');   // shows error.tsx
  const page: Page<Employee> = await res.json();

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Employees</h1>
      <EmployeeFilter />
      <ul>
        {page.content.map((e) => (
          <li key={e.id}>{e.name} · {e.department}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </main>
  );
}
'use client';

import { useState } from 'react';

export default function EmployeeFilter() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');          // state needs a Client Component
  return (
    <input value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)}
           placeholder="Filter employees" aria-label="Filter employees" />
  );
}
export async function GET() {
  return Response.json({ status: 'ok' });
}

Next.js changes between major versions

Next.js moves fast. Details such as how fetch results are cached by default, whether route params are passed as a promise, and which file name is used for request interception ("middleware") differ between major versions. The ideas on this page (App Router, Server and Client Components, route handlers) are stable, but check the current documentation at nextjs.org/docs before copying code from an older tutorial. React 19 and the App Router are the basis of current versions.

Next.js with a Spring Boot backend

Next.js does not replace Spring Boot. It replaces the Vite-and-React-Router part. Your Java API still owns the business rules, database and security. Two common ways to connect them:

  • Browser calls Spring Boot directly (as in Module 6) from Client Components, with CORS and JWT handling as before. Server Components can also call Spring Boot during rendering.
  • Next.js as a backend-for-frontend (BFF). The browser talks only to Next.js; Next.js server code (route handlers, Server Components) calls Spring Boot. The access token can then live in an httpOnly cookie set by Next.js and never be visible to browser JavaScript, which removes the XSS token-theft risk discussed in the JWT article. The price is one more server to run.

Do not put the business logic in Next.js "API routes"

It is tempting to write database access and rules in route handlers because it is quick. If you have a Spring Boot service, keep rules and data access there. Next.js route handlers should be thin: forward, attach cookies, shape data for the UI. Two places with business logic drift apart.

When to choose which

SituationBetter choiceWhy
Admin panel, CRM, internal dashboard behind loginVite SPANo SEO need; simplest; deploys as static files
Public e-commerce catalogue, blog, landing pagesNext.jsSEO, social previews, fast first paint
Mixed: marketing pages plus an appNext.jsStatic pages and app pages in one codebase
Team knows only React + Spring Boot and wants minimal moving partsVite SPAFewer concepts, no Node server in production
You want the token hidden from browser JavaScriptNext.js (BFF)Server-side cookie handling
Static hosting only (S3, GitHub Pages)Vite SPA (or Next.js static export)No server available to render

Pros of Next.js

  • SEO and fast first load through server rendering and static pages.
  • Routing, layouts, image and font handling included.
  • Large ecosystem, many jobs; easy deployment on Vercel.

Cons

  • More concepts: server vs client boundary, caching rules, hydration errors.
  • You must run a Node.js server (or use a platform that does), unless you export static files.
  • Fast-changing APIs; older tutorials mislead.
  • For a pure internal SPA it is extra complexity with no payoff.

Basics you should know

  • npx create-next-app@latest creates a project (with TypeScript if you choose it). next dev runs the dev server, next build builds, next start runs the production server.
  • Environment variables: only names starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ are sent to the browser; everything else stays on the server. The same warning as for VITE_: public means public. Compare with Vite env variables.
  • To deploy in Docker, Next.js can produce a smaller server bundle with the option output: 'standalone' in next.config (DevOps · Module 3).
  • A hydration error means the HTML rendered on the server differs from what React rendered in the browser (for example you print Date.now() or read localStorage during render). Move such code into an effect.

Common mistakes

  • Using useState or onClick in a Server Component. Add 'use client' to a small component, not to the whole page.
  • Marking a layout 'use client' and losing the benefits of server rendering for everything under it.
  • Reading browser-only things (window, localStorage) during server rendering.
  • Importing a server-only module (with secrets) into a Client Component.
  • Choosing Next.js because it is popular, for an app that needs none of its features.

Interview: "Would you use Next.js or a Vite SPA for this project?"

  • Ask whether the pages are public and need SEO or fast first paint. If yes: Next.js with SSR/SSG. If it is an authenticated dashboard: a Vite SPA is simpler and cheaper to host.
  • Explain the rendering modes (CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR) and the Server vs Client Component split.
  • Say that Spring Boot remains the API in both; Next.js may act as a BFF.

State management: Context, TanStack Query, Redux Toolkit and Zustand

Most "state" in a CRUD app is server data, which TanStack Query handles; keep UI state local, and reach for Redux Toolkit or Zustand only when many distant components share client-side state that changes often.

Five kinds of state

The first step in choosing a tool is to name the kind of state you have. Most confusion comes from putting everything in one global store.

KindExampleBest home
Local UI stateIs this dropdown open? Text in one inputuseState in the component
Form stateValues and errors while typinguseState or React Hook Form
URL stateCurrent page, filters, selected tabThe URL (useSearchParams)
Server stateEmployees from the API, with loading, caching, refetchingTanStack Query
Shared client stateShopping cart, theme, sidebar, multi-step wizard, notificationsContext for simple cases; Redux Toolkit or Zustand when it grows

If you use TanStack Query for server data and the URL for filters, the amount of leftover global state is small. Many apps never need Redux.

Why Context stops being enough

Context (Module 5) is built into React and perfect for values that change rarely: the logged-in user, the theme, the language. Its limit: when the value in a context changes, every component that calls useContext for it re-renders, even if it uses a part of the value that did not change. A context holding { items, total, coupon } re-renders the whole tree that reads it whenever the coupon changes. There is also no built-in way to select a slice, no dev tools and no middleware. That is where a state library helps.

Redux Toolkit

Redux keeps all shared state in one store. Components read it with a selector and change it by dispatching an action; a pure function called a reducer computes the next state. Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official, modern way to write Redux: it removes the boilerplate, and its createSlice lets you write "mutating" code that it turns into immutable updates (using a library called Immer).

import { createSlice, type PayloadAction } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

export interface CartItem { productId: number; name: string; price: number; qty: number }
interface CartState { items: CartItem[] }

const initialState: CartState = { items: [] };

const cartSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'cart',
  initialState,
  reducers: {
    added(state, action: PayloadAction<Omit<CartItem, 'qty'>>) {
      const existing = state.items.find((i) => i.productId === action.payload.productId);
      if (existing) existing.qty += 1;               // looks like mutation; Immer makes it safe
      else state.items.push({ ...action.payload, qty: 1 });
    },
    removed(state, action: PayloadAction<number>) {
      state.items = state.items.filter((i) => i.productId !== action.payload);
    },
    cleared(state) {
      state.items = [];
    },
  },
});

export const { added, removed, cleared } = cartSlice.actions;
export default cartSlice.reducer;
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
import { useDispatch, useSelector, type TypedUseSelectorHook } from 'react-redux';
import cartReducer from './cartSlice';

export const store = configureStore({
  reducer: { cart: cartReducer },        // add more slices here
});

export type RootState = ReturnType<typeof store.getState>;
export type AppDispatch = typeof store.dispatch;

// Typed hooks: use these instead of the plain ones
export const useAppDispatch = () => useDispatch<AppDispatch>();
export const useAppSelector: TypedUseSelectorHook<RootState> = useSelector;
// main.tsx: make the store available
import { Provider } from 'react-redux';
// <Provider store={store}><App /></Provider>

// CartBadge.tsx
function CartBadge() {
  const count = useAppSelector((s) => s.cart.items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0));
  return <span>Cart ({count})</span>;          // re-renders only when the count changes
}

// ProductCard.tsx
function AddButton({ product }: { product: Product }) {
  const dispatch = useAppDispatch();
  return <button onClick={() => dispatch(added(product))}>Add to cart</button>;
}

RTK also ships RTK Query, a data-fetching and caching tool (like TanStack Query but integrated with the store). If a team is already on Redux, they often use RTK Query for server state. Redux DevTools lets you see every action and travel back in time, which is a real help in large apps.

Zustand

Zustand (German for "state") is a very small library. You create a store with create; the store is a hook. There is no provider, no actions, no reducers: you write state and the functions that change it side by side.

import { create } from 'zustand';

export interface CartItem { productId: number; name: string; price: number; qty: number }

interface CartState {
  items: CartItem[];
  add: (item: Omit<CartItem, 'qty'>) => void;
  remove: (productId: number) => void;
  clear: () => void;
}

export const useCartStore = create<CartState>()((set) => ({
  items: [],
  add: (item) =>
    set((state) => {
      const existing = state.items.find((i) => i.productId === item.productId);
      return existing
        ? { items: state.items.map((i) =>
            i.productId === item.productId ? { ...i, qty: i.qty + 1 } : i) }
        : { items: [...state.items, { ...item, qty: 1 }] };
    }),
  remove: (productId) =>
    set((state) => ({ items: state.items.filter((i) => i.productId !== productId) })),
  clear: () => set({ items: [] }),
}));
function CartBadge() {
  // Select only what you need: re-renders only when this value changes
  const count = useCartStore((s) => s.items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0));
  return <span>Cart ({count})</span>;
}

function AddButton({ product }: { product: Product }) {
  const add = useCartStore((s) => s.add);
  return <button onClick={() => add(product)}>Add to cart</button>;
}

Zustand has optional middleware, for example persist (save the store to localStorage) and a Redux DevTools connector. As with any localStorage use, never persist tokens or secrets.

How they compare

ContextTanStack QueryRedux ToolkitZustand
ForRarely changing values (user, theme)Server dataLarge shared client stateSmall to medium shared client state
Built into ReactYesNoNoNo
BoilerplateLowLowMedium (slices, store, hooks)Very low
Selects a slice (fewer re-renders)NoYes (select)Yes (selectors)Yes (selectors)
Dev toolsReact DevTools onlyQuery devtoolsExcellent (Redux DevTools)Optional via middleware
Caching, refetching, retriesNoBuilt inRTK QueryNo
Typical inEvery appMost modern appsLarge, older or enterprise appsNewer, smaller teams

A sensible decision path

  1. Keep state as local as possible (useState); lift it only when siblings need it.
  2. Data from the API: TanStack Query. Do not copy it into a store.
  3. Filters, paging, selected tab: the URL.
  4. A few app-wide values that rarely change: Context.
  5. Complex client state used by many distant components, or frequent updates: Zustand (simple) or Redux Toolkit (large team, strict structure, great tooling).

Common mistakes

  • Copying API data into Redux or Zustand, then writing code to keep it in sync. Let TanStack Query own server data.
  • Putting everything in one global store "because we have Redux". Local state belongs in components.
  • Subscribing to the whole store (useStore() without a selector) so every change re-renders the component.
  • Returning a new object or array from a selector on every call, which causes needless re-renders. Select primitives, or select the stable reference and derive outside.
  • Mutating state outside createSlice in Redux (plain Redux requires immutability; only Immer inside slices allows "mutating" syntax). Also, non-serialisable values (Date, class instances, functions) in the store.

Interview: "When would you use Redux, and when not?"

  • Separate server state (TanStack Query / RTK Query) from client state. Most apps have little truly global client state.
  • Redux Toolkit when many components share complex state, you need predictable updates, time-travel debugging, middleware, or a strict structure for a big team.
  • Zustand when you want a small global store with almost no boilerplate. Context for stable values.
  • Explain the Redux flow: dispatch an action, the reducer returns new state, subscribers re-render. Mention that Redux Toolkit uses Immer so reducers can be written in a mutating style safely.

Testing the frontend: Vitest, React Testing Library, MSW and Playwright

Test what the user sees and does, not how the component is built: Vitest runs the tests, React Testing Library renders components and finds elements by role and label, MSW fakes the API at the network level, and a few Playwright tests check the whole app in a real browser.

What to test, and what not to

Frontend tests have a cost: they must be written and kept up to date. Spend that effort where bugs hurt. Think of a pyramid with many fast tests at the bottom and few slow ones at the top:

LevelToolTestsHow many
UnitVitestPure functions: formatters, validators, classifyErrorMany
Component / integrationVitest + React Testing Library (+ MSW)A form shows errors; a list shows loading, data, error; a button click calls the APIModerate: the sweet spot
End-to-end (E2E)PlaywrightLogin, create an employee, log out, in a real browser against a real or test backendFew: the critical journeys
  • Test behaviour: "when I submit an empty form, I see 'Name is required' and no request is sent". The user does not care that you used useState.
  • Do not test React itself, library internals, CSS details, or private state. A test that breaks when you refactor without changing behaviour is a bad test.
  • Backend rules (validation, security, transactions) are tested in Spring Boot (Spring Boot · Module 5). The frontend tests check that the UI reacts correctly to the responses.

Vitest: setup

Vitest is a test runner made for Vite projects. It reuses your Vite configuration, so imports, TypeScript and JSX just work, and it is fast. Its API (describe, it, expect) is almost the same as Jest, with vi instead of jest for mocks. React Testing Library (RTL) renders components into a simulated browser (jsdom, a Node.js implementation of the DOM) and gives you queries that find elements the way a user would.

$ npm install -D vitest jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom \
    @testing-library/user-event msw
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  test: {
    environment: 'jsdom',
    setupFiles: './src/test/setup.ts',
  },
});
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';   // adds toBeInTheDocument(), toBeDisabled(), ...
import { afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { cleanup } from '@testing-library/react';

afterEach(() => cleanup());                   // unmount rendered components after each test
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "vitest",
    "test:run": "vitest run"
  }
}

npm test starts watch mode (re-runs affected tests when you save); vitest run runs once, which is what a CI pipeline uses (DevOps · Module 4). Vite loads .env.test in test mode, so put VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8080/api there.

A first test: a pure function

import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { classifyError } from './errors';

describe('classifyError', () => {
  it('treats a missing response as a retryable network error', () => {
    const info = classifyError({ code: 'ERR_NETWORK' });       // no "response" property
    expect(info.kind).toBe('network');
    expect(info.retryable).toBe(true);
  });

  it('does not retry a 404', () => {
    const info = classifyError({ response: { status: 404, data: {} } });
    expect(info.kind).toBe('not-found');
    expect(info.retryable).toBe(false);
  });
});

Component tests with React Testing Library

The pattern is arrange, act, assert: render the component, act like a user (click, type), and check what is on the screen.

import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { EmployeeForm } from './EmployeeForm';

describe('EmployeeForm', () => {
  it('shows client errors and does not submit an empty form', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const onSubmit = vi.fn();                       // a spy function
    render(<EmployeeForm onSubmit={onSubmit} />);

    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /save/i }));

    expect(screen.getByText('Name is required')).toBeInTheDocument();
    expect(onSubmit).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  it('submits the typed values', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const onSubmit = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    render(<EmployeeForm onSubmit={onSubmit} />);

    await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Name'), 'Asha Rao');
    await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Email'), 'asha@acme.in');
    await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Department'), 'IT');
    await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Salary'), '50000');
    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /save/i }));

    expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({
      name: 'Asha Rao', email: 'asha@acme.in', department: 'IT', salary: 50000,
    });
  });
});

Which query to use: the priority order

RTL queries are ordered by how close they are to what a real user and assistive technology perceive. Use the first one that works. Choosing queries this way also pushes you to write accessible markup.

  1. getByRole('button', { name: /save/i }): the best default. Works for buttons, links, headings, textboxes, checkboxes.
  2. getByLabelText('Email'): form fields with a label.
  3. getByPlaceholderText, then getByText('Employee created'): visible text.
  4. getByDisplayValue, getByAltText, getByTitle.
  5. getByTestId('row-7'): the last resort, using a data-testid attribute that users cannot see.
Query familyNot foundUse it for
getBy…Throws an error at onceSomething that must be there now
queryBy…Returns nullAsserting that something is not there: expect(screen.queryByText('Error')).not.toBeInTheDocument()
findBy…Waits (default about one second), then throwsSomething that appears after an async step (API data)

Add All (getAllByRole) when several elements match. Always await userEvent calls; they are asynchronous.

Mocking the API with MSW

MSW (Mock Service Worker) intercepts HTTP requests at the network layer, so your real Axios code, interceptors and error handling run unchanged and only the server is fake. This is better than mocking Axios with vi.mock, which skips half of the code you want to test. In Node tests you use setupServer.

import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

export const handlers = [
  http.get('http://localhost:8080/api/employees', () =>
    HttpResponse.json({
      content: [{ id: 1, name: 'Asha Rao', email: 'asha@acme.in', department: 'IT', salary: 50000 }],
      page: 0, size: 10, totalElements: 1, totalPages: 1,
    }),
  ),
];

export const server = setupServer(...handlers);
import { afterAll, afterEach, beforeAll } from 'vitest';
import { server } from './server';

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));  // fail on unexpected calls
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());                          // undo per-test overrides
afterAll(() => server.close());
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { MemoryRouter } from 'react-router';
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { server } from '../test/server';
import EmployeeListPage from './EmployeeListPage';

function renderPage() {
  const client = new QueryClient({ defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: false } } }); // no retries
  return render(
    <QueryClientProvider client={client}>
      <MemoryRouter>
        <EmployeeListPage />
      </MemoryRouter>
    </QueryClientProvider>,
  );   // components that call useAuth also need a test AuthProvider around them
}

it('shows employees from the API', async () => {
  renderPage();
  expect(await screen.findByText('Asha Rao')).toBeInTheDocument();   // waits for the data
});

it('shows a friendly message when the server fails', async () => {
  server.use(   // override the default handler for this test only
    http.get('http://localhost:8080/api/employees', () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ title: 'Internal Server Error' }, { status: 500 })),
  );
  renderPage();
  expect(await screen.findByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent('Something went wrong on our side');
});

Notes: a fresh QueryClient per test avoids cached data leaking between tests; retry: false makes the error case fast; MemoryRouter provides routing without a browser URL.

Mocking modules with vi.mock

For things you do not want to run, use vi.mock('./employeeApi') to replace a module with mocks, and vi.fn() for spies. Use it for browser APIs, timers (vi.useFakeTimers()) and third-party modules, but prefer MSW for HTTP so that Axios, interceptors and error mapping are part of the test.

End-to-end tests with Playwright

Playwright drives a real browser (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) through your running app, as a user would. It catches what component tests cannot: CORS problems, wrong routing after deploy, a broken login against the real backend. Because E2E tests are slow and can be flaky, write few of them, for the journeys that must never break: login, the main create flow, checkout.

import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test';

test('a logged-out visitor is sent to login, then sees the employee list', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('http://localhost:5173/employees');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);              // the route guard worked

  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('admin@acme.in');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.E2E_PASSWORD ?? '');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Employees' })).toBeVisible();
});

Create the project with npm init playwright@latest and run tests with npx playwright test. Playwright's locators (getByRole, getByLabel) follow the same ideas as RTL. Use a dedicated test user and test database, and keep the password in an environment variable, not in the file.

Rules for good frontend tests

  • Each test is independent: no shared state, any order, can run alone.
  • Find elements by role or label before text, and by test id last.
  • Wait with findBy or waitFor, never with setTimeout or fixed sleeps.
  • No real network in unit and component tests. MSW answers; unknown requests fail the test.
  • Tests run in CI on every push.

Common mistakes

  • Testing implementation details (calling an internal function, checking state values) so tests break on every refactor.
  • Forgetting await on user.click or findBy: the assertion runs too early, or you see "not wrapped in act(...)" warnings.
  • Using getBy for data that loads later (throws immediately). Use findBy.
  • Asserting absence with getBy (it throws). Use queryBy.
  • Large snapshot tests that everybody updates without reading.
  • Not wrapping a component in the providers it needs (QueryClient, Router, Auth): "No QueryClient set" errors.
  • Reusing one QueryClient across tests, so cached results leak.

Interview: "How do you test a React component that calls an API?"

  • Vitest + React Testing Library; render inside the needed providers with a fresh QueryClient with retries off.
  • Fake the network with MSW (not by mocking Axios), so interceptors and error handling run.
  • Interact with userEvent, find elements by role/label, assert with findBy for async results, and test loading, success, empty and error states.
  • Add a few Playwright E2E tests for the critical journeys; leave rules and security to backend tests.

What to learn next for full-stack roles

After React and a working Spring Boot app, the next gains come from running software (Docker, CI/CD, cloud), designing systems, deeper backend skills and polish on the frontend; pick by what the jobs you target ask for, and always keep one real project moving.

Where you stand

If you can build and deploy the Employee Manager from Module 6, you can already do the core work of a junior full-stack developer: model data, expose a secured REST API, build a UI against it, and debug a failing request. What employers look for beyond that falls into four groups. Chips show how soon each matters for most job listings.

1. Ship and run it

TopicWhyWhere in these notes
Must DockerEvery team packages apps as containersDevOps · Module 3
Must CI/CD with GitHub ActionsTests and builds on every pushDevOps · Module 4
Good to know A cloud provider (deployment basics)Real hosting, databases, storageDevOps · Module 5
Good to know Logs, metrics, monitoringFinding problems in productionDevOps · Module 6
Later KubernetesLarge-scale container platformsDevOps · Module 6

2. Go deeper on the backend

TopicWhyWhere
Must Spring Security in depth, JWT and rolesEvery business app has login and rolesSpring Boot · Module 4
Must Backend testing (JUnit, Mockito, slice tests, Testcontainers)Teams expect tests with every pull requestSpring Boot · Module 5
Good to know JPA performance (N+1, indexes, transactions)The usual cause of slow APIsSpring Boot · Module 3, SQL · Module 5
Good to know Caching and RedisSpeed and load reductionSpring Boot · Module 6
Later Messaging (Kafka, RabbitMQ) and microservicesCommon in larger companiesSpring Boot · Module 7

3. Design and interviews

  • Must Data structures and algorithms. Service and product companies screen with them: DSA · Module 1 and onwards.
  • Must Core CS (OS, networks, DBMS, OOP theory) for interview rounds: CS Fundamentals.
  • Good to know Design patterns and low-level design: System Design · Module 2.
  • Good to know High-level system design (load balancers, caches, queues, databases at scale): System Design · Module 4.

4. Frontend polish

TopicWhat to do
Good to know A CSS framework or component libraryTailwind CSS, or a component set such as MUI or shadcn/ui; learn one so that apps look decent quickly
Good to know AccessibilitySemantic HTML, labels, keyboard use, focus handling, colour contrast; test with the keyboard only
Good to know Web performanceCode splitting with lazy routes, image sizes, Core Web Vitals, the browser Performance tab
Later Real-time featuresWebSockets or Server-Sent Events for live updates and notifications
Later GraphQLAn alternative to REST that some teams use; learn when a job needs it
Later Frontend securityXSS, CSRF, content security policy, safe handling of tokens

A practical order

  1. Finish and deploy Project 3 (React + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL) with a README, screenshots and a live link.
  2. Move the frontend to TypeScript, add Vitest tests for the form and list, and add a test for the backend endpoints.
  3. Containerise both apps with Docker and add a GitHub Actions workflow that tests and builds on every push.
  4. Deploy to a cloud provider with a managed database; add basic monitoring.
  5. Practise DSA and interview questions regularly alongside, not after, the projects.
  6. Build one more project that uses a new idea (caching, messaging, file upload, or real-time updates), then read about system design.

Let the job listings guide you

Pick ten job posts for the roles you want and count the keywords. Learn the top five that you do not have yet. Depth in a few things beats shallow contact with everything; a deployed, tested project that you can explain end to end is worth more than ten tutorials.

Interview: "What would you learn or improve next in this project?"

  • Show you think about production: tests in CI, Docker, monitoring, secure token handling, pagination and indexes for scale.
  • Name concrete trade-offs you would revisit (localStorage vs cookie tokens, offset vs cursor paging, SPA vs Next.js).

Interview questions — TypeScript, Next.js, state and testing

Why use TypeScript instead of JavaScript?

Static types catch typos, wrong argument types and missing null checks before the code runs. They give accurate autocomplete, safe refactoring across a large codebase, and living documentation for data shapes such as API DTOs. The cost is a build step and some extra writing. Types are erased, so they add no run-time overhead and also give no run-time protection.

What is the difference between any and unknown?

Both accept any value. any turns off type checking for it, so you can call anything on it and errors are hidden. unknown forces you to narrow the type (typeof, instanceof, a type guard) before you use it. Use unknown for external data and catch variables.

interface or type?

For object shapes they are nearly interchangeable. type can also name unions, tuples and primitives; interface supports extends and declaration merging. A common convention: interface for object shapes and props, type for unions and combinations. Consistency inside the project matters more.

What does this print or fail on? const [rows, setRows] = useState([]); setRows(data);

It runs, but with strict TypeScript the state type is inferred as never[], so setRows(data) is a compile error ("not assignable to never[]"). Fix it by giving the type: useState<Employee[]>([]).

How do you type an API response, and why is it not a guarantee?

Write an interface that mirrors the backend DTO and pass it as a generic: api.get<Page<Employee>>('/employees'). The compiler then checks your usage. It is a promise, not a check: TypeScript types do not exist at run time, so if the server sends another shape, the code still compiles. Close the gap with types generated from the OpenAPI document, schema validation such as Zod at the boundary, and API tests.

What does "strict": true do?

It enables a group of strict checks: strictNullChecks (null and undefined are separate types), noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictPropertyInitialization, useUnknownInCatchVariables and others. It catches the largest class of run-time errors ("cannot read property of undefined") at compile time. New projects should always start with it.

What is narrowing? Give two ways to do it.

Narrowing is the compiler refining a union type inside a branch after a check. Examples: typeof x === 'string', x instanceof Error, 'name' in x, an equality check against null, a discriminated-union switch (state.status), or a custom type guard function returning x is Employee.

How does TypeScript's type system differ from Java's?

TypeScript is structural: an object fits a type if it has the required properties, with no implements. Java is nominal. TypeScript types are erased and unavailable at run time; Java keeps class information for reflection. TypeScript has first-class unions and literal types, and heavy inference; null-safety comes from strictNullChecks.

Server-side rendering vs client-side rendering: what are the trade-offs?

With CSR (a Vite SPA) the browser downloads JavaScript, runs it and then fetches data, so the first content is late and crawlers or link previews may see an empty page. With SSR or static generation the server sends ready HTML, so content appears quickly and is indexable, then React hydrates it. SSR needs a server to run and adds the server/client boundary to think about. CSR is simpler and fine behind a login.

When would you choose Next.js over Vite and React Router with a Spring Boot backend?

Choose Next.js for public pages that need SEO, social previews and fast first load (catalogues, blogs, marketing), or when you want a backend-for-frontend layer that keeps tokens in httpOnly cookies. Choose a Vite SPA for internal dashboards and apps behind a login, for static hosting, and for the smallest number of moving parts. In both cases Spring Boot remains the API and owns the business rules.

What is the difference between a Server Component and a Client Component?

In the Next.js App Router, components are Server Components by default: they run on the server, can be async and read data directly, and send no component JavaScript to the browser. A file with 'use client' is a Client Component: it also runs in the browser and can use state, effects and event handlers. Keep the client part small and pass data down as props.

When do you need Redux or Zustand, given Context and TanStack Query exist?

Server data belongs to TanStack Query; URL state to the URL; local state to useState; stable app-wide values (user, theme) to Context. A store is for shared client state that is complex or changes often and is used by many distant components, such as a cart, a wizard or editor state. Context re-renders every consumer on any change, while stores let components select a slice. Redux Toolkit fits large teams and strict structure; Zustand fits small, simple global state.

How do you test a React component that fetches data?

Render it with Vitest and React Testing Library inside the required providers (a new QueryClient with retry off, a MemoryRouter). Fake the server with MSW so the real Axios code and interceptors run. Use await screen.findByText(...) for async results, userEvent for interaction, and test the loading, success, empty and error states. Override an MSW handler per test to simulate a 500.

Which RTL query should you reach for first, and what is the difference between getBy, queryBy and findBy?

getByRole first, then getByLabelText, then text, with getByTestId as the last resort. getBy throws immediately if nothing matches; queryBy returns null (use it to assert absence); findBy waits and retries until the element appears (use it for async UI).

What do you test with Playwright instead of component tests?

Whole journeys in a real browser against a running app and backend: login and redirect, creating a record, permissions. It finds integration problems such as CORS, routing and deployment settings. These tests are slower and more fragile, so keep them few and focused on critical paths.

Cheat sheet — TypeScript, Next.js, state and testing

  • TypeScript JavaScript plus static types; checked by tsc/editor, erased at build.
  • Vite + TS npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts; Vite strips types, tsc checks.
  • Basic types string, number, boolean, null, undefined, bigint, T[], [A, B].
  • Union / literal 'ADMIN' | 'USER', string | null; replaces most enums.
  • Discriminated union shared tag property (status) + switch for exact narrowing.
  • interface vs type objects: either; type for unions/tuples; interface merges and extends.
  • Optional / readonly phone?: string, readonly id: number (compile-time only).
  • Generics Page<T>, function f<T extends HasId>(x: T).
  • Narrowing typeof, instanceof, in, equality, type guards (x is T).
  • any / unknown / never unchecked / must narrow / impossible. Prefer unknown.
  • Utility types Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, Readonly, Required.
  • React typing props interface; ReactNode for children; useState<User | null>(null); ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>.
  • DTO mapping record → interface; LocalDate → string; enum → union; nullable → T | null.
  • Types are not checks validate with Zod or generate from OpenAPI.
  • tsconfig "strict": true always; noEmit; jsx: "react-jsx".
  • Structural typing shape decides compatibility; Java is nominal.
  • Next.js React framework: file routing, SSR/SSG/ISR, Server Components, route handlers, Server Actions.
  • Server vs Client Component default server; 'use client' for state/effects/events.
  • Choose Next.js for SEO and public pages; Vite SPA for logged-in dashboards.
  • Env vars (Next) only NEXT_PUBLIC_* reaches the browser.
  • State kinds local → useState; server → TanStack Query; URL → search params; shared → Context/Zustand/Redux.
  • Redux Toolkit createSlice + configureStore + Provider + useSelector/useDispatch; Immer inside.
  • Zustand create((set) => ({...})), no provider, select slices.
  • Vitest + RTL render, screen.getByRole, await userEvent, findBy for async.
  • Query order role → label → placeholder/text → display value → test id.
  • MSW http.get(url, () => HttpResponse.json(...)) + setupServer; fresh QueryClient, retry: false.
  • Playwright few E2E tests of critical journeys in a real browser.

Practice — TypeScript, Next.js, state and testing

  1. TypeScript warm-up (easy). In a scratch .ts file write: a union of string literals for roles, a discriminated union for a load state with an exhaustive switch, a generic Page<T> and a type guard isApiError. Done when the compiler flags a missing case after you add a new status.
  2. Type the DTOs (easy). Write TypeScript interfaces for every record your Spring Boot API returns, using Omit for request types. Done when api.get<Page<Employee>> autocompletes every field.
  3. Migrate Project 3's frontend to TypeScript (medium). Rename components to .tsx one at a time with strict on. Type props, state, events, context and the API module. Done when npm run build passes with no any except documented ones, and renaming a DTO field in one place shows errors everywhere it is used.
  4. Validate at the boundary (medium). Add a Zod schema for one response and parse it in the API function. Make the backend return a wrong field and watch the app fail with a clear error. Done when the type is derived with z.infer and you can explain why.
  5. Unit and component tests (medium). Set up Vitest, jsdom and React Testing Library. Test classifyError, then EmployeeForm (empty submit shows errors and does not call onSubmit; valid input calls it with the right values). Done when npm run test:run is green and all queries use role or label.
  6. Mock the API with MSW (medium). Test the list page for data, empty list, 500 and network error. Done when no test touches the real backend and unexpected requests fail the test.
  7. One E2E test (medium). Write a Playwright test for login and creating an employee against a local backend with a test user. Done when it passes headless and the password comes from an environment variable.
  8. A shared store (medium). Add a cart or notification feature with Zustand, then re-implement it with Redux Toolkit. Done when you can state which you would use for this app and why, and the cart badge re-renders only when its count changes.
  9. Next.js comparison (hard). Build a public, read-only "company directory" page in Next.js that renders the employee list on the server from your Spring Boot API, with a client-side search box. Done when "View page source" shows the names in the HTML, and you can write five lines on when you would not use Next.js.
  10. Plan your next quarter (easy). Choose ten job posts, list their required skills, and write a four-week plan from the "What to learn next" article. Done when each week has a concrete output (a deployed app, a pipeline, a test suite).
